Chapter 1 · Topic 1

Matter and its classification

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 1 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Matter and its classification: matter splits into pure substances and mixtures by uniformity of composition. Gay-Lussac law: at same \(T,P\), gas volumes combine in simple whole-number ratios equal to their mole ratios. Particle counts follow from moles: entities \(= n\times N_A\), with atomicity/ion multiplicity applied per formula unit.
Key formula(s). \[ \frac{n_1}{\nu_1}=\frac{n_2}{\nu_2}\,(mole\,bridge) \]
Key points.
  • For ions from a salt, multiply by the subscript: \(CaCl_2 \to 1\,Ca^{2+}+2\,Cl^-\).
  • Matter classes: elements and compounds are pure; mixtures (homogeneous/heterogeneous) vary in composition.
  • Volume ratios \(=\) mole ratios only when all substances are gases at the same \(T,P\).
  • Laws of combination: definite, multiple and reciprocal proportions fix formulas from mass data.
Example 1.

How many \(Cl^-\) ions in \(0.1\,mol\,MgCl_2\)?

  1. Each unit gives \(2\,Cl^-\): \(0.2\,mol\) ions.
  2. \(1.204\times10^{23}\) ions.

Answer: \(1.204\times10^{23}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Equal masses of \(CH_4\) and \(O_2\): compare their molecule counts.

  1. Moles \(\propto 1/M\): ratio \(32:16 = 2:1\).
  2. \(CH_4\) has twice as many.

Answer: \(CH_4\) double.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Applying volume ratios when water (liquid) is a product.
  • Missing the ion/atom multiplicity per formula unit.

Chapter 1 · Topic 2

Laws of chemical combination

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 2 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Laws of chemical combination: definite, multiple and reciprocal proportions fix compound formulas from mass data. Gay-Lussac law: at same \(T,P\), gas volumes combine in simple whole-number ratios equal to their mole ratios. Particle counts follow from moles: entities \(= n\times N_A\), with atomicity/ion multiplicity applied per formula unit.
Key formula(s). \[ \; atoms=n\times atomicity\times N_A,\;\frac{n_1}{\nu_1}=\frac{n_2}{\nu_2}\,(mole\,bridge) \]
Key points.
  • Volume ratios \(=\) mole ratios only when all substances are gases at the same \(T,P\).
  • Laws of combination: definite, multiple and reciprocal proportions fix formulas from mass data.
  • For ions from a salt, multiply by the subscript: \(CaCl_2 \to 1\,Ca^{2+}+2\,Cl^-\).
  • Matter classes: elements and compounds are pure; mixtures (homogeneous/heterogeneous) vary in composition.
Example 1.

\(10\,mL\,H_2 + 10\,mL\,Cl_2 \to HCl\). Find the volume of \(HCl\) formed at same \(T,P\).

  1. \(H_2+Cl_2\to2HCl\); volumes in ratio \(1:1:2\).
  2. Limiting pair gives \(20\,mL\,HCl\).

Answer: \(20\,mL\,HCl\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) How many oxygen atoms are in \(4.4\,g\,CO_2\)?

  1. Moles \(= 4.4/44 = 0.1\); molecules \(= 0.1N_A\).
  2. O atoms \(= 2\times0.1N_A = 1.204\times10^{23}\).

Answer: \(1.204\times10^{23}\) O atoms.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Applying volume ratios when water (liquid) is a product.
  • Missing the ion/atom multiplicity per formula unit.

Chapter 1 · Topic 3

Atomic mass

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 3 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Atomic mass: atomic mass is the weighted average over isotopes, with 1u = 1.66e-27 kg. Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance in \(g\,mol^{-1}\); numerically it equals the relative atomic/molecular mass. One mole of gas at STP occupies \(22.4\,L\) (molar volume).
Key formula(s). \[ (g\,mol^{-1}),\;\; V_m = 22.4\,L\,mol^{-1}\,(STP) \]
Key points.
  • Formula mass is used for ionic compounds (e.g. \(NaCl = 58.5\)) where discrete molecules do not exist.
  • Vapour density \(= M/2\); molecular mass \(= 2 \times\) vapour density.
  • Molar volume \(22.4\,L\) is valid only for gases at STP.
  • Atomic mass unit: \(1\,u = 1.66\times10^{-27}\,kg\); molar mass in grams is numerically equal to mass in \(u\).
Example 1.

\(2.24\,L\) of a gas at STP weighs \(2.9\,g\). Find its molar mass.

  1. Moles \(= 0.1\).
  2. \(M = 29\,g/mol\).

Answer: \(29\,g/mol\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) The vapour density of \(NO_2/ N_2O_4\) mixture is \(38\). Find average molar mass.

  1. \(M_{avg} = 2\times VD\).
  2. \(76\,g/mol\).

Answer: \(76\,g/mol\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using vapour density \(=\,M\) instead of \(M/2\).
  • Applying \(22.4\,L\) to liquids/solids.

Chapter 1 · Topic 4

Molecular mass

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 4 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Molecular mass: molecular mass is the sum of atomic masses in one covalent molecule. Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance in \(g\,mol^{-1}\); numerically it equals the relative atomic/molecular mass. One mole of gas at STP occupies \(22.4\,L\) (molar volume).
Key formula(s). \[ M = \frac{m}{n} \]
Key points.
  • Vapour density \(= M/2\); molecular mass \(= 2 \times\) vapour density.
  • Molar volume \(22.4\,L\) is valid only for gases at STP.
  • Atomic mass unit: \(1\,u = 1.66\times10^{-27}\,kg\); molar mass in grams is numerically equal to mass in \(u\).
  • Formula mass is used for ionic compounds (e.g. \(NaCl = 58.5\)) where discrete molecules do not exist.
Example 1.

How many moles are in \(4.4\,g\,CO_2\)? How many molecules?

  1. Moles \(= 4.4/44 = 0.1\).
  2. Molecules \(= 0.1N_A = 6.022\times10^{22}\).

Answer: \(0.1\,mol\), \(6.022\times10^{22}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) One mole of methane occupies what volume at STP?

  1. Molar volume of any ideal gas at STP.
  2. \(22.4\,L\).

Answer: \(22.4\,L\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using vapour density \(=\,M\) instead of \(M/2\).
  • Applying \(22.4\,L\) to liquids/solids.

Chapter 1 · Topic 5

Formula mass

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 5 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Formula mass: formula mass plays the role of molecular mass for ionic lattices that have no molecules. Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance in \(g\,mol^{-1}\); numerically it equals the relative atomic/molecular mass. One mole of gas at STP occupies \(22.4\,L\) (molar volume).
Key formula(s). \[ M = \frac{m}{n},\;(g\,mol^{-1}) \]
Key points.
  • Atomic mass unit: \(1\,u = 1.66\times10^{-27}\,kg\); molar mass in grams is numerically equal to mass in \(u\).
  • Formula mass is used for ionic compounds (e.g. \(NaCl = 58.5\)) where discrete molecules do not exist.
  • Vapour density \(= M/2\); molecular mass \(= 2 \times\) vapour density.
  • Molar volume \(22.4\,L\) is valid only for gases at STP.
Example 1.

Vapour density of a gas is \(23\). Find its molecular mass and the volume of \(4.6\,g\) at STP.

  1. \(M = 2\times23 = 46\,g\,mol^{-1}\).
  2. Moles \(= 4.6/46 = 0.1\); volume \(= 0.1\times22.4 = 2.24\,L\).

Answer: \(M = 46\), volume \(= 2.24\,L\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(1.12\,L\) of a gas at STP weighs \(1.43\,g\). Find its molar mass.

  1. Moles \(= 1.12/22.4 = 0.05\,mol\).
  2. \(M = 1.43/0.05 = 28.6\,g\,mol^{-1}\) (about \(N_2/CO\) range).

Answer: About \(28.6\,g\,mol^{-1}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using vapour density \(=\,M\) instead of \(M/2\).
  • Applying \(22.4\,L\) to liquids/solids.

Chapter 1 · Topic 6

Mole concept

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 6 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Mole concept: one mole is 6.022e23 entities, and every mass, number or gas-volume problem must pass through moles. Mole is the chemist counting unit: one mole contains \(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\) entities, and links mass, number and volume through \(n = m/M = N/N_A = V/22.4\,L\) at STP.
Key formula(s). \[ n = \frac{m}{M} = \frac{N}{N_A} = \frac{V(L)}{22.4\,(STP)},\;\; N_A = 6.022\times10^{23} \]
Key points.
  • At STP one mole of any gas occupies \(22.4\,L\); at NTP the same value is used in JEE.
  • Number of entities \(=\) moles \(\times N_A\); never multiply grams directly by \(N_A\).
  • For mixtures, total moles \(=\) sum of component moles; average molar mass \(=\) total mass/total moles.
  • JEE trap: STP volume applies only to gases, never to liquids or solids.
  • Always convert every quantity to moles first, then use the balanced-equation mole ratio.
Example 1.

How many moles and molecules are present in \(9\,g\) of water?

  1. Molar mass of \(H_2O = 18\,g\,mol^{-1}\), so \(n = 9/18 = 0.5\,mol\).
  2. Molecules \(= 0.5 \times 6.022\times10^{23} = 3.011\times10^{23}\).
  3. Atoms \(= 3 \times 3.011\times10^{23} = 9.03\times10^{23}\) since each water has 3 atoms.

Answer: \(0.5\,mol\), \(3.011\times10^{23}\) molecules.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) A mixture of \(CH_4\) and \(C_2H_6\) weighing \(8\,g\) occupies \(5.6\,L\) at STP. Find the mole fraction of \(CH_4\).

  1. Total moles \(= 5.6/22.4 = 0.25\,mol\); let \(x =\) moles of \(CH_4\).
  2. Mass: \(16x + 30(0.25-x) = 8 \Rightarrow 16x + 7.5 - 30x = 8 \Rightarrow x = -0.5/-14\), solving gives \(x \approx 0.036\,mol\).
  3. Mole fraction \(= 0.036/0.25 \approx 0.143\).

Answer: About \(0.14\) (solve mass + mole equations simultaneously).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(22.4\,L\) for non-gaseous substances.
  • Forgetting to multiply by atomicity when asked for atoms.
  • Mixing average molar mass with mole fraction weighting.

Chapter 1 · Topic 7

Avogadro number

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 7 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Avogadro number: Avogadro number converts the macroscopic gram scale into countable microscopic entities. Avogadro number \(N_A = 6.022\times10^{23}\,mol^{-1}\) is the number of entities per mole; it converts between the macroscopic gram scale and the microscopic particle scale.
Key formula(s). \[ N = n \times N_A,\;\; n = N/N_A \]
Key points.
  • For ions: count each ion type separately, e.g. \(Na_2SO_4\) gives \(2\,Na^+ + SO_4^{2-}\) per unit.
  • Mass of one atom/molecule \(=\) molar mass divided by \(N_A\).
  • One mole of anything contains \(6.022\times10^{23}\) formula units.
  • Charge on one mole of electrons (1 faraday) \(= N_A \times e \approx 96485\,C\).
Example 1.

Find the mass of one molecule of \(CO_2\) in grams.

  1. Molar mass \(= 44\,g\,mol^{-1}\).
  2. One molecule \(= 44/(6.022\times10^{23}) \approx 7.31\times10^{-23}\,g\).

Answer: About \(7.3\times10^{-23}\,g\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) How many \(Na^+\) ions are present in \(14.2\,g\) of \(Na_2SO_4\)?

  1. Moles \(= 14.2/142 = 0.1\,mol\).
  2. Each unit gives \(2\,Na^+\), so ions \(= 0.2 \times N_A = 1.204\times10^{23}\).

Answer: \(1.204\times10^{23}\) sodium ions.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Forgetting the subscript multiplier for polyatomic salts.
  • Confusing atoms with molecules (multiply by atomicity only when asked).

Chapter 1 · Topic 8

Molar mass

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 8 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Molar mass: molar mass is the grams-per-mole bridge between the balance and the mole. Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance in \(g\,mol^{-1}\); numerically it equals the relative atomic/molecular mass. One mole of gas at STP occupies \(22.4\,L\) (molar volume).
Key formula(s). \[ M = \frac{m}{n},\;(g\,mol^{-1}),\;\; V_m = 22.4\,L\,mol^{-1}\,(STP) \]
Key points.
  • Atomic mass unit: \(1\,u = 1.66\times10^{-27}\,kg\); molar mass in grams is numerically equal to mass in \(u\).
  • Formula mass is used for ionic compounds (e.g. \(NaCl = 58.5\)) where discrete molecules do not exist.
  • Vapour density \(= M/2\); molecular mass \(= 2 \times\) vapour density.
  • Molar volume \(22.4\,L\) is valid only for gases at STP.
Example 1.

Vapour density of a gas is \(23\). Find its molecular mass and the volume of \(4.6\,g\) at STP.

  1. \(M = 2\times23 = 46\,g\,mol^{-1}\).
  2. Moles \(= 4.6/46 = 0.1\); volume \(= 0.1\times22.4 = 2.24\,L\).

Answer: \(M = 46\), volume \(= 2.24\,L\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(1.12\,L\) of a gas at STP weighs \(1.43\,g\). Find its molar mass.

  1. Moles \(= 1.12/22.4 = 0.05\,mol\).
  2. \(M = 1.43/0.05 = 28.6\,g\,mol^{-1}\) (about \(N_2/CO\) range).

Answer: About \(28.6\,g\,mol^{-1}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using vapour density \(=\,M\) instead of \(M/2\).
  • Applying \(22.4\,L\) to liquids/solids.

Chapter 1 · Topic 9

Molar volume

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 9 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Molar volume: molar volume packs Avogadro number of gas particles into 22.4 L at STP. Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance in \(g\,mol^{-1}\); numerically it equals the relative atomic/molecular mass. One mole of gas at STP occupies \(22.4\,L\) (molar volume).
Key formula(s). \[ \; V_m = 22.4\,L\,mol^{-1}\,(STP) \]
Key points.
  • Formula mass is used for ionic compounds (e.g. \(NaCl = 58.5\)) where discrete molecules do not exist.
  • Vapour density \(= M/2\); molecular mass \(= 2 \times\) vapour density.
  • Molar volume \(22.4\,L\) is valid only for gases at STP.
  • Atomic mass unit: \(1\,u = 1.66\times10^{-27}\,kg\); molar mass in grams is numerically equal to mass in \(u\).
Example 1.

\(2.24\,L\) of a gas at STP weighs \(2.9\,g\). Find its molar mass.

  1. Moles \(= 0.1\).
  2. \(M = 29\,g/mol\).

Answer: \(29\,g/mol\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) The vapour density of \(NO_2/ N_2O_4\) mixture is \(38\). Find average molar mass.

  1. \(M_{avg} = 2\times VD\).
  2. \(76\,g/mol\).

Answer: \(76\,g/mol\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using vapour density \(=\,M\) instead of \(M/2\).
  • Applying \(22.4\,L\) to liquids/solids.

Chapter 1 · Topic 10

Number of particles

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 10 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Number of particles: particle counts come from moles times Avogadro number, never from grams directly. Gay-Lussac law: at same \(T,P\), gas volumes combine in simple whole-number ratios equal to their mole ratios. Particle counts follow from moles: entities \(= n\times N_A\), with atomicity/ion multiplicity applied per formula unit.
Key formula(s). \[ \; atoms=n\times atomicity\times N_A,\;ions=n\times ion\,count\times N_A \]
Key points.
  • For ions from a salt, multiply by the subscript: \(CaCl_2 \to 1\,Ca^{2+}+2\,Cl^-\).
  • Matter classes: elements and compounds are pure; mixtures (homogeneous/heterogeneous) vary in composition.
  • Volume ratios \(=\) mole ratios only when all substances are gases at the same \(T,P\).
  • Laws of combination: definite, multiple and reciprocal proportions fix formulas from mass data.
Example 1.

How many \(Cl^-\) ions in \(0.1\,mol\,MgCl_2\)?

  1. Each unit gives \(2\,Cl^-\): \(0.2\,mol\) ions.
  2. \(1.204\times10^{23}\) ions.

Answer: \(1.204\times10^{23}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Equal masses of \(CH_4\) and \(O_2\): compare their molecule counts.

  1. Moles \(\propto 1/M\): ratio \(32:16 = 2:1\).
  2. \(CH_4\) has twice as many.

Answer: \(CH_4\) double.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Applying volume ratios when water (liquid) is a product.
  • Missing the ion/atom multiplicity per formula unit.

Chapter 1 · Topic 11

Number of atoms

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 11 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Number of atoms: atom counts multiply molecules by atomicity before applying Avogadro number. Gay-Lussac law: at same \(T,P\), gas volumes combine in simple whole-number ratios equal to their mole ratios. Particle counts follow from moles: entities \(= n\times N_A\), with atomicity/ion multiplicity applied per formula unit.
Key formula(s). \[ \frac{V_1}{\nu_1}=\frac{V_2}{\nu_2}\,(same\,T,P),\;\; atoms=n\times atomicity\times N_A,\;\frac{n_1}{\nu_1}=\frac{n_2}{\nu_2}\,(mole\,bridge) \]
Key points.
  • Volume ratios \(=\) mole ratios only when all substances are gases at the same \(T,P\).
  • Laws of combination: definite, multiple and reciprocal proportions fix formulas from mass data.
  • For ions from a salt, multiply by the subscript: \(CaCl_2 \to 1\,Ca^{2+}+2\,Cl^-\).
  • Matter classes: elements and compounds are pure; mixtures (homogeneous/heterogeneous) vary in composition.
Example 1.

\(10\,mL\,H_2 + 10\,mL\,Cl_2 \to HCl\). Find the volume of \(HCl\) formed at same \(T,P\).

  1. \(H_2+Cl_2\to2HCl\); volumes in ratio \(1:1:2\).
  2. Limiting pair gives \(20\,mL\,HCl\).

Answer: \(20\,mL\,HCl\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) How many oxygen atoms are in \(4.4\,g\,CO_2\)?

  1. Moles \(= 4.4/44 = 0.1\); molecules \(= 0.1N_A\).
  2. O atoms \(= 2\times0.1N_A = 1.204\times10^{23}\).

Answer: \(1.204\times10^{23}\) O atoms.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Applying volume ratios when water (liquid) is a product.
  • Missing the ion/atom multiplicity per formula unit.

Chapter 1 · Topic 12

Number of molecules

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 12 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Number of molecules: molecule counts equal moles times Avogadro number. Gay-Lussac law: at same \(T,P\), gas volumes combine in simple whole-number ratios equal to their mole ratios. Particle counts follow from moles: entities \(= n\times N_A\), with atomicity/ion multiplicity applied per formula unit.
Key formula(s). \[ \; N=nN_A,\;\; atoms=n\times atomicity\times N_A,\;\frac{n_1}{\nu_1}=\frac{n_2}{\nu_2}\,(mole\,bridge) \]
Key points.
  • Laws of combination: definite, multiple and reciprocal proportions fix formulas from mass data.
  • For ions from a salt, multiply by the subscript: \(CaCl_2 \to 1\,Ca^{2+}+2\,Cl^-\).
  • Matter classes: elements and compounds are pure; mixtures (homogeneous/heterogeneous) vary in composition.
  • Volume ratios \(=\) mole ratios only when all substances are gases at the same \(T,P\).
Example 1.

How many hydrogen atoms are in \(1\,g\,H_2\)?

  1. Moles \(= 0.5\); molecules \(= 0.5N_A\).
  2. Atoms \(= 2\times0.5N_A = 6.022\times10^{23}\).

Answer: \(6.022\times10^{23}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(11.2\,L\,O_2\) at STP + \(5.6\,L\,H_2\) at STP: which has more molecules?

  1. Moles: \(0.5\) vs \(0.25\).
  2. Oxygen has double.

Answer: \(O_2\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Applying volume ratios when water (liquid) is a product.
  • Missing the ion/atom multiplicity per formula unit.

  • Volume ratios \(=\) mole ratios only when all substances are gases at the same \(T,P\).
  • Laws of combination: definite, multiple and reciprocal proportions fix formulas from mass data.
Example 1.

How many \(Cl^-\) ions in \(0.1\,mol\,MgCl_2\)?

  1. Each unit gives \(2\,Cl^-\): \(0.2\,mol\) ions.
  2. \(1.204\times10^{23}\) ions.

Answer: \(1.204\times10^{23}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Equal masses of \(CH_4\) and \(O_2\): compare their molecule counts.

  1. Moles \(\propto 1/M\): ratio \(32:16 = 2:1\).
  2. \(CH_4\) has twice as many.

Chapter 1 · Topic 14

Percentage composition

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 14 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Percentage composition: percentage composition reports each element's mass share of one mole of compound. Percentage composition is the mass share of each element in one mole of compound: \(\%E =\) (atoms \(\times\) atomic mass / molar mass) \(\times 100\). It is the bridge between analysis data and empirical formula.
Key formula(s). \[ \%E = \frac{n_E \times A_E}{M_{compound}}\times100 \]
Key points.
  • Sum of all percentages must equal \(100\%\) (check your arithmetic).
  • From \(\%\) composition divide each \(\%\) by atomic mass to get mole ratios.
  • Water of crystallisation counts in molar mass, e.g. \(CuSO_4\cdot5H_2O = 249.5\).
  • JEE often gives combustion data instead; convert \(CO_2 \to C\), \(H_2O \to H\) first.
Example 1.

Calculate the mass \(\%\) of \(N\) in urea, \((NH_2)_2CO\).

  1. Molar mass \(= 60\,g\,mol^{-1}\); \(N\) mass per mole \(= 28\,g\).
  2. \(\%N = 28/60\times100 = 46.7\%\).

Answer: \(46.7\%\) nitrogen.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) A compound contains \(40\%\,C\), \(6.7\%\,H\), rest \(O\). Find its empirical formula.

  1. Moles: \(C = 40/12 = 3.33\), \(H = 6.7/1 = 6.7\), \(O = 53.3/16 = 3.33\).
  2. Ratio \(1:2:1\), so empirical formula \(= CH_2O\).

Answer: \(CH_2O\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Forgetting waters of crystallisation in molar mass.
  • Rounding mole ratios too early; divide by the smallest last.

Index / Fundamentals
Chapter 1 · Topic 15

Empirical formula

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 15 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Empirical formula: empirical formula is the simplest whole-number atom ratio from analysis data. Empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; molecular formula is an integer multiple of it. \(n =\) molecular mass / empirical mass gives the multiplier.
Key formula(s). \[ \; n = \frac{M_{molecular}}{M_{empirical}} \]
Key points.
  • If a ratio is \(1.5\) or \(1.33\), multiply all by \(2\) or \(3\) to clear decimals.
  • Molecular formula needs molar mass from another experiment (vapour density, colligative, MS).
  • For combustion: moles \(C =\) moles \(CO_2\), moles \(H = 2\times\) moles \(H_2O\).
  • Steps: \(\% \to\) mass \(\to\) moles \(\to\) divide by smallest \(\to\) integers.
Example 1.

A compound with empirical formula \(CH_2O\) has molar mass \(180\). Find its molecular formula.

  1. Empirical mass \(= 30\); \(n = 180/30 = 6\).
  2. Molecular formula \(= C_6H_{12}O_6\).

Answer: \(C_6H_{12}O_6\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(0.46\,g\) of a compound gives \(0.88\,g\,CO_2\) and \(0.54\,g\,H_2O\) on combustion. Molar mass \(= 46\). Find MF.

  1. Moles \(C = 0.88/44 = 0.02\); moles \(H = 2\times(0.54/18) = 0.06\); mass \(C+H = 0.24+0.06 = 0.30\,g\).
  2. Oxygen mass \(= 0.46-0.30 = 0.16\,g = 0.01\,mol\); ratio \(C:H:O = 2:6:1\), EF \(= C_2H_6O\), mass \(46 =\) MF.

Answer: \(C_2H_6O\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Forgetting \(H_2O\) gives TWO hydrogens per mole.
  • Taking oxygen by difference incorrectly (subtract C and H masses first).

Index / Fundamentals
Chapter 1 · Topic 16

Molecular formula

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 16 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Molecular formula: molecular formula scales the empirical formula up by the measured molar mass. Stoichiometry converts the balanced equation coefficients into mole ratios. The limiting reagent is the reactant that finishes first; all product amounts are calculated from it, and \(\%\) yield \(=\) (actual/theoretical) \(\times 100\).
Key formula(s). \[ \frac{n_1}{\nu_1}=\frac{n_2}{\nu_2},\;\; purity=\frac{pure\,mass}{sample\,mass}\times100 \]
Key points.
  • Theoretical yield comes from the limiting reagent; excess reagent is left over.
  • Purity and yield corrections: multiply the impure mass by \(\%\) purity before converting to moles.
  • Balance the equation first; coefficients are mole ratios, not mass ratios.
  • Limiting reagent \(=\) smallest \((given\,moles)/(coefficient)\).
Example 1.

\(2.7\,g\,Al\) reacts with \(9.8\,g\,H_2SO_4\) (\(2Al+3H_2SO_4\to Al_2(SO_4)_3+3H_2\)). Identify the limiter and moles of \(H_2\).

  1. Moles: \(Al = 0.1\), acid \(= 0.1\); need \(0.15\,mol\) acid for all Al, so acid limits.
  2. \(H_2 = 0.1\,mol\) (1:1 with acid).

Answer: Acid limits; \(0.1\,mol\,H_2\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Theoretical yield \(= 20\,g\), actual \(= 17\,g\). Find percent yield.

  1. \(\% = 17/20\times100\).
  2. \(85\%\).

Answer: \(85\%\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Computing products from the excess reagent.
  • Using masses directly in the mole ratio without dividing by molar mass.
Back to Index
Index / Fundamentals
Chapter 1 · Topic 17

Stoichiometry

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 17 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Stoichiometry: stoichiometry reads the balanced-equation coefficients as a mole recipe. Stoichiometry converts the balanced equation coefficients into mole ratios. The limiting reagent is the reactant that finishes first; all product amounts are calculated from it, and \(\%\) yield \(=\) (actual/theoretical) \(\times 100\).
Key formula(s). \[ \frac{n_1}{\nu_1}=\frac{n_2}{\nu_2},\;\; \%\,yield=\frac{actual}{theoretical}\times100 \]
Key points.
  • Balance the equation first; coefficients are mole ratios, not mass ratios.
  • Limiting reagent \(=\) smallest \((given\,moles)/(coefficient)\).
  • Theoretical yield comes from the limiting reagent; excess reagent is left over.
  • Purity and yield corrections: multiply the impure mass by \(\%\) purity before converting to moles.
Example 1.

\(10\,g\,CaCO_3\) decomposes to \(CaO + CO_2\). Find the mass of \(CO_2\) formed.

  1. Moles \(CaCO_3 = 10/100 = 0.1\,mol\); 1:1 ratio gives \(0.1\,mol\,CO_2\).
  2. Mass \(= 0.1\times44 = 4.4\,g\).

Answer: \(4.4\,g\,CO_2\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(5.6\,L\,H_2\) at STP reacts with \(1.4\,L\,N_2\) at STP by \(N_2+3H_2\to2NH_3\). Find the mass of \(NH_3\) formed.

  1. Moles: \(H_2 = 0.25\), \(N_2 = 0.0625\); required ratio \(3:1\); available \(0.25/3 = 0.0833 > 0.0625\), so \(N_2\) limits.
  2. Moles \(NH_3 = 2\times0.0625 = 0.125\); mass \(= 0.125\times17 = 2.125\,g\).

Answer: \(2.125\,g\,NH_3\); \(N_2\) is limiting.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Computing products from the excess reagent.
  • Using masses directly in the mole ratio without dividing by molar mass.

Index / Fundamentals
Chapter 1 · Topic 18

Stoichiometric calculations

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 18 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Stoichiometric calculations: stoichiometric calculations convert given mass to moles, cross the mole bridge, and convert back. Stoichiometry converts the balanced equation coefficients into mole ratios. The limiting reagent is the reactant that finishes first; all product amounts are calculated from it, and \(\%\) yield \(=\) (actual/theoretical) \(\times 100\).
Key formula(s). \[ \; purity=\frac{pure\,mass}{sample\,mass}\times100 \]
Key points.
  • Limiting reagent \(=\) smallest \((given\,moles)/(coefficient)\).
  • Theoretical yield comes from the limiting reagent; excess reagent is left over.
  • Purity and yield corrections: multiply the impure mass by \(\%\) purity before converting to moles.
  • Balance the equation first; coefficients are mole ratios, not mass ratios.
Example 1.

\(4\,g\,H_2\) reacts with \(32\,g\,O_2\) (\(2H_2+O_2\to2H_2O\)). Find the mass of water formed.

  1. Moles: \(H_2 = 2\), \(O_2 = 1\); required ratio \(2:1\) exactly matches.
  2. Both fully consumed: \(2\,mol\,H_2O = 36\,g\).

Answer: \(36\,g\,H_2O\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(80\%\) pure \(CaCO_3\) sample (\(10\,g\)) is heated. Find \(CO_2\) released.

  1. Pure \(CaCO_3 = 8\,g = 0.08\,mol\).
  2. \(CO_2 = 0.08\times44 = 3.52\,g\).

Answer: \(3.52\,g\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Computing products from the excess reagent.
  • Using masses directly in the mole ratio without dividing by molar mass.

Limiting reagent

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 19 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Limiting reagent: the limiting reagent is the reactant with the smallest moles-per-coefficient value. Stoichiometry converts the balanced equation coefficients into mole ratios. The limiting reagent is the reactant that finishes first; all product amounts are calculated from it, and \(\%\) yield \(=\) (actual/theoretical) \(\times 100\).
Key formula(s). \[ \; purity=\frac{pure\,mass}{sample\,mass}\times100 \],\;\frac{n_1}{\nu_1}=\frac{n_2}{\nu_2} \]
Key points.
  • Theoretical yield comes from the limiting reagent; excess reagent is left over.
  • Purity and yield corrections: multiply the impure mass by \(\%\) purity before converting to moles.
  • Balance the equation first; coefficients are mole ratios, not mass ratios.
  • Limiting reagent \(=\) smallest \((given\,moles)/(coefficient)\).
Example 1.

\(2.7\,g\,Al\) reacts with \(9.8\,g\,H_2SO_4\) (\(2Al+3H_2SO_4\to Al_2(SO_4)_3+3H_2\)). Identify the limiter and moles of \(H_2\).

  1. Moles: \(Al = 0.1\), acid \(= 0.1\); need \(0.15\,mol\) acid for all Al, so acid limits.
  2. \(H_2 = 0.1\,mol\) (1:1 with acid).

Answer: Acid limits; \(0.1\,mol\,H_2\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Theoretical yield \(= 20\,g\), actual \(= 17\,g\). Find percent yield.

  1. \(\% = 17/20\times100\).
  2. \(85\%\).

Answer: \(85\%\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Computing products from the excess reagent.
  • Using masses directly in the mole ratio without dividing by molar mass.

Excess reagent

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 20 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Excess reagent: the excess reagent is whatever survives after the limiting reagent is exhausted. Stoichiometry converts the balanced equation coefficients into mole ratios. The limiting reagent is the reactant that finishes first; all product amounts are calculated from it, and \(\%\) yield \(=\) (actual/theoretical) \(\times 100\).
Key formula(s). \[ n_{excess}=n_{given}-n_{used} \]
Key points.
  • Balance the equation first; coefficients are mole ratios, not mass ratios.
  • Limiting reagent \(=\) smallest \((given\,moles)/(coefficient)\).
  • Theoretical yield comes from the limiting reagent; excess reagent is left over.
  • Purity and yield corrections: multiply the impure mass by \(\%\) purity before converting to moles.
Example 1.

\(10\,g\,CaCO_3\) decomposes to \(CaO + CO_2\). Find the mass of \(CO_2\) formed.

  1. Moles \(CaCO_3 = 10/100 = 0.1\,mol\); 1:1 ratio gives \(0.1\,mol\,CO_2\).
  2. Mass \(= 0.1\times44 = 4.4\,g\).

Answer: \(4.4\,g\,CO_2\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(5.6\,L\,H_2\) at STP reacts with \(1.4\,L\,N_2\) at STP by \(N_2+3H_2\to2NH_3\). Find the mass of \(NH_3\) formed.

  1. Moles: \(H_2 = 0.25\), \(N_2 = 0.0625\); required ratio \(3:1\); available \(0.25/3 = 0.0833 > 0.0625\), so \(N_2\) limits.
  2. Moles \(NH_3 = 2\times0.0625 = 0.125\); mass \(= 0.125\times17 = 2.125\,g\).

Answer: \(2.125\,g\,NH_3\); \(N_2\) is limiting.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Computing products from the excess reagent.
  • Using masses directly in the mole ratio without dividing by molar mass.

Chapter 1 · Topic 21

Theoretical yield

  • Limiting reagent \(=\) smallest \((given\,moles)/(coefficient)\).
  • Theoretical yield comes from the limiting reagent; excess reagent is left over.
  • Purity and yield corrections: multiply the impure mass by \(\%\) purity before converting to moles.
  • Balance the equation first; coefficients are mole ratios, not mass ratios.
Example 1.

\(4\,g\,H_2\) reacts with \(32\,g\,O_2\) (\(2H_2+O_2\to2H_2O\)). Find the mass of water formed.

  1. Moles: \(H_2 = 2\), \(O_2 = 1\); required ratio \(2:1\) exactly matches.
  2. Both fully consumed: \(2\,mol\,H_2O = 36\,g\).

Answer: \(36\,g\,H_2O\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(80\%\) pure \(CaCO_3\) sample (\(10\,g\)) is heated. Find \(CO_2\) released.

  1. Pure \(CaCO_3 = 8\,g = 0.08\,mol\).
  2. \(CO_2 = 0.08\times44 = 3.52\,g\).

Answer: \(3.52\,g\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Computing products from the excess reagent.
  • Using masses directly in the mole ratio without dividing by molar mass.

Chapter 1 · Topic 22

Percentage yield

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 22 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Percentage yield: percentage yield compares the actual harvest with the theoretical maximum. Stoichiometry converts the balanced equation coefficients into mole ratios. The limiting reagent is the reactant that finishes first; all product amounts are calculated from it, and \(\%\) yield \(=\) (actual/theoretical) \(\times 100\).
Key formula(s). \[ \; \%\,yield=\frac{actual}{theoretical}\times100 \]
Key points.
  • Theoretical yield comes from the limiting reagent; excess reagent is left over.
  • Purity and yield corrections: multiply the impure mass by \(\%\) purity before converting to moles.
  • Balance the equation first; coefficients are mole ratios, not mass ratios.
  • Limiting reagent \(=\) smallest \((given\,moles)/(coefficient)\).
Example 1.

\(2.7\,g\,Al\) reacts with \(9.8\,g\,H_2SO_4\) (\(2Al+3H_2SO_4\to Al_2(SO_4)_3+3H_2\)). Identify the limiter and moles of \(H_2\).

  1. Moles: \(Al = 0.1\), acid \(= 0.1\); need \(0.15\,mol\) acid for all Al, so acid limits.
  2. \(H_2 = 0.1\,mol\) (1:1 with acid).

Answer: Acid limits; \(0.1\,mol\,H_2\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Theoretical yield \(= 20\,g\), actual \(= 17\,g\). Find percent yield.

  1. \(\% = 17/20\times100\).
  2. \(85\%\).

Answer: \(85\%\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Computing products from the excess reagent.
  • Using masses directly in the mole ratio without dividing by molar mass.

Index / Fundamentals
Chapter 1 · Topic 23

Purity of substances

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 23 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Purity of substances: purity corrections multiply the sample mass by percent purity before any mole step. Stoichiometry converts the balanced equation coefficients into mole ratios. The limiting reagent is the reactant that finishes first; all product amounts are calculated from it, and \(\%\) yield \(=\) (actual/theoretical) \(\times 100\).
Key formula(s). \[ \%\,purity=m_{pure}/m_{sample}\times100 \]
Key points.
  • Balance the equation first; coefficients are mole ratios, not mass ratios.
  • Limiting reagent \(=\) smallest \((given\,moles)/(coefficient)\).
  • Theoretical yield comes from the limiting reagent; excess reagent is left over.
  • Purity and yield corrections: multiply the impure mass by \(\%\) purity before converting to moles.
Example 1.

\(10\,g\,CaCO_3\) decomposes to \(CaO + CO_2\). Find the mass of \(CO_2\) formed.

  1. Moles \(CaCO_3 = 10/100 = 0.1\,mol\); 1:1 ratio gives \(0.1\,mol\,CO_2\).
  2. Mass \(= 0.1\times44 = 4.4\,g\).

Answer: \(4.4\,g\,CO_2\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(5.6\,L\,H_2\) at STP reacts with \(1.4\,L\,N_2\) at STP by \(N_2+3H_2\to2NH_3\). Find the mass of \(NH_3\) formed.

  1. Moles: \(H_2 = 0.25\), \(N_2 = 0.0625\); required ratio \(3:1\); available \(0.25/3 = 0.0833 > 0.0625\), so \(N_2\) limits.
  2. Moles \(NH_3 = 2\times0.0625 = 0.125\); mass \(= 0.125\times17 = 2.125\,g\).

Answer: \(2.125\,g\,NH_3\); \(N_2\) is limiting.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Computing products from the excess reagent.
  • Using masses directly in the mole ratio without dividing by molar mass.

Chapter 1 · Topic 24

Equivalent mass

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 24 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Equivalent mass: equivalent mass is the mass that supplies or consumes one mole of the reacting unit. Equivalent mass \(= M/x\) where \(x\) (n-factor) is \(H^+\) given, \(OH^-\) given, electrons exchanged, or total cation charge. Normality \(N = M\times x\), and at equivalence \(N_1V_1 = N_2V_2\).
Key formula(s). \[ E = M/x,\;\; N = M\cdot x \]
Key points.
  • Redox: \(x =\) electrons gained/lost per molecule (\(KMnO_4\) acidic: \(5\); \(K_2Cr_2O_7\): \(6\)).
  • Salts: \(x =\) total charge of cation (\(Al_2(SO_4)_3: 2\times3 = 6\)).
  • n-factor can change with medium (e.g. \(KMnO_4\): acidic \(5\), neutral \(3\), basic \(1\)).
  • Acids: \(x =\) basicity (\(H_2SO_4:2\)); bases: \(x =\) acidity (\(Ca(OH)_2:2\)).
Example 1.

Find the equivalent mass of \(Ca(OH)_2\) (\(M = 74\)).

  1. Acidity \(= 2\) (\(2\,OH^-\)).
  2. \(E = 74/2 = 37\).

Answer: \(37\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(1\,M\,Al_2(SO_4)_3\): find its normality.

  1. Total cation charge \(= 2\times3 = 6\).
  2. \(N = 6\,N\).

Answer: \(6\,N\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using acid-base n-factor in a redox titration.
  • Forgetting that \(KMnO_4\) n-factor depends on medium.
Back to Index
Index / Fundamentals
Chapter 1 · Topic 25

Equivalent weight

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 25 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Equivalent weight: equivalent weight equals molar mass divided by the n-factor of that medium. Equivalent mass \(= M/x\) where \(x\) (n-factor) is \(H^+\) given, \(OH^-\) given, electrons exchanged, or total cation charge. Normality \(N = M\times x\), and at equivalence \(N_1V_1 = N_2V_2\).
Key formula(s). \[ E = M/x,\;\; N = M\cdot x,\;\; N_1V_1 = N_2V_2 \]
Key points.
  • Salts: \(x =\) total charge of cation (\(Al_2(SO_4)_3: 2\times3 = 6\)).
  • n-factor can change with medium (e.g. \(KMnO_4\): acidic \(5\), neutral \(3\), basic \(1\)).
  • Acids: \(x =\) basicity (\(H_2SO_4:2\)); bases: \(x =\) acidity (\(Ca(OH)_2:2\)).
  • Redox: \(x =\) electrons gained/lost per molecule (\(KMnO_4\) acidic: \(5\); \(K_2Cr_2O_7\): \(6\)).
Example 1.

\(25\,mL\) of \(0.2\,N\,Na_2CO_3\) reacts completely with acid. How many meq?

  1. meq \(= N\times V(mL)\).
  2. \(0.2\times25 = 5\,meq\).

Answer: \(5\,meq\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why is the n-factor of \(H_3PO_4\) sometimes \(1\), \(2\) or \(3\)?

  1. It depends on how many \(H^+\) the reaction consumes.
  2. Vs NaOH: 1, 2 or 3 with 1, 2, 3 moles of base.

Answer: Depends on neutralisation extent.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using acid-base n-factor in a redox titration.
  • Forgetting that \(KMnO_4\) n-factor depends on medium.

Chapter 1 · Topic 26

n-factor

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 26 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, n-factor: the n-factor counts H+, OH- or electrons exchanged per molecule in that specific reaction. Equivalent mass \(= M/x\) where \(x\) (n-factor) is \(H^+\) given, \(OH^-\) given, electrons exchanged, or total cation charge. Normality \(N = M\times x\), and at equivalence \(N_1V_1 = N_2V_2\).
Key formula(s). \[ E = M/x,\;\; N = M\cdot x,\;\; w = \frac{NEV(L)}{1000} \]
Key points.
  • Acids: \(x =\) basicity (\(H_2SO_4:2\)); bases: \(x =\) acidity (\(Ca(OH)_2:2\)).
  • Redox: \(x =\) electrons gained/lost per molecule (\(KMnO_4\) acidic: \(5\); \(K_2Cr_2O_7\): \(6\)).
  • Salts: \(x =\) total charge of cation (\(Al_2(SO_4)_3: 2\times3 = 6\)).
  • n-factor can change with medium (e.g. \(KMnO_4\): acidic \(5\), neutral \(3\), basic \(1\)).
Example 1.

Find the equivalent mass of \(H_2SO_4\) (\(M = 98\)) and normality of \(2\,M\,H_2SO_4\).

  1. Basicity \(= 2\), so \(E = 98/2 = 49\).
  2. \(N = 2\times2 = 4\,N\).

Answer: \(E = 49\), \(N = 4\,N\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(20\,mL\) of \(KMnO_4\) solution oxidises \(25\,mL\) of \(0.1\,N\) oxalic acid in acidic medium. Find normality of \(KMnO_4\).

  1. At equivalence \(N_1V_1 = N_2V_2\).
  2. \(N_{KMnO_4} = 0.1\times25/20 = 0.125\,N\).

Answer: \(0.125\,N\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using acid-base n-factor in a redox titration.
  • Forgetting that \(KMnO_4\) n-factor depends on medium.

Normality

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 27 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Normality: normality counts equivalents per litre, so N1V1 = N2V2 works at every endpoint. Equivalent mass \(= M/x\) where \(x\) (n-factor) is \(H^+\) given, \(OH^-\) given, electrons exchanged, or total cation charge. Normality \(N = M\times x\), and at equivalence \(N_1V_1 = N_2V_2\).
Key formula(s). \[ \; N = M\cdot x,\;\; N_1V_1 = N_2V_2 \]
Key points.
  • Redox: \(x =\) electrons gained/lost per molecule (\(KMnO_4\) acidic: \(5\); \(K_2Cr_2O_7\): \(6\)).
  • Salts: \(x =\) total charge of cation (\(Al_2(SO_4)_3: 2\times3 = 6\)).
  • n-factor can change with medium (e.g. \(KMnO_4\): acidic \(5\), neutral \(3\), basic \(1\)).
  • Acids: \(x =\) basicity (\(H_2SO_4:2\)); bases: \(x =\) acidity (\(Ca(OH)_2:2\)).
Example 1.

Find the equivalent mass of \(Ca(OH)_2\) (\(M = 74\)).

  1. Acidity \(= 2\) (\(2\,OH^-\)).
  2. \(E = 74/2 = 37\).

Answer: \(37\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(1\,M\,Al_2(SO_4)_3\): find its normality.

  1. Total cation charge \(= 2\times3 = 6\).
  2. \(N = 6\,N\).

Answer: \(6\,N\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using acid-base n-factor in a redox titration.
  • Forgetting that \(KMnO_4\) n-factor depends on medium.

Chapter 1 · Topic 28

Molarity

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 28 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Molarity: molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution and shifts with temperature. Molarity \(M = n/V(L)\) is temperature-dependent (volume changes); molality \(m = n/kg\,solvent\) and mole fraction are temperature-independent. Dilution obeys \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\).
Key formula(s). \[ M=\frac{n}{V(L)},\;M_1V_1=M_2V_2 \]
Key points.
  • Mole fractions in a mixture always add to \(1\).
  • On mixing: total moles conserved, \(M_{mix} = (M_1V_1+M_2V_2)/(V_1+V_2)\).
  • Molarity uses solution volume; molality uses solvent mass in kg.
  • ppm \(= (mass\,solute/mass\,solution)\times10^6\), used for trace quantities.
Example 1.

Fluoride in water is \(2\,mg/L\). Express it in ppm.

  1. \(1\,L\) water \(\approx 10^6\,mg\).
  2. \(2\,mg\) per \(10^6\,mg = 2\,ppm\).

Answer: \(2\,ppm\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(0.5\,mol\) solute is dissolved in \(250\,g\) water. Find molality.

  1. Solvent \(= 0.25\,kg\).
  2. \(m = 0.5/0.25 = 2\,m\).

Answer: \(2\,m\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using solution mass instead of solvent mass for molality.
  • Applying \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\) when a reaction occurs (use equivalents instead).

Chapter 1 · Topic 29

Molality

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 29 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Molality: molality is moles per kilogram of solvent, immune to temperature. Molarity \(M = n/V(L)\) is temperature-dependent (volume changes); molality \(m = n/kg\,solvent\) and mole fraction are temperature-independent. Dilution obeys \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\).
Key formula(s). \[ m=\frac{n}{kg} \]
Key points.
  • Molarity uses solution volume; molality uses solvent mass in kg.
  • ppm \(= (mass\,solute/mass\,solution)\times10^6\), used for trace quantities.
  • Mole fractions in a mixture always add to \(1\).
  • On mixing: total moles conserved, \(M_{mix} = (M_1V_1+M_2V_2)/(V_1+V_2)\).
Example 1.

\(4\,g\,NaOH\) is dissolved to make \(500\,mL\) solution. Find molarity.

  1. Moles \(= 4/40 = 0.1\,mol\); volume \(= 0.5\,L\).
  2. \(M = 0.1/0.5 = 0.2\,M\).

Answer: \(0.2\,M\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) What volume of water must be added to \(200\,mL\) of \(1.5\,M\) solution to make it \(0.5\,M\)?

  1. \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2 \Rightarrow V_2 = 1.5\times200/0.5 = 600\,mL\).
  2. Water added \(= 600-200 = 400\,mL\).

Answer: \(400\,mL\) water.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using solution mass instead of solvent mass for molality.
  • Applying \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\) when a reaction occurs (use equivalents instead).
Back to Index
Index / Fundamentals
Chapter 1 · Topic 30

Mole fraction

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 30 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Mole fraction: mole fraction is each component's mole share, and all fractions add to one. Molarity \(M = n/V(L)\) is temperature-dependent (volume changes); molality \(m = n/kg\,solvent\) and mole fraction are temperature-independent. Dilution obeys \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\).
Key formula(s). \[ M=\frac{n}{V(L)},\;\chi_i=\frac{n_i}{\sum n} \]
Key points.
  • ppm \(= (mass\,solute/mass\,solution)\times10^6\), used for trace quantities.
  • Mole fractions in a mixture always add to \(1\).
  • On mixing: total moles conserved, \(M_{mix} = (M_1V_1+M_2V_2)/(V_1+V_2)\).
  • Molarity uses solution volume; molality uses solvent mass in kg.
Example 1.

A \(10\%\,w/w\,NaOH\) solution has density \(1.1\,g/mL\). Find its molarity.

  1. \(100\,g\) solution carries \(10\,g\,NaOH = 0.25\,mol\); volume \(= 100/1.1 = 90.9\,mL\).
  2. \(M = 0.25/0.0909 \approx 2.75\,M\).

Answer: \(2.75\,M\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Mix \(100\,mL\,1\,M + 200\,mL\,2\,M\) of the same solute. Find final molarity.

  1. Total moles \(= 100 + 400 = 500\,mmol\); total volume \(= 300\,mL\).
  2. \(M = 500/300 \approx 1.67\,M\).

Answer: \(1.67\,M\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using solution mass instead of solvent mass for molality.
  • Applying \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\) when a reaction occurs (use equivalents instead).

  • Mole fractions in a mixture always add to \(1\).

  • ppm \(= (mass\,solute/mass\,solution)\times10^6\), used for trace quantities.

Fluoride in water is \(2\,mg/L\). Express it in ppm.

  2. \(2\,mg\) per \(10^6\,mg = 2\,ppm\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(0.5\,mol\) solute is dissolved in \(250\,g\) water. Find molality.

  2. \(m = 0.5/0.25 = 2\,m\).

Concentration conversions

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 32 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Concentration conversions: concentration conversions all pass through moles, using density to link mass and volume. Molarity \(M = n/V(L)\) is temperature-dependent (volume changes); molality \(m = n/kg\,solvent\) and mole fraction are temperature-independent. Dilution obeys \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\).

\(4\,g\,NaOH\) is dissolved to make \(500\,mL\) solution. Find molarity.

  1. Moles \(= 4/40 = 0.1\,mol\); volume \(= 0.5\,L\).

Answer: \(0.2\,M\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) What volume of water must be added to \(200\,mL\) of \(1.5\,M\) solution to make it \(0.5\,M\)?

  1. \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2 \Rightarrow V_2 = 1.5\times200/0.5 = 600\,mL\).

Chapter 1 · Topic 33

Stoichiometry of gaseous reactions

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 33 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Stoichiometry of gaseous reactions: gas volumes at the same T and P combine in the same ratio as their moles. Stoichiometry converts the balanced equation coefficients into mole ratios. The limiting reagent is the reactant that finishes first; all product amounts are calculated from it, and \(\%\) yield \(=\) (actual/theoretical) \(\times 100\).
Key formula(s). \[ V_1/\nu_1=V_2/\nu_2\,(same\,T,P) \]
Key points.
  • Limiting reagent \(=\) smallest \((given\,moles)/(coefficient)\).
  • Theoretical yield comes from the limiting reagent; excess reagent is left over.
  • Purity and yield corrections: multiply the impure mass by \(\%\) purity before converting to moles.
  • Balance the equation first; coefficients are mole ratios, not mass ratios.
Example 1.

\(4\,g\,H_2\) reacts with \(32\,g\,O_2\) (\(2H_2+O_2\to2H_2O\)). Find the mass of water formed.

  1. Moles: \(H_2 = 2\), \(O_2 = 1\); required ratio \(2:1\) exactly matches.
  2. Both fully consumed: \(2\,mol\,H_2O = 36\,g\).

Answer: \(36\,g\,H_2O\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(80\%\) pure \(CaCO_3\) sample (\(10\,g\)) is heated. Find \(CO_2\) released.

  1. Pure \(CaCO_3 = 8\,g = 0.08\,mol\).
  2. \(CO_2 = 0.08\times44 = 3.52\,g\).

Answer: \(3.52\,g\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Computing products from the excess reagent.
  • Using masses directly in the mole ratio without dividing by molar mass.

Chapter 1 · Topic 34

Redox stoichiometry

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 34 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Redox stoichiometry: redox stoichiometry balances electrons first, then spends the mole ratio on products. Stoichiometry converts the balanced equation coefficients into mole ratios. The limiting reagent is the reactant that finishes first; all product amounts are calculated from it, and \(\%\) yield \(=\) (actual/theoretical) \(\times 100\).
Key formula(s). \[ e^-_{lost}=e^-_{gained} \]
Key points.
  • Theoretical yield comes from the limiting reagent; excess reagent is left over.
  • Purity and yield corrections: multiply the impure mass by \(\%\) purity before converting to moles.
  • Balance the equation first; coefficients are mole ratios, not mass ratios.
  • Limiting reagent \(=\) smallest \((given\,moles)/(coefficient)\).
Example 1.

\(2.7\,g\,Al\) reacts with \(9.8\,g\,H_2SO_4\) (\(2Al+3H_2SO_4\to Al_2(SO_4)_3+3H_2\)). Identify the limiter and moles of \(H_2\).

  1. Moles: \(Al = 0.1\), acid \(= 0.1\); need \(0.15\,mol\) acid for all Al, so acid limits.
  2. \(H_2 = 0.1\,mol\) (1:1 with acid).

Answer: Acid limits; \(0.1\,mol\,H_2\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Theoretical yield \(= 20\,g\), actual \(= 17\,g\). Find percent yield.

  1. \(\% = 17/20\times100\).
  2. \(85\%\).

Answer: \(85\%\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Computing products from the excess reagent.
  • Using masses directly in the mole ratio without dividing by molar mass.

Index / Fundamentals
Chapter 1 · Topic 35

Mixture calculations

Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole ConceptFundamentalsTopic 35 of 35

Explanation

Concept. In Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry / Mole Concept, Mixture calculations: mixtures are solved by writing one mass equation plus one mole equation and solving them together. Mole is the chemist counting unit: one mole contains \(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\) entities, and links mass, number and volume through \(n = m/M = N/N_A = V/22.4\,L\) at STP.
Key formula(s). \[ mass\,eqn + mol\,eqn\,together \]
Key points.
  • Always convert every quantity to moles first, then use the balanced-equation mole ratio.
  • At STP one mole of any gas occupies \(22.4\,L\); at NTP the same value is used in JEE.
  • Number of entities \(=\) moles \(\times N_A\); never multiply grams directly by \(N_A\).
  • For mixtures, total moles \(=\) sum of component moles; average molar mass \(=\) total mass/total moles.
  • JEE trap: STP volume applies only to gases, never to liquids or solids.
Example 1.

How many moles and molecules are present in \(9\,g\) of water?

  1. Molar mass of \(H_2O = 18\,g\,mol^{-1}\), so \(n = 9/18 = 0.5\,mol\).
  2. Molecules \(= 0.5 \times 6.022\times10^{23} = 3.011\times10^{23}\).
  3. Atoms \(= 3 \times 3.011\times10^{23} = 9.03\times10^{23}\) since each water has 3 atoms.

Answer: \(0.5\,mol\), \(3.011\times10^{23}\) molecules.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) A mixture of \(CH_4\) and \(C_2H_6\) weighing \(8\,g\) occupies \(5.6\,L\) at STP. Find the mole fraction of \(CH_4\).

  1. Total moles \(= 5.6/22.4 = 0.25\,mol\); let \(x =\) moles of \(CH_4\).
  2. Mass: \(16x + 30(0.25-x) = 8 \Rightarrow 16x + 7.5 - 30x = 8 \Rightarrow x = -0.5/-14\), solving gives \(x \approx 0.036\,mol\).
  3. Mole fraction \(= 0.036/0.25 \approx 0.143\).

Answer: About \(0.14\) (solve mass + mole equations simultaneously).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(22.4\,L\) for non-gaseous substances.
  • Forgetting to multiply by atomicity when asked for atoms.
  • Mixing average molar mass with mole fraction weighting.

Chapter 2 · Topic 1

Fundamental particles

Atomic StructureFundamentalsTopic 1 of 46

Explanation

Concept. In Atomic Structure, Fundamental particles: electrons, protons and neutrons fix charge, mass and identity of every atom. Atom: electrons \((-e, 1/1837\,u)\), protons \((+e, 1\,u)\), neutrons (neutral, \(1\,u\)). EM waves satisfy \(c = \nu\lambda = 3\times10^8\,m/s\); wave number \(\bar\nu = 1/\lambda\).
Key formula(s). \[ e/m\,(Thomson),\,\alpha\!-\!scatter\,(Rutherford\,nucleus) \],\;c=\nu\lambda \]
Key points.
  • Rutherford scattering: most mass/positive charge sits in a tiny nucleus; electrons occupy the rest.
  • Thomson Plum-pudding gave \(e/m\); Millikan oil-drop gave \(e\); together they fixed \(m_e\).
  • Convert \(cm^{-1}\) to \(m^{-1}\) by \(\times100\) before using \(E = hc\bar\nu\).
  • Order of EM spectrum: gamma \(<\) X \(<\) UV \(<\) visible \(<\) IR \(<\) micro \(<\) radio (decreasing energy).
Example 1.

Frequency of yellow light \(\lambda = 580\,nm\)? Also its wave number.

  1. \(\nu = c/\lambda = 3\times10^8/5.8\times10^{-7} \approx 5.17\times10^{14}\,Hz\).
  2. \(\bar\nu = 1/\lambda \approx 1.72\times10^6\,m^{-1} = 17200\,cm^{-1}\).

Answer: \(5.17\times10^{14}\,Hz\), \(1.72\times10^4\,cm^{-1}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Energy of one mole of photons with \(\lambda = 400\,nm\)?

  1. Per photon \(E = hc/\lambda = 4.97\times10^{-19}\,J\).
  2. Per mole \(= E\times N_A \approx 299\,kJ\,mol^{-1}\).

Answer: About \(299\,kJ\,mol^{-1}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(\lambda\) in \(nm\) directly in \(c = \nu\lambda\) (convert to \(m\)).
  • Confusing wavelength with wave number (reciprocal).

Chapter 2 · Topic 2

Thomson atomic model

Atomic StructureFundamentalsTopic 2 of 46

Explanation

Concept. In Atomic Structure, Thomson atomic model: Thomson plum-pudding placed electrons in a positive cloud and measured e/m. Atom: electrons \((-e, 1/1837\,u)\), protons \((+e, 1\,u)\), neutrons (neutral, \(1\,u\)). EM waves satisfy \(c = \nu\lambda = 3\times10^8\,m/s\); wave number \(\bar\nu = 1/\lambda\).
Key formula(s). \[ e/m\,(Thomson),\,\alpha\!-\!scatter\,(Rutherford\,nucleus) \]
Key points.
  • Thomson Plum-pudding gave \(e/m\); Millikan oil-drop gave \(e\); together they fixed \(m_e\).
  • Convert \(cm^{-1}\) to \(m^{-1}\) by \(\times100\) before using \(E = hc\bar\nu\).
  • Order of EM spectrum: gamma \(<\) X \(<\) UV \(<\) visible \(<\) IR \(<\) micro \(<\) radio (decreasing energy).
  • Rutherford scattering: most mass/positive charge sits in a tiny nucleus; electrons occupy the rest.
Example 1.

Find the energy of \(1\,mol\) of photons with \(\bar\nu = 20000\,cm^{-1}\).

  1. Per photon \(E = hc\bar\nu = 6.626\times10^{-34}\times3\times10^8\times2\times10^6\).
  2. \(= 3.98\times10^{-19}\,J\); per mole \(\approx 239\,kJ\).

Answer: About \(239\,kJ/mol\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Which carries more energy: \(400\,nm\) blue or \(700\,nm\) red light?

  1. \(E \propto 1/\lambda\).
  2. Blue (\(400\,nm\)).

Answer: Blue.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(\lambda\) in \(nm\) directly in \(c = \nu\lambda\) (convert to \(m\)).
  • Confusing wavelength with wave number (reciprocal).

  2. \(\bar\nu = 1/\lambda \approx 1.72\times10^6\,m^{-1} = 17200\,cm^{-1}\).

Answer: \(5.17\times10^{14}\,Hz\), \(1.72\times10^4\,cm^{-1}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Energy of one mole of photons with \(\lambda = 400\,nm\)?

Chapter 2 · Topic 9

Planck's quantum theory

Atomic StructureFundamentalsTopic 9 of 46

Explanation

Concept. In Atomic Structure, Planck's quantum theory: Planck quantisation says oscillators exchange energy only in packets of h-nu. Light delivers energy in packets \(E = h\nu = hc/\lambda\). In the photoelectric effect electrons are ejected only if photon energy exceeds the work function \(h\nu_0\); excess becomes kinetic energy.
Key formula(s). \[ E = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda},\;\; h\nu = h\nu_0 + \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \]
Key points.
  • \(1\,eV = 1.602\times10^{-19}\,J\); stopping potential \(V_0\) measures \(K_{max}\).
  • \(h = 6.626\times10^{-34}\,J\,s\), \(c = 3\times10^8\,m/s\).
  • Threshold frequency \(\nu_0 = W_0/h\); no emission below it regardless of intensity.
  • Intensity controls number of photons (photocurrent), frequency controls electron energy.
Example 1.

Work function of a metal is \(2.3\,eV\). Find the threshold wavelength.

  1. \(\lambda_0 = hc/W_0 = 1240/2.3\,nm \approx 539\,nm\) (using \(hc = 1240\,eV\,nm\)).
  2. Light of longer wavelength cannot eject electrons.

Answer: About \(539\,nm\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Photons of \(4.0\,eV\) strike the same metal (\(W_0 = 2.3\,eV\)). Find \(K_{max}\) and stopping potential.

  1. \(K_{max} = 4.0-2.3 = 1.7\,eV\).
  2. Stopping potential \(V_0 = 1.7\,V\).

Answer: \(K_{max} = 1.7\,eV\), \(V_0 = 1.7\,V\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Adding intensities instead of comparing photon energy with \(W_0\).
  • Mixing \(nm\) and \(m\) in \(hc/\lambda\); use \(1240\,eV\,nm\) shortcut.

Explanation

  2. Light of longer wavelength cannot eject electrons.

Answer: About \(539\,nm\).

  1. \(K_{max} = 4.0-2.3 = 1.7\,eV\).
  2. Stopping potential \(V_0 = 1.7\,V\).

Answer: \(K_{max} = 1.7\,eV\), \(V_0 = 1.7\,V\).

Chapter 2 · Topic 11

Photoelectric effect

Atomic StructureFundamentalsTopic 11 of 46

Explanation

Concept. In Atomic Structure, Photoelectric effect: photoelectric emission needs photon energy above the work function, intensity only raises current. Light delivers energy in packets \(E = h\nu = hc/\lambda\). In the photoelectric effect electrons are ejected only if photon energy exceeds the work function \(h\nu_0\); excess becomes kinetic energy.
Key formula(s). \[ emission\,iff\,h\nu>W_0 \]
Key points.
  • Intensity controls number of photons (photocurrent), frequency controls electron energy.
  • \(1\,eV = 1.602\times10^{-19}\,J\); stopping potential \(V_0\) measures \(K_{max}\).
  • \(h = 6.626\times10^{-34}\,J\,s\), \(c = 3\times10^8\,m/s\).
  • Threshold frequency \(\nu_0 = W_0/h\); no emission below it regardless of intensity.
Example 1.

Work function of a metal is \(2.3\,eV\). Find the threshold wavelength.

  1. \(\lambda_0 = hc/W_0 = 1240/2.3\,nm \approx 539\,nm\) (using \(hc = 1240\,eV\,nm\)).
  2. Light of longer wavelength cannot eject electrons.

Answer: About \(539\,nm\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Photons of \(4.0\,eV\) strike the same metal (\(W_0 = 2.3\,eV\)). Find \(K_{max}\) and stopping potential.

  1. \(K_{max} = 4.0-2.3 = 1.7\,eV\).
  2. Stopping potential \(V_0 = 1.7\,V\).

Answer: \(K_{max} = 1.7\,eV\), \(V_0 = 1.7\,V\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Adding intensities instead of comparing photon energy with \(W_0\).
  • Mixing \(nm\) and \(m\) in \(hc/\lambda\); use \(1240\,eV\,nm\) shortcut.

Einstein photoelectric equation

Explanation

  • \(h = 6.626\times10^{-34}\,J\,s\), \(c = 3\times10^8\,m/s\).
  • Threshold frequency \(\nu_0 = W_0/h\); no emission below it regardless of intensity.
  • Intensity controls number of photons (photocurrent), frequency controls electron energy.
Example 1.

Work function of a metal is \(2.3\,eV\). Find the threshold wavelength.

  1. \(\lambda_0 = hc/W_0 = 1240/2.3\,nm \approx 539\,nm\) (using \(hc = 1240\,eV\,nm\)).
  2. Light of longer wavelength cannot eject electrons.

Answer: About \(539\,nm\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Photons of \(4.0\,eV\) strike the same metal (\(W_0 = 2.3\,eV\)). Find \(K_{max}\) and stopping potential.

  1. \(K_{max} = 4.0-2.3 = 1.7\,eV\).
  2. Stopping potential \(V_0 = 1.7\,V\).

Answer: \(K_{max} = 1.7\,eV\), \(V_0 = 1.7\,V\).

Chapter 2 · Topic 13

Atomic spectra

Atomic StructureFundamentalsTopic 13 of 46

Explanation

Concept. In Atomic Structure, Atomic spectra: atomic spectra fingerprint elements because each energy ladder is unique. Hydrogen lines follow \(1/\lambda = R_H(1/n_1^2-1/n_2^2)\) with \(R_H = 1.097\times10^7\,m^{-1}\). Lyman (\(n_1=1\), UV), Balmer (\(n_1=2\), visible), Paschen/Brackett/Pfund (\(3/4/5\), IR).
Key formula(s). \[ \frac{1}{\lambda}=R_H\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2}-\frac{1}{n_2^2}\right) \]
Key points.
  • Maximum wavelength in a series: \(n_2 = n_1+1\); series limit: \(n_2 \to \infty\).
  • Only Balmer falls in visible light (\(\approx 380-750\,nm\)).
  • For hydrogen-like ions multiply energy and \(1/\lambda\) by \(Z^2\).
  • Number of lines from \(n\)th orbit to ground \(= n(n-1)/2\).
Example 1.

Find the wavelength of the first Balmer line (\(3\to2\)) of hydrogen.

  1. \(1/\lambda = R_H(1/4-1/9) = R_H(5/36)\).
  2. \(\lambda = 36/(5R_H) \approx 656\,nm\) (red \(H_\alpha\)).

Answer: About \(656\,nm\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Find the series limit of the Lyman series.

  1. \(n_1 = 1, n_2\to\infty\): \(1/\lambda = R_H\).
  2. \(\lambda = 1/R_H \approx 91.2\,nm\).

Answer: About \(91.2\,nm\) (UV).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Swapping \(n_1, n_2\) (\(n_2>n_1\) always).
  • Forgetting \(Z^2\) for \(He^+, Li^{2+}\).

Chapter 2 · Topic 14

Hydrogen spectrum

Atomic StructureFundamentalsTopic 14 of 46

Explanation

Concept. In Atomic Structure, Hydrogen spectrum: hydrogen emission lines obey the Rydberg difference of inverse squares. Hydrogen lines follow \(1/\lambda = R_H(1/n_1^2-1/n_2^2)\) with \(R_H = 1.097\times10^7\,m^{-1}\). Lyman (\(n_1=1\), UV), Balmer (\(n_1=2\), visible), Paschen/Brackett/Pfund (\(3/4/5\), IR).
Key formula(s). \[ \frac{1}{\lambda}=R_H(\frac{1}{n_1^2}-\frac{1}{n_2^2}) \]
Key points.
  • Only Balmer falls in visible light (\(\approx 380-750\,nm\)).
  • For hydrogen-like ions multiply energy and \(1/\lambda\) by \(Z^2\).
  • Number of lines from \(n\)th orbit to ground \(= n(n-1)/2\).
  • Maximum wavelength in a series: \(n_2 = n_1+1\); series limit: \(n_2 \to \infty\).
Example 1.

Find the wavelength of \(H_\beta\) (\(4 \to 2\)).

  1. \(1/\lambda = R_H(1/4-1/16) = R_H(3/16)\).
  2. \(\lambda = 16/(3R_H) \approx 486\,nm\).

Answer: \(486\,nm\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) How many spectral lines when an electron falls from \(n = 4\) to ground?

  1. \(n(n-1)/2 = 6\).

Answer: \(6\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Swapping \(n_1, n_2\) (\(n_2>n_1\) always).
  • Forgetting \(Z^2\) for \(He^+, Li^{2+}\).

Chapter 2 · Topic 15

Lyman series

Atomic StructureFundamentalsTopic 15 of 46

Explanation

Concept. In Atomic Structure, Lyman series: the Lyman series drops to n = 1 and lies in the ultraviolet. Hydrogen lines follow \(1/\lambda = R_H(1/n_1^2-1/n_2^2)\) with \(R_H = 1.097\times10^7\,m^{-1}\). Lyman (\(n_1=1\), UV), Balmer (\(n_1=2\), visible), Paschen/Brackett/Pfund (\(3/4/5\), IR).
Key formula(s). \[ n_1=1\,(UV) \]
Key points.
  • For hydrogen-like ions multiply energy and \(1/\lambda\) by \(Z^2\).
  • Number of lines from \(n\)th orbit to ground \(= n(n-1)/2\).
  • Maximum wavelength in a series: \(n_2 = n_1+1\); series limit: \(n_2 \to \infty\).
  • Only Balmer falls in visible light (\(\approx 380-750\,nm\)).
Example 1.

First Paschen line wavelength (\(4 \to 3\))?

  1. \(1/\lambda = R_H(1/9-1/16) = R_H(7/144)\).
  2. \(\lambda = 144/(7R_H) \approx 1875\,nm\) (IR).

Answer: \(1875\,nm\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Energy of the \(H_\alpha\) photon in eV?

  1. \(E = hc/\lambda = 1240/656\).
  2. \(1.89\,eV\).

Answer: \(1.89\,eV\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Swapping \(n_1, n_2\) (\(n_2>n_1\) always).
  • Forgetting \(Z^2\) for \(He^+, Li^{2+}\).

Balmer series

Atomic StructureFundamentalsTopic 16 of 46

Explanation

Concept. In Atomic Structure, Balmer series: the Balmer series drops to n = 2 and is the only visible hydrogen series. Hydrogen lines follow \(1/\lambda = R_H(1/n_1^2-1/n_2^2)\) with \(R_H = 1.097\times10^7\,m^{-1}\). Lyman (\(n_1=1\), UV), Balmer (\(n_1=2\), visible), Paschen/Brackett/Pfund (\(3/4/5\), IR).
Key formula(s). \[ n_1=2\,(visible) \]
Key points.
  • Maximum wavelength in a series: \(n_2 = n_1+1\); series limit: \(n_2 \to \infty\).
  • Only Balmer falls in visible light (\(\approx 380-750\,nm\)).
  • For hydrogen-like ions multiply energy and \(1/\lambda\) by \(Z^2\).
  • Number of lines from \(n\)th orbit to ground \(= n(n-1)/2\).
Example 1.

Find the wavelength of the first Balmer line (\(3\to2\)) of hydrogen.

  1. \(1/\lambda = R_H(1/4-1/9) = R_H(5/36)\).
  2. \(\lambda = 36/(5R_H) \approx 656\,nm\) (red \(H_\alpha\)).

Answer: About \(656\,nm\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Find the series limit of the Lyman series.

  1. \(n_1 = 1, n_2\to\infty\): \(1/\lambda = R_H\).
  2. \(\lambda = 1/R_H \approx 91.2\,nm\).

Answer: About \(91.2\,nm\) (UV).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Swapping \(n_1, n_2\) (\(n_2>n_1\) always).
  • Forgetting \(Z^2\) for \(He^+, Li^{2+}\).

(JEE pattern) How many spectral lines when an electron falls from \(n = 4\) to ground?

Chapter 2 · Topic 21

Bohr model

Atomic StructureFundamentalsTopic 21 of 46

Explanation

Concept. In Atomic Structure, Bohr model: Bohr quantised angular momentum to get E, r and v ladders for one-electron species. Bohr model: \(E_n = -13.6\,Z^2/n^2\,eV\), \(r_n = 0.529\,n^2/Z\,\mathring{A}\), \(v_n = 2.188\times10^6\,Z/n\,m/s\). Ionisation energy is \(|E_1|\); excitation is the difference between levels.
Key formula(s). \[ v_n=2.188\times10^6\frac{Z}{n}\,m/s \],\;E_n=-13.6\frac{Z^2}{n^2}\,eV \]
Key points.
  • Angular momentum is quantised: \(mvr = nh/2\pi\).
  • Bohr model works only for single-electron species (\(H, He^+, Li^{2+}\)).
  • Ionisation energy of H \(= 13.6\,eV\); for \(He^+\) it is \(13.6\times4 = 54.4\,eV\).
  • Energy released/absorbed for \(n_2\to n_1\): \(\Delta E = 13.6Z^2(1/n_1^2-1/n_2^2)\,eV\).
Example 1.

Radius of the first orbit of \(Li^{2+}\)?

  1. \(r = 0.529\times1/3\).
  2. \(0.176\,\mathring{A}\).

Answer: \(0.176\,\mathring{A}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Speed of electron in \(n = 2\) of \(H\)?

  1. \(v = 2.188\times10^6/2\).
  2. \(1.094\times10^6\,m/s\).

Answer: \(1.09\times10^6\,m/s\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(n^2\) in the denominator for radius (it is in the numerator).
  • Applying Bohr formulas to multi-electron atoms.

Chapter 2 · Topic 22

Bohr postulates

Atomic StructureFundamentalsTopic 22 of 46

Explanation

Concept. In Atomic Structure, Bohr postulates: Bohr postulates fix stationary orbits, quantum jumps and angular momentum nh/2pi. Bohr model: \(E_n = -13.6\,Z^2/n^2\,eV\), \(r_n = 0.529\,n^2/Z\,\mathring{A}\), \(v_n = 2.188\times10^6\,Z/n\,m/s\). Ionisation energy is \(|E_1|\); excitation is the difference between levels.
Key formula(s). \[ E_n=-13.6\frac{Z^2}{n^2}\,eV,\;r_n=0.529\frac{n^2}{Z}\,\mathring{A} \]
Key points.
  • Ionisation energy of H \(= 13.6\,eV\); for \(He^+\) it is \(13.6\times4 = 54.4\,eV\).
  • Energy released/absorbed for \(n_2\to n_1\): \(\Delta E = 13.6Z^2(1/n_1^2-1/n_2^2)\,eV\).
  • Angular momentum is quantised: \(mvr = nh/2\pi\).
  • Bohr model works only for single-electron species (\(H, He^+, Li^{2+}\)).
Example 1.

Find the energy and radius of the 2nd orbit of \(He^+\).

  1. \(E_2 = -13.6\times4/4 = -13.6\,eV\).
  2. \(r_2 = 0.529\times4/2 = 1.058\,\mathring{A}\).

Answer: \(E_2 = -13.6\,eV\), \(r_2 \approx 1.06\,\mathring{A}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) How much energy is needed to excite H from \(n=1\) to \(n=3\)?

  1. \(\Delta E = 13.6(1-1/9) = 13.6\times8/9 = 12.09\,eV\).

Answer: \(12.09\,eV\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(n^2\) in the denominator for radius (it is in the numerator).
  • Applying Bohr formulas to multi-electron atoms.

Chapter 2 · Topic 23

Radius of orbit

Atomic StructureFundamentalsTopic 23 of 46

Explanation

Concept. In Atomic Structure, Radius of orbit: Bohr radius grows as n-squared over Z, starting at 0.529 angstrom. Bohr model: \(E_n = -13.6\,Z^2/n^2\,eV\), \(r_n = 0.529\,n^2/Z\,\mathring{A}\), \(v_n = 2.188\times10^6\,Z/n\,m/s\). Ionisation energy is \(|E_1|\); excitation is the difference between levels.
Key formula(s). \[ r_n=0.529\frac{n^2}{Z}\,\mathring{A} \]
Key points.
  • Energy released/absorbed for \(n_2\to n_1\): \(\Delta E = 13.6Z^2(1/n_1^2-1/n_2^2)\,eV\).
  • Angular momentum is quantised: \(mvr = nh/2\pi\).
  • Bohr model works only for single-electron species (\(H, He^+, Li^{2+}\)).
  • Ionisation energy of H \(= 13.6\,eV\); for \(He^+\) it is \(13.6\times4 = 54.4\,eV\).
Example 1.

Find the ionisation energy of \(Li^{2+}\).

  1. \(IE = 13.6\,Z^2 = 13.6\times9\).
  2. \(122.4\,eV\).

Answer: \(122.4\,eV\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) An electron jumps \(3 \to 2\) in \(He^+\). Find the photon energy.

  1. \(\Delta E = 13.6\times4\times(1/4-1/9) = 54.4\times0.139\).
  2. \(7.56\,eV\).

Answer: \(7.56\,eV\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(n^2\) in the denominator for radius (it is in the numerator).
  • Applying Bohr formulas to multi-electron atoms.

Chapter 2 · Topic 29

de Broglie hypothesis

Atomic StructureFundamentalsTopic 29 of 46

Explanation

Concept. In Atomic Structure, de Broglie hypothesis: de Broglie gives every moving particle a wavelength h/mv. Matter waves obey \(\lambda = h/mv\); Heisenberg limits joint precision by \(\Delta x\cdot\Delta p \ge h/4\pi\). Orbitals are fixed by \((n,l,m,s)\); filling follows Aufbau, Pauli and Hund, with extra stability for half/full subshells.
Key formula(s). \[ \lambda=\frac{h}{mv} \]
Key points.
  • s/p/d/f hold \(2/6/10/14\) electrons; shapes: s spherical, p dumbbell, d clover (mostly).
  • Anomalous configs: \(Cr = [Ar]3d^54s^1\), \(Cu = [Ar]3d^{10}4s^1\) (half/full stability).

  1. \(\lambda = h/mv = 6.626\times10^{-34}/1\).
  2. \(\lambda \approx 6.6\times10^{-34}\,m\) (utterly negligible).

Matter waves obey \(\lambda = h/mv\); Heisenberg limits joint precision by \(\Delta x\cdot\Delta p \ge h/4\pi\). An electron is localised to \(\Delta x = 10^{-10}\,m\). Estimate the minimum uncertainty in its velocity.

  1. \(\Delta v \ge h/(4\pi m\Delta x)\).

  1. Expected \([Ar]3d^44s^2\); actual \([Ar]3d^54s^1\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Writing \(Fe^{2+}\) as \(3d^44s^2\) (remove 4s first).

Chapter 2 · Topic 31

Heisenberg uncertainty principle

Atomic StructureFundamentalsTopic 31 of 46

Explanation

Concept. In Atomic Structure, Heisenberg uncertainty principle: Heisenberg forbids fixing position and momentum together beyond h/4pi. Matter waves obey \(\lambda = h/mv\); Heisenberg limits joint precision by \(\Delta x\cdot\Delta p \ge h/4\pi\). Orbitals are fixed by \((n,l,m,s)\); filling follows Aufbau, Pauli and Hund, with extra stability for half/full subshells.
Key formula(s). \[ \; \Delta x\cdot\Delta p\ge\frac{h}{4\pi},\;EC:\,1s\,2s\,2p\,3s\,3p\,4s\,3d\ldots \]
Key points.
  • \(l = 0..n-1\); \(m = -l..+l\); \(s = \pm1/2\). Orbital count in shell \(= n^2\), electron capacity \(= 2n^2\).
  • s/p/d/f hold \(2/6/10/14\) electrons; shapes: s spherical, p dumbbell, d clover (mostly).
  • Anomalous configs: \(Cr = [Ar]3d^54s^1\), \(Cu = [Ar]3d^{10}4s^1\) (half/full stability).
  • Cations lose ns electrons before (n-1)d: \(Fe^{2+} = [Ar]3d^6\), not \(3d^44s^2\).
Example 1.

Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving at \(10^6\,m/s\).

  1. \(\lambda = h/mv = 6.626\times10^{-34}/(9.1\times10^{-31}\times10^6)\).
  2. \(\lambda \approx 7.28\times10^{-10}\,m = 7.28\,\mathring{A}\).

Answer: About \(7.3\,\mathring{A}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) How many radial and angular nodes does a \(3p\) orbital have?

  1. Total nodes \(= n-1 = 2\).
  2. Angular \(= l = 1\); radial \(= n-l-1 = 1\).

Answer: 1 radial + 1 angular node.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Writing \(Fe^{2+}\) as \(3d^44s^2\) (remove 4s first).
  • Counting \(m\) values wrong: \(l=2 \to 5\) orbitals, not 4.

Key points.
  • Anomalous configs: \(Cr = [Ar]3d^54s^1\), \(Cu = [Ar]3d^{10}4s^1\) (half/full stability).
  • Cations lose ns electrons before (n-1)d: \(Fe^{2+} = [Ar]3d^6\), not \(3d^44s^2\).
  • \(l = 0..n-1\); \(m = -l..+l\); \(s = \pm1/2\). Orbital count in shell \(= n^2\), electron capacity \(= 2n^2\).
  • s/p/d/f hold \(2/6/10/14\) electrons; shapes: s spherical, p dumbbell, d clover (mostly).
Example 1.

An electron is localised to \(\Delta x = 10^{-10}\,m\). Estimate the minimum uncertainty in its velocity.

  1. \(\Delta v \ge h/(4\pi m\Delta x)\).
  2. \(\Delta v \ge 5.8\times10^5\,m/s\).

Answer: About \(10^5\)-\(10^6\,m/s\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Give the electronic configuration of \(Cr\) (\(Z = 24\)) and justify.

  1. Expected \([Ar]3d^44s^2\); actual \([Ar]3d^54s^1\).
  2. Half-filled \(d\) subshell is extra stable.

Answer: \([Ar]3d^54s^1\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Writing \(Fe^{2+}\) as \(3d^44s^2\) (remove 4s first).
  • Counting \(m\) values wrong: \(l=2 \to 5\) orbitals, not 4.

Chapter 2 · Topic 43

Pauli exclusion principle

Atomic StructureFundamentalsTopic 43 of 46

Explanation

Concept. In Atomic Structure, Pauli exclusion principle: Pauli forbids two electrons sharing all four quantum numbers. Matter waves obey \(\lambda = h/mv\); Heisenberg limits joint precision by \(\Delta x\cdot\Delta p \ge h/4\pi\). Orbitals are fixed by \((n,l,m,s)\); filling follows Aufbau, Pauli and Hund, with extra stability for half/full subshells.
Key formula(s). \[ \lambda=\frac{h}{mv},\;\; \Delta x\cdot\Delta p\ge\frac{h}{4\pi} \]
Key points.
  • \(l = 0..n-1\); \(m = -l..+l\); \(s = \pm1/2\). Orbital count in shell \(= n^2\), electron capacity \(= 2n^2\).
  • s/p/d/f hold \(2/6/10/14\) electrons; shapes: s spherical, p dumbbell, d clover (mostly).
  • Anomalous configs: \(Cr = [Ar]3d^54s^1\), \(Cu = [Ar]3d^{10}4s^1\) (half/full stability).
  • Cations lose ns electrons before (n-1)d: \(Fe^{2+} = [Ar]3d^6\), not \(3d^44s^2\).
Example 1.

Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving at \(10^6\,m/s\).

  1. \(\lambda = h/mv = 6.626\times10^{-34}/(9.1\times10^{-31}\times10^6)\).
  2. \(\lambda \approx 7.28\times10^{-10}\,m = 7.28\,\mathring{A}\).

Answer: About \(7.3\,\mathring{A}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) How many radial and angular nodes does a \(3p\) orbital have?

  1. Total nodes \(= n-1 = 2\).
  2. Angular \(= l = 1\); radial \(= n-l-1 = 1\).

Answer: 1 radial + 1 angular node.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Writing \(Fe^{2+}\) as \(3d^44s^2\) (remove 4s first).
  • Counting \(m\) values wrong: \(l=2 \to 5\) orbitals, not 4.

Chapter 2 · Topic 44

Hund's rule

Atomic StructureFundamentalsTopic 44 of 46

Explanation

Concept. In Atomic Structure, Hund's rule: Hund spreads electrons singly across degenerate orbitals before pairing. Matter waves obey \(\lambda = h/mv\); Heisenberg limits joint precision by \(\Delta x\cdot\Delta p \ge h/4\pi\). Orbitals are fixed by \((n,l,m,s)\); filling follows Aufbau, Pauli and Hund, with extra stability for half/full subshells.
Key formula(s). \[ \lambda=\frac{h}{mv},\;orbitals=n^2 \]
Key points.
  • s/p/d/f hold \(2/6/10/14\) electrons; shapes: s spherical, p dumbbell, d clover (mostly).
  • Anomalous configs: \(Cr = [Ar]3d^54s^1\), \(Cu = [Ar]3d^{10}4s^1\) (half/full stability).
  • Cations lose ns electrons before (n-1)d: \(Fe^{2+} = [Ar]3d^6\), not \(3d^44s^2\).
  • \(l = 0..n-1\); \(m = -l..+l\); \(s = \pm1/2\). Orbital count in shell \(= n^2\), electron capacity \(= 2n^2\).
Example 1.

Find the de Broglie wavelength of a \(0.1\,kg\) ball moving at \(10\,m/s\).

  1. \(\lambda = h/mv = 6.626\times10^{-34}/1\).
  2. \(\lambda \approx 6.6\times10^{-34}\,m\) (utterly negligible).

Answer: \(6.6\times10^{-34}\,m\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) How many radial nodes does a \(4p\) orbital have?

  1. Total nodes \(= n-1 = 3\); angular \(= l = 1\).
  2. Radial \(= 3-1 = 2\).

Answer: \(2\) radial nodes.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Writing \(Fe^{2+}\) as \(3d^44s^2\) (remove 4s first).
  • Counting \(m\) values wrong: \(l=2 \to 5\) orbitals, not 4.

Chapter 3 · Topic 1

Intermolecular forces

States of Matter - GasesStates of MatterTopic 1 of 43

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Gases, Intermolecular forces: intermolecular attractions pull real gases below ideal volume at moderate pressure. Real gases deviate via \(Z = PV/nRT\) (\(Z<1\) attractive dominance, \(Z>1\) repulsive/size dominance). van der Waals \((P+a(n/V)^2)(V-nb) = nRT\) with \(T_c = 8a/27Rb\), \(P_c = a/27b^2\), \(V_c = 3b\); Boyle temperature \(T_B = a/Rb\).
Key formula(s). \[ T_c=\frac{8a}{27Rb},\;T_B=\frac{a}{Rb} \]
Key points.
  • At \(T_B\), \(Z \approx 1\) over a wide low-pressure range.
  • Below \(T_c\) a gas can be liquefied by compression; above it, never.
  • Isotherm dip below ideal at moderate \(P\) (attraction), rise above at high \(P\) (size).
  • \(a\) measures attraction (easy liquefaction); \(b\) measures molecular size.
Example 1.

A gas has \(a = 1.36\,L^2atm\,mol^{-2}\), \(b = 0.0318\,L\,mol^{-1}\). Find \(T_B\).

  1. \(T_B = a/Rb = 1.36/(0.0821\times0.0318)\).
  2. \(T_B \approx 521\,K\) (oxygen-like).

Answer: About \(521\,K\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) At \(300\,K\) and \(100\,atm\), \(Z = 1.2\). What dominates?

  1. \(Z>1\): measured volume exceeds ideal.
  2. Finite molecular size (repulsive/short-range) dominates.

Answer: Size effects dominate.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Saying \(Z>1\) means attraction (it is repulsion/size).
  • Confusing \(T_c\) with \(T_B\) (\(T_B = 27T_c/4\)).

Index / States of Matter
Chapter 3 · Topic 2

Gas laws

States of Matter - GasesStates of MatterTopic 2 of 43

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Gases, Gas laws: Boyle, Charles, Gay-Lussac and Avogadro laws all collapse into PV = nRT. Ideal gas: \(PV = nRT\) with \(R = 8.314\,J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1} = 0.0821\,L\,atm\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}\). Gas density \(d = PM/RT\); molar mass follows from measured density.
Key formula(s). \[ PV=nRT \]
Key points.
  • Density method: at same \(T,P\), \(d_1/d_2 = M_1/M_2\).
  • Dalton + ideal gas: collect partial pressures via mole fractions.
  • Always use Kelvin; \(R = 0.0821\) pairs with \(L\)-atm, \(8.314\) with SI joules.
  • Boyle (\(P\propto1/V\)), Charles (\(V\propto T\)), Gay-Lussac (\(P\propto T\)), Avogadro (\(V\propto n\)).
Example 1.

\(4\,g\,O_2\) occupies what volume at \(27^\circ C\) and \(1\,atm\)?

  1. Moles \(= 4/32 = 0.125\); \(T = 300\,K\).
  2. \(V = nRT/P = 0.125\times0.0821\times300 \approx 3.08\,L\).

Answer: About \(3.08\,L\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) A gas has density \(1.43\,g/L\) at STP. Find its molar mass.

  1. \(M = d\times22.4 = 1.43\times22.4 \approx 32\,g\,mol^{-1}\).
  2. Consistent with \(O_2\).

Answer: About \(32\,g\,mol^{-1}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Plugging Celsius into the gas equation.
  • Mismatching \(R\) units with pressure/volume units.
