Boyle's law

States of Matter - GasesStates of MatterTopic 3 of 43

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Gases, Boyle's law: Boyle law says pressure times volume stays constant at fixed T and moles. Ideal gas: \(PV = nRT\) with \(R = 8.314\,J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1} = 0.0821\,L\,atm\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}\). Gas density \(d = PM/RT\); molar mass follows from measured density.
Key formula(s). \[ \; \frac{P_1V_1}{T_1}=\frac{P_2V_2}{T_2} \]
Key points.
  • Always use Kelvin; \(R = 0.0821\) pairs with \(L\)-atm, \(8.314\) with SI joules.
  • Boyle (\(P\propto1/V\)), Charles (\(V\propto T\)), Gay-Lussac (\(P\propto T\)), Avogadro (\(V\propto n\)).
  • Density method: at same \(T,P\), \(d_1/d_2 = M_1/M_2\).
  • Dalton + ideal gas: collect partial pressures via mole fractions.
Example 1.

\(4\,g\,O_2\) occupies what volume at \(27^\circ C\) and \(1\,atm\)?

  1. Moles \(= 4/32 = 0.125\); \(T = 300\,K\).
  2. \(V = nRT/P = 0.125\times0.0821\times300 \approx 3.08\,L\).

Answer: About \(3.08\,L\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) A gas has density \(1.43\,g/L\) at STP. Find its molar mass.

  1. \(M = d\times22.4 = 1.43\times22.4 \approx 32\,g\,mol^{-1}\).
  2. Consistent with \(O_2\).

Answer: About \(32\,g\,mol^{-1}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Plugging Celsius into the gas equation.
  • Mismatching \(R\) units with pressure/volume units.

Chapter 3 · Topic 4

Charles' law

States of Matter - GasesStates of MatterTopic 4 of 43

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Gases, Charles' law: Charles law says volume over temperature stays constant at fixed P. Ideal gas: \(PV = nRT\) with \(R = 8.314\,J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1} = 0.0821\,L\,atm\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}\). Gas density \(d = PM/RT\); molar mass follows from measured density.
Key formula(s). \[ \; \frac{P_1V_1}{T_1}=\frac{P_2V_2}{T_2},\;\; M=\frac{dRT}{P} \]
Key points.
  • Boyle (\(P\propto1/V\)), Charles (\(V\propto T\)), Gay-Lussac (\(P\propto T\)), Avogadro (\(V\propto n\)).
  • Density method: at same \(T,P\), \(d_1/d_2 = M_1/M_2\).
  • Dalton + ideal gas: collect partial pressures via mole fractions.
  • Always use Kelvin; \(R = 0.0821\) pairs with \(L\)-atm, \(8.314\) with SI joules.
Example 1.

A gas occupies \(300\,mL\) at \(27^\circ C\) and \(1\,atm\). Find its volume at STP.

  1. \(V_2 = P_1V_1T_2/(T_1P_2) = 1\times300\times273/(300\times1)\).
  2. \(V_2 = 273\,mL\).

Answer: \(273\,mL\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(2\,g\,H_2\) vs \(16\,g\,O_2\) at same \(T,V\): compare pressures.

  1. Moles: \(H_2 = 1\), \(O_2 = 0.5\).
  2. \(P_{H_2} = 2\,P_{O_2}\).

Answer: Hydrogen pressure is double.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Plugging Celsius into the gas equation.
  • Mismatching \(R\) units with pressure/volume units.

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Gases, Gas constant R: R is 8.314 with joules and 0.0821 with litre-atm. Ideal gas: \(PV = nRT\) with \(R = 8.314\,J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1} = 0.0821\,L\,atm\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}\). Gas density \(d = PM/RT\); molar mass follows from measured density.
Key formula(s). \[ PV=nRT,\;\; \frac{P_1V_1}{T_1}=\frac{P_2V_2}{T_2},\;\; d=\frac{PM}{RT} \]
Key points.
  • Always use Kelvin; \(R = 0.0821\) pairs with \(L\)-atm, \(8.314\) with SI joules.
  • Boyle (\(P\propto1/V\)), Charles (\(V\propto T\)), Gay-Lussac (\(P\propto T\)), Avogadro (\(V\propto n\)).
  • Density method: at same \(T,P\), \(d_1/d_2 = M_1/M_2\).
  • Dalton + ideal gas: collect partial pressures via mole fractions.
Example 1.

\(4\,g\,O_2\) occupies what volume at \(27^\circ C\) and \(1\,atm\)?

  1. Moles \(= 4/32 = 0.125\); \(T = 300\,K\).
  2. \(V = nRT/P = 0.125\times0.0821\times300 \approx 3.08\,L\).

Answer: About \(3.08\,L\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) A gas has density \(1.43\,g/L\) at STP. Find its molar mass.

  1. \(M = d\times22.4 = 1.43\times22.4 \approx 32\,g\,mol^{-1}\).
  2. Consistent with \(O_2\).

Answer: About \(32\,g\,mol^{-1}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Plugging Celsius into the gas equation.
  • Mismatching \(R\) units with pressure/volume units.

Answer: Hydrogen pressure is double.

Chapter 3 · Topic 13

Dalton's law of partial pressures

States of Matter - GasesStates of MatterTopic 13 of 43

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Gases, Dalton's law of partial pressures: Dalton adds partial pressures, each being mole fraction times total. Dalton law: \(P_{total} = \sum p_i\) with \(p_i = \chi_i P_{total}\). A gas collected over water is moist: \(p_{dry} = P_{total} -\) aqueous tension at that temperature.
Key formula(s). \[ P_{tot}=\sum p_i \]
Key points.
  • Always subtract aqueous tension for gases collected over water.
  • Partial pressure ratio \(=\) mole ratio \(=\) volume ratio (same \(T\)).
  • JEE gives aqueous tension tables; read the value at the experimental temperature.
  • Mole fraction in vapour \(\ne\) mole fraction in liquid (more volatile enriched).
Example 1.

A mixture has \(2\,mol\,N_2 + 3\,mol\,O_2\) at \(5\,atm\). Find each partial pressure.

  1. \(\chi_{N_2} = 0.4\), \(\chi_{O_2} = 0.6\).
  2. \(p_{N_2} = 2\,atm\), \(p_{O_2} = 3\,atm\).

Answer: \(2\,atm\) and \(3\,atm\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(H_2\) collected over water at \(25^\circ C\), \(755\,mmHg\); aqueous tension \(= 23.8\,mmHg\). Find dry pressure.

  1. \(p_{dry} = 755-23.8 = 731.2\,mmHg\).
  2. Use this corrected pressure in \(PV = nRT\).

Answer: \(731.2\,mmHg\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Forgetting to subtract aqueous tension.
  • Using liquid mole fractions for vapour pressures (apply Raoult instead).

Chapter 3 · Topic 17

Kinetic theory of gases

States of Matter - GasesStates of MatterTopic 17 of 43

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Gases, Kinetic theory of gases: kinetic theory derives pressure from molecular collisions on walls. Kinetic theory: \(u_{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M}\), \(u_{av} = \sqrt{8RT/\pi M}\), \(u_{mp} = \sqrt{2RT/M}\) (ratio \(1:1.128:1.225\) for mp:av:rms). Average KE per mole \(= 3RT/2\), independent of gas identity.
Key formula(s). \[ u_{rms}=\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}},\;\frac{u_{mp}}{u_{av}}{u_{rms}}=1:1.128:1.224 \]
Key points.
  • Degrees of freedom: mono \(3\), linear \(5\), non-linear \(6\); \(C_v = fR/2\).
  • Mean free path \(\lambda \propto T/(P\sigma^2)\): rises with \(T\), falls with \(P\).
  • Use molar mass in \(kg\,mol^{-1}\) with \(R = 8.314\) to get \(m/s\).
  • At fixed \(T\), lighter gases move faster: \(u \propto 1/\sqrt{M}\).
Example 1.

Which has larger \(u_{rms}\) at same \(T\): \(H_2\) or \(CO_2\), and by what factor?

  1. \(u \propto 1/\sqrt M\); ratio \(= \sqrt{44/2} = \sqrt{22}\).
  2. \(H_2\) is \(4.69\) times faster.

Answer: \(H_2\), \(4.69\times\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(C_v\) of a linear triatomic gas (\(CO_2\)) per mole?

  1. Degrees of freedom \(= 5\); \(C_v = fR/2\).
  2. \(C_v = 5R/2\).

Answer: \(5R/2\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(M\) in \(g/mol\) with SI \(R\) (speeds come out \(\sqrt{1000}\times\) off).
  • Mixing up the speed order: \(u_{mp}<u_{av}<u_{rms}\).

Chapter 3 · Topic 18

Assumptions of kinetic theory

States of Matter - GasesStates of MatterTopic 18 of 43

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Gases, Assumptions of kinetic theory: point masses, elastic hits and random motion underpin the whole kinetic derivation. Kinetic theory: \(u_{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M}\), \(u_{av} = \sqrt{8RT/\pi M}\), \(u_{mp} = \sqrt{2RT/M}\) (ratio \(1:1.128:1.225\) for mp:av:rms). Average KE per mole \(= 3RT/2\), independent of gas identity.
Key formula(s). \[ u_{rms}=\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}},\;\bar{E}_k=\frac{3}{2}RT,\;\frac{u_{mp}}{u_{av}}{u_{rms}}=1:1.128:1.224 \]
Key points.
  • Use molar mass in \(kg\,mol^{-1}\) with \(R = 8.314\) to get \(m/s\).
  • At fixed \(T\), lighter gases move faster: \(u \propto 1/\sqrt{M}\).
  • Degrees of freedom: mono \(3\), linear \(5\), non-linear \(6\); \(C_v = fR/2\).
  • Mean free path \(\lambda \propto T/(P\sigma^2)\): rises with \(T\), falls with \(P\).
Example 1.

Find \(u_{rms}\) of \(O_2\) at \(300\,K\).

  1. \(M = 0.032\,kg/mol\); \(u_{rms} = \sqrt{3\times8.314\times300/0.032}\).
  2. \(u_{rms} \approx 483\,m/s\).

Answer: About \(483\,m/s\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) At what temperature will \(u_{rms}\) of \(He\) equal that of \(O_2\) at \(300\,K\)?

  1. Same \(u\): \(T/M\) equal, so \(T_{He} = 300\times(4/32) = 37.5\,K\).

Answer: \(37.5\,K\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(M\) in \(g/mol\) with SI \(R\) (speeds come out \(\sqrt{1000}\times\) off).
  • Mixing up the speed order: \(u_{mp}<u_{av}<u_{rms}\).

Pressure from kinetic theory

States of Matter - GasesStates of MatterTopic 19 of 43

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Gases, Pressure from kinetic theory: pressure equals two-thirds of the translational energy density. Kinetic theory: \(u_{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M}\), \(u_{av} = \sqrt{8RT/\pi M}\), \(u_{mp} = \sqrt{2RT/M}\) (ratio \(1:1.128:1.225\) for mp:av:rms). Average KE per mole \(= 3RT/2\), independent of gas identity.
Key formula(s). \[ u_{rms}=\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}},\;\frac{u_{mp}}{u_{av}}{u_{rms}}=1:1.128:1.224,\;C_v=fR/2 \]
Key points.
  • At fixed \(T\), lighter gases move faster: \(u \propto 1/\sqrt{M}\).
  • Degrees of freedom: mono \(3\), linear \(5\), non-linear \(6\); \(C_v = fR/2\).
  • Mean free path \(\lambda \propto T/(P\sigma^2)\): rises with \(T\), falls with \(P\).
  • Use molar mass in \(kg\,mol^{-1}\) with \(R = 8.314\) to get \(m/s\).
Example 1.

How does mean free path change if pressure is doubled at fixed \(T\)?

  1. \(\lambda \propto 1/P\) (denser gas, more collisions).
  2. It halves.

Answer: Halved.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(u_{av}\) of \(N_2\) at \(300\,K\)? (\(M = 0.028\,kg/mol\))

  1. \(u_{av} = \sqrt{8RT/\pi M} = \sqrt{8\times8.314\times300/(3.14\times0.028)}\).
  2. \(\approx 476\,m/s\).

Answer: About \(476\,m/s\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(M\) in \(g/mol\) with SI \(R\) (speeds come out \(\sqrt{1000}\times\) off).
  • Mixing up the speed order: \(u_{mp}<u_{av}<u_{rms}\).

Key formula(s). \[ u_{rms}=\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}},\;\bar{E}_k=\frac{3}{2}RT,\;\frac{u_{mp}}{u_{av}}{u_{rms}}=1:1.128:1.224,\;C_v=fR/2,\;\lambda_{mfp}\propto T/P \]
Key points.
  • Degrees of freedom: mono \(3\), linear \(5\), non-linear \(6\); \(C_v = fR/2\).
  • Mean free path \(\lambda \propto T/(P\sigma^2)\): rises with \(T\), falls with \(P\).
  • Use molar mass in \(kg\,mol^{-1}\) with \(R = 8.314\) to get \(m/s\).
  • At fixed \(T\), lighter gases move faster: \(u \propto 1/\sqrt{M}\).
Example 1.

Which has larger \(u_{rms}\) at same \(T\): \(H_2\) or \(CO_2\), and by what factor?

  1. \(u \propto 1/\sqrt M\); ratio \(= \sqrt{44/2} = \sqrt{22}\).
  2. \(H_2\) is \(4.69\) times faster.

Answer: \(H_2\), \(4.69\times\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(C_v\) of a linear triatomic gas (\(CO_2\)) per mole?

  1. Degrees of freedom \(= 5\); \(C_v = fR/2\).
  2. \(C_v = 5R/2\).

Answer: \(5R/2\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(M\) in \(g/mol\) with SI \(R\) (speeds come out \(\sqrt{1000}\times\) off).
  • Mixing up the speed order: \(u_{mp}<u_{av}<u_{rms}\).

Degrees of freedom

Explanation

How does mean free path change if pressure is doubled at fixed \(T\)?

(JEE pattern) \(u_{av}\) of \(N_2\) at \(300\,K\)? (\(M = 0.028\,kg/mol\))

  1. \(u_{av} = \sqrt{8RT/\pi M} = \sqrt{8\times8.314\times300/(3.14\times0.028)}\).
  2. \(\approx 476\,m/s\).

Answer: About \(476\,m/s\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(M\) in \(g/mol\) with SI \(R\) (speeds come out \(\sqrt{1000}\times\) off).
  • Mixing up the speed order: \(u_{mp}<u_{av}<u_{rms}\).

Chapter 3 · Topic 29

Graham's law

States of Matter - GasesStates of MatterTopic 29 of 43

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Gases, Graham's law: Graham law makes diffusion speed fall as one over root molar mass. Graham law: rate of diffusion/effusion \(r \propto 1/\sqrt{M}\) at same \(T,P\). Rate \(=\) volume/time or moles/time; compare two gases through \(r_1/r_2 = \sqrt{M_2/M_1}\).
Key formula(s). \[ r\propto1/\sqrt M \]
Key points.
  • Time ratio inverts: \(t_1/t_2 = \sqrt{M_1/M_2}\).
  • Effusion through a pinhole follows the same law as diffusion.
  • Same conditions required (same \(T,P\) and same hole/conditions).
  • Lighter gas diffuses faster; for mixtures the composition shifts over time.
Example 1.

\(100\,mL\,H_2\) effuses in \(20\,s\). How long for \(100\,mL\,O_2\) under identical conditions?

  1. \(t_{O_2}/t_{H_2} = \sqrt{32/2} = 4\).
  2. \(t = 80\,s\).

Answer: \(80\,s\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) A gas diffuses \(1/3\) as fast as \(He\). Find its molar mass.

  1. \(r/r_{He} = 1/3 = \sqrt{4/M}\).
  2. \(M = 36\,g\,mol^{-1}\).

Answer: \(36\,g\,mol^{-1}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Inverting the mass ratio (heavier \(=\) slower).
  • Using different \(T,P\) for the two gases.

Index / States of Matter
Chapter 3 · Topic 32

Real gases

States of Matter - GasesStates of MatterTopic 32 of 43

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Gases, Real gases: real gases deviate because molecules attract at range and occupy volume. Real gases deviate via \(Z = PV/nRT\) (\(Z<1\) attractive dominance, \(Z>1\) repulsive/size dominance). van der Waals \((P+a(n/V)^2)(V-nb) = nRT\) with \(T_c = 8a/27Rb\), \(P_c = a/27b^2\), \(V_c = 3b\); Boyle temperature \(T_B = a/Rb\).
Key formula(s). \[ Z=\frac{PV}{nRT} \]
Key points.
  • Below \(T_c\) a gas can be liquefied by compression; above it, never.
  • Isotherm dip below ideal at moderate \(P\) (attraction), rise above at high \(P\) (size).
  • \(a\) measures attraction (easy liquefaction); \(b\) measures molecular size.
  • At \(T_B\), \(Z \approx 1\) over a wide low-pressure range.
Example 1.

For a gas \(a = 3.6\,L^2atm\,mol^{-2}, b = 0.04\,L\,mol^{-1}\). Find \(T_c\).

  1. \(T_c = 8a/(27Rb) = 8\times3.6/(27\times0.0821\times0.04)\).
  2. \(T_c \approx 324.7\,K\).

Answer: About \(325\,K\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(Z = 0.9\) at some \(P\). What dominates?

  1. \(Z<1\) means measured volume below ideal: attractive forces dominate.
  2. Typical of moderate pressure, below \(T_B\).

Answer: Attractive forces dominate.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Saying \(Z>1\) means attraction (it is repulsion/size).
  • Confusing \(T_c\) with \(T_B\) (\(T_B = 27T_c/4\)).

  2. \(T_c \approx 324.7\,K\).

Answer: About \(325\,K\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.

Answer: Size effects dominate.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.

  • Isotherm dip below ideal at moderate \(P\) (attraction), rise above at high \(P\) (size).
  • \(a\) measures attraction (easy liquefaction); \(b\) measures molecular size.
Example 1.

A gas has \(a = 1.36\,L^2atm\,mol^{-2}\), \(b = 0.0318\,L\,mol^{-1}\). Find \(T_B\).

  1. \(T_B = a/Rb = 1.36/(0.0821\times0.0318)\).
  2. \(T_B \approx 521\,K\) (oxygen-like).

Answer: About \(521\,K\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) At \(300\,K\) and \(100\,atm\), \(Z = 1.2\). What dominates?

  1. \(Z>1\): measured volume exceeds ideal.
  2. Finite molecular size (repulsive/short-range) dominates.

Answer: Size effects dominate.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Saying \(Z>1\) means attraction (it is repulsion/size).
  • Confusing \(T_c\) with \(T_B\) (\(T_B = 27T_c/4\)).

Critical pressure

States of Matter - GasesStates of MatterTopic 38 of 43

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Gases, Critical pressure: critical pressure is the isotherm inflection pressure at Tc. Real gases deviate via \(Z = PV/nRT\) (\(Z<1\) attractive dominance, \(Z>1\) repulsive/size dominance). van der Waals \((P+a(n/V)^2)(V-nb) = nRT\) with \(T_c = 8a/27Rb\), \(P_c = a/27b^2\), \(V_c = 3b\); Boyle temperature \(T_B = a/Rb\).
Key formula(s). \[ Z=\frac{PV}{nRT},\;T_c=\frac{8a}{27Rb} \]
Key points.
  • Below \(T_c\) a gas can be liquefied by compression; above it, never.

  • At \(T_B\), \(Z \approx 1\) over a wide low-pressure range.
Example 1.

For a gas \(a = 3.6\,L^2atm\,mol^{-2}, b = 0.04\,L\,mol^{-1}\). Find \(T_c\).

  1. \(T_c = 8a/(27Rb) = 8\times3.6/(27\times0.0821\times0.04)\).
  2. \(T_c \approx 324.7\,K\).

Answer: About \(325\,K\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(Z = 0.9\) at some \(P\). What dominates?

  1. \(Z<1\) means measured volume below ideal: attractive forces dominate.
  2. Typical of moderate pressure, below \(T_B\).

Answer: Attractive forces dominate.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Saying \(Z>1\) means attraction (it is repulsion/size).
  • Confusing \(T_c\) with \(T_B\) (\(T_B = 27T_c/4\)).

Chapter 3 · Topic 42

Boyle temperature

States of Matter - GasesStates of MatterTopic 42 of 43

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Gases, Boyle temperature: at Boyle temperature Z hugs one across a wide low-pressure range. Ideal gas: \(PV = nRT\) with \(R = 8.314\,J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1} = 0.0821\,L\,atm\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}\). Gas density \(d = PM/RT\); molar mass follows from measured density.
Key formula(s). \[ T_B=a/Rb \]
Key points.
  • Always use Kelvin; \(R = 0.0821\) pairs with \(L\)-atm, \(8.314\) with SI joules.
  • Boyle (\(P\propto1/V\)), Charles (\(V\propto T\)), Gay-Lussac (\(P\propto T\)), Avogadro (\(V\propto n\)).
  • Density method: at same \(T,P\), \(d_1/d_2 = M_1/M_2\).
  • Dalton + ideal gas: collect partial pressures via mole fractions.
Example 1.

\(4\,g\,O_2\) occupies what volume at \(27^\circ C\) and \(1\,atm\)?

  1. Moles \(= 4/32 = 0.125\); \(T = 300\,K\).
  2. \(V = nRT/P = 0.125\times0.0821\times300 \approx 3.08\,L\).

Answer: About \(3.08\,L\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) A gas has density \(1.43\,g/L\) at STP. Find its molar mass.

  1. \(M = d\times22.4 = 1.43\times22.4 \approx 32\,g\,mol^{-1}\).
  2. Consistent with \(O_2\).

Answer: About \(32\,g\,mol^{-1}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Plugging Celsius into the gas equation.
  • Mismatching \(R\) units with pressure/volume units.

Chapter 4 · Topic 1

Intermolecular forces in liquids

States of Matter - Liquids and SolidsStates of MatterTopic 1 of 40

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Liquids and Solids, Intermolecular forces in liquids: dipole, dispersion and hydrogen bonds in liquids decide VP, boiling and viscosity. Vapour pressure rises with \(T\) (Clausius-Clapeyron); boiling occurs when VP \(=\) external pressure. Surface tension and viscosity both fall with rising \(T\); capillary rise \(h = 2T\cos\theta/(r\rho g)\).
Key formula(s). \[ boiling:\,VP=P_{ext},\;F=\eta A\frac{dv}{dx} \]
Key points.
  • Stokes terminal velocity \(v_t = 2r^2(\rho-\sigma)g/9\eta\): bigger/denser spheres fall faster.
  • Surfactants lower surface tension; temperature rise lowers both \(T\)-tension and \(\eta\).
  • Boiling point is pressure-dependent (vacuum distillation lowers it).
  • Stronger intermolecular forces \(\to\) higher VP deficit, boiling point, surface tension, viscosity.
Example 1.

Two soap bubbles of radii \(r\) and \(2r\) coalesce. What decides the final shape?

  1. System minimises total surface area (surface energy \(= T\times\Delta A\)).
  2. Smaller bubble (higher excess pressure \(4T/r\)) empties into the larger.

Answer: Area minimisation; small drains into large.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why do small drops have higher vapour pressure (Kelvin effect)?

  1. High curvature raises the chemical potential of the liquid.
  2. VP rises as droplet radius falls.

Answer: Curvature raises VP.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling boiling point a constant (it needs the pressure).
  • Mixing adhesion (wall) with cohesion (liquid-liquid).
Back to Index
Index / States of Matter
Chapter 4 · Topic 2

Vapour pressure

States of Matter - Liquids and SolidsStates of MatterTopic 2 of 40

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Liquids and Solids, Vapour pressure: vapour pressure is the escaping tendency of a liquid at fixed T. Vapour pressure rises with \(T\) (Clausius-Clapeyron); boiling occurs when VP \(=\) external pressure. Surface tension and viscosity both fall with rising \(T\); capillary rise \(h = 2T\cos\theta/(r\rho g)\).
Key formula(s). \[ \ln\frac{P_2}{P_1}=-\frac{\Delta H_{vap}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2}-\frac{1}{T_1}\right),\;boiling:\,VP=P_{ext} \]
Key points.
  • Boiling point is pressure-dependent (vacuum distillation lowers it).
  • Stronger intermolecular forces \(\to\) higher VP deficit, boiling point, surface tension, viscosity.
  • Stokes terminal velocity \(v_t = 2r^2(\rho-\sigma)g/9\eta\): bigger/denser spheres fall faster.
  • Surfactants lower surface tension; temperature rise lowers both \(T\)-tension and \(\eta\).
Example 1.

Why does water boil below \(100^\circ C\) on mountains?

  1. External pressure is lower, so VP equals it at a lower temperature.
  2. Boiling condition is \(VP = P_{ext}\), not a fixed temperature.

Answer: Lower \(P_{ext}\) gives lower boiling point.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Capillary of radius \(0.1\,mm\) in water (\(T = 0.072\,N/m\), \(\theta \approx 0\)). Find rise.

  1. \(h = 2\times0.072/(10^{-4}\times1000\times9.8)\).
  2. \(h \approx 0.147\,m \approx 14.7\,cm\).

Answer: About \(14.7\,cm\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling boiling point a constant (it needs the pressure).
  • Mixing adhesion (wall) with cohesion (liquid-liquid).

Chapter 4 · Topic 3

Boiling point

States of Matter - Liquids and SolidsStates of MatterTopic 3 of 40

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Liquids and Solids, Boiling point: boiling starts exactly where vapour pressure meets external pressure. Vapour pressure rises with \(T\) (Clausius-Clapeyron); boiling occurs when VP \(=\) external pressure. Surface tension and viscosity both fall with rising \(T\); capillary rise \(h = 2T\cos\theta/(r\rho g)\).
Key formula(s). \[ \ln\frac{P_2}{P_1}=-\frac{\Delta H_{vap}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2}-\frac{1}{T_1}\right),\;h=\frac{2T\cos\theta}{r\rho g},\;boiling:\,VP=P_{ext} \]
Key points.
  • Stronger intermolecular forces \(\to\) higher VP deficit, boiling point, surface tension, viscosity.
  • Stokes terminal velocity \(v_t = 2r^2(\rho-\sigma)g/9\eta\): bigger/denser spheres fall faster.
  • Surfactants lower surface tension; temperature rise lowers both \(T\)-tension and \(\eta\).
  • Boiling point is pressure-dependent (vacuum distillation lowers it).
Example 1.

Mercury has very high surface tension yet falls in a capillary. Why?

  1. Contact angle \(\theta \approx 140^\circ > 90^\circ\): \(\cos\theta\) is negative.
  2. Cohesion beats adhesion, giving capillary depression.

Answer: Negative \(\cos\theta\) (non-wetting).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Hot water cleans better than cold water. Explain via surface tension.

  1. Surface tension falls as \(T\) rises.
  2. Lower tension wets fabrics and lifts grease better.

Answer: Lower \(T\)-tension at high \(T\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling boiling point a constant (it needs the pressure).
  • Mixing adhesion (wall) with cohesion (liquid-liquid).

  • Surfactants lower surface tension; temperature rise lowers both \(T\)-tension and \(\eta\).
Example 1.

Why does water boil below \(100^\circ C\) on mountains?

  1. External pressure is lower, so VP equals it at a lower temperature.
  2. Boiling condition is \(VP = P_{ext}\), not a fixed temperature.

Answer: Lower \(P_{ext}\) gives lower boiling point.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Capillary of radius \(0.1\,mm\) in water (\(T = 0.072\,N/m\), \(\theta \approx 0\)). Find rise.

  1. \(h = 2\times0.072/(10^{-4}\times1000\times9.8)\).
  2. \(h \approx 0.147\,m \approx 14.7\,cm\).

Answer: About \(14.7\,cm\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling boiling point a constant (it needs the pressure).
  • Mixing adhesion (wall) with cohesion (liquid-liquid).

Chapter 4 · Topic 9

Stokes' law

States of Matter - Liquids and SolidsStates of MatterTopic 9 of 40

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Liquids and Solids, Stokes' law: Stokes drag 6-pi-eta-r-v governs slow spheres in fluids. Vapour pressure rises with \(T\) (Clausius-Clapeyron); boiling occurs when VP \(=\) external pressure. Surface tension and viscosity both fall with rising \(T\); capillary rise \(h = 2T\cos\theta/(r\rho g)\).
Key formula(s). \[ h=\frac{2T\cos\theta}{r\rho g},\;F=\eta A\frac{dv}{dx},\;v_t=\frac{2r^2g}{9\eta} \]
Key points.
  • Stronger intermolecular forces \(\to\) higher VP deficit, boiling point, surface tension, viscosity.
  • Stokes terminal velocity \(v_t = 2r^2(\rho-\sigma)g/9\eta\): bigger/denser spheres fall faster.
  • Surfactants lower surface tension; temperature rise lowers both \(T\)-tension and \(\eta\).
  • Boiling point is pressure-dependent (vacuum distillation lowers it).
Example 1.

Mercury has very high surface tension yet falls in a capillary. Why?

  1. Contact angle \(\theta \approx 140^\circ > 90^\circ\): \(\cos\theta\) is negative.
  2. Cohesion beats adhesion, giving capillary depression.

Answer: Negative \(\cos\theta\) (non-wetting).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Hot water cleans better than cold water. Explain via surface tension.

  1. Surface tension falls as \(T\) rises.
  2. Lower tension wets fabrics and lifts grease better.

Answer: Lower \(T\)-tension at high \(T\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling boiling point a constant (it needs the pressure).
  • Mixing adhesion (wall) with cohesion (liquid-liquid).

Chapter 4 · Topic 10

Terminal velocity

States of Matter - Liquids and SolidsStates of MatterTopic 10 of 40

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Liquids and Solids, Terminal velocity: terminal velocity balances weight against Stokes drag plus buoyancy. Vapour pressure rises with \(T\) (Clausius-Clapeyron); boiling occurs when VP \(=\) external pressure. Surface tension and viscosity both fall with rising \(T\); capillary rise \(h = 2T\cos\theta/(r\rho g)\).
Key formula(s). \[ v_t=\frac{2r^2g}{9\eta} \],\;\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1}=-\frac{\Delta H_{vap}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2}-\frac{1}{T_1}\right) \]
Key points.
  • Stokes terminal velocity \(v_t = 2r^2(\rho-\sigma)g/9\eta\): bigger/denser spheres fall faster.
  • Surfactants lower surface tension; temperature rise lowers both \(T\)-tension and \(\eta\).
  • Boiling point is pressure-dependent (vacuum distillation lowers it).
  • Stronger intermolecular forces \(\to\) higher VP deficit, boiling point, surface tension, viscosity.
Example 1.

Two soap bubbles of radii \(r\) and \(2r\) coalesce. What decides the final shape?

  1. System minimises total surface area (surface energy \(= T\times\Delta A\)).
  2. Smaller bubble (higher excess pressure \(4T/r\)) empties into the larger.

Answer: Area minimisation; small drains into large.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why do small drops have higher vapour pressure (Kelvin effect)?

  1. High curvature raises the chemical potential of the liquid.
  2. VP rises as droplet radius falls.

Answer: Curvature raises VP.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Calling boiling point a constant (it needs the pressure).
  • Mixing adhesion (wall) with cohesion (liquid-liquid).

Chapter 4 · Topic 14

Solids

States of Matter - Liquids and SolidsStates of MatterTopic 14 of 40

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Liquids and Solids, Solids: solids lock particles in fixed positions with long-range order or glassy disorder. Cubic cells: sc (\(Z=1\), CN 6, 52.4\(\%\)), bcc (\(Z=2\), CN 8, 68\(\%\)), fcc (\(Z=4\), CN 12, 74\(\%\)). Density \(d = ZM/(a^3N_A)\); \(r = a/2\) (sc), \(\sqrt3a/4\) (bcc), \(a/2\sqrt2\) (fcc).
Key formula(s). \[ r_{fcc}=\frac{a}{2\sqrt2},\;Z:\,sc=1,\,bcc=2,\,fcc=4 \]
Key points.
  • Count atoms: corners \(\times1/8\), faces \(\times1/2\), body centre \(\times1\), edges \(\times1/4\).
  • Voids in ccp: octahedral \(= N\), tetrahedral \(= 2N\) per \(N\) atoms.
  • Convert \(a\) from \(pm\) to \(cm\) (\(\times10^{-10}\)) before density in \(g/cm^3\).
  • Amorphous solids (glass) have no long-range order and melt over a range.
Example 1.

An fcc metal has \(a = 400\,pm\), \(M = 64\). Find its density.

  1. \(Z = 4\); \(a = 4\times10^{-8}\,cm\); \(a^3 = 6.4\times10^{-23}\,cm^3\).
  2. \(d = 4\times64/(6.4\times10^{-23}\times6.022\times10^{23}) \approx 6.64\,g/cm^3\).

Answer: About \(6.64\,g/cm^3\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) If atoms occupy all octahedral voids of ccp oxide \(O^{2-}\) lattice with \(M^{2+}\), find the formula.

  1. ccp \(O\): \(N\) atoms; octahedral voids \(= N\), all filled by \(M\).
  2. Formula \(= MO\) (rock-salt type).

Answer: \(MO\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(Z = 8\) for corners (each corner is shared by 8 cells).
  • Forgetting \(pm\to cm\) conversion in density.

Chapter 4 · Topic 15

Crystalline solids

States of Matter - Liquids and SolidsStates of MatterTopic 15 of 40

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Liquids and Solids, Crystalline solids: crystals repeat a unit cell in perfect three-dimensional order. Cubic cells: sc (\(Z=1\), CN 6, 52.4\(\%\)), bcc (\(Z=2\), CN 8, 68\(\%\)), fcc (\(Z=4\), CN 12, 74\(\%\)). Density \(d = ZM/(a^3N_A)\); \(r = a/2\) (sc), \(\sqrt3a/4\) (bcc), \(a/2\sqrt2\) (fcc).
Key formula(s). \[ Z:\,sc=1,\,bcc=2,\,fcc=4,\;PE:\,74/68/52.4\% \,(fcc/bcc/sc) \]
Key points.
  • Voids in ccp: octahedral \(= N\), tetrahedral \(= 2N\) per \(N\) atoms.
  • Convert \(a\) from \(pm\) to \(cm\) (\(\times10^{-10}\)) before density in \(g/cm^3\).
  • Amorphous solids (glass) have no long-range order and melt over a range.
  • Count atoms: corners \(\times1/8\), faces \(\times1/2\), body centre \(\times1\), edges \(\times1/4\).
Example 1.

A bcc metal has edge \(a = 300\,pm\). Find its atomic radius.

  1. For bcc, \(r = \sqrt3\,a/4\).
  2. \(r = 1.732\times300/4 \approx 130\,pm\).

Answer: About \(130\,pm\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Sulphide ions form ccp; \(Zn^{2+}\) fills half the tetrahedral voids. Give the formula.

  1. ccp \(S\): \(N\) atoms; tetrahedral voids \(= 2N\); half filled \(= N\,Zn\).
  2. Formula \(= ZnS\).

Answer: \(ZnS\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(Z = 8\) for corners (each corner is shared by 8 cells).
  • Forgetting \(pm\to cm\) conversion in density.

Amorphous solids

Explanation

Cubic cells: sc (\(Z=1\), CN 6, 52.4\(\%\)), bcc (\(Z=2\), CN 8, 68\(\%\)), fcc (\(Z=4\), CN 12, 74\(\%\)). Density \(d = ZM/(a^3N_A)\); \(r = a/2\) (sc), \(\sqrt3a/4\) (bcc), \(a/2\sqrt2\) (fcc).
Key formula(s). \[ PE:\,74/68/52.4\% \,(fcc/bcc/sc),\;voids:\,oct=N \]
Key points.
  • Convert \(a\) from \(pm\) to \(cm\) (\(\times10^{-10}\)) before density in \(g/cm^3\).

  • Voids in ccp: octahedral \(= N\), tetrahedral \(= 2N\) per \(N\) atoms.
Example 1.

How many atoms per simple cubic cell, and its packing efficiency?

  1. Corners only: \(8\times1/8 = 1\) atom.
  2. Efficiency \(= \pi/6 \approx 52.4\%\).

Answer: \(Z = 1\), \(52.4\%\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(KCl\) has similar-size ions. Which defect does it show?

  1. Similar sizes favour paired vacancies.
  2. Schottky defect.

Answer: Schottky.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(Z = 8\) for corners (each corner is shared by 8 cells).
  • Forgetting \(pm\to cm\) conversion in density.

Chapter 4 · Topic 23

Packing efficiency

States of Matter - Liquids and SolidsStates of MatterTopic 23 of 40

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Liquids and Solids, Packing efficiency: packing efficiency is the hard-sphere volume share of the cell. Cubic cells: sc (\(Z=1\), CN 6, 52.4\(\%\)), bcc (\(Z=2\), CN 8, 68\(\%\)), fcc (\(Z=4\), CN 12, 74\(\%\)). Density \(d = ZM/(a^3N_A)\); \(r = a/2\) (sc), \(\sqrt3a/4\) (bcc), \(a/2\sqrt2\) (fcc).
Key formula(s). \[ PE:\,74/68/52.4\% \,(fcc/bcc/sc) \]
Key points.
  • Count atoms: corners \(\times1/8\), faces \(\times1/2\), body centre \(\times1\), edges \(\times1/4\).
  • Voids in ccp: octahedral \(= N\), tetrahedral \(= 2N\) per \(N\) atoms.
  • Convert \(a\) from \(pm\) to \(cm\) (\(\times10^{-10}\)) before density in \(g/cm^3\).
  • Amorphous solids (glass) have no long-range order and melt over a range.
Example 1.

An fcc metal has \(a = 400\,pm\), \(M = 64\). Find its density.

  1. \(Z = 4\); \(a = 4\times10^{-8}\,cm\); \(a^3 = 6.4\times10^{-23}\,cm^3\).
  2. \(d = 4\times64/(6.4\times10^{-23}\times6.022\times10^{23}) \approx 6.64\,g/cm^3\).

Answer: About \(6.64\,g/cm^3\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) If atoms occupy all octahedral voids of ccp oxide \(O^{2-}\) lattice with \(M^{2+}\), find the formula.

  1. ccp \(O\): \(N\) atoms; octahedral voids \(= N\), all filled by \(M\).
  2. Formula \(= MO\) (rock-salt type).

Answer: \(MO\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(Z = 8\) for corners (each corner is shared by 8 cells).
  • Forgetting \(pm\to cm\) conversion in density.

Number of atoms per unit cell

States of Matter - Liquids and SolidsStates of MatterTopic 24 of 40

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Liquids and Solids, Number of atoms per unit cell: corner atoms count 1/8, face atoms 1/2, and the body centre counts whole. Cubic cells: sc (\(Z=1\), CN 6, 52.4\(\%\)), bcc (\(Z=2\), CN 8, 68\(\%\)), fcc (\(Z=4\), CN 12, 74\(\%\)). Density \(d = ZM/(a^3N_A)\); \(r = a/2\) (sc), \(\sqrt3a/4\) (bcc), \(a/2\sqrt2\) (fcc).
Key formula(s). \[ d=\frac{ZM}{a^3N_A},\;r_{fcc}=\frac{a}{2\sqrt2},\;Z:\,sc=1,\,bcc=2,\,fcc=4 \]
Key points.
  • Voids in ccp: octahedral \(= N\), tetrahedral \(= 2N\) per \(N\) atoms.
  • Convert \(a\) from \(pm\) to \(cm\) (\(\times10^{-10}\)) before density in \(g/cm^3\).
  • Amorphous solids (glass) have no long-range order and melt over a range.
  • Count atoms: corners \(\times1/8\), faces \(\times1/2\), body centre \(\times1\), edges \(\times1/4\).
Example 1.

A bcc metal has edge \(a = 300\,pm\). Find its atomic radius.

  1. For bcc, \(r = \sqrt3\,a/4\).
  2. \(r = 1.732\times300/4 \approx 130\,pm\).

Answer: About \(130\,pm\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Sulphide ions form ccp; \(Zn^{2+}\) fills half the tetrahedral voids. Give the formula.

  1. ccp \(S\): \(N\) atoms; tetrahedral voids \(= 2N\); half filled \(= N\,Zn\).
  2. Formula \(= ZnS\).

Answer: \(ZnS\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(Z = 8\) for corners (each corner is shared by 8 cells).
  • Forgetting \(pm\to cm\) conversion in density.

Chapter 4 · Topic 31

Schottky defect

States of Matter - Liquids and SolidsStates of MatterTopic 31 of 40

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Liquids and Solids, Schottky defect: Schottky pairs vacancies of cation and anion and lowers density. Schottky: paired cation+anion vacancies (density falls, e.g. \(NaCl\)); Frenkel: ion displaced to interstitial (density unchanged, e.g. \(AgCl\)). Metal excess via F-centres gives colour; metal deficiency (\(Fe_{0.93}O\)) raises oxidation states.
Key formula(s). \[ Schottky:\,\rho\downarrow \]
Key points.
  • Metal-deficient \(FeO\) is always non-stoichiometric in practice.
  • Doping \(Si\) with \(P\) gives n-type; with \(B\) gives p-type.
  • Schottky favoured by similar-size ions; Frenkel by large size difference.
  • F-centres: anion vacancy traps electron \(\to\) yellow (\(NaCl\)), pink (\(KCl\)).
Example 1.

Which defect: \(AgBr\) shows both vacancy pairs and displaced \(Ag^+\)?

  1. Vacancy pairs \(=\) Schottky; displaced ion \(=\) Frenkel.
  2. \(AgBr\) shows both (intermediate size difference).

Answer: Both Schottky and Frenkel.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Doping Si with group-15 element gives which semiconductor?

  1. Extra electron beyond the lattice bonds.
  2. n-type semiconductor.

Answer: n-type.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Saying Frenkel lowers density (it does not).
  • Swapping n-type and p-type dopant groups.

(JEE pattern) Sulphide ions form ccp; \(Zn^{2+}\) fills half the tetrahedral voids. Give the formula.

  1. ccp \(S\): \(N\) atoms; tetrahedral voids \(= 2N\); half filled \(= N\,Zn\).
  2. Formula \(= ZnS\).

Answer: \(ZnS\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(Z = 8\) for corners (each corner is shared by 8 cells).
  • Forgetting \(pm\to cm\) conversion in density.

Chapter 4 · Topic 37

Molecular solids

States of Matter - Liquids and SolidsStates of MatterTopic 37 of 40

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Liquids and Solids, Molecular solids: molecular solids are soft low-melting van der Waals crystals. Cubic cells: sc (\(Z=1\), CN 6, 52.4\(\%\)), bcc (\(Z=2\), CN 8, 68\(\%\)), fcc (\(Z=4\), CN 12, 74\(\%\)). Density \(d = ZM/(a^3N_A)\); \(r = a/2\) (sc), \(\sqrt3a/4\) (bcc), \(a/2\sqrt2\) (fcc).
Key formula(s). \[ d=\frac{ZM}{a^3N_A},\;voids:\,oct=N,\;tetra=2N \]
Key points.
  • Convert \(a\) from \(pm\) to \(cm\) (\(\times10^{-10}\)) before density in \(g/cm^3\).
  • Amorphous solids (glass) have no long-range order and melt over a range.
  • Count atoms: corners \(\times1/8\), faces \(\times1/2\), body centre \(\times1\), edges \(\times1/4\).
  • Voids in ccp: octahedral \(= N\), tetrahedral \(= 2N\) per \(N\) atoms.
Example 1.

How many atoms per simple cubic cell, and its packing efficiency?

  1. Corners only: \(8\times1/8 = 1\) atom.
  2. Efficiency \(= \pi/6 \approx 52.4\%\).

Answer: \(Z = 1\), \(52.4\%\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(KCl\) has similar-size ions. Which defect does it show?

  1. Similar sizes favour paired vacancies.
  2. Schottky defect.

Answer: Schottky.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(Z = 8\) for corners (each corner is shared by 8 cells).
  • Forgetting \(pm\to cm\) conversion in density.

Chapter 4 · Topic 38

Ionic solids

States of Matter - Liquids and SolidsStates of MatterTopic 38 of 40

Explanation

Concept. In States of Matter - Liquids and Solids, Ionic solids: ionic solids are hard brittle high-melting Coulomb lattices. Cubic cells: sc (\(Z=1\), CN 6, 52.4\(\%\)), bcc (\(Z=2\), CN 8, 68\(\%\)), fcc (\(Z=4\), CN 12, 74\(\%\)). Density \(d = ZM/(a^3N_A)\); \(r = a/2\) (sc), \(\sqrt3a/4\) (bcc), \(a/2\sqrt2\) (fcc).
Key formula(s). \[ r_{fcc}=\frac{a}{2\sqrt2},\;Z:\,sc=1,\,bcc=2,\,fcc=4,\;PE:\,74/68/52.4\% \,(fcc/bcc/sc),\;voids:\,oct=N \]
Key points.
  • Count atoms: corners \(\times1/8\), faces \(\times1/2\), body centre \(\times1\), edges \(\times1/4\).
  • Voids in ccp: octahedral \(= N\), tetrahedral \(= 2N\) per \(N\) atoms.
  • Convert \(a\) from \(pm\) to \(cm\) (\(\times10^{-10}\)) before density in \(g/cm^3\).
  • Amorphous solids (glass) have no long-range order and melt over a range.
Example 1.

An fcc metal has \(a = 400\,pm\), \(M = 64\). Find its density.

  1. \(Z = 4\); \(a = 4\times10^{-8}\,cm\); \(a^3 = 6.4\times10^{-23}\,cm^3\).
  2. \(d = 4\times64/(6.4\times10^{-23}\times6.022\times10^{23}) \approx 6.64\,g/cm^3\).

Answer: About \(6.64\,g/cm^3\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) If atoms occupy all octahedral voids of ccp oxide \(O^{2-}\) lattice with \(M^{2+}\), find the formula.

  1. ccp \(O\): \(N\) atoms; octahedral voids \(= N\), all filled by \(M\).
  2. Formula \(= MO\) (rock-salt type).

Answer: \(MO\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(Z = 8\) for corners (each corner is shared by 8 cells).
  • Forgetting \(pm\to cm\) conversion in density.

Index / Energy & Equilibrium
Chapter 5 · Topic 1

System and surroundings

ThermodynamicsEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 1 of 51

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics, System and surroundings: the system is the watched region, everything else is surroundings. First law: \(\Delta U = q + w\) (chemistry sign: work done BY the system is negative). \(U, H, G, S\) are state functions; \(q, w\) are path functions. Zeroth law founds temperature; equilibrium needs thermal, mechanical and chemical balance.
Key formula(s). \[ q=-w \],\;\Delta U = q + w \]
Key points.
  • Signs: heat absorbed by system \(+\); work done BY system \(-\). Free expansion against vacuum: \(w = 0\).
  • Reversible work magnitude exceeds irreversible work between the same states.
  • Intensive (\(T, P, \rho\)) vs extensive (\(V, n, U\)): only extensive scales with amount.
  • Cyclic process: \(\Delta U = 0\), so \(q = -w\).
Example 1.

\(2\,mol\) ideal gas expands reversibly and isothermally at \(300\,K\) from \(5\,L\) to \(15\,L\). Find \(w\).

  1. \(w = -nRT\ln(V_2/V_1) = -2\times8.314\times300\times\ln3\).
  2. \(w \approx -5483\,J \approx -5.48\,kJ\). For isothermal ideal gas \(\Delta U = 0\), so \(q = +5.48\,kJ\).

Answer: \(w \approx -5.48\,kJ\), \(q \approx +5.48\,kJ\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) One mole of gas expands against \(1\,atm\) external pressure from \(2\,L\) to \(7\,L\). Find irreversible work in \(L\,atm\) and joules.

  1. \(w = -P_{ext}\Delta V = -1\times5 = -5\,L\,atm\).
  2. In joules: \(-5\times101.3 = -506.5\,J\).

Answer: \(-5\,L\,atm\) (\(-506.5\,J\)).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using physics sign convention (work by system positive) in chemistry problems.
  • Forgetting free expansion \(w = 0\) because \(P_{ext} = 0\).
Back to Index
Index / Energy & Equilibrium
Chapter 5 · Topic 2

Open system

ThermodynamicsEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 2 of 51

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics, Open system: open systems trade both matter and energy across the boundary. First law: \(\Delta U = q + w\) (chemistry sign: work done BY the system is negative). \(U, H, G, S\) are state functions; \(q, w\) are path functions. Zeroth law founds temperature; equilibrium needs thermal, mechanical and chemical balance.
Key formula(s). \[ \Delta U = q + w,\;w_{rev} = -nRT\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1} \]
Key points.
  • Reversible work magnitude exceeds irreversible work between the same states.
  • Intensive (\(T, P, \rho\)) vs extensive (\(V, n, U\)): only extensive scales with amount.
  • Cyclic process: \(\Delta U = 0\), so \(q = -w\).
  • Signs: heat absorbed by system \(+\); work done BY system \(-\). Free expansion against vacuum: \(w = 0\).
Example 1.

An ideal gas expands adiabatically into vacuum (free expansion). Give \(w, q, \Delta U\).

  1. Against zero external pressure \(w = 0\); insulated so \(q = 0\).
  2. \(\Delta U = 0\); temperature unchanged for an ideal gas.

Answer: All zero; \(\Delta T = 0\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(1\,mol\) gas is compressed with \(P_{ext} = 5\,atm\) from \(10\,L\) to \(2\,L\). Find \(w\).

  1. \(w = -P_{ext}\Delta V = -5\times(2-10) = +40\,L\,atm\).
  2. \(+40\times101.3 = +4052\,J\) (work done ON the system).

Answer: \(+40\,L\,atm\) (\(+4.05\,kJ\)).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using physics sign convention (work by system positive) in chemistry problems.
  • Forgetting free expansion \(w = 0\) because \(P_{ext} = 0\).
Back to Index
Index / Energy & Equilibrium
Chapter 5 · Topic 3

Closed system

ThermodynamicsEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 3 of 51

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics, Closed system: closed systems trade energy but seal matter inside. First law: \(\Delta U = q + w\) (chemistry sign: work done BY the system is negative). \(U, H, G, S\) are state functions; \(q, w\) are path functions. Zeroth law founds temperature; equilibrium needs thermal, mechanical and chemical balance.
Key formula(s). \[ w_{rev} = -nRT\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1},\;w_{irr} = -P_{ext}\Delta V \]
Key points.
  • Intensive (\(T, P, \rho\)) vs extensive (\(V, n, U\)): only extensive scales with amount.
  • Cyclic process: \(\Delta U = 0\), so \(q = -w\).
  • Signs: heat absorbed by system \(+\); work done BY system \(-\). Free expansion against vacuum: \(w = 0\).
  • Reversible work magnitude exceeds irreversible work between the same states.
Example 1.

In an isothermal change \(q = +2\,kJ\) for an ideal gas. Find \(w\) and \(\Delta U\).

  1. Isothermal ideal gas: \(\Delta U = 0\).
  2. \(w = -q = -2\,kJ\).

Answer: \(\Delta U = 0\), \(w = -2\,kJ\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(1\,mol\) expands at \(300\,K\) from \(1\,L\) to \(10\,L\): compare reversible vs \(1\,atm\) irreversible work.

  1. Reversible: \(-8.314\times300\times\ln10 \approx -5744\,J\).
  2. Irreversible: \(-1\times9\,L\,atm = -912\,J\) (much smaller magnitude).

Answer: \(-5.74\,kJ\) vs \(-0.91\,kJ\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using physics sign convention (work by system positive) in chemistry problems.
  • Forgetting free expansion \(w = 0\) because \(P_{ext} = 0\).

  1. \(w = -nRT\ln(V_2/V_1) = -2\times8.314\times300\times\ln3\).
  2. \(w \approx -5483\,J \approx -5.48\,kJ\). For isothermal ideal gas \(\Delta U = 0\), so \(q = +5.48\,kJ\).

Answer: \(w \approx -5.48\,kJ\), \(q \approx +5.48\,kJ\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) One mole of gas expands against \(1\,atm\) external pressure from \(2\,L\) to \(7\,L\). Find irreversible work in \(L\,atm\) and joules.

  1. \(w = -P_{ext}\Delta V = -1\times5 = -5\,L\,atm\).
  2. In joules: \(-5\times101.3 = -506.5\,J\).

Answer: \(-5\,L\,atm\) (\(-506.5\,J\)).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using physics sign convention (work by system positive) in chemistry problems.
  • Forgetting free expansion \(w = 0\) because \(P_{ext} = 0\).

  2. \(\Delta U = 0\); temperature unchanged for an ideal gas.

Answer: All zero; \(\Delta T = 0\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(1\,mol\) gas is compressed with \(P_{ext} = 5\,atm\) from \(10\,L\) to \(2\,L\). Find \(w\).

  1. \(w = -P_{ext}\Delta V = -5\times(2-10) = +40\,L\,atm\).
  2. \(+40\times101.3 = +4052\,J\) (work done ON the system).

Answer: \(+40\,L\,atm\) (\(+4.05\,kJ\)).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using physics sign convention (work by system positive) in chemistry problems.
  • Forgetting free expansion \(w = 0\) because \(P_{ext} = 0\).

Chapter 5 · Topic 10

Zeroth law

ThermodynamicsEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 10 of 51

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics, Zeroth law: the zeroth law founds temperature through mutual thermal equilibrium. First law: \(\Delta U = q + w\) (chemistry sign: work done BY the system is negative). \(U, H, G, S\) are state functions; \(q, w\) are path functions. Zeroth law founds temperature; equilibrium needs thermal, mechanical and chemical balance.
Key formula(s). \[ Zeroth:\,T_1=T_2=T_3 \]
Key points.
  • Signs: heat absorbed by system \(+\); work done BY system \(-\). Free expansion against vacuum: \(w = 0\).
  • Reversible work magnitude exceeds irreversible work between the same states.
  • Intensive (\(T, P, \rho\)) vs extensive (\(V, n, U\)): only extensive scales with amount.
  • Cyclic process: \(\Delta U = 0\), so \(q = -w\).
Example 1.

\(2\,mol\) ideal gas expands reversibly and isothermally at \(300\,K\) from \(5\,L\) to \(15\,L\). Find \(w\).

  1. \(w = -nRT\ln(V_2/V_1) = -2\times8.314\times300\times\ln3\).
  2. \(w \approx -5483\,J \approx -5.48\,kJ\). For isothermal ideal gas \(\Delta U = 0\), so \(q = +5.48\,kJ\).

Answer: \(w \approx -5.48\,kJ\), \(q \approx +5.48\,kJ\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) One mole of gas expands against \(1\,atm\) external pressure from \(2\,L\) to \(7\,L\). Find irreversible work in \(L\,atm\) and joules.

  1. \(w = -P_{ext}\Delta V = -1\times5 = -5\,L\,atm\).
  2. In joules: \(-5\times101.3 = -506.5\,J\).

Answer: \(-5\,L\,atm\) (\(-506.5\,J\)).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using physics sign convention (work by system positive) in chemistry problems.
  • Forgetting free expansion \(w = 0\) because \(P_{ext} = 0\).

Internal energy

ThermodynamicsEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 11 of 51

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics, Internal energy: internal energy banks every microscopic kinetic and potential bit. First law: \(\Delta U = q + w\) (chemistry sign: work done BY the system is negative). \(U, H, G, S\) are state functions; \(q, w\) are path functions. Zeroth law founds temperature; equilibrium needs thermal, mechanical and chemical balance.
Key formula(s). \[ w_{irr} = -P_{ext}\Delta V,\;isolated:\,\Delta U=const \]
Key points.
  • Reversible work magnitude exceeds irreversible work between the same states.
  • Intensive (\(T, P, \rho\)) vs extensive (\(V, n, U\)): only extensive scales with amount.
  • Cyclic process: \(\Delta U = 0\), so \(q = -w\).
  • Signs: heat absorbed by system \(+\); work done BY system \(-\). Free expansion against vacuum: \(w = 0\).
Example 1.

An ideal gas expands adiabatically into vacuum (free expansion). Give \(w, q, \Delta U\).

  1. Against zero external pressure \(w = 0\); insulated so \(q = 0\).
  2. \(\Delta U = 0\); temperature unchanged for an ideal gas.

Answer: All zero; \(\Delta T = 0\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(1\,mol\) gas is compressed with \(P_{ext} = 5\,atm\) from \(10\,L\) to \(2\,L\). Find \(w\).

  1. \(w = -P_{ext}\Delta V = -5\times(2-10) = +40\,L\,atm\).
  2. \(+40\times101.3 = +4052\,J\) (work done ON the system).

Answer: \(+40\,L\,atm\) (\(+4.05\,kJ\)).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using physics sign convention (work by system positive) in chemistry problems.
  • Forgetting free expansion \(w = 0\) because \(P_{ext} = 0\).

Heat

Explanation

In an isothermal change \(q = +2\,kJ\) for an ideal gas. Find \(w\) and \(\Delta U\).

Chapter 5 · Topic 16

Delta-U calculations

ThermodynamicsEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 16 of 51

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics, Delta-U calculations: delta-U is path-independent, so pick the easiest route between states. Enthalpy \(H = U + PV\); at constant pressure \(q_p = \Delta H\). Key links: \(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_gRT\), \(C_p - C_v = R\), Hess law (enthalpy is a state function), \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) with spontaneity at \(\Delta G<0\).
Key formula(s). \[ \Delta H=\Delta U+\Delta n_gRT,\;Hess:\,\sum\Delta H\,path\,independent \]
Key points.
  • Standard formation enthalpy of elements in reference state \(= 0\).
  • Strong acid + strong base neutralisation \(\approx -57.1\,kJ/eq\); weaker if weak electrolyte involved (ionisation absorbs heat).
  • Bond enthalpy route: \(\Delta H = \sum BE(reactants) - \sum BE(products)\).
  • Kirchhoff: \(\Delta H_2-\Delta H_1 = \Delta C_p(T_2-T_1)\); entropy of heating: \(\Delta S = C\ln(T_2/T_1)\).
Example 1.

For \(2H_2+O_2\to2H_2O(l)\), \(\Delta U = -750\,kJ\) at \(300\,K\). Find \(\Delta H\).

  1. \(\Delta n_g = 0-3 = -3\).
  2. \(\Delta H = -750 + (-3)(8.314\times10^{-3})(300) = -750-7.48 = -757.5\,kJ\).

Answer: About \(-757.5\,kJ\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(\Delta H = -100\,kJ\), \(\Delta S = -200\,J/K\). Above what \(T\) does the reaction become non-spontaneous?

  1. Set \(\Delta G = 0\): \(T = \Delta H/\Delta S = (-100000)/(-200) = 500\,K\).
  2. Below \(500\,K\) spontaneous; above, \(\Delta G>0\).

Answer: \(500\,K\) (spontaneous below it).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Including solids/liquids in \(\Delta n_g\) (gases only).
  • Using \(kJ\) and \(J\) together without converting in \(\Delta G = \Delta H-T\Delta S\).

  1. \(\Delta n_g = 2-4 = -2\).
  2. \(\Delta U = \Delta H - \Delta n_gRT = -92 - (-2)(2.478) = -87.0\,kJ\).

Answer: About \(-87.0\,kJ\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Ice melts with \(\Delta H = +6.0\,kJ/mol\), \(\Delta S = +22\,J/mol/K\). Above what \(T\) is melting spontaneous?

  1. \(T = 6000/22 \approx 273\,K\).
  2. Melting spontaneous above \(273\,K\) at \(1\,atm\).

Answer: \(273\,K\).

  • Including solids/liquids in \(\Delta n_g\) (gases only).

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics, Isobaric process: isobaric fixes pressure, so heat equals delta-H. Enthalpy \(H = U + PV\); at constant pressure \(q_p = \Delta H\). Key links: \(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_gRT\), \(C_p - C_v = R\), Hess law (enthalpy is a state function), \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) with spontaneity at \(\Delta G<0\).
Key formula(s). \[ q_p=\Delta H \]
Key points.
  • Strong acid + strong base neutralisation \(\approx -57.1\,kJ/eq\); weaker if weak electrolyte involved (ionisation absorbs heat).
  • Bond enthalpy route: \(\Delta H = \sum BE(reactants) - \sum BE(products)\).
  • Kirchhoff: \(\Delta H_2-\Delta H_1 = \Delta C_p(T_2-T_1)\); entropy of heating: \(\Delta S = C\ln(T_2/T_1)\).
  • Standard formation enthalpy of elements in reference state \(= 0\).
Example 1.

\(2CO + O_2 \to 2CO_2\): \(\Delta U = -564\,kJ\) at \(298\,K\). Find \(\Delta H\).

  1. Gases: products \(2\), reactants \(3\), so \(\Delta n_g = -1\).
  2. \(\Delta H = -564 + (-1)(8.314\times10^{-3})(298) = -566.5\,kJ\).

Answer: About \(-566.5\,kJ\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) A reaction has \(\Delta H = -92\,kJ\), \(\Delta S = -199\,J/K\). Below what \(T\) is it spontaneous?

  1. \(T = \Delta H/\Delta S = 92000/199 \approx 462\,K\).
  2. Spontaneous below \(462\,K\) (Haber-type sign pair).

Answer: \(462\,K\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Including solids/liquids in \(\Delta n_g\) (gases only).
  • Using \(kJ\) and \(J\) together without converting in \(\Delta G = \Delta H-T\Delta S\).

Isochoric process

ThermodynamicsEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 24 of 51

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics, Isochoric process: isochoric fixes volume, so heat equals delta-U with zero work. Enthalpy \(H = U + PV\); at constant pressure \(q_p = \Delta H\). Key links: \(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_gRT\), \(C_p - C_v = R\), Hess law (enthalpy is a state function), \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) with spontaneity at \(\Delta G<0\).
Key formula(s). \[ \Delta H=\Delta U+\Delta n_gRT,\;\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S \]
Key points.
  • Bond enthalpy route: \(\Delta H = \sum BE(reactants) - \sum BE(products)\).
  • Kirchhoff: \(\Delta H_2-\Delta H_1 = \Delta C_p(T_2-T_1)\); entropy of heating: \(\Delta S = C\ln(T_2/T_1)\).
  • Standard formation enthalpy of elements in reference state \(= 0\).
  • Strong acid + strong base neutralisation \(\approx -57.1\,kJ/eq\); weaker if weak electrolyte involved (ionisation absorbs heat).
Example 1.

For \(N_2 + 3H_2 \to 2NH_3\), \(\Delta H = -92\,kJ\) at \(298\,K\). Find \(\Delta U\).

  1. \(\Delta n_g = 2-4 = -2\).
  2. \(\Delta U = \Delta H - \Delta n_gRT = -92 - (-2)(2.478) = -87.0\,kJ\).

Answer: About \(-87.0\,kJ\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Ice melts with \(\Delta H = +6.0\,kJ/mol\), \(\Delta S = +22\,J/mol/K\). Above what \(T\) is melting spontaneous?

  1. \(T = 6000/22 \approx 273\,K\).
  2. Melting spontaneous above \(273\,K\) at \(1\,atm\).

Answer: \(273\,K\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Including solids/liquids in \(\Delta n_g\) (gases only).
  • Using \(kJ\) and \(J\) together without converting in \(\Delta G = \Delta H-T\Delta S\).

Chapter 5 · Topic 25

Enthalpy

ThermodynamicsEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 25 of 51

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics, Enthalpy: enthalpy H = U + PV makes constant-pressure heat bookkeeping trivial. Enthalpy \(H = U + PV\); at constant pressure \(q_p = \Delta H\). Key links: \(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_gRT\), \(C_p - C_v = R\), Hess law (enthalpy is a state function), \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) with spontaneity at \(\Delta G<0\).
Key formula(s). \[ \Delta H=\Delta U+\Delta n_gRT,\;\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S,\;Hess:\,\sum\Delta H\,path\,independent \]
Key points.
  • Standard formation enthalpy of elements in reference state \(= 0\).
  • Strong acid + strong base neutralisation \(\approx -57.1\,kJ/eq\); weaker if weak electrolyte involved (ionisation absorbs heat).
  • Bond enthalpy route: \(\Delta H = \sum BE(reactants) - \sum BE(products)\).
  • Kirchhoff: \(\Delta H_2-\Delta H_1 = \Delta C_p(T_2-T_1)\); entropy of heating: \(\Delta S = C\ln(T_2/T_1)\).
Example 1.

For \(2H_2+O_2\to2H_2O(l)\), \(\Delta U = -750\,kJ\) at \(300\,K\). Find \(\Delta H\).

  1. \(\Delta n_g = 0-3 = -3\).
  2. \(\Delta H = -750 + (-3)(8.314\times10^{-3})(300) = -750-7.48 = -757.5\,kJ\).

Answer: About \(-757.5\,kJ\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(\Delta H = -100\,kJ\), \(\Delta S = -200\,J/K\). Above what \(T\) does the reaction become non-spontaneous?

  1. Set \(\Delta G = 0\): \(T = \Delta H/\Delta S = (-100000)/(-200) = 500\,K\).
  2. Below \(500\,K\) spontaneous; above, \(\Delta G>0\).

Answer: \(500\,K\) (spontaneous below it).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Including solids/liquids in \(\Delta n_g\) (gases only).
  • Using \(kJ\) and \(J\) together without converting in \(\Delta G = \Delta H-T\Delta S\).

Chapter 5 · Topic 27

Heat capacity

ThermodynamicsEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 27 of 51

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics, Heat capacity: heat capacity is the heat price of one degree for the whole object. First law: \(\Delta U = q + w\) (chemistry sign: work done BY the system is negative). \(U, H, G, S\) are state functions; \(q, w\) are path functions. Zeroth law founds temperature; equilibrium needs thermal, mechanical and chemical balance.
Key formula(s). \[ \Delta U = q + w,\;isolated:\,\Delta U=const,\;q=-w \]
Key points.
  • Intensive (\(T, P, \rho\)) vs extensive (\(V, n, U\)): only extensive scales with amount.
  • Cyclic process: \(\Delta U = 0\), so \(q = -w\).
  • Signs: heat absorbed by system \(+\); work done BY system \(-\). Free expansion against vacuum: \(w = 0\).
  • Reversible work magnitude exceeds irreversible work between the same states.
Example 1.

In an isothermal change \(q = +2\,kJ\) for an ideal gas. Find \(w\) and \(\Delta U\).

  1. Isothermal ideal gas: \(\Delta U = 0\).
  2. \(w = -q = -2\,kJ\).

Answer: \(\Delta U = 0\), \(w = -2\,kJ\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(1\,mol\) expands at \(300\,K\) from \(1\,L\) to \(10\,L\): compare reversible vs \(1\,atm\) irreversible work.

  1. Reversible: \(-8.314\times300\times\ln10 \approx -5744\,J\).
  2. Irreversible: \(-1\times9\,L\,atm = -912\,J\) (much smaller magnitude).

Answer: \(-5.74\,kJ\) vs \(-0.91\,kJ\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using physics sign convention (work by system positive) in chemistry problems.
  • Forgetting free expansion \(w = 0\) because \(P_{ext} = 0\).

Chapter 5 · Topic 28

Specific heat

ThermodynamicsEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 28 of 51

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics, Specific heat: specific heat prices one degree per gram. First law: \(\Delta U = q + w\) (chemistry sign: work done BY the system is negative). \(U, H, G, S\) are state functions; \(q, w\) are path functions. Zeroth law founds temperature; equilibrium needs thermal, mechanical and chemical balance.
Key formula(s). \[ \Delta U = q + w,\;Zeroth:\,T_1=T_2=T_3,\;q=-w \]
Key points.
  • Signs: heat absorbed by system \(+\); work done BY system \(-\). Free expansion against vacuum: \(w = 0\).
  • Reversible work magnitude exceeds irreversible work between the same states.
  • Intensive (\(T, P, \rho\)) vs extensive (\(V, n, U\)): only extensive scales with amount.
  • Cyclic process: \(\Delta U = 0\), so \(q = -w\).
Example 1.

\(2\,mol\) ideal gas expands reversibly and isothermally at \(300\,K\) from \(5\,L\) to \(15\,L\). Find \(w\).

  1. \(w = -nRT\ln(V_2/V_1) = -2\times8.314\times300\times\ln3\).
  2. \(w \approx -5483\,J \approx -5.48\,kJ\). For isothermal ideal gas \(\Delta U = 0\), so \(q = +5.48\,kJ\).

Answer: \(w \approx -5.48\,kJ\), \(q \approx +5.48\,kJ\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) One mole of gas expands against \(1\,atm\) external pressure from \(2\,L\) to \(7\,L\). Find irreversible work in \(L\,atm\) and joules.

  1. \(w = -P_{ext}\Delta V = -1\times5 = -5\,L\,atm\).
  2. In joules: \(-5\times101.3 = -506.5\,J\).

Answer: \(-5\,L\,atm\) (\(-506.5\,J\)).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using physics sign convention (work by system positive) in chemistry problems.
  • Forgetting free expansion \(w = 0\) because \(P_{ext} = 0\).

Chapter 5 · Topic 29

Molar heat capacity

ThermodynamicsEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 29 of 51

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics, Molar heat capacity: molar heat capacity prices one degree per mole. First law: \(\Delta U = q + w\) (chemistry sign: work done BY the system is negative). \(U, H, G, S\) are state functions; \(q, w\) are path functions. Zeroth law founds temperature; equilibrium needs thermal, mechanical and chemical balance.
Key formula(s). \[ \Delta U = q + w,\;w_{rev} = -nRT\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1},\;cyclic:\,\Delta U=0,\;q=-w \]
Key points.
  • Reversible work magnitude exceeds irreversible work between the same states.
  • Intensive (\(T, P, \rho\)) vs extensive (\(V, n, U\)): only extensive scales with amount.
  • Cyclic process: \(\Delta U = 0\), so \(q = -w\).
  • Signs: heat absorbed by system \(+\); work done BY system \(-\). Free expansion against vacuum: \(w = 0\).
Example 1.

An ideal gas expands adiabatically into vacuum (free expansion). Give \(w, q, \Delta U\).

  1. Against zero external pressure \(w = 0\); insulated so \(q = 0\).
  2. \(\Delta U = 0\); temperature unchanged for an ideal gas.

Answer: All zero; \(\Delta T = 0\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(1\,mol\) gas is compressed with \(P_{ext} = 5\,atm\) from \(10\,L\) to \(2\,L\). Find \(w\).

  1. \(w = -P_{ext}\Delta V = -5\times(2-10) = +40\,L\,atm\).
  2. \(+40\times101.3 = +4052\,J\) (work done ON the system).

Answer: \(+40\,L\,atm\) (\(+4.05\,kJ\)).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using physics sign convention (work by system positive) in chemistry problems.
  • Forgetting free expansion \(w = 0\) because \(P_{ext} = 0\).

Explanation

Key formula(s). \[ \Delta U=q+w,\;\Delta H=\Delta U+\Delta n_gRT \]
Key points.
  • Reversible work exceeds irreversible in magnitude.
  • Elements in reference state have zero formation enthalpy.
  • Convert kJ and J before using G = H-TS.
  • Chemistry sign: work by system is negative.
Example 1.

Isothermal reversible expansion of 1 mol at 300 K, 2 L -> 6 L. Find w.

  1. w = -nRT ln(3) = -8.314x300x1.0986.
  2. w = -2740 J.

Answer: -2.74 kJ.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) dH = -120 kJ, dS = -300 J/K. Spontaneous below what T?

  1. T = dH/dS = 400 K.
  2. Spontaneous below 400 K.

Answer: 400 K.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Solids in delta-ng.
  • kJ/J mixing in Gibbs.

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics, Gibbs energy and equilibrium: the focus here is Gibbs energy and equilibrium, worked through the Thermodynamics toolkit below. Enthalpy \(H = U + PV\); at constant pressure \(q_p = \Delta H\). Key links: \(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_gRT\), \(C_p - C_v = R\), Hess law (enthalpy is a state function), \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) with spontaneity at \(\Delta G<0\).
Key formula(s). \[ \Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S,\;\Delta G^\circ=-RT\ln K,\;2nd\,law:\,\Delta S_{univ}>0 \]
Key points.
  • Bond enthalpy route: \(\Delta H = \sum BE(reactants) - \sum BE(products)\).
  • Kirchhoff: \(\Delta H_2-\Delta H_1 = \Delta C_p(T_2-T_1)\); entropy of heating: \(\Delta S = C\ln(T_2/T_1)\).
  • Standard formation enthalpy of elements in reference state \(= 0\).
  • Strong acid + strong base neutralisation \(\approx -57.1\,kJ/eq\); weaker if weak electrolyte involved (ionisation absorbs heat).
Example 1.

For \(N_2 + 3H_2 \to 2NH_3\), \(\Delta H = -92\,kJ\) at \(298\,K\). Find \(\Delta U\).

  1. \(\Delta n_g = 2-4 = -2\).
  2. \(\Delta U = \Delta H - \Delta n_gRT = -92 - (-2)(2.478) = -87.0\,kJ\).

Answer: About \(-87.0\,kJ\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Ice melts with \(\Delta H = +6.0\,kJ/mol\), \(\Delta S = +22\,J/mol/K\). Above what \(T\) is melting spontaneous?

  1. \(T = 6000/22 \approx 273\,K\).
  2. Melting spontaneous above \(273\,K\) at \(1\,atm\).

Answer: \(273\,K\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Including solids/liquids in \(\Delta n_g\) (gases only).
  • Using \(kJ\) and \(J\) together without converting in \(\Delta G = \Delta H-T\Delta S\).

Chapter 5 · Topic 49

Standard Gibbs energy

ThermodynamicsEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 49 of 51

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics, Standard Gibbs energy: the focus here is Standard Gibbs energy, worked through the Thermodynamics toolkit below. Enthalpy \(H = U + PV\); at constant pressure \(q_p = \Delta H\). Key links: \(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_gRT\), \(C_p - C_v = R\), Hess law (enthalpy is a state function), \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) with spontaneity at \(\Delta G<0\).
Key formula(s). \[ \Delta H=\Delta U+\Delta n_gRT,\;C_p-C_v=R,\;\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S,\;\Delta G^\circ=-RT\ln K \]
Key points.
  • Standard formation enthalpy of elements in reference state \(= 0\).
  • Strong acid + strong base neutralisation \(\approx -57.1\,kJ/eq\); weaker if weak electrolyte involved (ionisation absorbs heat).
  • Bond enthalpy route: \(\Delta H = \sum BE(reactants) - \sum BE(products)\).
  • Kirchhoff: \(\Delta H_2-\Delta H_1 = \Delta C_p(T_2-T_1)\); entropy of heating: \(\Delta S = C\ln(T_2/T_1)\).
Example 1.

For \(2H_2+O_2\to2H_2O(l)\), \(\Delta U = -750\,kJ\) at \(300\,K\). Find \(\Delta H\).

  1. \(\Delta n_g = 0-3 = -3\).
  2. \(\Delta H = -750 + (-3)(8.314\times10^{-3})(300) = -750-7.48 = -757.5\,kJ\).

Answer: About \(-757.5\,kJ\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(\Delta H = -100\,kJ\), \(\Delta S = -200\,J/K\). Above what \(T\) does the reaction become non-spontaneous?

  1. Set \(\Delta G = 0\): \(T = \Delta H/\Delta S = (-100000)/(-200) = 500\,K\).
  2. Below \(500\,K\) spontaneous; above, \(\Delta G>0\).

Answer: \(500\,K\) (spontaneous below it).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Including solids/liquids in \(\Delta n_g\) (gases only).
  • Using \(kJ\) and \(J\) together without converting in \(\Delta G = \Delta H-T\Delta S\).

Chapter 5 · Topic 50

Spontaneous and non-spontaneous processes

ThermodynamicsEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 50 of 51

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics, Spontaneous and non-spontaneous processes: sign of Delta-G separates processes that run from those needing drive. This Thermodynamics topic follows the state-function chain: first law for work and heat, enthalpy corrections with delta-ng RT, Hess summation, and the Gibbs spontaneity test.
Key formula(s). \[ \Delta G<0\,runs \]
Key points.
  • Reversible work exceeds irreversible in magnitude.
  • Elements in reference state have zero formation enthalpy.
  • Convert kJ and J before using G = H-TS.
  • Chemistry sign: work by system is negative.
Example 1.

Isothermal reversible expansion of 1 mol at 300 K, 2 L -> 6 L. Find w.

  1. w = -nRT ln(3) = -8.314x300x1.0986.
  2. w = -2740 J.

Answer: -2.74 kJ.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) dH = -120 kJ, dS = -300 J/K. Spontaneous below what T?

  1. T = dH/dS = 400 K.
  2. Spontaneous below 400 K.

Answer: 400 K.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Solids in delta-ng.
  • kJ/J mixing in Gibbs.

Chapter 6 · Topic 1

Dynamic equilibrium

Chemical EquilibriumEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 1 of 27

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Equilibrium, Dynamic equilibrium: dynamic equilibrium balances equal opposite rates with constant concentrations. At equilibrium \(Q = K\); \(K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}\). Reaction moves forward if \(Q<K\), backward if \(Q>K\). \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K\) ties \(K\) to thermodynamics; van It Hoff gives temperature dependence.
Key formula(s). \[ Le\,Chatelier:\,stress\to opposite\,shift \]
Key points.
  • Catalyst never changes \(K\), only the speed of approach.
  • Le Chatelier: pressure/utting shifts toward fewer gas moles; inert gas at constant \(P\) dilutes like expansion.
  • For \(N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2\) with degree \(\alpha\): \(K_p = 4\alpha^2P/(1-\alpha^2)\).
  • Pure solids/liquids are omitted from \(K\) and \(Q\) expressions.
Example 1.

For \(H_2 + I_2 \rightleftharpoons 2HI\), \(K_c = 50\). Start with \(1\,M\) each of \(H_2, I_2\). Find \([HI]\) at equilibrium.

  1. Let \(x\) reacted: \(K_c = (2x)^2/(1-x)^2 = 50\), so \(2x/(1-x) = 7.07\).
  2. \(x = 7.07/9.07 \approx 0.78\); \([HI] = 1.56\,M\).

Answer: About \(1.56\,M\,HI\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(PCl_5\) dissociates \(40\%\) at total pressure \(2\,atm\). Find \(K_p\).

  1. \(K_p = 4\alpha^2P/(1-\alpha^2) = 4(0.16)(2)/(0.84)\).
  2. \(K_p \approx 1.52\,atm\).

Answer: \(1.52\,atm\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Writing \(K_p\) with wrong \(\Delta n_g\) sign.
  • Including solids (e.g. \(CaCO_3\)) in the equilibrium expression.

Index / Energy & Equilibrium
Chapter 6 · Topic 2

Characteristics of equilibrium

Chemical EquilibriumEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 2 of 27

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Equilibrium, Characteristics of equilibrium: equilibrium is dynamic, needs closed vessels, and keeps K fixed at fixed T. At equilibrium \(Q = K\); \(K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}\). Reaction moves forward if \(Q<K\), backward if \(Q>K\). \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K\) ties \(K\) to thermodynamics; van It Hoff gives temperature dependence.
Key formula(s). \[ \Delta G^\circ=-RT\ln K,\;\ln\frac{K_2}{K_1}=-\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2}-\frac{1}{T_1}\right) \]
Key points.
  • Le Chatelier: pressure/utting shifts toward fewer gas moles; inert gas at constant \(P\) dilutes like expansion.
  • For \(N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2\) with degree \(\alpha\): \(K_p = 4\alpha^2P/(1-\alpha^2)\).
  • Pure solids/liquids are omitted from \(K\) and \(Q\) expressions.
  • Catalyst never changes \(K\), only the speed of approach.
Example 1.

\(\Delta G^\circ = -30\,kJ\) at \(300\,K\). Find \(K\).

  1. \(\ln K = 30000/(8.314\times300) = 12.03\).
  2. \(K = e^{12.03} \approx 1.68\times10^5\).

Answer: About \(1.7\times10^5\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(N_2 + O_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NO\) is endothermic. What happens to \(K\) on heating?

  1. Heat favours the endothermic (forward) side.
  2. \(K\) increases with \(T\).

Answer: \(K\) increases.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Writing \(K_p\) with wrong \(\Delta n_g\) sign.
  • Including solids (e.g. \(CaCO_3\)) in the equilibrium expression.
Back to Index
Index / Energy & Equilibrium
Chapter 6 · Topic 3

Physical equilibrium

Chemical EquilibriumEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 3 of 27

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Equilibrium, Physical equilibrium: phase equilibria like liquid-vapour balance rates at fixed vapour pressure. At equilibrium \(Q = K\); \(K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}\). Reaction moves forward if \(Q<K\), backward if \(Q>K\). \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K\) ties \(K\) to thermodynamics; van It Hoff gives temperature dependence.
Key formula(s). \[ \ln\frac{K_2}{K_1}=-\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2}-\frac{1}{T_1}\right),\;Q<K\to forward \]
Key points.
  • Pure solids/liquids are omitted from \(K\) and \(Q\) expressions.
  • Catalyst never changes \(K\), only the speed of approach.
  • Le Chatelier: pressure/utting shifts toward fewer gas moles; inert gas at constant \(P\) dilutes like expansion.
  • For \(N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2\) with degree \(\alpha\): \(K_p = 4\alpha^2P/(1-\alpha^2)\).
Example 1.

For \(N_2+3H_2\rightleftharpoons2NH_3\), \(K_c = 0.5\) at some \(T\). Find \(K_p\) at \(700\,K\).

  1. \(\Delta n_g = 2-4 = -2\).
  2. \(K_p = 0.5\times(0.0821\times700)^{-2} = 0.5/(57.47)^2 \approx 1.51\times10^{-4}\).

Answer: About \(1.5\times10^{-4}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(1\,mol\,N_2O_4\) dissociates \(20\%\) at total pressure \(1\,atm\). Find \(K_p\).

  1. \(\alpha = 0.2\); \(K_p = 4(0.04)(1)/(1-0.04) = 0.16/0.96\).
  2. \(K_p \approx 0.167\,atm\).

Answer: About \(0.167\,atm\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Writing \(K_p\) with wrong \(\Delta n_g\) sign.
  • Including solids (e.g. \(CaCO_3\)) in the equilibrium expression.

For \(H_2 + I_2 \rightleftharpoons 2HI\), \(K_c = 50\). Start with \(1\,M\) each of \(H_2, I_2\). Find \([HI]\) at equilibrium.

  1. Let \(x\) reacted: \(K_c = (2x)^2/(1-x)^2 = 50\), so \(2x/(1-x) = 7.07\).
  2. \(x = 7.07/9.07 \approx 0.78\); \([HI] = 1.56\,M\).

Answer: About \(1.56\,M\,HI\).

(JEE pattern) \(PCl_5\) dissociates \(40\%\) at total pressure \(2\,atm\). Find \(K_p\).

  1. \(K_p = 4\alpha^2P/(1-\alpha^2) = 4(0.16)(2)/(0.84)\).

Chapter 6 · Topic 11

Homogeneous equilibrium

Chemical EquilibriumEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 11 of 27

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Equilibrium, Homogeneous equilibrium: homogeneous equilibria keep every player in one phase. At equilibrium \(Q = K\); \(K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}\). Reaction moves forward if \(Q<K\), backward if \(Q>K\). \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K\) ties \(K\) to thermodynamics; van It Hoff gives temperature dependence.
Key formula(s). \[ Q<K\to forward,\;Q>K\to backward,\;K_p=\frac{4\alpha^2P}{1-\alpha^2}\,(dissociation) \]
Key points.
  • Le Chatelier: pressure/utting shifts toward fewer gas moles; inert gas at constant \(P\) dilutes like expansion.
  • For \(N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2\) with degree \(\alpha\): \(K_p = 4\alpha^2P/(1-\alpha^2)\).
  • Pure solids/liquids are omitted from \(K\) and \(Q\) expressions.
  • Catalyst never changes \(K\), only the speed of approach.
Example 1.

\(\Delta G^\circ = -30\,kJ\) at \(300\,K\). Find \(K\).

  1. \(\ln K = 30000/(8.314\times300) = 12.03\).
  2. \(K = e^{12.03} \approx 1.68\times10^5\).

Answer: About \(1.7\times10^5\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(N_2 + O_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NO\) is endothermic. What happens to \(K\) on heating?

  1. Heat favours the endothermic (forward) side.
  2. \(K\) increases with \(T\).

Answer: \(K\) increases.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Writing \(K_p\) with wrong \(\Delta n_g\) sign.
  • Including solids (e.g. \(CaCO_3\)) in the equilibrium expression.

Answer: About \(1.7\times10^5\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(N_2 + O_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NO\) is endothermic. What happens to \(K\) on heating?

  1. Heat favours the endothermic (forward) side.
  2. \(K\) increases with \(T\).

Answer: \(K\) increases.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Writing \(K_p\) with wrong \(\Delta n_g\) sign.
  • Including solids (e.g. \(CaCO_3\)) in the equilibrium expression.

Chapter 6 · Topic 24

Relationship of K with thermodynamics

Chemical EquilibriumEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 24 of 27

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Equilibrium, Relationship of K with thermodynamics: Delta-G-zero equals -RT ln K, wedding kinetics-free thermo to K. At equilibrium \(Q = K\); \(K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}\). Reaction moves forward if \(Q<K\), backward if \(Q>K\). \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K\) ties \(K\) to thermodynamics; van It Hoff gives temperature dependence.
Key formula(s). \[ K_p=K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g},\;\Delta G^\circ=-RT\ln K,\;\ln\frac{K_2}{K_1}=-\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2}-\frac{1}{T_1}\right),\;Q<K\to forward \]
Key points.
  • Pure solids/liquids are omitted from \(K\) and \(Q\) expressions.
  • Catalyst never changes \(K\), only the speed of approach.
  • Le Chatelier: pressure/utting shifts toward fewer gas moles; inert gas at constant \(P\) dilutes like expansion.
  • For \(N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2\) with degree \(\alpha\): \(K_p = 4\alpha^2P/(1-\alpha^2)\).
Example 1.

For \(N_2+3H_2\rightleftharpoons2NH_3\), \(K_c = 0.5\) at some \(T\). Find \(K_p\) at \(700\,K\).

  1. \(\Delta n_g = 2-4 = -2\).
  2. \(K_p = 0.5\times(0.0821\times700)^{-2} = 0.5/(57.47)^2 \approx 1.51\times10^{-4}\).

Answer: About \(1.5\times10^{-4}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(1\,mol\,N_2O_4\) dissociates \(20\%\) at total pressure \(1\,atm\). Find \(K_p\).

  1. \(\alpha = 0.2\); \(K_p = 4(0.04)(1)/(1-0.04) = 0.16/0.96\).
  2. \(K_p \approx 0.167\,atm\).

Answer: About \(0.167\,atm\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Writing \(K_p\) with wrong \(\Delta n_g\) sign.
  • Including solids (e.g. \(CaCO_3\)) in the equilibrium expression.

Chapter 6 · Topic 25

Delta-G and K

Chemical EquilibriumEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 25 of 27

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Equilibrium, Delta-G and K: large K means strongly negative Delta-G-zero. At equilibrium \(Q = K\); \(K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}\). Reaction moves forward if \(Q<K\), backward if \(Q>K\). \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K\) ties \(K\) to thermodynamics; van It Hoff gives temperature dependence.
Key formula(s). \[ K_p=K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g},\;\Delta G^\circ=-RT\ln K,\;Q<K\to forward \]
Key points.
  • Catalyst never changes \(K\), only the speed of approach.
  • Le Chatelier: pressure/utting shifts toward fewer gas moles; inert gas at constant \(P\) dilutes like expansion.
  • For \(N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2\) with degree \(\alpha\): \(K_p = 4\alpha^2P/(1-\alpha^2)\).
  • Pure solids/liquids are omitted from \(K\) and \(Q\) expressions.
Example 1.

For \(H_2 + I_2 \rightleftharpoons 2HI\), \(K_c = 50\). Start with \(1\,M\) each of \(H_2, I_2\). Find \([HI]\) at equilibrium.

  1. Let \(x\) reacted: \(K_c = (2x)^2/(1-x)^2 = 50\), so \(2x/(1-x) = 7.07\).
  2. \(x = 7.07/9.07 \approx 0.78\); \([HI] = 1.56\,M\).

Answer: About \(1.56\,M\,HI\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(PCl_5\) dissociates \(40\%\) at total pressure \(2\,atm\). Find \(K_p\).

  1. \(K_p = 4\alpha^2P/(1-\alpha^2) = 4(0.16)(2)/(0.84)\).
  2. \(K_p \approx 1.52\,atm\).

Answer: \(1.52\,atm\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Writing \(K_p\) with wrong \(\Delta n_g\) sign.
  • Including solids (e.g. \(CaCO_3\)) in the equilibrium expression.
