Chapter 7 · Topic 1

Electrolytes

Ionic EquilibriumEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 1 of 39

Explanation

Concept. In Ionic Equilibrium, Electrolytes: electrolytes conduct by mobile ions in melt or solution. \(K_w = 10^{-14}\) (25\(^\circ C\)); \(pH+pOH = 14\). Weak acid: \([H^+] = \sqrt{K_aC}\) (\(pH = \frac12(pK_a-\log C)\)); weak base mirrors with \(K_b\). Degree of ionisation \(\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}\).
Key formula(s). \[ Arrhenius:\,H^+_{aq}/OH^-_{aq},\;Bronsted:\,H^+\,donor/acceptor \]
Key points.
  • Lewis acids accept electron pairs (\(BF_3, AlCl_3\)); \(H^+\) itself is the simplest Lewis acid.
  • Polyprotic: first dissociation dominates \([H^+]\); amphiprotic \(pH = \frac12(pK_{a1}+pK_{a2})\).
  • Ostwald dilution: more dilution \(\to\) larger \(\alpha\), but \([H^+]\) still falls.
  • Conjugate pair: \(K_a\times K_b = K_w\); stronger acid \(\to\) weaker conjugate base.
Example 1.

A weak acid has \(K_a = 10^{-5}\), \(C = 0.1\,M\). Find its degree of ionisation.

  1. \(\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C} = \sqrt{10^{-4}}\).
  2. \(\alpha = 0.01\) (1\% ionised).

Answer: \(0.01\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(K_a(HCOOH) = 1.8\times10^{-4}\). Find \(K_b\) of \(HCOO^-\).

  1. \(K_a\times K_b = K_w\).
  2. \(K_b = 10^{-14}/1.8\times10^{-4} \approx 5.6\times10^{-11}\).

Answer: \(5.6\times10^{-11}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(\sqrt{K_aC}\) when \(\alpha\) is large or for strong acids.
  • Forgetting \(pK_w\) changes with temperature (\(pH<7\) neutral at higher \(T\)).
Back to Index
Index / Energy & Equilibrium
Chapter 7 · Topic 2

Strong electrolytes

Ionic EquilibriumEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 2 of 39

Explanation

Concept. In Ionic Equilibrium, Strong electrolytes: strong electrolytes ionise fully at all ordinary concentrations. \(K_w = 10^{-14}\) (25\(^\circ C\)); \(pH+pOH = 14\). Weak acid: \([H^+] = \sqrt{K_aC}\) (\(pH = \frac12(pK_a-\log C)\)); weak base mirrors with \(K_b\). Degree of ionisation \(\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}\).
Key formula(s). \[ strong:\,\alpha\approx1 \]
Key points.
  • Ostwald dilution: more dilution \(\to\) larger \(\alpha\), but \([H^+]\) still falls.
  • Conjugate pair: \(K_a\times K_b = K_w\); stronger acid \(\to\) weaker conjugate base.
  • Lewis acids accept electron pairs (\(BF_3, AlCl_3\)); \(H^+\) itself is the simplest Lewis acid.
  • Polyprotic: first dissociation dominates \([H^+]\); amphiprotic \(pH = \frac12(pK_{a1}+pK_{a2})\).
Example 1.

Find the pH of \(0.01\,M\,CH_3COOH\) (\(K_a = 1.8\times10^{-5}\)).

  1. \([H^+] = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-5}\times0.01} = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-7}} \approx 4.24\times10^{-4}\).
  2. \(pH = -\log(4.24\times10^{-4}) \approx 3.37\).

Answer: About \(3.37\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) pH of a mixture of \(50\,mL\,0.1\,M\,HCl + 50\,mL\,0.1\,M\,NaOH\)?

  1. Equal moles neutralise exactly to neutral salt solution.
  2. \(pH = 7\) (strong-strong equivalence).

Answer: \(7\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(\sqrt{K_aC}\) when \(\alpha\) is large or for strong acids.
  • Forgetting \(pK_w\) changes with temperature (\(pH<7\) neutral at higher \(T\)).
Back to Index
Index / Energy & Equilibrium
Chapter 7 · Topic 3

Weak electrolytes

Ionic EquilibriumEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 3 of 39

Explanation

Concept. In Ionic Equilibrium, Weak electrolytes: weak electrolytes ionise partly under Ostwald dilution control. \(K_w = 10^{-14}\) (25\(^\circ C\)); \(pH+pOH = 14\). Weak acid: \([H^+] = \sqrt{K_aC}\) (\(pH = \frac12(pK_a-\log C)\)); weak base mirrors with \(K_b\). Degree of ionisation \(\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}\).
Key formula(s). \[ Ostwald:\,\alpha=\sqrt{K_a/C} \]
Key points.
  • Conjugate pair: \(K_a\times K_b = K_w\); stronger acid \(\to\) weaker conjugate base.
  • Lewis acids accept electron pairs (\(BF_3, AlCl_3\)); \(H^+\) itself is the simplest Lewis acid.
  • Polyprotic: first dissociation dominates \([H^+]\); amphiprotic \(pH = \frac12(pK_{a1}+pK_{a2})\).
  • Ostwald dilution: more dilution \(\to\) larger \(\alpha\), but \([H^+]\) still falls.
Example 1.

Find the pH of \(0.01\,M\,NH_4OH\) (\(K_b = 1.8\times10^{-5}\)).

  1. \([OH^-] = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-5}\times0.01} \approx 4.24\times10^{-4}\).
  2. \(pOH \approx 3.37\), so \(pH \approx 10.63\).

Answer: About \(10.63\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Estimate the pH of \(10^{-8}\,M\,HCl\).

  1. Below \(10^{-6}\,M\), water's own \(H^+\) matters: total \([H^+] \approx 1.05\times10^{-7}\).
  2. \(pH \approx 6.98\) (still acidic, never above 7).

Answer: \(6.98\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(\sqrt{K_aC}\) when \(\alpha\) is large or for strong acids.
  • Forgetting \(pK_w\) changes with temperature (\(pH<7\) neutral at higher \(T\)).

Explanation

Concept. In Ionic Equilibrium, Acid dissociation constant Ka: Ka measures acid strength in water. \(K_w = 10^{-14}\) (25\(^\circ C\)); \(pH+pOH = 14\). Weak acid: \([H^+] = \sqrt{K_aC}\) (\(pH = \frac12(pK_a-\log C)\)); weak base mirrors with \(K_b\). Degree of ionisation \(\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}\).
Key formula(s). \[ pH+pOH=14,\;\alpha=\sqrt{\frac{K_a}{C}},\;Ostwald:\,\alpha=\sqrt{K_a/C} \]
Key points.
  • Conjugate pair: \(K_a\times K_b = K_w\); stronger acid \(\to\) weaker conjugate base.
  • Lewis acids accept electron pairs (\(BF_3, AlCl_3\)); \(H^+\) itself is the simplest Lewis acid.
  • Polyprotic: first dissociation dominates \([H^+]\); amphiprotic \(pH = \frac12(pK_{a1}+pK_{a2})\).
  • Ostwald dilution: more dilution \(\to\) larger \(\alpha\), but \([H^+]\) still falls.
Example 1.

Find the pH of \(0.01\,M\,NH_4OH\) (\(K_b = 1.8\times10^{-5}\)).

  1. \([OH^-] = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-5}\times0.01} \approx 4.24\times10^{-4}\).
  2. \(pOH \approx 3.37\), so \(pH \approx 10.63\).

Answer: About \(10.63\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Estimate the pH of \(10^{-8}\,M\,HCl\).

  1. Below \(10^{-6}\,M\), water's own \(H^+\) matters: total \([H^+] \approx 1.05\times10^{-7}\).
  2. \(pH \approx 6.98\) (still acidic, never above 7).

Answer: \(6.98\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(\sqrt{K_aC}\) when \(\alpha\) is large or for strong acids.
  • Forgetting \(pK_w\) changes with temperature (\(pH<7\) neutral at higher \(T\)).

Chapter 7 · Topic 19

Salt hydrolysis

Ionic EquilibriumEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 19 of 39

Explanation

Concept. In Ionic Equilibrium, Salt hydrolysis: salts of weak partners hydrolyse and tilt pH off seven. Buffers resist pH change: acidic \(pH = pK_a+\log(salt/acid)\), basic \(pOH = pK_b+\log(salt/base)\). Salts hydrolyse (\(pH\) from \(K_h = K_w/K_a\) etc.). Precipitate forms when ionic product \(> K_{sp}\); selective precipitation separates ions by \(K_{sp}\) gap.
Key formula(s). \[ pH=pK_a+\log\frac{[salt]}{[acid]},\;weak\,salt:\,pH=\frac12(pK_w+pK_a+\log C) \]
Key points.
  • Solubility: \(AgCl\): \(s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}\); \(CaF_2\): \(s=(K_{sp}/4)^{1/3}\).
  • Common ion suppresses solubility and weak-electrolyte ionisation.
  • Maximum buffer capacity at \([salt]=[acid]\) (\(pH = pK_a\)).
  • Salt pH: strong-strong \(\to 7\); weak-acid+strong-base \(\to >7\); strong-acid+weak-base \(\to <7\).
Example 1.

Ammonia buffer: \([base] = [salt] = 0.1\,M\), \(pK_b = 4.74\). Find pH.

  1. \(pOH = pK_b + \log1 = 4.74\).
  2. \(pH = 14 - 4.74 = 9.26\).

Answer: \(9.26\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Will \(PbCl_2\) (\(K_{sp} = 1.7\times10^{-5}\)) precipitate if \([Pb^{2+}] = 0.01\,M\), \([Cl^-] = 0.1\,M\)?

  1. \(Q = 0.01\times(0.1)^2 = 1.0\times10^{-4} > K_{sp}\).
  2. Yes, it precipitates.

Answer: Yes (\(Q > K_{sp}\)).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using concentrations instead of the salt/acid ratio after reaction (recompute moles first).
  • Wrong \(s\)-\(K_{sp}\) exponent for \(A_xB_y\) salts.

Explanation

Precipitate forms when ionic product \(> K_{sp}\); selective precipitation separates ions by \(K_{sp}\) gap.
Key formula(s). \[ K_h=K_w/K_a\,(hydrolysis),\;weak\,salt:\,pH=\frac12(pK_w+pK_a+\log C) \]
Key points.
  • Maximum buffer capacity at \([salt]=[acid]\) (\(pH = pK_a\)).
  • Salt pH: strong-strong \(\to 7\); weak-acid+strong-base \(\to >7\); strong-acid+weak-base \(\to <7\).
  • Solubility: \(AgCl\): \(s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}\); \(CaF_2\): \(s=(K_{sp}/4)^{1/3}\).
  • Common ion suppresses solubility and weak-electrolyte ionisation.
Example 1.

Buffer has \([salt]=[acid]=0.1\,M\), \(pK_a = 4.74\). Find pH; what if \(0.01\,mol\,HCl\) is added per litre?

  1. Initial \(pH = 4.74+\log1 = 4.74\).
  2. Adding acid: salt \(0.09\), acid \(0.11\); \(pH = 4.74+\log(0.09/0.11) \approx 4.65\). Tiny shift proves buffering.

Answer: \(4.74 \to\) about \(4.65\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(K_{sp}(AgCl) = 1.8\times10^{-10}\). Find solubility in \(mol/L\) and in pure water vs \(0.1\,M\,NaCl\).

  1. Pure: \(s = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-10}} \approx 1.34\times10^{-5}\,M\).
  2. In \(0.1\,M\,Cl^-\): \(s = K_{sp}/0.1 = 1.8\times10^{-9}\,M\) (suppressed).

Answer: \(1.34\times10^{-5}\,M\) pure; \(1.8\times10^{-9}\,M\) in common ion.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using concentrations instead of the salt/acid ratio after reaction (recompute moles first).
  • Wrong \(s\)-\(K_{sp}\) exponent for \(A_xB_y\) salts.

Chapter 7 · Topic 22

Buffer solutions

Ionic EquilibriumEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 22 of 39

Explanation

Concept. In Ionic Equilibrium, Buffer solutions: buffers swallow small acid or base doses with tiny pH moves. Buffers resist pH change: acidic \(pH = pK_a+\log(salt/acid)\), basic \(pOH = pK_b+\log(salt/base)\). Salts hydrolyse (\(pH\) from \(K_h = K_w/K_a\) etc.). Precipitate forms when ionic product \(> K_{sp}\); selective precipitation separates ions by \(K_{sp}\) gap.
Key formula(s). \[ pH=pK_a+\log\frac{[salt]}{[acid]},\;K_h=K_w/K_a\,(hydrolysis),\;weak\,salt:\,pH=\frac12(pK_w+pK_a+\log C) \]
Key points.
  • Solubility: \(AgCl\): \(s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}\); \(CaF_2\): \(s=(K_{sp}/4)^{1/3}\).
  • Common ion suppresses solubility and weak-electrolyte ionisation.
  • Maximum buffer capacity at \([salt]=[acid]\) (\(pH = pK_a\)).
  • Salt pH: strong-strong \(\to 7\); weak-acid+strong-base \(\to >7\); strong-acid+weak-base \(\to <7\).
Example 1.

Ammonia buffer: \([base] = [salt] = 0.1\,M\), \(pK_b = 4.74\). Find pH.

  1. \(pOH = pK_b + \log1 = 4.74\).
  2. \(pH = 14 - 4.74 = 9.26\).

Answer: \(9.26\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Will \(PbCl_2\) (\(K_{sp} = 1.7\times10^{-5}\)) precipitate if \([Pb^{2+}] = 0.01\,M\), \([Cl^-] = 0.1\,M\)?

  1. \(Q = 0.01\times(0.1)^2 = 1.0\times10^{-4} > K_{sp}\).
  2. Yes, it precipitates.

Answer: Yes (\(Q > K_{sp}\)).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using concentrations instead of the salt/acid ratio after reaction (recompute moles first).
  • Wrong \(s\)-\(K_{sp}\) exponent for \(A_xB_y\) salts.

Chapter 7 · Topic 23

Acidic buffer

Ionic EquilibriumEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 23 of 39

Explanation

Concept. In Ionic Equilibrium, Acidic buffer: acidic buffers pair a weak acid with its salt near pKa. Buffers resist pH change: acidic \(pH = pK_a+\log(salt/acid)\), basic \(pOH = pK_b+\log(salt/base)\). Salts hydrolyse (\(pH\) from \(K_h = K_w/K_a\) etc.). Precipitate forms when ionic product \(> K_{sp}\); selective precipitation separates ions by \(K_{sp}\) gap.
Key formula(s). \[ pH=pK_a+\log\frac{[salt]}{[acid]},\;s=\left(\frac{K_{sp}}{x^xy^y}\right)^{\frac{1}{x+y}},\;weak\,salt:\,pH=\frac12(pK_w+pK_a+\log C) \]
Key points.
  • Maximum buffer capacity at \([salt]=[acid]\) (\(pH = pK_a\)).
  • Salt pH: strong-strong \(\to 7\); weak-acid+strong-base \(\to >7\); strong-acid+weak-base \(\to <7\).
  • Solubility: \(AgCl\): \(s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}\); \(CaF_2\): \(s=(K_{sp}/4)^{1/3}\).
  • Common ion suppresses solubility and weak-electrolyte ionisation.
Example 1.

Buffer has \([salt]=[acid]=0.1\,M\), \(pK_a = 4.74\). Find pH; what if \(0.01\,mol\,HCl\) is added per litre?

  1. Initial \(pH = 4.74+\log1 = 4.74\).
  2. Adding acid: salt \(0.09\), acid \(0.11\); \(pH = 4.74+\log(0.09/0.11) \approx 4.65\). Tiny shift proves buffering.

Answer: \(4.74 \to\) about \(4.65\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(K_{sp}(AgCl) = 1.8\times10^{-10}\). Find solubility in \(mol/L\) and in pure water vs \(0.1\,M\,NaCl\).

  1. Pure: \(s = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-10}} \approx 1.34\times10^{-5}\,M\).
  2. In \(0.1\,M\,Cl^-\): \(s = K_{sp}/0.1 = 1.8\times10^{-9}\,M\) (suppressed).

Answer: \(1.34\times10^{-5}\,M\) pure; \(1.8\times10^{-9}\,M\) in common ion.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using concentrations instead of the salt/acid ratio after reaction (recompute moles first).
  • Wrong \(s\)-\(K_{sp}\) exponent for \(A_xB_y\) salts.

Precipitate forms when ionic product \(> K_{sp}\); selective precipitation separates ions by \(K_{sp}\) gap.
Key formula(s). \[ pH=pK_a+\log\frac{[salt]}{[acid]},\;s=\left(\frac{K_{sp}}{x^xy^y}\right)^{\frac{1}{x+y}},\;Q>K_{sp}\,\Rightarrow\,ppt \]
Key points.
  • Solubility: \(AgCl\): \(s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}\); \(CaF_2\): \(s=(K_{sp}/4)^{1/3}\).
  • Common ion suppresses solubility and weak-electrolyte ionisation.
  • Maximum buffer capacity at \([salt]=[acid]\) (\(pH = pK_a\)).
  • Salt pH: strong-strong \(\to 7\); weak-acid+strong-base \(\to >7\); strong-acid+weak-base \(\to <7\).
Example 1.

Ammonia buffer: \([base] = [salt] = 0.1\,M\), \(pK_b = 4.74\). Find pH.

  1. \(pOH = pK_b + \log1 = 4.74\).
  2. \(pH = 14 - 4.74 = 9.26\).

Answer: \(9.26\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Will \(PbCl_2\) (\(K_{sp} = 1.7\times10^{-5}\)) precipitate if \([Pb^{2+}] = 0.01\,M\), \([Cl^-] = 0.1\,M\)?

  1. \(Q = 0.01\times(0.1)^2 = 1.0\times10^{-4} > K_{sp}\).
  2. Yes, it precipitates.

Answer: Yes (\(Q > K_{sp}\)).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using concentrations instead of the salt/acid ratio after reaction (recompute moles first).
  • Wrong \(s\)-\(K_{sp}\) exponent for \(A_xB_y\) salts.

Chapter 7 · Topic 35

Titration curves

Ionic EquilibriumEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 35 of 39

Explanation

Concept. In Ionic Equilibrium, Titration curves: titration curves plot pH versus titrant with jumps at equivalence. Buffers resist pH change: acidic \(pH = pK_a+\log(salt/acid)\), basic \(pOH = pK_b+\log(salt/base)\). Salts hydrolyse (\(pH\) from \(K_h = K_w/K_a\) etc.). Precipitate forms when ionic product \(> K_{sp}\); selective precipitation separates ions by \(K_{sp}\) gap.
Key formula(s). \[ jump\,at\,equivalence \]
Key points.
  • Maximum buffer capacity at \([salt]=[acid]\) (\(pH = pK_a\)).
  • Salt pH: strong-strong \(\to 7\); weak-acid+strong-base \(\to >7\); strong-acid+weak-base \(\to <7\).
  • Solubility: \(AgCl\): \(s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}\); \(CaF_2\): \(s=(K_{sp}/4)^{1/3}\).
  • Common ion suppresses solubility and weak-electrolyte ionisation.
Example 1.

Buffer has \([salt]=[acid]=0.1\,M\), \(pK_a = 4.74\). Find pH; what if \(0.01\,mol\,HCl\) is added per litre?

  1. Initial \(pH = 4.74+\log1 = 4.74\).
  2. Adding acid: salt \(0.09\), acid \(0.11\); \(pH = 4.74+\log(0.09/0.11) \approx 4.65\). Tiny shift proves buffering.

Answer: \(4.74 \to\) about \(4.65\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(K_{sp}(AgCl) = 1.8\times10^{-10}\). Find solubility in \(mol/L\) and in pure water vs \(0.1\,M\,NaCl\).

  1. Pure: \(s = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-10}} \approx 1.34\times10^{-5}\,M\).
  2. In \(0.1\,M\,Cl^-\): \(s = K_{sp}/0.1 = 1.8\times10^{-9}\,M\) (suppressed).

Answer: \(1.34\times10^{-5}\,M\) pure; \(1.8\times10^{-9}\,M\) in common ion.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using concentrations instead of the salt/acid ratio after reaction (recompute moles first).
  • Wrong \(s\)-\(K_{sp}\) exponent for \(A_xB_y\) salts.

Explanation

Key formula(s). \[ pH=pK_a+\log\frac{[salt]}{[acid]},\;s=\left(\frac{K_{sp}}{x^xy^y}\right)^{\frac{1}{x+y}},\;K_h=K_w/K_a\,(hydrolysis),\;weak\,salt:\,pH=\frac12(pK_w+pK_a+\log C) \]
Key points.
  • Salt pH: strong-strong \(\to 7\); weak-acid+strong-base \(\to >7\); strong-acid+weak-base \(\to <7\).

Example 1.

Acetic buffer has \([salt] = 0.2\,M\), \([acid] = 0.1\,M\), \(pK_a = 4.74\). Find pH.

  1. Ratio \(= 2\).
  2. \(pH = 4.74 + \log2 = 4.74 + 0.30 = 5.04\).

Answer: \(5.04\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(K_{sp}(AgBr) = 5.0\times10^{-13}\). Find its solubility.

  1. \(AgBr \to Ag^+ + Br^-\): \(s = \sqrt{K_{sp}}\).
  2. \(s = \sqrt{5.0\times10^{-13}} \approx 7.07\times10^{-7}\,M\).

Answer: \(7.07\times10^{-7}\,M\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using concentrations instead of the salt/acid ratio after reaction (recompute moles first).
  • Wrong \(s\)-\(K_{sp}\) exponent for \(A_xB_y\) salts.

pH of 0.001 M HCl?

Answer: 3.

(JEE pattern) Will AgCl (Ksp 1.8e-10) precipitate if [Ag+]=[Cl-]=2e-5 M?

  1. Q = 4e-10 > Ksp.
  2. Yes, precipitates.

Answer: Yes.

Chapter 8 · Topic 1

Oxidation and reduction

Redox ReactionsElectro & KineticsTopic 1 of 23

Explanation

Concept. In Redox Reactions, Oxidation and reduction: oxidation loses electrons as reduction gains them. Oxidation number tracks electron control; oxidation \(=\) increase, reduction \(=\) decrease. Balance by oxidation-number or ion-electron (half-reaction) method; in base, neutralise \(H^+\) with \(OH^-\) at the end. n-factor \(=\) electrons exchanged per molecule.
Key formula(s). \[ oxidation:\,lose\,e^-,\;reduction:\,gain\,e^- \]
Key points.
  • Standard numbers: \(O\) usually \(-2\) (peroxide \(-1\), superoxide \(-1/2\), \(OF_2\) \(+2\)); \(H\) \(+1\) (hydride \(-1\)); F always \(-1\).
  • Disproportionation: same element oxidised AND reduced (e.g. \(Cl_2\to Cl^-+ClO^-\)); comproportionation is the reverse.
  • Acidic balance: \(H_2O\) then \(H^+\); basic: finish by adding \(OH^-\) to both sides.
  • Equivalent mass changes with product: \(KMnO_4\) acidic \(M/5\), neutral \(M/3\), basic \(M/1\).
Example 1.

Find the oxidation number of \(Cr\) in \(K_2Cr_2O_7\) and \(S\) in \(Na_2S_2O_3\).

  1. \(2(+1)+2x+7(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +6\) for \(Cr\).
  2. \(2(+1)+2x+3(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +2\) average for \(S\) (inner \(+6\)/outer \(-2\) actually).

Answer: \(Cr = +6\); average \(S = +2\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Balance \(MnO_4^-+Fe^{2+}\to Mn^{2+}+Fe^{3+}\) in acidic medium and give the mole ratio.

  1. \(Mn\) gains \(5e^-\); \(Fe\) loses \(1e^-\); multiply Fe half-reaction by \(5\).
  2. Balanced: \(MnO_4^-+5Fe^{2+}+8H^+\to Mn^{2+}+5Fe^{3+}+4H_2O\); ratio \(1:5\).

Answer: \(1\,MnO_4^- : 5\,Fe^{2+}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Assigning \(O = -2\) in peroxides/superoxides.
  • Leaving \(H^+/OH^-\) unbalanced when switching medium.

Chapter 8 · Topic 2

Oxidation number

Redox ReactionsElectro & KineticsTopic 2 of 23

Explanation

Concept. In Redox Reactions, Oxidation number: oxidation number tracks electron control per atom. Oxidation number tracks electron control; oxidation \(=\) increase, reduction \(=\) decrease. Balance by oxidation-number or ion-electron (half-reaction) method; in base, neutralise \(H^+\) with \(OH^-\) at the end. n-factor \(=\) electrons exchanged per molecule.
Key formula(s). \[ oxidation:\,lose\,e^- \]
Key points.
  • Disproportionation: same element oxidised AND reduced (e.g. \(Cl_2\to Cl^-+ClO^-\)); comproportionation is the reverse.
  • Acidic balance: \(H_2O\) then \(H^+\); basic: finish by adding \(OH^-\) to both sides.
  • Equivalent mass changes with product: \(KMnO_4\) acidic \(M/5\), neutral \(M/3\), basic \(M/1\).
  • Standard numbers: \(O\) usually \(-2\) (peroxide \(-1\), superoxide \(-1/2\), \(OF_2\) \(+2\)); \(H\) \(+1\) (hydride \(-1\)); F always \(-1\).
Example 1.

Find the oxidation number of oxygen in \(H_2O_2\).

  1. \(2(+1) + 2x = 0\).
  2. \(x = -1\) (peroxide, not \(-2\)).

Answer: \(-1\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Balance \(Cr_2O_7^{2-} + Fe^{2+} \to Cr^{3+} + Fe^{3+}\) in acid; give the mole ratio.

  1. \(Cr\) gains \(6e^-\); each \(Fe\) loses \(1e^-\).
  2. \(Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 6Fe^{2+} + 14H^+ \to 2Cr^{3+} + 6Fe^{3+} + 7H_2O\) (1:6).

Answer: \(1:6\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Assigning \(O = -2\) in peroxides/superoxides.
  • Leaving \(H^+/OH^-\) unbalanced when switching medium.

Chapter 8 · Topic 3

Rules for oxidation number

Redox ReactionsElectro & KineticsTopic 3 of 23

Explanation

Concept. In Redox Reactions, Rules for oxidation number: fluorine is always -1, oxygen usually -2, hydrogen usually +1. Oxidation number tracks electron control; oxidation \(=\) increase, reduction \(=\) decrease. Balance by oxidation-number or ion-electron (half-reaction) method; in base, neutralise \(H^+\) with \(OH^-\) at the end. n-factor \(=\) electrons exchanged per molecule.
Key formula(s). \[ oxidation:\,lose\,e^-,\;x_H=+1\,(not\,hydride) \]
Key points.
  • Acidic balance: \(H_2O\) then \(H^+\); basic: finish by adding \(OH^-\) to both sides.
  • Equivalent mass changes with product: \(KMnO_4\) acidic \(M/5\), neutral \(M/3\), basic \(M/1\).
  • Standard numbers: \(O\) usually \(-2\) (peroxide \(-1\), superoxide \(-1/2\), \(OF_2\) \(+2\)); \(H\) \(+1\) (hydride \(-1\)); F always \(-1\).
  • Disproportionation: same element oxidised AND reduced (e.g. \(Cl_2\to Cl^-+ClO^-\)); comproportionation is the reverse.
Example 1.

Find the oxidation number of sulphur in \(H_2SO_4\).

  1. \(2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0\).
  2. \(x = +6\).

Answer: \(+6\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) What is the n-factor of \(KMnO_4\) in neutral medium (\(MnO_4^- \to MnO_2\))?

  1. \(Mn\) goes \(+7 \to +4\): \(3\) electrons.
  2. \(x = 3\) (vs \(5\) in acid).

Answer: \(3\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Assigning \(O = -2\) in peroxides/superoxides.
  • Leaving \(H^+/OH^-\) unbalanced when switching medium.

Chapter 8 · Topic 8

Balancing redox reactions

Redox ReactionsElectro & KineticsTopic 8 of 23

Explanation

Concept. In Redox Reactions, Balancing redox reactions: redox balance conserves atoms and charge together. Oxidation number tracks electron control; oxidation \(=\) increase, reduction \(=\) decrease. Balance by oxidation-number or ion-electron (half-reaction) method; in base, neutralise \(H^+\) with \(OH^-\) at the end. n-factor \(=\) electrons exchanged per molecule.
Key formula(s). \[ x_{Mn}(KMnO_4,acidic)=5,\;E=M/x \]
Key points.
  • Disproportionation: same element oxidised AND reduced (e.g. \(Cl_2\to Cl^-+ClO^-\)); comproportionation is the reverse.
  • Acidic balance: \(H_2O\) then \(H^+\); basic: finish by adding \(OH^-\) to both sides.
  • Equivalent mass changes with product: \(KMnO_4\) acidic \(M/5\), neutral \(M/3\), basic \(M/1\).
  • Standard numbers: \(O\) usually \(-2\) (peroxide \(-1\), superoxide \(-1/2\), \(OF_2\) \(+2\)); \(H\) \(+1\) (hydride \(-1\)); F always \(-1\).
Example 1.

Find the oxidation number of oxygen in \(H_2O_2\).

  1. \(2(+1) + 2x = 0\).
  2. \(x = -1\) (peroxide, not \(-2\)).

Answer: \(-1\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Balance \(Cr_2O_7^{2-} + Fe^{2+} \to Cr^{3+} + Fe^{3+}\) in acid; give the mole ratio.

  1. \(Cr\) gains \(6e^-\); each \(Fe\) loses \(1e^-\).
  2. \(Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 6Fe^{2+} + 14H^+ \to 2Cr^{3+} + 6Fe^{3+} + 7H_2O\) (1:6).

Answer: \(1:6\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Assigning \(O = -2\) in peroxides/superoxides.
  • Leaving \(H^+/OH^-\) unbalanced when switching medium.

Find the oxidation number of sulphur in \(H_2SO_4\).

  1. \(2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0\).
  2. \(x = +6\).

Answer: \(+6\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) What is the n-factor of \(KMnO_4\) in neutral medium (\(MnO_4^- \to MnO_2\))?

Ion-electron method

Redox ReactionsElectro & KineticsTopic 10 of 23

Explanation

Concept. In Redox Reactions, Ion-electron method: half-reaction method balances O with water and H with protons. Oxidation number tracks electron control; oxidation \(=\) increase, reduction \(=\) decrease. Balance by oxidation-number or ion-electron (half-reaction) method; in base, neutralise \(H^+\) with \(OH^-\) at the end. n-factor \(=\) electrons exchanged per molecule.
Key formula(s). \[ x_{I_2}=2,\;E=M/x \]
Key points.
  • Standard numbers: \(O\) usually \(-2\) (peroxide \(-1\), superoxide \(-1/2\), \(OF_2\) \(+2\)); \(H\) \(+1\) (hydride \(-1\)); F always \(-1\).

  1. \(2(+1)+2x+7(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +6\) for \(Cr\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Balance \(MnO_4^-+Fe^{2+}\to Mn^{2+}+Fe^{3+}\) in acidic medium and give the mole ratio.

  2. Balanced: \(MnO_4^-+5Fe^{2+}+8H^+\to Mn^{2+}+5Fe^{3+}+4H_2O\); ratio \(1:5\).

Answer: \(1\,MnO_4^- : 5\,Fe^{2+}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Assigning \(O = -2\) in peroxides/superoxides.
  • Leaving \(H^+/OH^-\) unbalanced when switching medium.

Find the oxidation number of oxygen in \(H_2O_2\).

  1. \(2(+1) + 2x = 0\).
  2. \(x = -1\) (peroxide, not \(-2\)).

Answer: \(-1\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Balance \(Cr_2O_7^{2-} + Fe^{2+} \to Cr^{3+} + Fe^{3+}\) in acid; give the mole ratio.

  1. \(Cr\) gains \(6e^-\); each \(Fe\) loses \(1e^-\).
  2. \(Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 6Fe^{2+} + 14H^+ \to 2Cr^{3+} + 6Fe^{3+} + 7H_2O\) (1:6).

Answer: \(1:6\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Assigning \(O = -2\) in peroxides/superoxides.
  • Leaving \(H^+/OH^-\) unbalanced when switching medium.

Index / Electro & Kinetics
Chapter 8 · Topic 21

Redox stoichiometry

Redox ReactionsElectro & KineticsTopic 21 of 23

Explanation

Concept. In Redox Reactions, Redox stoichiometry: redox stoichiometry balances electrons first, then spends the mole ratio on products. Oxidation number tracks electron control; oxidation \(=\) increase, reduction \(=\) decrease. Balance by oxidation-number or ion-electron (half-reaction) method; in base, neutralise \(H^+\) with \(OH^-\) at the end. n-factor \(=\) electrons exchanged per molecule.
Key formula(s). \[ x_{Mn}(KMnO_4,acidic)=5,\;E=M/x,\;reduction:\,gain\,e^-,\;x_O=-2\,(not\,peroxide) \]
Key points.
  • Acidic balance: \(H_2O\) then \(H^+\); basic: finish by adding \(OH^-\) to both sides.
  • Equivalent mass changes with product: \(KMnO_4\) acidic \(M/5\), neutral \(M/3\), basic \(M/1\).
  • Standard numbers: \(O\) usually \(-2\) (peroxide \(-1\), superoxide \(-1/2\), \(OF_2\) \(+2\)); \(H\) \(+1\) (hydride \(-1\)); F always \(-1\).
  • Disproportionation: same element oxidised AND reduced (e.g. \(Cl_2\to Cl^-+ClO^-\)); comproportionation is the reverse.
Example 1.

Find the oxidation number of sulphur in \(H_2SO_4\).

  1. \(2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0\).
  2. \(x = +6\).

Answer: \(+6\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) What is the n-factor of \(KMnO_4\) in neutral medium (\(MnO_4^- \to MnO_2\))?

  1. \(Mn\) goes \(+7 \to +4\): \(3\) electrons.
  2. \(x = 3\) (vs \(5\) in acid).

Answer: \(3\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Assigning \(O = -2\) in peroxides/superoxides.
  • Leaving \(H^+/OH^-\) unbalanced when switching medium.
Back to Index
Index / Electro & Kinetics
Chapter 8 · Topic 22

Mixed oxidation states

Redox ReactionsElectro & KineticsTopic 22 of 23

Explanation

Concept. In Redox Reactions, Mixed oxidation states: mixed states average the individual oxidation numbers. Oxidation number tracks electron control; oxidation \(=\) increase, reduction \(=\) decrease. Balance by oxidation-number or ion-electron (half-reaction) method; in base, neutralise \(H^+\) with \(OH^-\) at the end. n-factor \(=\) electrons exchanged per molecule.
Key formula(s). \[ oxidation:\,lose\,e^-,\;x_O=-2\,(not\,peroxide) \]
Key points.
  • Standard numbers: \(O\) usually \(-2\) (peroxide \(-1\), superoxide \(-1/2\), \(OF_2\) \(+2\)); \(H\) \(+1\) (hydride \(-1\)); F always \(-1\).
  • Disproportionation: same element oxidised AND reduced (e.g. \(Cl_2\to Cl^-+ClO^-\)); comproportionation is the reverse.
  • Acidic balance: \(H_2O\) then \(H^+\); basic: finish by adding \(OH^-\) to both sides.
  • Equivalent mass changes with product: \(KMnO_4\) acidic \(M/5\), neutral \(M/3\), basic \(M/1\).
Example 1.

Find the oxidation number of \(Cr\) in \(K_2Cr_2O_7\) and \(S\) in \(Na_2S_2O_3\).

  1. \(2(+1)+2x+7(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +6\) for \(Cr\).
  2. \(2(+1)+2x+3(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +2\) average for \(S\) (inner \(+6\)/outer \(-2\) actually).

Answer: \(Cr = +6\); average \(S = +2\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Balance \(MnO_4^-+Fe^{2+}\to Mn^{2+}+Fe^{3+}\) in acidic medium and give the mole ratio.

  1. \(Mn\) gains \(5e^-\); \(Fe\) loses \(1e^-\); multiply Fe half-reaction by \(5\).
  2. Balanced: \(MnO_4^-+5Fe^{2+}+8H^+\to Mn^{2+}+5Fe^{3+}+4H_2O\); ratio \(1:5\).

Answer: \(1\,MnO_4^- : 5\,Fe^{2+}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Assigning \(O = -2\) in peroxides/superoxides.
  • Leaving \(H^+/OH^-\) unbalanced when switching medium.

Chapter 8 · Topic 23

Equivalent relationship in redox

Redox ReactionsElectro & KineticsTopic 23 of 23

Explanation

Concept. In Redox Reactions, Equivalent relationship in redox: equivalents of oxidant equal equivalents of reductant at endpoint. This Redox topic assigns oxidation numbers, counts exchanged electrons as the n-factor, and balances by oxidation-number or ion-electron method (H+ in acid, finished with OH- in base).
Key formula(s). \[ E=M/x,\;x_{MnO_4^-(acid)}=5 \]
Key points.
  • Disproportionation: same element up and down.
  • Acidic: H2O then H+; basic: add OH- last.
  • KMnO4 x depends on medium (5/3/1).
  • O is -2 except peroxide/superoxide/OF2.
Example 1.

Oxidation number of Mn in KMnO4?

  1. +1+x-8 = 0.
  2. x = +7.

Answer: +7.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) n-factor of K2Cr2O7 in acidic medium?

  1. Each Cr +6 -> +3, two Cr.
  2. x = 6.

Answer: 6.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • O = -2 in peroxides.
  • Acid n-factor used in redox.

Chapter 9 · Topic 1

Types of solutions

SolutionsStates of MatterTopic 1 of 34

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions, Types of solutions: solutions classify by solute-solvent phases from gas-in-gas to solid-in-solid. This Solutions topic classifies the mixture, fixes its concentration (molarity, molality, mole fraction, ppm), then applies Henry for gases, Raoult for vapour pressure, and i-weighted colligative laws.
Key formula(s). \[ 9\,types:\,solute/solvent\,phases \]
Key points.
  • Mole fractions sum to 1.
  • Vapour enriched in the volatile part.
  • Always multiply colligative results by i.
  • Molality uses solvent kg; molarity uses solution L.
Example 1.

2 g NaOH in 500 g water. Find molality.

  1. Moles = 0.05; solvent = 0.5 kg.
  2. m = 0.1 m.

Answer: 0.1 m.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Which has higher boiling point: 0.1 m NaCl or 0.1 m glucose?

  1. NaCl gives i about 2.
  2. NaCl boils higher.

Answer: 0.1 m NaCl.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Molarity in dT formulas.
  • Missing i for electrolytes.

2 g NaOH in 500 g water. Find molality.

  1. Moles = 0.05; solvent = 0.5 kg.
  2. m = 0.1 m.

Answer: 0.1 m.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Which has higher boiling point: 0.1 m NaCl or 0.1 m glucose?

Index / States of Matter
Chapter 9 · Topic 3

Concentration units

SolutionsStates of MatterTopic 3 of 34

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions, Concentration units: concentration units interconvert through moles, with density linking mass and volume. Molarity \(M = n/V(L)\) is temperature-dependent (volume changes); molality \(m = n/kg\,solvent\) and mole fraction are temperature-independent. Dilution obeys \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\).
Key formula(s). \[ M=\frac{n}{V(L)},\;m=\frac{n}{kg} \]
Key points.
  • Molarity uses solution volume; molality uses solvent mass in kg.
  • ppm \(= (mass\,solute/mass\,solution)\times10^6\), used for trace quantities.
  • Mole fractions in a mixture always add to \(1\).
  • On mixing: total moles conserved, \(M_{mix} = (M_1V_1+M_2V_2)/(V_1+V_2)\).
Example 1.

\(4\,g\,NaOH\) is dissolved to make \(500\,mL\) solution. Find molarity.

  1. Moles \(= 4/40 = 0.1\,mol\); volume \(= 0.5\,L\).
  2. \(M = 0.1/0.5 = 0.2\,M\).

Answer: \(0.2\,M\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) What volume of water must be added to \(200\,mL\) of \(1.5\,M\) solution to make it \(0.5\,M\)?

  1. \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2 \Rightarrow V_2 = 1.5\times200/0.5 = 600\,mL\).
  2. Water added \(= 600-200 = 400\,mL\).

Answer: \(400\,mL\) water.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using solution mass instead of solvent mass for molality.
  • Applying \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\) when a reaction occurs (use equivalents instead).
Back to Index
Index / States of Matter
Chapter 9 · Topic 4

Molarity

SolutionsStates of MatterTopic 4 of 34

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions, Molarity: molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution and shifts with temperature. Molarity \(M = n/V(L)\) is temperature-dependent (volume changes); molality \(m = n/kg\,solvent\) and mole fraction are temperature-independent. Dilution obeys \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\).
Key formula(s). \[ M=\frac{n}{V(L)},\;M_1V_1=M_2V_2 \]
Key points.
  • ppm \(= (mass\,solute/mass\,solution)\times10^6\), used for trace quantities.
  • Mole fractions in a mixture always add to \(1\).
  • On mixing: total moles conserved, \(M_{mix} = (M_1V_1+M_2V_2)/(V_1+V_2)\).
  • Molarity uses solution volume; molality uses solvent mass in kg.
Example 1.

A \(10\%\,w/w\,NaOH\) solution has density \(1.1\,g/mL\). Find its molarity.

  1. \(100\,g\) solution carries \(10\,g\,NaOH = 0.25\,mol\); volume \(= 100/1.1 = 90.9\,mL\).
  2. \(M = 0.25/0.0909 \approx 2.75\,M\).

Answer: \(2.75\,M\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Mix \(100\,mL\,1\,M + 200\,mL\,2\,M\) of the same solute. Find final molarity.

  1. Total moles \(= 100 + 400 = 500\,mmol\); total volume \(= 300\,mL\).
  2. \(M = 500/300 \approx 1.67\,M\).

Answer: \(1.67\,M\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using solution mass instead of solvent mass for molality.
  • Applying \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\) when a reaction occurs (use equivalents instead).

Chapter 9 · Topic 5

Molality

SolutionsStates of MatterTopic 5 of 34

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions, Molality: molality is moles per kilogram of solvent, immune to temperature. Molarity \(M = n/V(L)\) is temperature-dependent (volume changes); molality \(m = n/kg\,solvent\) and mole fraction are temperature-independent. Dilution obeys \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\).
Key formula(s). \[ m=\frac{n}{kg} \]
Key points.
  • Mole fractions in a mixture always add to \(1\).
  • On mixing: total moles conserved, \(M_{mix} = (M_1V_1+M_2V_2)/(V_1+V_2)\).
  • Molarity uses solution volume; molality uses solvent mass in kg.
  • ppm \(= (mass\,solute/mass\,solution)\times10^6\), used for trace quantities.
Example 1.

Fluoride in water is \(2\,mg/L\). Express it in ppm.

  1. \(1\,L\) water \(\approx 10^6\,mg\).
  2. \(2\,mg\) per \(10^6\,mg = 2\,ppm\).

Answer: \(2\,ppm\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(0.5\,mol\) solute is dissolved in \(250\,g\) water. Find molality.

  1. Solvent \(= 0.25\,kg\).
  2. \(m = 0.5/0.25 = 2\,m\).

Answer: \(2\,m\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using solution mass instead of solvent mass for molality.
  • Applying \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\) when a reaction occurs (use equivalents instead).

SolutionsStates of MatterTopic 6 of 34

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions, Mole fraction: mole fraction is each component's mole share, and all fractions add to one. Molarity \(M = n/V(L)\) is temperature-dependent (volume changes); molality \(m = n/kg\,solvent\) and mole fraction are temperature-independent. Dilution obeys \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\).

Key points.
  • Molarity uses solution volume; molality uses solvent mass in kg.
  • ppm \(= (mass\,solute/mass\,solution)\times10^6\), used for trace quantities.
  • Mole fractions in a mixture always add to \(1\).
  • On mixing: total moles conserved, \(M_{mix} = (M_1V_1+M_2V_2)/(V_1+V_2)\).
Example 1.

\(4\,g\,NaOH\) is dissolved to make \(500\,mL\) solution. Find molarity.

  1. Moles \(= 4/40 = 0.1\,mol\); volume \(= 0.5\,L\).
  2. \(M = 0.1/0.5 = 0.2\,M\).

Answer: \(0.2\,M\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) What volume of water must be added to \(200\,mL\) of \(1.5\,M\) solution to make it \(0.5\,M\)?

  1. \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2 \Rightarrow V_2 = 1.5\times200/0.5 = 600\,mL\).
  2. Water added \(= 600-200 = 400\,mL\).

Answer: \(400\,mL\) water.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using solution mass instead of solvent mass for molality.
  • Applying \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\) when a reaction occurs (use equivalents instead).

Chapter 9 · Topic 12

Solubility of gases in liquids

SolutionsStates of MatterTopic 12 of 34

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions, Solubility of gases in liquids: gas solubility falls with temperature and rises with pressure. Henry law: solubility of a gas \(\propto\) its partial pressure, \(p = K_H\chi\) (or \(C = K_H'p\)). \(K_H\) rises with temperature (solubility falls); deep-sea divers exhale \(N_2\) slowly to avoid bends from this law.
Key formula(s). \[ (\text{higher }K_H \Rightarrow \text{lower solubility}),\;scuba:\,He\,over\,N_2\,(low\,solubility) \]
Key points.
  • Units of \(K_H\) fix the form used; check whether mole fraction or concentration version is given.
  • Scuba/aerated-drink problems are Henry-law flags.
  • Solubility of solids usually rises with \(T\); gases always fall.
  • Convert pressure to the same units as \(K_H\) before multiplying.
Example 1.

\(K_H(N_2) = 76\,kbar\) at 298 K. Find mole fraction dissolved at \(p_{N_2} = 0.8\,bar\).

  1. Convert: \(p = 0.8\,bar = 8\times10^{-4}\,kbar\).
  2. \(\chi = p/K_H = 8\times10^{-4}/76 \approx 1.05\times10^{-5}\).

Answer: About \(1.05\times10^{-5}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why do divers use He-diluted air?

  1. \(He\) has much higher \(K_H\) (lower blood solubility) than \(N_2\).
  2. Less dissolved gas \(\to\) lower bends risk on ascent.

Answer: Lower solubility of He reduces nitrogen-bubble risk.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Inverting \(K_H\) meaning (large \(K_H\) = LESS soluble).
  • Forgetting to match pressure units with \(K_H\).

Chapter 9 · Topic 13

Henry's law

SolutionsStates of MatterTopic 13 of 34

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions, Henry's law: Henry law makes dissolved gas proportional to its partial pressure. Henry law: solubility of a gas \(\propto\) its partial pressure, \(p = K_H\chi\) (or \(C = K_H'p\)). \(K_H\) rises with temperature (solubility falls); deep-sea divers exhale \(N_2\) slowly to avoid bends from this law.
Key formula(s). \[ p=K_H\chi,\;(\text{higher }K_H \Rightarrow \text{lower solubility}) \]
Key points.
  • Scuba/aerated-drink problems are Henry-law flags.
  • Solubility of solids usually rises with \(T\); gases always fall.
  • Convert pressure to the same units as \(K_H\) before multiplying.
  • Units of \(K_H\) fix the form used; check whether mole fraction or concentration version is given.
Example 1.

\(K_H(N_2) = 76\,kbar\) at 298 K. Find mole fraction dissolved at \(p_{N_2} = 0.8\,bar\).

  1. Convert: \(p = 0.8\,bar = 8\times10^{-4}\,kbar\).
  2. \(\chi = p/K_H = 8\times10^{-4}/76 \approx 1.05\times10^{-5}\).

Answer: About \(1.05\times10^{-5}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why do divers use He-diluted air?

  1. \(He\) has much higher \(K_H\) (lower blood solubility) than \(N_2\).
  2. Less dissolved gas \(\to\) lower bends risk on ascent.

Answer: Lower solubility of He reduces nitrogen-bubble risk.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Inverting \(K_H\) meaning (large \(K_H\) = LESS soluble).
  • Forgetting to match pressure units with \(K_H\).

Chapter 9 · Topic 14

Vapour pressure

SolutionsStates of MatterTopic 14 of 34

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions, Vapour pressure: vapour pressure is the escaping tendency of a liquid at fixed T. Raoult: \(p_i = \chi_ip_i^0\); total \(P = \sum p_i\). Ideal solutions obey at all compositions (\(\Delta H_{mix} = 0\)); positive deviation (weak A-B, e.g. ethanol+acetone, minimum-boiling azeotrope) and negative deviation (strong A-B, e.g. \(HNO_3\)+water, maximum-boiling azeotrope).
Key formula(s). \[ P=\chi_Ap_A^0+\chi_Bp_B^0 \]
Key points.
  • Colligative properties depend on particle count: always multiply by van It Hoff \(i\).
  • For volatile-nonvolatile: relative lowering \(\Delta p/p^0 = \chi_{solute}\).
  • Vapour is richer in the more volatile component; distillate composition follows the \(y\)-\(x\) curve.
  • Azeotropes distil unchanged (cannot be separated by simple distillation).
Example 1.

\(CS_2\) + acetone shows which deviation, and why?

  1. Mixing breaks the stronger pure-liquid attractions (positive \(\Delta H_{mix}\)).
  2. Positive deviation (higher VP than Raoult).

Answer: Positive deviation.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(HNO_3\) + water is a maximum-boiling azeotrope. What does that imply about A-B forces?

  1. Boiling point rises: VP is lower than ideal.
  2. Strong A-B attraction (negative deviation).

Answer: Strong unlike attraction.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using liquid mole fractions as vapour composition.
  • Missing \(i\) in colligative numericals with electrolytes.

Chapter 9 · Topic 15

Raoult's law

SolutionsStates of MatterTopic 15 of 34

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions, Raoult's law: Raoult prices each vapour share at mole fraction times pure pressure. Raoult: \(p_i = \chi_ip_i^0\); total \(P = \sum p_i\). Ideal solutions obey at all compositions (\(\Delta H_{mix} = 0\)); positive deviation (weak A-B, e.g. ethanol+acetone, minimum-boiling azeotrope) and negative deviation (strong A-B, e.g. \(HNO_3\)+water, maximum-boiling azeotrope).
Key formula(s). \[ \pi=iCRT \],\;p_i=\chi_ip_i^0 \]
Key points.
  • Vapour is richer in the more volatile component; distillate composition follows the \(y\)-\(x\) curve.
  • Azeotropes distil unchanged (cannot be separated by simple distillation).
  • Colligative properties depend on particle count: always multiply by van It Hoff \(i\).
  • For volatile-nonvolatile: relative lowering \(\Delta p/p^0 = \chi_{solute}\).
Example 1.

Benzene (\(p^0 = 75\,mmHg\)) + toluene (\(p^0 = 22\,mmHg\)), \(\chi_{benz} = 0.6\). Find total VP.

  1. \(p_{benz} = 0.6\times75 = 45\); \(p_{tol} = 0.4\times22 = 8.8\).
  2. \(P = 53.8\,mmHg\).

Answer: \(53.8\,mmHg\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(1\,mol\) non-volatile solute in \(10\,mol\) water (\(p^0 = 23.8\,mmHg\)). Find VP lowering.

  1. \(\chi_{solute} = 1/11 \approx 0.0909\).
  2. \(\Delta p = 0.0909\times23.8 \approx 2.16\,mmHg\).

Answer: About \(2.16\,mmHg\) lowering.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using liquid mole fractions as vapour composition.
  • Missing \(i\) in colligative numericals with electrolytes.

Ideal solutions

SolutionsStates of MatterTopic 16 of 34

Explanation

Ideal solutions obey at all compositions (\(\Delta H_{mix} = 0\)); positive deviation (weak A-B, e.g. ethanol+acetone, minimum-boiling azeotrope) and negative deviation (strong A-B, e.g. \(HNO_3\)+water, maximum-boiling azeotrope).

  • For volatile-nonvolatile: relative lowering \(\Delta p/p^0 = \chi_{solute}\).
  • Vapour is richer in the more volatile component; distillate composition follows the \(y\)-\(x\) curve.
Example 1.

Ethanol-water forms a minimum-boiling azeotrope at \(95.6\%\) ethanol. Can simple distillation give absolute alcohol?

  1. The azeotrope distils unchanged at fixed composition.
  2. No; special methods (molecular sieves) are needed.

Answer: No (azeotropic barrier).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(p^\circ = 100\,mmHg\), \(\chi_{solute} = 0.05\) (non-volatile). Find the vapour-pressure lowering.

  1. \(\Delta p = p^\circ\chi_{solute}\).
  2. \(\Delta p = 5\,mmHg\).

Answer: \(5\,mmHg\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using liquid mole fractions as vapour composition.
  • Missing \(i\) in colligative numericals with electrolytes.

Chapter 9 · Topic 21

Colligative properties

SolutionsStates of MatterTopic 21 of 34

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions, Colligative properties: colligative properties count particles, not identities. Colligative: \(\Delta T_b = iK_bm\), \(\Delta T_f = iK_fm\), \(\pi = iCRT\), \(\Delta p/p^0 = i\chi_{solute}\). van It Hoff \(i =\) observed/calculated; association gives \(i<1\), dissociation \(i>1\). Abnormal molar mass \(= M_{true}/i\).
Key formula(s). \[ i=1+(n-1)\alpha\;(dissociation),\;i=1-\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)\beta\;(association) \]
Key points.
  • Molality (not molarity) in \(\Delta T\) formulas; \(R = 0.0821\,L\,atm\) in \(\pi = CRT\).
  • Isotonic solutions have equal \(\pi\) (same \(iC\) at same \(T\)).
  • Reverse osmosis needs applied \(P>\pi\) (desalination).
  • Degree of dissociation from \(i\) first, then \(K\) if asked.
Example 1.

Find \(\Delta T_f\) for \(0.1\,m\,NaCl\) (\(K_f = 1.86\), \(i = 1.9\)).

  1. \(\Delta T_f = 1.9\times1.86\times0.1 = 0.353\,K\).
  2. Freezing point \(\approx -0.35^\circ C\).

Answer: About \(0.35\,K\) depression.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(K_4[Fe(CN)_6]\) dissociates fully; how is its \(\pi\) related to a non-electrolyte of same \(C\)?

  1. \(n = 5\) ions, so \(i \approx 5\).
  2. \(\pi\) is about \(5\times\) larger.

Answer: Five times larger.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using molarity in \(\Delta T_f\) (use molality).
  • Taking \(i = n\) without checking \(\alpha\) (weak electrolytes partly dissociate).

  • Reverse osmosis needs applied \(P>\pi\) (desalination).
  • Degree of dissociation from \(i\) first, then \(K\) if asked.
  • Molality (not molarity) in \(\Delta T\) formulas; \(R = 0.0821\,L\,atm\) in \(\pi = CRT\).
Example 1.

Find \(\Delta T_b\) for \(0.2\,m\) glucose (\(K_b = 0.52\)).

  1. Glucose is a non-electrolyte: \(i = 1\).
  2. \(\Delta T_b = 1\times0.52\times0.2 = 0.104\,K\).

Answer: \(0.104\,K\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Find the osmotic pressure of \(0.01\,M\) sucrose at \(300\,K\).

  1. \(\pi = iCRT = 1\times0.01\times0.0821\times300\).
  2. \(\pi \approx 0.246\,atm\).

Answer: \(0.246\,atm\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using molarity in \(\Delta T_f\) (use molality).
  • Taking \(i = n\) without checking \(\alpha\) (weak electrolytes partly dissociate).

Chapter 9 · Topic 29

Association

SolutionsStates of MatterTopic 29 of 34

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions, Association: association merges particles, pushing van't Hoff i below one. Colligative: \(\Delta T_b = iK_bm\), \(\Delta T_f = iK_fm\), \(\pi = iCRT\), \(\Delta p/p^0 = i\chi_{solute}\). van It Hoff \(i =\) observed/calculated; association gives \(i<1\), dissociation \(i>1\). Abnormal molar mass \(= M_{true}/i\).
Key formula(s). \[ \Delta T_f=iK_fm,\;i=1+(n-1)\alpha\;(dissociation),\;i=1-\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)\beta\;(association) \]
Key points.
  • Reverse osmosis needs applied \(P>\pi\) (desalination).
  • Degree of dissociation from \(i\) first, then \(K\) if asked.
  • Molality (not molarity) in \(\Delta T\) formulas; \(R = 0.0821\,L\,atm\) in \(\pi = CRT\).
  • Isotonic solutions have equal \(\pi\) (same \(iC\) at same \(T\)).
Example 1.

\(0.1\,M\,CaCl_2\) has \(\alpha = 0.9\). Find its van't Hoff factor.

  1. \(n = 3\) ions; \(i = 1 + (n-1)\alpha = 1 + 2(0.9)\).
  2. \(i = 2.8\).

Answer: \(2.8\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Acetic acid (\(M = 60\)) dimerises in benzene; observed molar mass \(= 120\). Find \(i\).

  1. \(i = M_{true}/M_{obs} = 60/120\).
  2. \(i = 0.5\) (association).

Answer: \(0.5\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using molarity in \(\Delta T_f\) (use molality).
  • Taking \(i = n\) without checking \(\alpha\) (weak electrolytes partly dissociate).

Chapter 10 · Topic 1

Electrochemical cells

ElectrochemistryElectro & KineticsTopic 1 of 36

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry, Electrochemical cells: cells convert chemical energy to electrical through split half-reactions. This Electrochemistry topic builds the cell (anode = oxidation, cathode = reduction, salt bridge completes it), reads EMF from standard potentials, corrects with Nernst, and weighs deposits with Faraday law.
Key formula(s). \[ w=\frac{MIt}{nF} \],\;E^\circ_{cell}=E^\circ_{c}-E^\circ_{a} \]
Key points.
  • Concentration cell has E0 = 0.
  • Series cells share the same charge.
  • Ecell>0 means spontaneous galvanic.
  • Never multiply E by stoichiometric factors.
Example 1.

Standard Zn-Cu cell EMF if E0(Cu)=+0.34, E0(Zn)=-0.76 V?

  1. Cathode Cu, anode Zn.
  2. E0 = 0.34-(-0.76) = 1.10 V.

Answer: 1.10 V.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Which electrode is negative in a galvanic cell?

  1. Oxidation occurs at anode.
  2. Anode is negative in galvanic mode.

Answer: The anode.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Multiplying E with equations.
  • Anode/cathode sign flip in electrolysis.
Back to Index
Index / Electro & Kinetics
Chapter 10 · Topic 2

Galvanic cells

ElectrochemistryElectro & KineticsTopic 2 of 36

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry, Galvanic cells: galvanic cells run spontaneously with positive EMF. Cell: \(E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode}-E^\circ_{anode}\); Nernst \(E = E^\circ-(0.0591/n)\log Q\) at 298 K. Links: \(\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ\), \(\log K = nE^\circ/0.0591\). Anode \(=\) oxidation (negative in galvanic).
Key formula(s). \[ \log K=\frac{nE^\circ}{0.0591},\;SHE:\,Pt|H_2(1atm)|H^+(1M)=0.00V \]
Key points.
  • \(E^\circ_{cell}>0 \Rightarrow\) spontaneous galvanic; \(E^\circ_{cell}<0 \Rightarrow\) needs electrolysis.
  • Salt bridge completes the circuit and preserves neutrality; no salt bridge \(\to\) no sustained current.
  • Concentration cell: \(E^\circ = 0\), \(E = (0.0591/n)\log(C_{cath}/C_{an})\); current flows to equalise.
  • Multiply half-reactions freely, but NEVER multiply \(E^\circ\) (intensive).
Example 1.

\(Zn|Zn^{2+}(0.1M)||Cu^{2+}(1M)|Cu\), \(E^\circ = 1.10\,V\), \(n = 2\). Find \(E\).

  1. \(Q = 0.1/1 = 0.1\); \(E = 1.10-(0.0591/2)\log(0.1)\).
  2. \(E = 1.10+0.0296 = 1.1296\,V\).

Answer: About \(1.13\,V\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(E^\circ = 0.46\,V\), \(n = 2\). Find \(K\).

  1. \(\log K = 2\times0.46/0.0591 \approx 15.57\).
  2. \(K \approx 3.7\times10^{15}\).

Answer: About \(10^{15.6}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Multiplying \(E^\circ\) when multiplying half-equations.
  • Wrong \(Q\) (products/reactants of the CELL reaction, solids omitted).
Back to Index
Index / Electro & Kinetics
Chapter 10 · Topic 3

Electrolytic cells

ElectrochemistryElectro & KineticsTopic 3 of 36

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry, Electrolytic cells: electrolytic cells spend external voltage to force non-spontaneous change. Cell: \(E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode}-E^\circ_{anode}\); Nernst \(E = E^\circ-(0.0591/n)\log Q\) at 298 K. Links: \(\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ\), \(\log K = nE^\circ/0.0591\). Anode \(=\) oxidation (negative in galvanic).
Key formula(s). \[ SHE:\,Pt|H_2(1atm)|H^+(1M)=0.00V,\;E_{conc}=\frac{0.0591}{n}\log\frac{C_{cath}}{C_{an}} \]
Key points.
  • Salt bridge completes the circuit and preserves neutrality; no salt bridge \(\to\) no sustained current.
  • Concentration cell: \(E^\circ = 0\), \(E = (0.0591/n)\log(C_{cath}/C_{an})\); current flows to equalise.
  • Multiply half-reactions freely, but NEVER multiply \(E^\circ\) (intensive).
  • \(E^\circ_{cell}>0 \Rightarrow\) spontaneous galvanic; \(E^\circ_{cell}<0 \Rightarrow\) needs electrolysis.
Example 1.

For \(Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \to Cu\), \(E^\circ = +0.34\,V\). Find \(E\) when \([Cu^{2+}] = 0.01\,M\).

  1. \(E = 0.34 - (0.0591/2)\log(1/0.01) = 0.34 - 0.0591\).
  2. \(E \approx 0.281\,V\).

Answer: \(0.281\,V\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) The Daniell cell has \(E^\circ = 1.10\,V\), \(n = 2\). Estimate its equilibrium constant.

  1. \(\log K = 2\times1.10/0.0591 \approx 37.2\).
  2. \(K \approx 1.6\times10^{37}\).

Answer: About \(10^{37}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Multiplying \(E^\circ\) when multiplying half-equations.
  • Wrong \(Q\) (products/reactants of the CELL reaction, solids omitted).

  • Concentration cell: \(E^\circ = 0\), \(E = (0.0591/n)\log(C_{cath}/C_{an})\); current flows to equalise.

  • \(E^\circ_{cell}>0 \Rightarrow\) spontaneous galvanic; \(E^\circ_{cell}<0 \Rightarrow\) needs electrolysis.
  • Salt bridge completes the circuit and preserves neutrality; no salt bridge \(\to\) no sustained current.
Example 1.

A silver concentration cell has \(0.1\,M\) vs \(1\,M\,Ag^+\). Find its EMF.

  1. \(E^\circ = 0\); \(E = (0.0591/1)\log(1/0.1)\).
  2. \(E = 0.0591\,V\).

Answer: \(0.0591\,V\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) What are the standard conditions defining the SHE (\(E^\circ = 0\))?

  1. \(Pt|H_2(1\,atm)|H^+(1\,M)\) at \(298\,K\).
  2. All ion activities unity by definition.

Answer: \(1\,M\,H^+\), \(1\,atm\,H_2\), \(Pt\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Multiplying \(E^\circ\) when multiplying half-equations.
  • Wrong \(Q\) (products/reactants of the CELL reaction, solids omitted).

Chapter 10 · Topic 16

Relationship between K and EMF

ElectrochemistryElectro & KineticsTopic 16 of 36

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry, Relationship between K and EMF: log K equals n E-zero over 0.0591. This Electrochemistry topic builds the cell (anode = oxidation, cathode = reduction, salt bridge completes it), reads EMF from standard potentials, corrects with Nernst, and weighs deposits with Faraday law.
Key formula(s). \[ E^\circ_{cell}=E^\circ_{c}-E^\circ_{a},\;E=E^\circ-\frac{0.0591}{n}\log Q \]
Key points.
  • Concentration cell has E0 = 0.
  • Series cells share the same charge.
  • Ecell>0 means spontaneous galvanic.
  • Never multiply E by stoichiometric factors.
Example 1.

Standard Zn-Cu cell EMF if E0(Cu)=+0.34, E0(Zn)=-0.76 V?

  1. Cathode Cu, anode Zn.
  2. E0 = 0.34-(-0.76) = 1.10 V.

Answer: 1.10 V.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Which electrode is negative in a galvanic cell?

  1. Oxidation occurs at anode.
  2. Anode is negative in galvanic mode.

Answer: The anode.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Multiplying E with equations.
  • Anode/cathode sign flip in electrolysis.

Chapter 10 · Topic 17

Electrolysis

ElectrochemistryElectro & KineticsTopic 17 of 36

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry, Electrolysis: electrolysis spends charge to deposit, liberate or decompose. Faraday: \(w = ZQ = (M/nF)It\). Products follow discharge order (lower \(E^\circ\) cation discharges first at cathode; concentrated \(Cl^-\) can beat \(O_2\) at anode). Corrosion is Fe oxidation; protection via galvanisation, alloying, cathodic protection.
Key formula(s). \[ w=\frac{MIt}{nF} \]
Key points.
  • Series cells: same \(Q\) passes; moles deposited \(\propto M/n\).
  • \(NaCl\)(aq): cathode \(H_2\), anode \(Cl_2\) (conc.) vs \(O_2\) (dilute); molten \(NaCl\): \(Na\) + \(Cl_2\).
  • Batteries: dry cell \(1.5\,V\), lead storage \(2\,V\)/cell, \(H_2\)-\(O_2\) fuel cell clean (water product).
  • Rusting needs both air AND moisture; \(E^\circ(Fe^{2+}/Fe) = -0.44\,V\).
Example 1.

How long must \(2\,A\) pass to deposit \(5.4\,g\,Ag\) (\(M = 108\), \(n = 1\))?

  1. Moles \(e^- = 5.4/108 = 0.05\); \(Q = 0.05\times96485 = 4824\,C\).
  2. \(t = 4824/2 = 2412\,s \approx 40.2\,min\).

Answer: About \(40\,min\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Same \(Q\) through \(AgNO_3\) and \(CuSO_4\) deposits \(10.8\,g\,Ag\). Find \(Cu\) mass.

  1. Moles \(e^- = 0.1\); \(Cu^{2+}\) needs \(2e^-\), so \(0.05\,mol\,Cu\).
  2. Mass \(= 0.05\times63.5 = 3.175\,g\).

Answer: \(3.175\,g\,Cu\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Forgetting \(n\) (valency) in \(w = MIt/nF\).
  • Wrong discharge order in aqueous electrolysis.

Chapter 10 · Topic 18

Faraday's first law

ElectrochemistryElectro & KineticsTopic 18 of 36

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry, Faraday's first law: deposited mass is proportional to charge passed. Faraday: \(w = ZQ = (M/nF)It\). Products follow discharge order (lower \(E^\circ\) cation discharges first at cathode; concentrated \(Cl^-\) can beat \(O_2\) at anode). Corrosion is Fe oxidation; protection via galvanisation, alloying, cathodic protection.
Key formula(s). \[ w=\frac{MIt}{nF},\;Q=It \]
Key points.
  • \(NaCl\)(aq): cathode \(H_2\), anode \(Cl_2\) (conc.) vs \(O_2\) (dilute); molten \(NaCl\): \(Na\) + \(Cl_2\).
  • Batteries: dry cell \(1.5\,V\), lead storage \(2\,V\)/cell, \(H_2\)-\(O_2\) fuel cell clean (water product).
  • Rusting needs both air AND moisture; \(E^\circ(Fe^{2+}/Fe) = -0.44\,V\).
  • Series cells: same \(Q\) passes; moles deposited \(\propto M/n\).
Example 1.

How much copper (\(Cu^{2+}\), \(M = 63.5\)) deposits with \(19300\,C\)?

  1. Moles \(e^- = 19300/96485 = 0.2\); \(Cu = 0.1\,mol\).
  2. Mass \(= 0.1\times63.5 = 6.35\,g\).

Answer: \(6.35\,g\,Cu\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Molten \(MgCl_2\) is electrolysed with \(2\,A\) for \(1\,h\). Find moles of \(Mg\).

  1. \(Q = 2\times3600 = 7200\,C\); \(e^- = 0.0746\,mol\).
  2. \(Mg = 0.0373\,mol\) (2 electrons each).

Answer: \(0.0373\,mol\,Mg\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Forgetting \(n\) (valency) in \(w = MIt/nF\).
  • Wrong discharge order in aqueous electrolysis.

Faraday's second law

ElectrochemistryElectro & KineticsTopic 19 of 36

Explanation

Products follow discharge order (lower \(E^\circ\) cation discharges first at cathode; concentrated \(Cl^-\) can beat \(O_2\) at anode). Corrosion is Fe oxidation; protection via galvanisation, alloying, cathodic protection.

  • Batteries: dry cell \(1.5\,V\), lead storage \(2\,V\)/cell, \(H_2\)-\(O_2\) fuel cell clean (water product).

  • \(NaCl\)(aq): cathode \(H_2\), anode \(Cl_2\) (conc.) vs \(O_2\) (dilute); molten \(NaCl\): \(Na\) + \(Cl_2\).
Example 1.

Why does aqueous \(NaCl\) give \(H_2\) at the cathode instead of \(Na\)?

  1. \(H_2O/H_2\) reduces far more easily than \(Na^+/Na\) (\(-0.83\) vs \(-2.71\,V\)).
  2. Water discharges preferentially.

Answer: Water reduces more easily.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) EMF of the lead-storage cell on discharge?

  1. \(Pb + PbO_2 + 2H_2SO_4 \to 2PbSO_4 + 2H_2O\).
  2. About \(2.0\,V\) per cell.

Answer: \(2.0\,V\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Forgetting \(n\) (valency) in \(w = MIt/nF\).
  • Wrong discharge order in aqueous electrolysis.

Chapter 10 · Topic 21

Conductance

ElectrochemistryElectro & KineticsTopic 21 of 36

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry, Conductance: conductance is reciprocal resistance in siemens. Conductance \(G = 1/R\); conductivity \(\kappa = G\cdot(l/A)\); molar \(\Lambda_m = \kappa\times1000/M\). \(\Lambda_m\) rises with dilution (weak: steeply near infinite dilution). Kohlrausch: \(\Lambda^\circ = \sum\nu_i\lambda_i^\circ\); \(\alpha = \Lambda_m/\Lambda^\circ\).
Key formula(s). \[ \Lambda_m=\frac{\kappa\times1000}{M},\;\kappa=G\cdot const \]
Key points.
  • Cell constant \(= l/A\); calibrate with standard \(KCl\).
  • Weak-electrolyte \(K_a\) from conductivity via \(\alpha\) then Ostwald formula.
  • \(\Lambda^\circ\) of weak electrolytes cannot be measured directly (extrapolation via Kohlrausch).
  • Units: \(\kappa\) \(S\,cm^{-1}\); \(\Lambda_m\) \(S\,cm^2mol^{-1}\).
Example 1.

\(\Lambda^\circ(K^+) = 73.5\), \(\Lambda^\circ(Br^-) = 78.1\). Find \(\Lambda^\circ(KBr)\).

  1. Kohlrausch: \(\Lambda^\circ = \lambda_+^\circ + \lambda_-^\circ\).
  2. \(\Lambda^\circ = 151.6\,S\,cm^2mol^{-1}\).

Answer: \(151.6\,S\,cm^2mol^{-1}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Cell constant \(= 0.5\,cm^{-1}\), \(R = 200\,\Omega\). Find \(\kappa\).

  1. \(\kappa = G\times(l/A) = (1/200)\times0.5\).
  2. \(\kappa = 2.5\times10^{-3}\,S/cm\).

Answer: \(2.5\times10^{-3}\,S/cm\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.

Chapter 10 · Topic 22

Resistance

ElectrochemistryElectro & KineticsTopic 22 of 36

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry, Resistance: resistance follows rho length over area. Conductance \(G = 1/R\); conductivity \(\kappa = G\cdot(l/A)\); molar \(\Lambda_m = \kappa\times1000/M\). \(\Lambda_m\) rises with dilution (weak: steeply near infinite dilution). Kohlrausch: \(\Lambda^\circ = \sum\nu_i\lambda_i^\circ\); \(\alpha = \Lambda_m/\Lambda^\circ\).
Key formula(s). \[ K_a=\frac{C\alpha^2}{1-\alpha},\;cell\,const=l/A \]
Key points.
  • Weak-electrolyte \(K_a\) from conductivity via \(\alpha\) then Ostwald formula.
  • \(\Lambda^\circ\) of weak electrolytes cannot be measured directly (extrapolation via Kohlrausch).
  • Units: \(\kappa\) \(S\,cm^{-1}\); \(\Lambda_m\) \(S\,cm^2mol^{-1}\).
  • Cell constant \(= l/A\); calibrate with standard \(KCl\).
Example 1.

Why is \(\Lambda_m\) of \(CH_3COOH\) at \(0.001\,M\) much larger than at \(0.1\,M\)?

  1. Dilution drives ionisation up (Ostwald: \(\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}\)).
  2. More ions per mole \(\to\) larger \(\Lambda_m\).

Answer: Ionisation rises with dilution.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(\Lambda_m = 20\), \(\Lambda^\circ = 400\) (\(S\,cm^2mol^{-1}\)). Find \(\alpha\).

  1. \(\alpha = 20/400\).
  2. \(\alpha = 0.05\).

Answer: \(0.05\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Missing the 1000 factor in \(\Lambda_m\).
  • Extrapolating weak-electrolyte curves directly to get \(\Lambda^\circ\).

Conductivity

ElectrochemistryElectro & KineticsTopic 23 of 36

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry, Conductivity: conductivity is conductance times cell constant. Conductance \(G = 1/R\); conductivity \(\kappa = G\cdot(l/A)\); molar \(\Lambda_m = \kappa\times1000/M\). \(\Lambda_m\) rises with dilution (weak: steeply near infinite dilution). Kohlrausch: \(\Lambda^\circ = \sum\nu_i\lambda_i^\circ\); \(\alpha = \Lambda_m/\Lambda^\circ\).
Key formula(s). \[ \Lambda_m=\frac{\kappa\times1000}{M},\;\alpha=\frac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda^\circ} \]
Key points.
  • Units: \(\kappa\) \(S\,cm^{-1}\); \(\Lambda_m\) \(S\,cm^2mol^{-1}\).
  • Cell constant \(= l/A\); calibrate with standard \(KCl\).
  • Weak-electrolyte \(K_a\) from conductivity via \(\alpha\) then Ostwald formula.
  • \(\Lambda^\circ\) of weak electrolytes cannot be measured directly (extrapolation via Kohlrausch).
Example 1.

\(\kappa = 0.001\,S/cm\) for \(0.01\,M\,CH_3COOH\). \(\Lambda^\circ = 390\). Find \(\alpha\) and \(K_a\).

  1. \(\Lambda_m = 0.001\times1000/0.01 = 100\); \(\alpha = 100/390 \approx 0.256\).
  2. \(K_a = 0.01(0.256)^2/(0.744) \approx 8.8\times10^{-4}\) (order check vs \(1.8\times10^{-5}\): here data illustrative).

Answer: \(\alpha \approx 0.26\) (method as shown).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why does \(\Lambda_m(NaCl)\) rise only slowly with dilution but \(CH_3COOH\) steeply?

  1. Strong electrolyte already fully ionised; only interionic drag falls.
  2. Weak electrolyte ionisation itself jumps with dilution (Ostwald).

Answer: Dilution ionises weak electrolytes further.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Missing the 1000 factor in \(\Lambda_m\).
  • Extrapolating weak-electrolyte curves directly to get \(\Lambda^\circ\).

Chapter 10 · Topic 31

Batteries

ElectrochemistryElectro & KineticsTopic 31 of 36

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry, Batteries: batteries package galvanic chemistry at fixed voltages. Faraday: \(w = ZQ = (M/nF)It\). Products follow discharge order (lower \(E^\circ\) cation discharges first at cathode; concentrated \(Cl^-\) can beat \(O_2\) at anode). Corrosion is Fe oxidation; protection via galvanisation, alloying, cathodic protection.
Key formula(s). \[ molten:\,Na+Cl_2 \],\;w=\frac{MIt}{nF} \]
Key points.
  • Batteries: dry cell \(1.5\,V\), lead storage \(2\,V\)/cell, \(H_2\)-\(O_2\) fuel cell clean (water product).
  • Rusting needs both air AND moisture; \(E^\circ(Fe^{2+}/Fe) = -0.44\,V\).
  • Series cells: same \(Q\) passes; moles deposited \(\propto M/n\).
  • \(NaCl\)(aq): cathode \(H_2\), anode \(Cl_2\) (conc.) vs \(O_2\) (dilute); molten \(NaCl\): \(Na\) + \(Cl_2\).
Example 1.

Why does aqueous \(NaCl\) give \(H_2\) at the cathode instead of \(Na\)?

  1. \(H_2O/H_2\) reduces far more easily than \(Na^+/Na\) (\(-0.83\) vs \(-2.71\,V\)).
  2. Water discharges preferentially.

Answer: Water reduces more easily.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) EMF of the lead-storage cell on discharge?

  1. \(Pb + PbO_2 + 2H_2SO_4 \to 2PbSO_4 + 2H_2O\).
  2. About \(2.0\,V\) per cell.

Answer: \(2.0\,V\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Forgetting \(n\) (valency) in \(w = MIt/nF\).
  • Wrong discharge order in aqueous electrolysis.

Chapter 10 · Topic 32

Primary cells

ElectrochemistryElectro & KineticsTopic 32 of 36

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry, Primary cells: primary cells like dry cells are single-use 1.5 V packs. This Electrochemistry topic builds the cell (anode = oxidation, cathode = reduction, salt bridge completes it), reads EMF from standard potentials, corrects with Nernst, and weighs deposits with Faraday law.
Key formula(s). \[ \Delta G^\circ=-nFE^\circ,\;w=\frac{MIt}{nF} \]
Key points.
  • Ecell>0 means spontaneous galvanic.
  • Never multiply E by stoichiometric factors.
  • Concentration cell has E0 = 0.
  • Series cells share the same charge.
Example 1.

Standard Zn-Cu cell EMF if E0(Cu)=+0.34, E0(Zn)=-0.76 V?

  1. Cathode Cu, anode Zn.
  2. E0 = 0.34-(-0.76) = 1.10 V.

Answer: 1.10 V.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Which electrode is negative in a galvanic cell?

  1. Oxidation occurs at anode.
  2. Anode is negative in galvanic mode.

Answer: The anode.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Multiplying E with equations.
  • Anode/cathode sign flip in electrolysis.

Chapter 10 · Topic 35

Corrosion

ElectrochemistryElectro & KineticsTopic 35 of 36

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry, Corrosion: rusting is iron oxidation needing both air and moisture. Faraday: \(w = ZQ = (M/nF)It\). Products follow discharge order (lower \(E^\circ\) cation discharges first at cathode; concentrated \(Cl^-\) can beat \(O_2\) at anode). Corrosion is Fe oxidation; protection via galvanisation, alloying, cathodic protection.
Key formula(s). \[ series:\,same\,Q,\,moles\propto M/n,\;NaCl(aq):\,H_2+Cl_2 \]
Key points.
  • Series cells: same \(Q\) passes; moles deposited \(\propto M/n\).
  • \(NaCl\)(aq): cathode \(H_2\), anode \(Cl_2\) (conc.) vs \(O_2\) (dilute); molten \(NaCl\): \(Na\) + \(Cl_2\).
  • Batteries: dry cell \(1.5\,V\), lead storage \(2\,V\)/cell, \(H_2\)-\(O_2\) fuel cell clean (water product).
  • Rusting needs both air AND moisture; \(E^\circ(Fe^{2+}/Fe) = -0.44\,V\).
Example 1.

How long must \(2\,A\) pass to deposit \(5.4\,g\,Ag\) (\(M = 108\), \(n = 1\))?

  1. Moles \(e^- = 5.4/108 = 0.05\); \(Q = 0.05\times96485 = 4824\,C\).
  2. \(t = 4824/2 = 2412\,s \approx 40.2\,min\).

Answer: About \(40\,min\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Same \(Q\) through \(AgNO_3\) and \(CuSO_4\) deposits \(10.8\,g\,Ag\). Find \(Cu\) mass.

  1. Moles \(e^- = 0.1\); \(Cu^{2+}\) needs \(2e^-\), so \(0.05\,mol\,Cu\).
  2. Mass \(= 0.05\times63.5 = 3.175\,g\).

Answer: \(3.175\,g\,Cu\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Forgetting \(n\) (valency) in \(w = MIt/nF\).
  • Wrong discharge order in aqueous electrolysis.

Chapter 10 · Topic 36

Prevention of corrosion

ElectrochemistryElectro & KineticsTopic 36 of 36

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry, Prevention of corrosion: galvanising, alloying and cathodic protection all guard iron. Faraday: \(w = ZQ = (M/nF)It\). Products follow discharge order (lower \(E^\circ\) cation discharges first at cathode; concentrated \(Cl^-\) can beat \(O_2\) at anode). Corrosion is Fe oxidation; protection via galvanisation, alloying, cathodic protection.
Key formula(s). \[ NaCl(aq):\,H_2+Cl_2,\;molten:\,Na+Cl_2 \]
Key points.
  • \(NaCl\)(aq): cathode \(H_2\), anode \(Cl_2\) (conc.) vs \(O_2\) (dilute); molten \(NaCl\): \(Na\) + \(Cl_2\).
  • Batteries: dry cell \(1.5\,V\), lead storage \(2\,V\)/cell, \(H_2\)-\(O_2\) fuel cell clean (water product).
  • Rusting needs both air AND moisture; \(E^\circ(Fe^{2+}/Fe) = -0.44\,V\).
  • Series cells: same \(Q\) passes; moles deposited \(\propto M/n\).
Example 1.

How much copper (\(Cu^{2+}\), \(M = 63.5\)) deposits with \(19300\,C\)?

  1. Moles \(e^- = 19300/96485 = 0.2\); \(Cu = 0.1\,mol\).
  2. Mass \(= 0.1\times63.5 = 6.35\,g\).

Answer: \(6.35\,g\,Cu\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Molten \(MgCl_2\) is electrolysed with \(2\,A\) for \(1\,h\). Find moles of \(Mg\).

  1. \(Q = 2\times3600 = 7200\,C\); \(e^- = 0.0746\,mol\).
  2. \(Mg = 0.0373\,mol\) (2 electrons each).

Answer: \(0.0373\,mol\,Mg\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Forgetting \(n\) (valency) in \(w = MIt/nF\).
  • Wrong discharge order in aqueous electrolysis.

Index / Electro & Kinetics
Chapter 11 · Topic 1

Rate of reaction

Chemical KineticsElectro & KineticsTopic 1 of 32

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Kinetics, Rate of reaction: rate is concentration change per time with sign fixed positive. Rate law \(rate = k[A]^m[B]^n\) comes from experiment only; order \(= m+n\), molecularity \(=\) molecules in an elementary step. First order: \(k = (2.303/t)\log(a/(a-x))\), \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/k\); zero: \(t_{1/2} = a/2k\). Units of \(k\): \((mol/L)^{1-n}s^{-1}\).
Key formula(s). \[ k=\frac{2.303}{t}\log\frac{a}{a-x},\;t_{1/2}(1st)=\frac{0.693}{k} \]
Key points.
  • Order can be zero, fractional or negative; molecularity is a positive integer \(1,2,3\).
  • Slowest elementary step \(=\) rate-determining; its stoichiometry (with pre-equilibria) sets the law.
  • Pseudo-first-order: excess reactant hides true order (e.g. ester hydrolysis in water).
  • Graphs: 1st order \(\ln[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; 2nd order \(1/[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; zero \([A]\) vs \(t\) linear.
Example 1.

A first-order reaction is \(75\%\) complete in \(60\,min\). Find \(k\).

  1. \(k = (2.303/60)\log(100/25) = (2.303/60)\log4\).
  2. \(k = (2.303\times0.602/60) \approx 0.0231\,min^{-1}\).

Answer: About \(0.0231\,min^{-1}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Doubling \([A]\) doubles rate, doubling \([B]\) quadruples it. Give orders and \(k\) units.

  1. Order in A \(= 1\), in B \(= 2\); overall \(= 3\).
  2. Units \(= M^{-2}s^{-1}\) (\(L^2mol^{-2}s^{-1}\)).

Answer: 3rd order; \(M^{-2}s^{-1}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reading order from balanced-equation coefficients.
  • Using \(\log\) vs \(\ln\) inconsistently (factor 2.303).

Index / Electro & Kinetics
Chapter 11 · Topic 2

Average rate

Chemical KineticsElectro & KineticsTopic 2 of 32

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Kinetics, Average rate: average rate divides the interval change by interval time. Rate law \(rate = k[A]^m[B]^n\) comes from experiment only; order \(= m+n\), molecularity \(=\) molecules in an elementary step. First order: \(k = (2.303/t)\log(a/(a-x))\), \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/k\); zero: \(t_{1/2} = a/2k\). Units of \(k\): \((mol/L)^{1-n}s^{-1}\).
Key formula(s). \[ k=\frac{2.303}{t}\log\frac{a}{a-x},\;t_{1/2}(1st)=\frac{0.693}{k},\;t_{1/2}(2)=\frac{1}{k[A]_0} \]
Key points.
  • Slowest elementary step \(=\) rate-determining; its stoichiometry (with pre-equilibria) sets the law.
  • Pseudo-first-order: excess reactant hides true order (e.g. ester hydrolysis in water).
  • Graphs: 1st order \(\ln[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; 2nd order \(1/[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; zero \([A]\) vs \(t\) linear.
  • Order can be zero, fractional or negative; molecularity is a positive integer \(1,2,3\).
Example 1.

A first-order reaction is \(50\%\) complete in \(30\,min\). Find \(k\).

  1. This is one half-life: \(t_{1/2} = 30\,min\).
  2. \(k = 0.693/30 \approx 0.0231\,min^{-1}\).

Answer: \(0.0231\,min^{-1}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Doubling \([A]\) has no effect; tripling \([B]\) triples the rate. Give orders and overall units of \(k\).

  1. Order \(0\) in A, \(1\) in B; overall \(1\).
  2. Units \(= s^{-1}\).

Answer: First order overall; \(s^{-1}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reading order from balanced-equation coefficients.
  • Using \(\log\) vs \(\ln\) inconsistently (factor 2.303).

Chapter 11 · Topic 3

Instantaneous rate

Chemical KineticsElectro & KineticsTopic 3 of 32

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Kinetics, Instantaneous rate: instantaneous rate is the tangent slope at one instant. Rate law \(rate = k[A]^m[B]^n\) comes from experiment only; order \(= m+n\), molecularity \(=\) molecules in an elementary step. First order: \(k = (2.303/t)\log(a/(a-x))\), \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/k\); zero: \(t_{1/2} = a/2k\). Units of \(k\): \((mol/L)^{1-n}s^{-1}\).
Key formula(s). \[ k=\frac{2.303}{t}\log\frac{a}{a-x},\;t_{1/2}(1st)=\frac{0.693}{k},\;order=m+n\,(expt) \]
Key points.
  • Pseudo-first-order: excess reactant hides true order (e.g. ester hydrolysis in water).
  • Graphs: 1st order \(\ln[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; 2nd order \(1/[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; zero \([A]\) vs \(t\) linear.
  • Order can be zero, fractional or negative; molecularity is a positive integer \(1,2,3\).
  • Slowest elementary step \(=\) rate-determining; its stoichiometry (with pre-equilibria) sets the law.
Example 1.

A zero-order reaction has \([A]_0 = 0.5\,M\), \(k = 0.01\,M/min\). Find \(t_{1/2}\).

  1. Zero order: \(t_{1/2} = [A]_0/2k\).
  2. \(t_{1/2} = 0.5/0.02 = 25\,min\).

Answer: \(25\,min\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Which plot is linear for a second-order reaction?

  1. Integrated form: \(1/[A] = 1/[A]_0 + kt\).
  2. \(1/[A]\) vs \(t\).

Answer: \(1/[A]\) vs time.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reading order from balanced-equation coefficients.
  • Using \(\log\) vs \(\ln\) inconsistently (factor 2.303).

  • Pseudo-first-order: excess reactant hides true order (e.g. ester hydrolysis in water).

  • Slowest elementary step \(=\) rate-determining; its stoichiometry (with pre-equilibria) sets the law.

A zero-order reaction has \([A]_0 = 0.5\,M\), \(k = 0.01\,M/min\). Find \(t_{1/2}\).

  1. Zero order: \(t_{1/2} = [A]_0/2k\).
  2. \(t_{1/2} = 0.5/0.02 = 25\,min\).

Answer: \(25\,min\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Which plot is linear for a second-order reaction?

  1. Integrated form: \(1/[A] = 1/[A]_0 + kt\).

Answer: \(1/[A]\) vs time.

Half-life

Chemical KineticsElectro & KineticsTopic 13 of 32

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Kinetics, Half-life: half-life is the time to halve the reactant. Rate law \(rate = k[A]^m[B]^n\) comes from experiment only; order \(= m+n\), molecularity \(=\) molecules in an elementary step. First order: \(k = (2.303/t)\log(a/(a-x))\), \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/k\); zero: \(t_{1/2} = a/2k\). Units of \(k\): \((mol/L)^{1-n}s^{-1}\).
Key formula(s). \[ k=\frac{2.303}{t}\log\frac{a}{a-x},\;t_{1/2}(1st)=\frac{0.693}{k},\;units(k)=(M)^{1-n}s^{-1} \]
Key points.
  • Order can be zero, fractional or negative; molecularity is a positive integer \(1,2,3\).
  • Slowest elementary step \(=\) rate-determining; its stoichiometry (with pre-equilibria) sets the law.
  • Pseudo-first-order: excess reactant hides true order (e.g. ester hydrolysis in water).
  • Graphs: 1st order \(\ln[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; 2nd order \(1/[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; zero \([A]\) vs \(t\) linear.
Example 1.

A first-order reaction is \(75\%\) complete in \(60\,min\). Find \(k\).

  1. \(k = (2.303/60)\log(100/25) = (2.303/60)\log4\).
  2. \(k = (2.303\times0.602/60) \approx 0.0231\,min^{-1}\).

Answer: About \(0.0231\,min^{-1}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Doubling \([A]\) doubles rate, doubling \([B]\) quadruples it. Give orders and \(k\) units.

  1. Order in A \(= 1\), in B \(= 2\); overall \(= 3\).
  2. Units \(= M^{-2}s^{-1}\) (\(L^2mol^{-2}s^{-1}\)).

Answer: 3rd order; \(M^{-2}s^{-1}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reading order from balanced-equation coefficients.
  • Using \(\log\) vs \(\ln\) inconsistently (factor 2.303).

A first-order reaction is \(50\%\) complete in \(30\,min\). Find \(k\).

  2. \(k = 0.693/30 \approx 0.0231\,min^{-1}\).

Answer: \(0.0231\,min^{-1}\).

  1. Order \(0\) in A, \(1\) in B; overall \(1\).
  2. Units \(= s^{-1}\).

Answer: First order overall; \(s^{-1}\).

Chapter 11 · Topic 18

Arrhenius equation

Chemical KineticsElectro & KineticsTopic 18 of 32

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Kinetics, Arrhenius equation: Arrhenius makes k exponential in minus Ea over RT. Arrhenius \(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\); two-temperature form \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (E_a/2.303R)(1/T_1-1/T_2)\). Catalyst lowers \(E_a\) (new path), raising \(k\) without changing \(K\); threshold energy \(=\) \(E_a +\) average reactant energy.
Key formula(s). \[ k=Ae^{-E_a/RT},\;k=pZ\,e^{-E_a/RT}\,(steric\,p) \]
Key points.
  • Effective collisions need energy \(\ge E_a\) AND correct orientation (steric factor \(p\)).
  • Parallel paths: \(k_{net} = k_1+k_2\); consecutive: slowest step dominates.
  • Rough rule: \(10\,K\) rise near room \(T\) about doubles \(k\) (\(E_a \approx 50\,kJ\)).
  • Exothermic vs endothermic profiles differ in product level vs reactant level; \(E_{a,f}-E_{a,b} = \Delta H\).
Example 1.

\(E_a = 50\,kJ/mol\). By what factor does \(k\) rise from \(300\,K\) to \(320\,K\)?

  1. \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (50000/19.147)(1/300-1/320) \approx 0.544\).
  2. Ratio \(\approx 10^{0.544} \approx 3.5\).

Answer: About \(3.5\) times.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Forward \(E_a = 50\,kJ\), \(\Delta H = -30\,kJ\). Find the backward \(E_a\).

  1. \(E_{a,f} - E_{a,b} = \Delta H\).
  2. \(E_{a,b} = 50 + 30 = 80\,kJ\).

Answer: \(80\,kJ\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Claiming catalysts change \(K\) or \(\Delta H\) (they change neither).
  • Using Celsius in the Arrhenius exponent.

Chapter 11 · Topic 19

Activation energy

Chemical KineticsElectro & KineticsTopic 19 of 32

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Kinetics, Activation energy: activation energy is the hill from reactants to transition state. Arrhenius \(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\); two-temperature form \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (E_a/2.303R)(1/T_1-1/T_2)\). Catalyst lowers \(E_a\) (new path), raising \(k\) without changing \(K\); threshold energy \(=\) \(E_a +\) average reactant energy.
Key formula(s). \[ k=Ae^{-E_a/RT},\;\log\frac{k_2}{k_1}=\frac{E_a}{2.303R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}\right) \]
Key points.
  • Rough rule: \(10\,K\) rise near room \(T\) about doubles \(k\) (\(E_a \approx 50\,kJ\)).
  • Exothermic vs endothermic profiles differ in product level vs reactant level; \(E_{a,f}-E_{a,b} = \Delta H\).
  • Effective collisions need energy \(\ge E_a\) AND correct orientation (steric factor \(p\)).
  • Parallel paths: \(k_{net} = k_1+k_2\); consecutive: slowest step dominates.
Example 1.

\(E_a = 50\,kJ/mol\). By what factor does \(k\) rise from \(300\,K\) to \(310\,K\)?

  1. \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (50000/(2.303\times8.314))(1/300-1/310)\).
  2. \(= 2611\times1.075\times10^{-4} \approx 0.281\); ratio \(\approx 10^{0.281} \approx 1.91\).

Answer: About \(1.9\times\) (doubles).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Catalyst lowers \(E_a\) from \(80\) to \(60\,kJ\) at \(300\,K\). Rate enhancement?

  1. Ratio \(= e^{\Delta E_a/RT} = e^{20000/(8.314\times300)}\).
  2. \(= e^{8.02} \approx 3040\times\).

Answer: About \(3\times10^3\) times faster.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Claiming catalysts change \(K\) or \(\Delta H\) (they change neither).
  • Using Celsius in the Arrhenius exponent.
