Frequency factor

Chemical KineticsElectro & KineticsTopic 20 of 32

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Kinetics, Frequency factor: the frequency factor A counts correctly-oriented collisions per second in Arrhenius theory. Arrhenius \(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\); two-temperature form \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (E_a/2.303R)(1/T_1-1/T_2)\). Catalyst lowers \(E_a\) (new path), raising \(k\) without changing \(K\); threshold energy \(=\) \(E_a +\) average reactant energy.
Key formula(s). \[ E_{a,f}-E_{a,b}=\Delta H \]
Key points.
  • Exothermic vs endothermic profiles differ in product level vs reactant level; \(E_{a,f}-E_{a,b} = \Delta H\).
  • Effective collisions need energy \(\ge E_a\) AND correct orientation (steric factor \(p\)).
  • Parallel paths: \(k_{net} = k_1+k_2\); consecutive: slowest step dominates.
  • Rough rule: \(10\,K\) rise near room \(T\) about doubles \(k\) (\(E_a \approx 50\,kJ\)).
Example 1.

\(k = 10^{-3}\,s^{-1}\) at \(300\,K\), \(E_a = 60\,kJ/mol\). Estimate \(k\) at \(310\,K\).

  1. \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (60000/19.147)(1/300-1/310) \approx 0.337\).
  2. \(k_2 \approx 2.17\times10^{-3}\,s^{-1}\).

Answer: About \(2.2\times10^{-3}\,s^{-1}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) A catalyst cuts \(E_a\) from \(90\) to \(60\,kJ\) at \(300\,K\). By what factor does the rate rise?

  1. Factor \(= e^{\Delta E_a/RT} = e^{30000/2494} = e^{12.03}\).
  2. About \(1.7\times10^5\) times.

Answer: About \(10^5\) times.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Claiming catalysts change \(K\) or \(\Delta H\) (they change neither).
  • Using Celsius in the Arrhenius exponent.

Chapter 11 · Topic 25

Catalysis

Chemical KineticsElectro & KineticsTopic 25 of 32

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Kinetics, Catalysis: catalysts open low-Ea paths without touching K or Delta-H. Arrhenius \(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\); two-temperature form \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (E_a/2.303R)(1/T_1-1/T_2)\). Catalyst lowers \(E_a\) (new path), raising \(k\) without changing \(K\); threshold energy \(=\) \(E_a +\) average reactant energy.
Key formula(s). \[ k=Ae^{-E_a/RT},\;\log\frac{k_2}{k_1}=\frac{E_a}{2.303R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}\right),\;catalyst:\,new\,path,\,lower\,E_a \]
Key points.
  • Rough rule: \(10\,K\) rise near room \(T\) about doubles \(k\) (\(E_a \approx 50\,kJ\)).
  • Exothermic vs endothermic profiles differ in product level vs reactant level; \(E_{a,f}-E_{a,b} = \Delta H\).
  • Effective collisions need energy \(\ge E_a\) AND correct orientation (steric factor \(p\)).
  • Parallel paths: \(k_{net} = k_1+k_2\); consecutive: slowest step dominates.
Example 1.

\(E_a = 50\,kJ/mol\). By what factor does \(k\) rise from \(300\,K\) to \(310\,K\)?

  1. \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (50000/(2.303\times8.314))(1/300-1/310)\).
  2. \(= 2611\times1.075\times10^{-4} \approx 0.281\); ratio \(\approx 10^{0.281} \approx 1.91\).

Answer: About \(1.9\times\) (doubles).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Catalyst lowers \(E_a\) from \(80\) to \(60\,kJ\) at \(300\,K\). Rate enhancement?

  1. Ratio \(= e^{\Delta E_a/RT} = e^{20000/(8.314\times300)}\).
  2. \(= e^{8.02} \approx 3040\times\).

Answer: About \(3\times10^3\) times faster.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Claiming catalysts change \(K\) or \(\Delta H\) (they change neither).
  • Using Celsius in the Arrhenius exponent.

Chapter 11 · Topic 26

Homogeneous catalysis

Chemical KineticsElectro & KineticsTopic 26 of 32

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Kinetics, Homogeneous catalysis: same-phase catalysts like NOx cycle intermediates invisibly. Arrhenius \(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\); two-temperature form \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (E_a/2.303R)(1/T_1-1/T_2)\). Catalyst lowers \(E_a\) (new path), raising \(k\) without changing \(K\); threshold energy \(=\) \(E_a +\) average reactant energy.
Key formula(s). \[ catalyst:\,new\,path,\,lower\,E_a,\;E_{a,f}-E_{a,b}=\Delta H \]
Key points.
  • Exothermic vs endothermic profiles differ in product level vs reactant level; \(E_{a,f}-E_{a,b} = \Delta H\).
  • Effective collisions need energy \(\ge E_a\) AND correct orientation (steric factor \(p\)).
  • Parallel paths: \(k_{net} = k_1+k_2\); consecutive: slowest step dominates.
  • Rough rule: \(10\,K\) rise near room \(T\) about doubles \(k\) (\(E_a \approx 50\,kJ\)).
Example 1.

\(k = 10^{-3}\,s^{-1}\) at \(300\,K\), \(E_a = 60\,kJ/mol\). Estimate \(k\) at \(310\,K\).

  1. \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (60000/19.147)(1/300-1/310) \approx 0.337\).
  2. \(k_2 \approx 2.17\times10^{-3}\,s^{-1}\).

Answer: About \(2.2\times10^{-3}\,s^{-1}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) A catalyst cuts \(E_a\) from \(90\) to \(60\,kJ\) at \(300\,K\). By what factor does the rate rise?

  1. Factor \(= e^{\Delta E_a/RT} = e^{30000/2494} = e^{12.03}\).
  2. About \(1.7\times10^5\) times.

Answer: About \(10^5\) times.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Claiming catalysts change \(K\) or \(\Delta H\) (they change neither).
  • Using Celsius in the Arrhenius exponent.

Chapter 11 · Topic 27

Heterogeneous catalysis

Chemical KineticsElectro & KineticsTopic 27 of 32

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Kinetics, Heterogeneous catalysis: surface catalysts adsorb, react and desorb in steps. Arrhenius \(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\); two-temperature form \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (E_a/2.303R)(1/T_1-1/T_2)\). Catalyst lowers \(E_a\) (new path), raising \(k\) without changing \(K\); threshold energy \(=\) \(E_a +\) average reactant energy.
Key formula(s). \[ k=Ae^{-E_a/RT},\;\log\frac{k_2}{k_1}=\frac{E_a}{2.303R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}\right),\;E_{a,f}-E_{a,b}=\Delta H,\;k=pZ\,e^{-E_a/RT}\,(steric\,p) \]
Key points.
  • Effective collisions need energy \(\ge E_a\) AND correct orientation (steric factor \(p\)).
  • Parallel paths: \(k_{net} = k_1+k_2\); consecutive: slowest step dominates.
  • Rough rule: \(10\,K\) rise near room \(T\) about doubles \(k\) (\(E_a \approx 50\,kJ\)).
  • Exothermic vs endothermic profiles differ in product level vs reactant level; \(E_{a,f}-E_{a,b} = \Delta H\).
Example 1.

\(E_a = 50\,kJ/mol\). By what factor does \(k\) rise from \(300\,K\) to \(320\,K\)?

  1. \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (50000/19.147)(1/300-1/320) \approx 0.544\).
  2. Ratio \(\approx 10^{0.544} \approx 3.5\).

Answer: About \(3.5\) times.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Forward \(E_a = 50\,kJ\), \(\Delta H = -30\,kJ\). Find the backward \(E_a\).

  1. \(E_{a,f} - E_{a,b} = \Delta H\).
  2. \(E_{a,b} = 50 + 30 = 80\,kJ\).

Answer: \(80\,kJ\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Claiming catalysts change \(K\) or \(\Delta H\) (they change neither).
  • Using Celsius in the Arrhenius exponent.

Chapter 11 · Topic 31

Rate-determining step

Chemical KineticsElectro & KineticsTopic 31 of 32

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Kinetics, Rate-determining step: the slowest elementary step dictates the observed law. Rate law \(rate = k[A]^m[B]^n\) comes from experiment only; order \(= m+n\), molecularity \(=\) molecules in an elementary step. First order: \(k = (2.303/t)\log(a/(a-x))\), \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/k\); zero: \(t_{1/2} = a/2k\). Units of \(k\): \((mol/L)^{1-n}s^{-1}\).
Key formula(s). \[ k=\frac{2.303}{t}\log\frac{a}{a-x},\;t_{1/2}(1st)=\frac{0.693}{k},\;molecularity=1/2/3,\;1st:\,\ln[A]-t\,linear \]
Key points.
  • Order can be zero, fractional or negative; molecularity is a positive integer \(1,2,3\).
  • Slowest elementary step \(=\) rate-determining; its stoichiometry (with pre-equilibria) sets the law.
  • Pseudo-first-order: excess reactant hides true order (e.g. ester hydrolysis in water).
  • Graphs: 1st order \(\ln[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; 2nd order \(1/[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; zero \([A]\) vs \(t\) linear.
Example 1.

A first-order reaction is \(75\%\) complete in \(60\,min\). Find \(k\).

  1. \(k = (2.303/60)\log(100/25) = (2.303/60)\log4\).
  2. \(k = (2.303\times0.602/60) \approx 0.0231\,min^{-1}\).

Answer: About \(0.0231\,min^{-1}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Doubling \([A]\) doubles rate, doubling \([B]\) quadruples it. Give orders and \(k\) units.

  1. Order in A \(= 1\), in B \(= 2\); overall \(= 3\).
  2. Units \(= M^{-2}s^{-1}\) (\(L^2mol^{-2}s^{-1}\)).

Answer: 3rd order; \(M^{-2}s^{-1}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reading order from balanced-equation coefficients.
  • Using \(\log\) vs \(\ln\) inconsistently (factor 2.303).

Chapter 11 · Topic 32

Mechanism and rate law

Chemical KineticsElectro & KineticsTopic 32 of 32

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Kinetics, Mechanism and rate law: mechanisms are proved when the slow step plus pre-equilibria match the law. Rate law \(rate = k[A]^m[B]^n\) comes from experiment only; order \(= m+n\), molecularity \(=\) molecules in an elementary step. First order: \(k = (2.303/t)\log(a/(a-x))\), \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/k\); zero: \(t_{1/2} = a/2k\). Units of \(k\): \((mol/L)^{1-n}s^{-1}\).
Key formula(s). \[ k=\frac{2.303}{t}\log\frac{a}{a-x},\;t_{1/2}(1st)=\frac{0.693}{k},\;1st:\,\ln[A]-t\,linear \]
Key points.
  • Slowest elementary step \(=\) rate-determining; its stoichiometry (with pre-equilibria) sets the law.
  • Pseudo-first-order: excess reactant hides true order (e.g. ester hydrolysis in water).
  • Graphs: 1st order \(\ln[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; 2nd order \(1/[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; zero \([A]\) vs \(t\) linear.
  • Order can be zero, fractional or negative; molecularity is a positive integer \(1,2,3\).
Example 1.

A first-order reaction is \(50\%\) complete in \(30\,min\). Find \(k\).

  1. This is one half-life: \(t_{1/2} = 30\,min\).
  2. \(k = 0.693/30 \approx 0.0231\,min^{-1}\).

Answer: \(0.0231\,min^{-1}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Doubling \([A]\) has no effect; tripling \([B]\) triples the rate. Give orders and overall units of \(k\).

  1. Order \(0\) in A, \(1\) in B; overall \(1\).
  2. Units \(= s^{-1}\).

Answer: First order overall; \(s^{-1}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reading order from balanced-equation coefficients.
  • Using \(\log\) vs \(\ln\) inconsistently (factor 2.303).

Index / Surface, Nuclear & Mastery
Chapter 12 · Topic 1

Adsorption

Surface ChemistrySurface, Nuclear & MasteryTopic 1 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Surface Chemistry, Adsorption: adsorption gathers molecules on surfaces exothermically. Adsorption is surface accumulation (exothermic, \(\Delta H<0\), \(\Delta S<0\), favoured at low \(T\)). Freundlich \(x/m = kP^{1/n}\) (\(\log\)-\(\log\) slope \(1/n\)); Langmuir monolayer \(\theta = KP/(1+KP)\). Chemisorption is specific, high-enthalpy, monolayer and often irreversible.
Key formula(s). \[ physisorption:\,weak,\,multilayer,\,reversible,\;chemisorption:\,monolayer,\,specific,\,high\,\Delta H \]
Key points.
  • \(1/n\) between \(0\)-\(1\); \(1/n = 0\) means saturated (pressure-independent).
  • Applications: gas masks (charcoal), decolourising sugar, silica-gel drying, catalysis beds.
  • Enzyme catalysis: lock-and-key, optimum \(T\)/pH, inhibited by poisons.
  • Physisorption: van der Waals, multilayer, reversible, low \(\Delta H\) (\(\approx 20\)-\(40\,kJ\)); chemisorption: chemical bonds, monolayer, high \(\Delta H\) (\(40\)-\(400\,kJ\)).
Example 1.

At low pressure, what order does Langmuir adsorption follow?

  1. \(\theta = KP/(1+KP) \approx KP\).
  2. First order in \(P\).

Answer: First order.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) At very high pressure, how does surface coverage change with \(P\)?

  1. \(\theta \to 1\) (saturated monolayer).
  2. Zero order (independent of \(P\)).

Answer: Saturates (zero order).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Applying Freundlich \(1/n>1\) uncritically (unphysical for chemisorption fits).
  • Calling absorption (bulk uptake) adsorption.

Chapter 12 · Topic 2

Absorption

Surface ChemistrySurface, Nuclear & MasteryTopic 2 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Surface Chemistry, Absorption: absorption soaks molecules into bulk, unlike surface adsorption. Adsorption is surface accumulation (exothermic, \(\Delta H<0\), \(\Delta S<0\), favoured at low \(T\)). Freundlich \(x/m = kP^{1/n}\) (\(\log\)-\(\log\) slope \(1/n\)); Langmuir monolayer \(\theta = KP/(1+KP)\). Chemisorption is specific, high-enthalpy, monolayer and often irreversible.
Key formula(s). \[ chemisorption:\,monolayer,\,specific,\,high\,\Delta H \],\;\frac{x}{m}=kP^{1/n} \]
Key points.
  • Applications: gas masks (charcoal), decolourising sugar, silica-gel drying, catalysis beds.
  • Enzyme catalysis: lock-and-key, optimum \(T\)/pH, inhibited by poisons.
  • Physisorption: van der Waals, multilayer, reversible, low \(\Delta H\) (\(\approx 20\)-\(40\,kJ\)); chemisorption: chemical bonds, monolayer, high \(\Delta H\) (\(40\)-\(400\,kJ\)).
  • \(1/n\) between \(0\)-\(1\); \(1/n = 0\) means saturated (pressure-independent).
Example 1.

Why is chemisorption usually irreversible while physisorption reverses easily?

  1. Chemisorption makes true chemical bonds (high \(\Delta H\)).
  2. Breaking them needs large activation energy.

Answer: Chemical bonds vs weak forces.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Which will adsorb more on nickel: \(NH_3\) or \(N_2\)?

  1. Chemisorption is specific; \(NH_3\) donates its lone pair to Ni.
  2. \(NH_3\).

Answer: \(NH_3\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Applying Freundlich \(1/n>1\) uncritically (unphysical for chemisorption fits).
  • Calling absorption (bulk uptake) adsorption.

Chapter 12 · Topic 3

Adsorption vs absorption

Surface ChemistrySurface, Nuclear & MasteryTopic 3 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Surface Chemistry, Adsorption vs absorption: adsorption is surface, absorption is bulk penetration. Adsorption is surface accumulation (exothermic, \(\Delta H<0\), \(\Delta S<0\), favoured at low \(T\)). Freundlich \(x/m = kP^{1/n}\) (\(\log\)-\(\log\) slope \(1/n\)); Langmuir monolayer \(\theta = KP/(1+KP)\). Chemisorption is specific, high-enthalpy, monolayer and often irreversible.
Key formula(s). \[ \frac{x}{m}=kP^{1/n},\;\log\frac{x}{m}=\log k+\frac{1}{n}\log P \]
Key points.
  • Physisorption: van der Waals, multilayer, reversible, low \(\Delta H\) (\(\approx 20\)-\(40\,kJ\)); chemisorption: chemical bonds, monolayer, high \(\Delta H\) (\(40\)-\(400\,kJ\)).
  • \(1/n\) between \(0\)-\(1\); \(1/n = 0\) means saturated (pressure-independent).
  • Applications: gas masks (charcoal), decolourising sugar, silica-gel drying, catalysis beds.
  • Enzyme catalysis: lock-and-key, optimum \(T\)/pH, inhibited by poisons.
Example 1.

Plot of \(\log(x/m)\) vs \(\log P\) has slope \(0.4\), intercept \(0.3\). Find \(n\) and \(k\).

  1. Slope \(= 1/n = 0.4 \Rightarrow n = 2.5\).
  2. Intercept \(= \log k = 0.3 \Rightarrow k = 10^{0.3} \approx 2.0\).

Answer: \(n = 2.5\), \(k \approx 2.0\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Which adsorbs more on charcoal at same \(P\): \(SO_2\) or \(H_2\)? Why?

  1. Easily liquefiable gases adsorb more (higher critical \(T\)).
  2. \(SO_2\) (\(T_c = 630\,K\)) far exceeds \(H_2\) (\(33\,K\)).

Answer: \(SO_2\) adsorbs much more.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Applying Freundlich \(1/n>1\) uncritically (unphysical for chemisorption fits).
  • Calling absorption (bulk uptake) adsorption.

  • Applications: gas masks (charcoal), decolourising sugar, silica-gel drying, catalysis beds.
  • Enzyme catalysis: lock-and-key, optimum \(T\)/pH, inhibited by poisons.
  • Physisorption: van der Waals, multilayer, reversible, low \(\Delta H\) (\(\approx 20\)-\(40\,kJ\)); chemisorption: chemical bonds, monolayer, high \(\Delta H\) (\(40\)-\(400\,kJ\)).
  • \(1/n\) between \(0\)-\(1\); \(1/n = 0\) means saturated (pressure-independent).
Example 1.

Why is chemisorption usually irreversible while physisorption reverses easily?

  1. Chemisorption makes true chemical bonds (high \(\Delta H\)).
  2. Breaking them needs large activation energy.

Answer: Chemical bonds vs weak forces.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Which will adsorb more on nickel: \(NH_3\) or \(N_2\)?

  1. Chemisorption is specific; \(NH_3\) donates its lone pair to Ni.
  2. \(NH_3\).

Answer: \(NH_3\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Applying Freundlich \(1/n>1\) uncritically (unphysical for chemisorption fits).
  • Calling absorption (bulk uptake) adsorption.

Factors affecting adsorption

Surface ChemistrySurface, Nuclear & MasteryTopic 6 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Surface Chemistry, Factors affecting adsorption: pressure, temperature, gas nature and surface area steer uptake. Adsorption is surface accumulation (exothermic, \(\Delta H<0\), \(\Delta S<0\), favoured at low \(T\)). Freundlich \(x/m = kP^{1/n}\) (\(\log\)-\(\log\) slope \(1/n\)); Langmuir monolayer \(\theta = KP/(1+KP)\). Chemisorption is specific, high-enthalpy, monolayer and often irreversible.
Key formula(s). \[ \frac{x}{m}=kP^{1/n},\;physisorption:\,weak,\,multilayer,\,reversible,\;chemisorption:\,monolayer,\,specific,\,high\,\Delta H \]
Key points.
  • Physisorption: van der Waals, multilayer, reversible, low \(\Delta H\) (\(\approx 20\)-\(40\,kJ\)); chemisorption: chemical bonds, monolayer, high \(\Delta H\) (\(40\)-\(400\,kJ\)).
  • \(1/n\) between \(0\)-\(1\); \(1/n = 0\) means saturated (pressure-independent).
  • Applications: gas masks (charcoal), decolourising sugar, silica-gel drying, catalysis beds.
  • Enzyme catalysis: lock-and-key, optimum \(T\)/pH, inhibited by poisons.
Example 1.

Plot of \(\log(x/m)\) vs \(\log P\) has slope \(0.4\), intercept \(0.3\). Find \(n\) and \(k\).

  1. Slope \(= 1/n = 0.4 \Rightarrow n = 2.5\).
  2. Intercept \(= \log k = 0.3 \Rightarrow k = 10^{0.3} \approx 2.0\).

Answer: \(n = 2.5\), \(k \approx 2.0\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Which adsorbs more on charcoal at same \(P\): \(SO_2\) or \(H_2\)? Why?

  1. Easily liquefiable gases adsorb more (higher critical \(T\)).
  2. \(SO_2\) (\(T_c = 630\,K\)) far exceeds \(H_2\) (\(33\,K\)).

Answer: \(SO_2\) adsorbs much more.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Applying Freundlich \(1/n>1\) uncritically (unphysical for chemisorption fits).
  • Calling absorption (bulk uptake) adsorption.

Freundlich adsorption isotherm

Surface ChemistrySurface, Nuclear & MasteryTopic 7 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Surface Chemistry, Freundlich adsorption isotherm: Freundlich fits x-over-m to k P to the one-over-n. Adsorption is surface accumulation (exothermic, \(\Delta H<0\), \(\Delta S<0\), favoured at low \(T\)). Freundlich \(x/m = kP^{1/n}\) (\(\log\)-\(\log\) slope \(1/n\)); Langmuir monolayer \(\theta = KP/(1+KP)\). Chemisorption is specific, high-enthalpy, monolayer and often irreversible.
Key formula(s). \[ \frac{x}{m}=kP^{1/n},\;\log\frac{x}{m}=\log k+\frac{1}{n}\log P,\;chemisorption:\,monolayer,\,specific,\,high\,\Delta H \]
Key points.
  • \(1/n\) between \(0\)-\(1\); \(1/n = 0\) means saturated (pressure-independent).
  • Applications: gas masks (charcoal), decolourising sugar, silica-gel drying, catalysis beds.
  • Enzyme catalysis: lock-and-key, optimum \(T\)/pH, inhibited by poisons.
  • Physisorption: van der Waals, multilayer, reversible, low \(\Delta H\) (\(\approx 20\)-\(40\,kJ\)); chemisorption: chemical bonds, monolayer, high \(\Delta H\) (\(40\)-\(400\,kJ\)).
Example 1.

At low pressure, what order does Langmuir adsorption follow?

  1. \(\theta = KP/(1+KP) \approx KP\).
  2. First order in \(P\).

Answer: First order.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) At very high pressure, how does surface coverage change with \(P\)?

  1. \(\theta \to 1\) (saturated monolayer).
  2. Zero order (independent of \(P\)).

Answer: Saturates (zero order).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Applying Freundlich \(1/n>1\) uncritically (unphysical for chemisorption fits).
  • Calling absorption (bulk uptake) adsorption.

Chapter 12 · Topic 10

Catalysis

Surface ChemistrySurface, Nuclear & MasteryTopic 10 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Surface Chemistry, Catalysis: catalysts open low-Ea paths without touching K or Delta-H. Arrhenius \(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\); two-temperature form \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (E_a/2.303R)(1/T_1-1/T_2)\). Catalyst lowers \(E_a\) (new path), raising \(k\) without changing \(K\); threshold energy \(=\) \(E_a +\) average reactant energy.
Key formula(s). \[ k=Ae^{-E_a/RT},\;\log\frac{k_2}{k_1}=\frac{E_a}{2.303R}\left(\frac{1}{T_1}-\frac{1}{T_2}\right) \]
Key points.
  • Exothermic vs endothermic profiles differ in product level vs reactant level; \(E_{a,f}-E_{a,b} = \Delta H\).
  • Effective collisions need energy \(\ge E_a\) AND correct orientation (steric factor \(p\)).
  • Parallel paths: \(k_{net} = k_1+k_2\); consecutive: slowest step dominates.
  • Rough rule: \(10\,K\) rise near room \(T\) about doubles \(k\) (\(E_a \approx 50\,kJ\)).
Example 1.

\(k = 10^{-3}\,s^{-1}\) at \(300\,K\), \(E_a = 60\,kJ/mol\). Estimate \(k\) at \(310\,K\).

  1. \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (60000/19.147)(1/300-1/310) \approx 0.337\).
  2. \(k_2 \approx 2.17\times10^{-3}\,s^{-1}\).

Answer: About \(2.2\times10^{-3}\,s^{-1}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) A catalyst cuts \(E_a\) from \(90\) to \(60\,kJ\) at \(300\,K\). By what factor does the rate rise?

  1. Factor \(= e^{\Delta E_a/RT} = e^{30000/2494} = e^{12.03}\).
  2. About \(1.7\times10^5\) times.

Answer: About \(10^5\) times.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Claiming catalysts change \(K\) or \(\Delta H\) (they change neither).
  • Using Celsius in the Arrhenius exponent.

Homogeneous catalysis

Surface ChemistrySurface, Nuclear & MasteryTopic 11 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Surface Chemistry, Homogeneous catalysis: same-phase catalysts like NOx cycle intermediates invisibly. Arrhenius \(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\); two-temperature form \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (E_a/2.303R)(1/T_1-1/T_2)\). Catalyst lowers \(E_a\) (new path), raising \(k\) without changing \(K\); threshold energy \(=\) \(E_a +\) average reactant energy.
Key formula(s). \[ E_{a,f}-E_{a,b}=\Delta H,\;k=pZ\,e^{-E_a/RT}\,(steric\,p) \]
Key points.
  • Effective collisions need energy \(\ge E_a\) AND correct orientation (steric factor \(p\)).
  • Parallel paths: \(k_{net} = k_1+k_2\); consecutive: slowest step dominates.
  • Rough rule: \(10\,K\) rise near room \(T\) about doubles \(k\) (\(E_a \approx 50\,kJ\)).
  • Exothermic vs endothermic profiles differ in product level vs reactant level; \(E_{a,f}-E_{a,b} = \Delta H\).
Example 1.

\(E_a = 50\,kJ/mol\). By what factor does \(k\) rise from \(300\,K\) to \(320\,K\)?

  1. \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (50000/19.147)(1/300-1/320) \approx 0.544\).
  2. Ratio \(\approx 10^{0.544} \approx 3.5\).

Answer: About \(3.5\) times.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Forward \(E_a = 50\,kJ\), \(\Delta H = -30\,kJ\). Find the backward \(E_a\).

  1. \(E_{a,f} - E_{a,b} = \Delta H\).
  2. \(E_{a,b} = 50 + 30 = 80\,kJ\).

Answer: \(80\,kJ\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Claiming catalysts change \(K\) or \(\Delta H\) (they change neither).
  • Using Celsius in the Arrhenius exponent.

Heterogeneous catalysis

Surface ChemistrySurface, Nuclear & MasteryTopic 12 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Surface Chemistry, Heterogeneous catalysis: surface catalysts adsorb, react and desorb in steps. Arrhenius \(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\); two-temperature form \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (E_a/2.303R)(1/T_1-1/T_2)\). Catalyst lowers \(E_a\) (new path), raising \(k\) without changing \(K\); threshold energy \(=\) \(E_a +\) average reactant energy.
Key formula(s). \[ k=pZ\,e^{-E_a/RT}\,(steric\,p) \],\;k=Ae^{-E_a/RT} \]
Key points.
  • Rough rule: \(10\,K\) rise near room \(T\) about doubles \(k\) (\(E_a \approx 50\,kJ\)).
  • Exothermic vs endothermic profiles differ in product level vs reactant level; \(E_{a,f}-E_{a,b} = \Delta H\).
  • Effective collisions need energy \(\ge E_a\) AND correct orientation (steric factor \(p\)).
  • Parallel paths: \(k_{net} = k_1+k_2\); consecutive: slowest step dominates.
Example 1.

\(E_a = 50\,kJ/mol\). By what factor does \(k\) rise from \(300\,K\) to \(310\,K\)?

  1. \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (50000/(2.303\times8.314))(1/300-1/310)\).
  2. \(= 2611\times1.075\times10^{-4} \approx 0.281\); ratio \(\approx 10^{0.281} \approx 1.91\).

Answer: About \(1.9\times\) (doubles).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Catalyst lowers \(E_a\) from \(80\) to \(60\,kJ\) at \(300\,K\). Rate enhancement?

  1. Ratio \(= e^{\Delta E_a/RT} = e^{20000/(8.314\times300)}\).
  2. \(= e^{8.02} \approx 3040\times\).

Answer: About \(3\times10^3\) times faster.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Claiming catalysts change \(K\) or \(\Delta H\) (they change neither).
  • Using Celsius in the Arrhenius exponent.

Chapter 12 · Topic 14

Colloids

Surface ChemistrySurface, Nuclear & MasteryTopic 14 of 30

Explanation

Concept. In Surface Chemistry, Colloids: colloids span 1 to 1000 nm with Tyndall and Brownian signatures. Colloids (1-\(1000\,nm\)) show Tyndall scattering and Brownian motion. Lyophilic are stable/reversible (gum, starch); lyophobic need stabilisers (metal sols). Coagulation follows Hardy-Schulze: power \(\propto\) (charge)\(^n\); gold number measures protective power.
Key formula(s). \[ Tyndall:\,light\,scattering\,by\,sols \]
Key points.
  • Emulsions: oil-in-water (milk) vs water-in-oil (butter); emulsifiers stabilise the interface.
  • Peptisation converts precipitate to colloid; dialysis purifies it.
  • Electrophoresis: particles migrate; electro-osmosis: medium moves (particles fixed).
  • CMC: above it surfactants form associated (micelle) colloids.
Example 1.

Rank \(Na^+, Ba^{2+}, Al^{3+}\) for coagulating a negative sol.

  1. Opposite charge coagulates; higher charge \(=\) stronger (Hardy-Schulze).
  2. Order: \(Al^{3+}>Ba^{2+}>Na^+\).

Answer: \(Al^{3+}>Ba^{2+}>Na^+\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Which is lyophilic: gelatin or \(Fe(OH)_3\) sol? Which is reversible?

  1. Gelatin (protein-water affinity) is lyophilic and reversible on evaporation.
  2. \(Fe(OH)_3\) is lyophobic and irreversible.

Answer: Gelatin; reversible.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using same-sign ions for coagulation (need opposite charge).
  • Swapping electrophoresis with electro-osmosis.

Explanation

  • Adsorption is exothermic, favoured cold.
  • 1/n in (0,1); 0 means saturated.
Example 1.

  1. Slope = 1/n.
  2. n = 2.

Answer: 2.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Protective power: gold numbers 0.01 vs 0.1. Which protects better?

  1. Smaller gold number wins.
  2. 0.01.

Answer: Gold number 0.01.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.

Chapter 13 · Topic 1

Classification of solids

Solid StateStates of MatterTopic 1 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Solid State, Classification of solids: the focus here is Classification of solids, worked through the Solid State toolkit below. Cubic cells: sc (\(Z=1\), CN 6, 52.4\(\%\)), bcc (\(Z=2\), CN 8, 68\(\%\)), fcc (\(Z=4\), CN 12, 74\(\%\)). Density \(d = ZM/(a^3N_A)\); \(r = a/2\) (sc), \(\sqrt3a/4\) (bcc), \(a/2\sqrt2\) (fcc).
Key formula(s). \[ tetra=2N,\;CN:\,6/8/12\,(sc/bcc/fcc) \]
Key points.
  • Convert \(a\) from \(pm\) to \(cm\) (\(\times10^{-10}\)) before density in \(g/cm^3\).
  • Amorphous solids (glass) have no long-range order and melt over a range.
  • Count atoms: corners \(\times1/8\), faces \(\times1/2\), body centre \(\times1\), edges \(\times1/4\).
  • Voids in ccp: octahedral \(= N\), tetrahedral \(= 2N\) per \(N\) atoms.
Example 1.

How many atoms per simple cubic cell, and its packing efficiency?

  1. Corners only: \(8\times1/8 = 1\) atom.
  2. Efficiency \(= \pi/6 \approx 52.4\%\).

Answer: \(Z = 1\), \(52.4\%\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(KCl\) has similar-size ions. Which defect does it show?

  1. Similar sizes favour paired vacancies.
  2. Schottky defect.

Answer: Schottky.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(Z = 8\) for corners (each corner is shared by 8 cells).
  • Forgetting \(pm\to cm\) conversion in density.

Index / States of Matter
Chapter 13 · Topic 2

Crystalline solids

Solid StateStates of MatterTopic 2 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Solid State, Crystalline solids: crystals repeat a unit cell in perfect three-dimensional order. Cubic cells: sc (\(Z=1\), CN 6, 52.4\(\%\)), bcc (\(Z=2\), CN 8, 68\(\%\)), fcc (\(Z=4\), CN 12, 74\(\%\)). Density \(d = ZM/(a^3N_A)\); \(r = a/2\) (sc), \(\sqrt3a/4\) (bcc), \(a/2\sqrt2\) (fcc).
Key formula(s). \[ CN:\,6/8/12\,(sc/bcc/fcc) \],\;d=\frac{ZM}{a^3N_A} \]
Key points.
  • Count atoms: corners \(\times1/8\), faces \(\times1/2\), body centre \(\times1\), edges \(\times1/4\).
  • Voids in ccp: octahedral \(= N\), tetrahedral \(= 2N\) per \(N\) atoms.
  • Convert \(a\) from \(pm\) to \(cm\) (\(\times10^{-10}\)) before density in \(g/cm^3\).
  • Amorphous solids (glass) have no long-range order and melt over a range.
Example 1.

An fcc metal has \(a = 400\,pm\), \(M = 64\). Find its density.

  1. \(Z = 4\); \(a = 4\times10^{-8}\,cm\); \(a^3 = 6.4\times10^{-23}\,cm^3\).
  2. \(d = 4\times64/(6.4\times10^{-23}\times6.022\times10^{23}) \approx 6.64\,g/cm^3\).

Answer: About \(6.64\,g/cm^3\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) If atoms occupy all octahedral voids of ccp oxide \(O^{2-}\) lattice with \(M^{2+}\), find the formula.

  1. ccp \(O\): \(N\) atoms; octahedral voids \(= N\), all filled by \(M\).
  2. Formula \(= MO\) (rock-salt type).

Answer: \(MO\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(Z = 8\) for corners (each corner is shared by 8 cells).
  • Forgetting \(pm\to cm\) conversion in density.

Chapter 13 · Topic 3

Amorphous solids

Explanation

Concept. In Solid State, Amorphous solids: glasses freeze disorder and soften over a range instead of melting sharp. Cubic cells: sc (\(Z=1\), CN 6, 52.4\(\%\)), bcc (\(Z=2\), CN 8, 68\(\%\)), fcc (\(Z=4\), CN 12, 74\(\%\)). Density \(d = ZM/(a^3N_A)\); \(r = a/2\) (sc), \(\sqrt3a/4\) (bcc), \(a/2\sqrt2\) (fcc).
Key formula(s). \[ d=\frac{ZM}{a^3N_A},\;r_{bcc}=\frac{\sqrt3a}{4} \]
Key points.
  • Voids in ccp: octahedral \(= N\), tetrahedral \(= 2N\) per \(N\) atoms.
  • Convert \(a\) from \(pm\) to \(cm\) (\(\times10^{-10}\)) before density in \(g/cm^3\).

  • Count atoms: corners \(\times1/8\), faces \(\times1/2\), body centre \(\times1\), edges \(\times1/4\).
Example 1.

A bcc metal has edge \(a = 300\,pm\). Find its atomic radius.

  1. For bcc, \(r = \sqrt3\,a/4\).
  2. \(r = 1.732\times300/4 \approx 130\,pm\).

Answer: About \(130\,pm\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Sulphide ions form ccp; \(Zn^{2+}\) fills half the tetrahedral voids. Give the formula.

  1. ccp \(S\): \(N\) atoms; tetrahedral voids \(= 2N\); half filled \(= N\,Zn\).
  2. Formula \(= ZnS\).

Answer: \(ZnS\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(Z = 8\) for corners (each corner is shared by 8 cells).
  • Forgetting \(pm\to cm\) conversion in density.

Chapter 13 · Topic 5

Primitive unit cell

Solid StateStates of MatterTopic 5 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Solid State, Primitive unit cell: primitive cells hold lattice points at corners only. Cubic cells: sc (\(Z=1\), CN 6, 52.4\(\%\)), bcc (\(Z=2\), CN 8, 68\(\%\)), fcc (\(Z=4\), CN 12, 74\(\%\)). Density \(d = ZM/(a^3N_A)\); \(r = a/2\) (sc), \(\sqrt3a/4\) (bcc), \(a/2\sqrt2\) (fcc).
Key formula(s). \[ r_{fcc}=\frac{a}{2\sqrt2},\;Z:\,sc=1,\,bcc=2,\,fcc=4 \]
Key points.
  • Count atoms: corners \(\times1/8\), faces \(\times1/2\), body centre \(\times1\), edges \(\times1/4\).
  • Voids in ccp: octahedral \(= N\), tetrahedral \(= 2N\) per \(N\) atoms.
  • Convert \(a\) from \(pm\) to \(cm\) (\(\times10^{-10}\)) before density in \(g/cm^3\).
  • Amorphous solids (glass) have no long-range order and melt over a range.
Example 1.

An fcc metal has \(a = 400\,pm\), \(M = 64\). Find its density.

  1. \(Z = 4\); \(a = 4\times10^{-8}\,cm\); \(a^3 = 6.4\times10^{-23}\,cm^3\).
  2. \(d = 4\times64/(6.4\times10^{-23}\times6.022\times10^{23}) \approx 6.64\,g/cm^3\).

Answer: About \(6.64\,g/cm^3\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) If atoms occupy all octahedral voids of ccp oxide \(O^{2-}\) lattice with \(M^{2+}\), find the formula.

  1. ccp \(O\): \(N\) atoms; octahedral voids \(= N\), all filled by \(M\).
  2. Formula \(= MO\) (rock-salt type).

Answer: \(MO\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(Z = 8\) for corners (each corner is shared by 8 cells).
  • Forgetting \(pm\to cm\) conversion in density.

Chapter 13 · Topic 6

Centred unit cells

Solid StateStates of MatterTopic 6 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Solid State, Centred unit cells: the focus here is Centred unit cells, worked through the Solid State toolkit below. Cubic cells: sc (\(Z=1\), CN 6, 52.4\(\%\)), bcc (\(Z=2\), CN 8, 68\(\%\)), fcc (\(Z=4\), CN 12, 74\(\%\)). Density \(d = ZM/(a^3N_A)\); \(r = a/2\) (sc), \(\sqrt3a/4\) (bcc), \(a/2\sqrt2\) (fcc).
Key formula(s). \[ Z:\,sc=1,\,bcc=2,\,fcc=4,\;PE:\,74/68/52.4\% \,(fcc/bcc/sc) \]
Key points.
  • Voids in ccp: octahedral \(= N\), tetrahedral \(= 2N\) per \(N\) atoms.
  • Convert \(a\) from \(pm\) to \(cm\) (\(\times10^{-10}\)) before density in \(g/cm^3\).
  • Amorphous solids (glass) have no long-range order and melt over a range.
  • Count atoms: corners \(\times1/8\), faces \(\times1/2\), body centre \(\times1\), edges \(\times1/4\).
Example 1.

A bcc metal has edge \(a = 300\,pm\). Find its atomic radius.

  1. For bcc, \(r = \sqrt3\,a/4\).
  2. \(r = 1.732\times300/4 \approx 130\,pm\).

Answer: About \(130\,pm\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Sulphide ions form ccp; \(Zn^{2+}\) fills half the tetrahedral voids. Give the formula.

  1. ccp \(S\): \(N\) atoms; tetrahedral voids \(= 2N\); half filled \(= N\,Zn\).
  2. Formula \(= ZnS\).

Answer: \(ZnS\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(Z = 8\) for corners (each corner is shared by 8 cells).
  • Forgetting \(pm\to cm\) conversion in density.

Chapter 13 · Topic 7

Simple cubic

Solid StateStates of MatterTopic 7 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Solid State, Simple cubic: simple cubic holds one atom at a sparse 52.4 percent. This Solid State topic counts atoms per cell (corners 1/8, faces 1/2), converts edge to radius, weighs density with d = ZM/(a^3 Na), and names Schottky vs Frenkel defects with doping outcomes.
Key formula(s). \[ Z_{fcc}=4 \]
Key points.
  • Schottky drops density; Frenkel keeps it.
  • P-doping gives n-type; B gives p-type.
  • CN: sc 6, bcc 8, fcc 12.
  • Tetra voids = 2N, octa = N.
Example 1.

Atoms per bcc unit cell?

  1. 8 corners x 1/8 + 1 body.
  2. Z = 2.

Answer: 2.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Packing efficiency of simple cubic?

  1. Sphere pi/6 of cube.
  2. 52.4%.

Answer: 52.4%.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Corner counted whole (divide by 8).
  • pm-cm conversion missed.

Chapter 13 · Topic 14

Radius-edge relationships

Solid StateStates of MatterTopic 14 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Solid State, Radius-edge relationships: sc halves the edge, bcc uses root-3-over-4, fcc root-2-over-4. Close packing: ABAB (hcp, 74\(\%\)) and ABCABC (ccp/fcc, 74\(\%\)); voids: tetrahedral \(2N\), octahedral \(N\). Limiting radius ratios: tetrahedral \(0.225\)-\(0.414\), octahedral \(0.414\)-\(0.732\). Conductivity: conductors \(\approx 10^7\), semiconductors \(10^{-6}\)-\(10^4\), insulators tiny \(S/m\).
Key formula(s). \[ r^+/r^-\,(oct)\ge0.414,\;d=\frac{ZM}{a^3N_A} \]
Key points.
  • hcp and ccp both 74\(\%\); bcc 68\(\%\); sc 52.4\(\%\); diamond cubic only 34\(\%\).
  • Radius-ratio predicts coordination: \(<0.155\) linear(2), \(0.414\) octahedral(6), \(>0.732\) cubic(8).
  • Magnetism: para (unpaired, attracted), dia (all paired, repelled), ferro (domains, permanent), ferri/anti-ferro variants.
  • n-type (group-15 donor) vs p-type (group-13 acceptor) from doping.
Example 1.

How many tetrahedral voids in an fcc lattice with \(4\) atoms per unit cell?

  1. Tetrahedral \(= 2N = 8\) per cell.
  2. Octahedral \(= 4\) per cell.

Answer: 8 tetrahedral, 4 octahedral.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(Na^+\) (\(102\,pm\)) in \(Cl^-\) (\(181\,pm\)) lattice: predict coordination.

  1. Ratio \(= 102/181 \approx 0.563\) (octahedral range).
  2. Coordination \(6\) (rock-salt).

Answer: 6:6 octahedral.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Claiming hcp packs worse than bcc (hcp 74\(\%\) is densest with ccp).
  • Mixing void counts (tetra \(= 2\times\) octa).

Example 1.

What is the coordination number of an octahedral void?

  1. An octahedral void touches \(6\) surrounding atoms.
  2. Coordination number \(= 6\).

(JEE pattern) What is the packing efficiency of hcp?

  1. hcp is a closest packing like ccp.
  2. \(74\%\).

Answer: \(74\%\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Claiming hcp packs worse than bcc (hcp 74\(\%\) is densest with ccp).

Key formula(s). \[ PE_{hcp/ccp}=74\%,\;ccp=ABCABC\,(both\,74\%) \]
Key points.
  • Magnetism: para (unpaired, attracted), dia (all paired, repelled), ferro (domains, permanent), ferri/anti-ferro variants.
  • n-type (group-15 donor) vs p-type (group-13 acceptor) from doping.
  • hcp and ccp both 74\(\%\); bcc 68\(\%\); sc 52.4\(\%\); diamond cubic only 34\(\%\).
  • Radius-ratio predicts coordination: \(<0.155\) linear(2), \(0.414\) octahedral(6), \(>0.732\) cubic(8).
Example 1.

\(Cs^+\) (\(174\,pm\)) sits in \(Cl^-\) (\(181\,pm\)) cubic voids. Predict coordination.

  1. Ratio \(= 174/181 \approx 0.96\) (cubic range, above \(0.732\)).
  2. Coordination \(8:8\) (CsCl type).

Answer: \(8:8\) cubic.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) What is the packing efficiency of diamond cubic?

  1. Diamond has a very open tetrahedral network.
  2. Only \(34\%\).

Answer: \(34\%\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Claiming hcp packs worse than bcc (hcp 74\(\%\) is densest with ccp).
  • Mixing void counts (tetra \(= 2\times\) octa).

What is the coordination number of an octahedral void?

  1. An octahedral void touches \(6\) surrounding atoms.
  2. Coordination number \(= 6\).

Answer: \(6\).

(JEE pattern) What is the packing efficiency of hcp?

Chapter 13 · Topic 22

Defects in solids

Solid StateStates of MatterTopic 22 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Solid State, Defects in solids: defects are missing or misplaced ions that tune colour and conductivity. Cubic cells: sc (\(Z=1\), CN 6, 52.4\(\%\)), bcc (\(Z=2\), CN 8, 68\(\%\)), fcc (\(Z=4\), CN 12, 74\(\%\)). Density \(d = ZM/(a^3N_A)\); \(r = a/2\) (sc), \(\sqrt3a/4\) (bcc), \(a/2\sqrt2\) (fcc).
Key formula(s). \[ Z:\,sc=1,\,bcc=2,\,fcc=4,\;PE:\,74/68/52.4\% \,(fcc/bcc/sc),\;voids:\,oct=N \]
Key points.
  • Convert \(a\) from \(pm\) to \(cm\) (\(\times10^{-10}\)) before density in \(g/cm^3\).
  • Amorphous solids (glass) have no long-range order and melt over a range.
  • Count atoms: corners \(\times1/8\), faces \(\times1/2\), body centre \(\times1\), edges \(\times1/4\).
  • Voids in ccp: octahedral \(= N\), tetrahedral \(= 2N\) per \(N\) atoms.
Example 1.

How many atoms per simple cubic cell, and its packing efficiency?

  1. Corners only: \(8\times1/8 = 1\) atom.
  2. Efficiency \(= \pi/6 \approx 52.4\%\).

Answer: \(Z = 1\), \(52.4\%\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(KCl\) has similar-size ions. Which defect does it show?

  1. Similar sizes favour paired vacancies.
  2. Schottky defect.

Answer: Schottky.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(Z = 8\) for corners (each corner is shared by 8 cells).
  • Forgetting \(pm\to cm\) conversion in density.

Chapter 13 · Topic 24

Schottky defect

Solid StateStates of MatterTopic 24 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Solid State, Schottky defect: Schottky pairs vacancies of cation and anion and lowers density. Schottky: paired cation+anion vacancies (density falls, e.g. \(NaCl\)); Frenkel: ion displaced to interstitial (density unchanged, e.g. \(AgCl\)). Metal excess via F-centres gives colour; metal deficiency (\(Fe_{0.93}O\)) raises oxidation states.
Key formula(s). \[ Schottky:\,\rho\downarrow \]
Key points.
  • F-centres: anion vacancy traps electron \(\to\) yellow (\(NaCl\)), pink (\(KCl\)).
  • Metal-deficient \(FeO\) is always non-stoichiometric in practice.
  • Doping \(Si\) with \(P\) gives n-type; with \(B\) gives p-type.
  • Schottky favoured by similar-size ions; Frenkel by large size difference.
Example 1.

\(ZnS\) (large size gap between \(Zn^{2+}\) and \(S^{2-}\)) shows which defect?

  1. Big size difference lets the small ion slip interstitial.
  2. Frenkel.

Answer: Frenkel.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Doping germanium with arsenic gives which type?

  1. Group-15 donor adds a free electron.
  2. n-type.

Answer: n-type.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Saying Frenkel lowers density (it does not).
  • Swapping n-type and p-type dopant groups.

Index / States of Matter
Chapter 13 · Topic 25

Frenkel defect

Solid StateStates of MatterTopic 25 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Solid State, Frenkel defect: Frenkel displaces an ion interstitially and keeps density unchanged. Schottky: paired cation+anion vacancies (density falls, e.g. \(NaCl\)); Frenkel: ion displaced to interstitial (density unchanged, e.g. \(AgCl\)). Metal excess via F-centres gives colour; metal deficiency (\(Fe_{0.93}O\)) raises oxidation states.
Key formula(s). \[ \; Frenkel:\,\rho\,same \]
Key points.
  • Metal-deficient \(FeO\) is always non-stoichiometric in practice.
  • Doping \(Si\) with \(P\) gives n-type; with \(B\) gives p-type.
  • Schottky favoured by similar-size ions; Frenkel by large size difference.
  • F-centres: anion vacancy traps electron \(\to\) yellow (\(NaCl\)), pink (\(KCl\)).
Example 1.

Which defect: \(AgBr\) shows both vacancy pairs and displaced \(Ag^+\)?

  1. Vacancy pairs \(=\) Schottky; displaced ion \(=\) Frenkel.
  2. \(AgBr\) shows both (intermediate size difference).

Answer: Both Schottky and Frenkel.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Doping Si with group-15 element gives which semiconductor?

  1. Extra electron beyond the lattice bonds.
  2. n-type semiconductor.

Answer: n-type.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Saying Frenkel lowers density (it does not).
  • Swapping n-type and p-type dopant groups.

  2. Coordination \(8:8\) (CsCl type).

Answer: \(8:8\) cubic.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) What is the packing efficiency of diamond cubic?

  1. Diamond has a very open tetrahedral network.
  2. Only \(34\%\).

Answer: \(34\%\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Claiming hcp packs worse than bcc (hcp 74\(\%\) is densest with ccp).
  • Mixing void counts (tetra \(= 2\times\) octa).

p-type semiconductor

Solid StateStates of MatterTopic 35 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Solid State, p-type semiconductor: group-13 doping leaves mobile holes for p-type conduction. Close packing: ABAB (hcp, 74\(\%\)) and ABCABC (ccp/fcc, 74\(\%\)); voids: tetrahedral \(2N\), octahedral \(N\). Limiting radius ratios: tetrahedral \(0.225\)-\(0.414\), octahedral \(0.414\)-\(0.732\). Conductivity: conductors \(\approx 10^7\), semiconductors \(10^{-6}\)-\(10^4\), insulators tiny \(S/m\).
Key formula(s). \[ PE_{hcp/ccp}=74\%,\;r^+/r^-\,(oct)\ge0.414,\;d=\frac{ZM}{a^3N_A},\;hcp=ABAB \]
Key points.
  • hcp and ccp both 74\(\%\); bcc 68\(\%\); sc 52.4\(\%\); diamond cubic only 34\(\%\).
  • Radius-ratio predicts coordination: \(<0.155\) linear(2), \(0.414\) octahedral(6), \(>0.732\) cubic(8).
  • Magnetism: para (unpaired, attracted), dia (all paired, repelled), ferro (domains, permanent), ferri/anti-ferro variants.
  • n-type (group-15 donor) vs p-type (group-13 acceptor) from doping.
Example 1.

How many tetrahedral voids in an fcc lattice with \(4\) atoms per unit cell?

  1. Tetrahedral \(= 2N = 8\) per cell.
  2. Octahedral \(= 4\) per cell.

Answer: 8 tetrahedral, 4 octahedral.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(Na^+\) (\(102\,pm\)) in \(Cl^-\) (\(181\,pm\)) lattice: predict coordination.

  1. Ratio \(= 102/181 \approx 0.563\) (octahedral range).
  2. Coordination \(6\) (rock-salt).

Answer: 6:6 octahedral.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Claiming hcp packs worse than bcc (hcp 74\(\%\) is densest with ccp).
  • Mixing void counts (tetra \(= 2\times\) octa).

Chapter 13 · Topic 36

Magnetic properties

Solid StateStates of MatterTopic 36 of 41

Explanation

Concept. In Solid State, Magnetic properties: para, dia, ferro, ferri and antiferro cover all spin orderings. Schottky: paired cation+anion vacancies (density falls, e.g. \(NaCl\)); Frenkel: ion displaced to interstitial (density unchanged, e.g. \(AgCl\)). Metal excess via F-centres gives colour; metal deficiency (\(Fe_{0.93}O\)) raises oxidation states.
Key formula(s). \[ Schottky:\,\rho\downarrow,\;\; Frenkel:\,\rho\,same,\;\; F-centre+e^-\,trapped \to colour \]
Key points.
  • F-centres: anion vacancy traps electron \(\to\) yellow (\(NaCl\)), pink (\(KCl\)).
  • Metal-deficient \(FeO\) is always non-stoichiometric in practice.
  • Doping \(Si\) with \(P\) gives n-type; with \(B\) gives p-type.
  • Schottky favoured by similar-size ions; Frenkel by large size difference.
Example 1.

\(ZnS\) (large size gap between \(Zn^{2+}\) and \(S^{2-}\)) shows which defect?

  1. Big size difference lets the small ion slip interstitial.
  2. Frenkel.

Answer: Frenkel.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Doping germanium with arsenic gives which type?

  1. Group-15 donor adds a free electron.
  2. n-type.

Answer: n-type.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Saying Frenkel lowers density (it does not).
  • Swapping n-type and p-type dopant groups.

  • P-doping gives n-type; B gives p-type.
Example 1.

Atoms per bcc unit cell?

  1. 8 corners x 1/8 + 1 body.
  2. Z = 2.

Answer: 2.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Packing efficiency of simple cubic?

  1. Sphere pi/6 of cube.
  2. 52.4%.

Answer: 52.4%.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.

Chapter 14 · Topic 1

Concentration conversion

Solutions & Colligative Properties - AdvancedStates of MatterTopic 1 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions and Colligative Properties - Advanced, Concentration conversion: density bridges mass-based and volume-based concentrations. Molarity \(M = n/V(L)\) is temperature-dependent (volume changes); molality \(m = n/kg\,solvent\) and mole fraction are temperature-independent. Dilution obeys \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\).
Key formula(s). \[ M_1V_1=M_2V_2 \],\;M=\frac{n}{V(L)} \]
Key points.
  • Molarity uses solution volume; molality uses solvent mass in kg.
  • ppm \(= (mass\,solute/mass\,solution)\times10^6\), used for trace quantities.
  • Mole fractions in a mixture always add to \(1\).
  • On mixing: total moles conserved, \(M_{mix} = (M_1V_1+M_2V_2)/(V_1+V_2)\).
Example 1.

\(4\,g\,NaOH\) is dissolved to make \(500\,mL\) solution. Find molarity.

  1. Moles \(= 4/40 = 0.1\,mol\); volume \(= 0.5\,L\).
  2. \(M = 0.1/0.5 = 0.2\,M\).

Answer: \(0.2\,M\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) What volume of water must be added to \(200\,mL\) of \(1.5\,M\) solution to make it \(0.5\,M\)?

  1. \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2 \Rightarrow V_2 = 1.5\times200/0.5 = 600\,mL\).
  2. Water added \(= 600-200 = 400\,mL\).

Answer: \(400\,mL\) water.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using solution mass instead of solvent mass for molality.
  • Applying \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\) when a reaction occurs (use equivalents instead).
Back to Index
Index / States of Matter
Chapter 14 · Topic 2

Mixing solutions

Solutions & Colligative Properties - AdvancedStates of MatterTopic 2 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions and Colligative Properties - Advanced, Mixing solutions: the focus here is Mixing solutions, worked through the Solutions and Colligative Properties - Advanced toolkit below. Molarity \(M = n/V(L)\) is temperature-dependent (volume changes); molality \(m = n/kg\,solvent\) and mole fraction are temperature-independent. Dilution obeys \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\).
Key formula(s). \[ M=\frac{n}{V(L)},\;m=\frac{n}{kg} \]
Key points.
  • ppm \(= (mass\,solute/mass\,solution)\times10^6\), used for trace quantities.
  • Mole fractions in a mixture always add to \(1\).
  • On mixing: total moles conserved, \(M_{mix} = (M_1V_1+M_2V_2)/(V_1+V_2)\).
  • Molarity uses solution volume; molality uses solvent mass in kg.
Example 1.

A \(10\%\,w/w\,NaOH\) solution has density \(1.1\,g/mL\). Find its molarity.

  1. \(100\,g\) solution carries \(10\,g\,NaOH = 0.25\,mol\); volume \(= 100/1.1 = 90.9\,mL\).
  2. \(M = 0.25/0.0909 \approx 2.75\,M\).

Answer: \(2.75\,M\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Mix \(100\,mL\,1\,M + 200\,mL\,2\,M\) of the same solute. Find final molarity.

  1. Total moles \(= 100 + 400 = 500\,mmol\); total volume \(= 300\,mL\).
  2. \(M = 500/300 \approx 1.67\,M\).

Answer: \(1.67\,M\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using solution mass instead of solvent mass for molality.
  • Applying \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\) when a reaction occurs (use equivalents instead).

Chapter 14 · Topic 3

Dilution

Solutions & Colligative Properties - AdvancedStates of MatterTopic 3 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions and Colligative Properties - Advanced, Dilution: dilution conserves moles as M1V1 equals M2V2. Molarity \(M = n/V(L)\) is temperature-dependent (volume changes); molality \(m = n/kg\,solvent\) and mole fraction are temperature-independent. Dilution obeys \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\).
Key formula(s). \[ M=\frac{n}{V(L)},\;M_1V_1=M_2V_2 \]
Key points.
  • Mole fractions in a mixture always add to \(1\).
  • On mixing: total moles conserved, \(M_{mix} = (M_1V_1+M_2V_2)/(V_1+V_2)\).
  • Molarity uses solution volume; molality uses solvent mass in kg.
  • ppm \(= (mass\,solute/mass\,solution)\times10^6\), used for trace quantities.
Example 1.

Fluoride in water is \(2\,mg/L\). Express it in ppm.

  1. \(1\,L\) water \(\approx 10^6\,mg\).
  2. \(2\,mg\) per \(10^6\,mg = 2\,ppm\).

Answer: \(2\,ppm\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(0.5\,mol\) solute is dissolved in \(250\,g\) water. Find molality.

  1. Solvent \(= 0.25\,kg\).
  2. \(m = 0.5/0.25 = 2\,m\).

Answer: \(2\,m\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using solution mass instead of solvent mass for molality.
  • Applying \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\) when a reaction occurs (use equivalents instead).

Chapter 14 · Topic 4

Vapour pressure calculations

Solutions & Colligative Properties - AdvancedStates of MatterTopic 4 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions and Colligative Properties - Advanced, Vapour pressure calculations: vapour-pressure math applies Raoult share by share. Raoult: \(p_i = \chi_ip_i^0\); total \(P = \sum p_i\). Ideal solutions obey at all compositions (\(\Delta H_{mix} = 0\)); positive deviation (weak A-B, e.g. ethanol+acetone, minimum-boiling azeotrope) and negative deviation (strong A-B, e.g. \(HNO_3\)+water, maximum-boiling azeotrope).
Key formula(s). \[ P=\chi_Ap_A^0+\chi_Bp_B^0 \]
Key points.
  • Vapour is richer in the more volatile component; distillate composition follows the \(y\)-\(x\) curve.
  • Azeotropes distil unchanged (cannot be separated by simple distillation).
  • Colligative properties depend on particle count: always multiply by van It Hoff \(i\).
  • For volatile-nonvolatile: relative lowering \(\Delta p/p^0 = \chi_{solute}\).
Example 1.

Benzene (\(p^0 = 75\,mmHg\)) + toluene (\(p^0 = 22\,mmHg\)), \(\chi_{benz} = 0.6\). Find total VP.

  1. \(p_{benz} = 0.6\times75 = 45\); \(p_{tol} = 0.4\times22 = 8.8\).
  2. \(P = 53.8\,mmHg\).

Answer: \(53.8\,mmHg\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(1\,mol\) non-volatile solute in \(10\,mol\) water (\(p^0 = 23.8\,mmHg\)). Find VP lowering.

  1. \(\chi_{solute} = 1/11 \approx 0.0909\).
  2. \(\Delta p = 0.0909\times23.8 \approx 2.16\,mmHg\).

Answer: About \(2.16\,mmHg\) lowering.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using liquid mole fractions as vapour composition.
  • Missing \(i\) in colligative numericals with electrolytes.
Back to Index
Index / States of Matter
Chapter 14 · Topic 5

Raoult's law numericals

Solutions & Colligative Properties - AdvancedStates of MatterTopic 5 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions and Colligative Properties - Advanced, Raoult's law numericals: Raoult numericals add the component shares for total pressure. Raoult: \(p_i = \chi_ip_i^0\); total \(P = \sum p_i\). Ideal solutions obey at all compositions (\(\Delta H_{mix} = 0\)); positive deviation (weak A-B, e.g. ethanol+acetone, minimum-boiling azeotrope) and negative deviation (strong A-B, e.g. \(HNO_3\)+water, maximum-boiling azeotrope).
Key formula(s). \[ \pi=iCRT \],\;p_i=\chi_ip_i^0 \]
Key points.
  • Azeotropes distil unchanged (cannot be separated by simple distillation).
  • Colligative properties depend on particle count: always multiply by van It Hoff \(i\).
  • For volatile-nonvolatile: relative lowering \(\Delta p/p^0 = \chi_{solute}\).
  • Vapour is richer in the more volatile component; distillate composition follows the \(y\)-\(x\) curve.
Example 1.

Ethanol-water forms a minimum-boiling azeotrope at \(95.6\%\) ethanol. Can simple distillation give absolute alcohol?

  1. The azeotrope distils unchanged at fixed composition.
  2. No; special methods (molecular sieves) are needed.

Answer: No (azeotropic barrier).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(p^\circ = 100\,mmHg\), \(\chi_{solute} = 0.05\) (non-volatile). Find the vapour-pressure lowering.

  1. \(\Delta p = p^\circ\chi_{solute}\).
  2. \(\Delta p = 5\,mmHg\).

Answer: \(5\,mmHg\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using liquid mole fractions as vapour composition.
  • Missing \(i\) in colligative numericals with electrolytes.

Chapter 14 · Topic 6

Partial vapour pressure

Solutions & Colligative Properties - AdvancedStates of MatterTopic 6 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions and Colligative Properties - Advanced, Partial vapour pressure: each component contributes its own mole-fraction share. Raoult: \(p_i = \chi_ip_i^0\); total \(P = \sum p_i\). Ideal solutions obey at all compositions (\(\Delta H_{mix} = 0\)); positive deviation (weak A-B, e.g. ethanol+acetone, minimum-boiling azeotrope) and negative deviation (strong A-B, e.g. \(HNO_3\)+water, maximum-boiling azeotrope).
Key formula(s). \[ p_i=\chi_ip_i^0,\;P=\chi_Ap_A^0+\chi_Bp_B^0 \]
Key points.
  • Colligative properties depend on particle count: always multiply by van It Hoff \(i\).
  • For volatile-nonvolatile: relative lowering \(\Delta p/p^0 = \chi_{solute}\).
  • Vapour is richer in the more volatile component; distillate composition follows the \(y\)-\(x\) curve.
  • Azeotropes distil unchanged (cannot be separated by simple distillation).
Example 1.

\(CS_2\) + acetone shows which deviation, and why?

  1. Mixing breaks the stronger pure-liquid attractions (positive \(\Delta H_{mix}\)).
  2. Positive deviation (higher VP than Raoult).

Answer: Positive deviation.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(HNO_3\) + water is a maximum-boiling azeotrope. What does that imply about A-B forces?

  1. Boiling point rises: VP is lower than ideal.
  2. Strong A-B attraction (negative deviation).

Answer: Strong unlike attraction.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using liquid mole fractions as vapour composition.
  • Missing \(i\) in colligative numericals with electrolytes.

  • For volatile-nonvolatile: relative lowering \(\Delta p/p^0 = \chi_{solute}\).

  1. \(p_{benz} = 0.6\times75 = 45\); \(p_{tol} = 0.4\times22 = 8.8\).
  2. \(P = 53.8\,mmHg\).

Answer: \(53.8\,mmHg\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(1\,mol\) non-volatile solute in \(10\,mol\) water (\(p^0 = 23.8\,mmHg\)). Find VP lowering.

  1. \(\chi_{solute} = 1/11 \approx 0.0909\).
  2. \(\Delta p = 0.0909\times23.8 \approx 2.16\,mmHg\).

Answer: About \(2.16\,mmHg\) lowering.

Chapter 14 · Topic 8

Non-ideal solution numericals

Solutions & Colligative Properties - AdvancedStates of MatterTopic 8 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions and Colligative Properties - Advanced, Non-ideal solution numericals: deviation problems compare measured VP against Raoult prediction. Raoult: \(p_i = \chi_ip_i^0\); total \(P = \sum p_i\). Ideal solutions obey at all compositions (\(\Delta H_{mix} = 0\)); positive deviation (weak A-B, e.g. ethanol+acetone, minimum-boiling azeotrope) and negative deviation (strong A-B, e.g. \(HNO_3\)+water, maximum-boiling azeotrope).
Key formula(s). \[ P=\chi_Ap_A^0+\chi_Bp_B^0,\;\Delta T_b=K_bm \]
Key points.
  • Azeotropes distil unchanged (cannot be separated by simple distillation).
  • Colligative properties depend on particle count: always multiply by van It Hoff \(i\).
  • For volatile-nonvolatile: relative lowering \(\Delta p/p^0 = \chi_{solute}\).
  • Vapour is richer in the more volatile component; distillate composition follows the \(y\)-\(x\) curve.
Example 1.

Ethanol-water forms a minimum-boiling azeotrope at \(95.6\%\) ethanol. Can simple distillation give absolute alcohol?

  1. The azeotrope distils unchanged at fixed composition.
  2. No; special methods (molecular sieves) are needed.

Answer: No (azeotropic barrier).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(p^\circ = 100\,mmHg\), \(\chi_{solute} = 0.05\) (non-volatile). Find the vapour-pressure lowering.

  1. \(\Delta p = p^\circ\chi_{solute}\).
  2. \(\Delta p = 5\,mmHg\).

Answer: \(5\,mmHg\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using liquid mole fractions as vapour composition.
  • Missing \(i\) in colligative numericals with electrolytes.

Chapter 14 · Topic 9

Azeotrope problems

Solutions & Colligative Properties - AdvancedStates of MatterTopic 9 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions and Colligative Properties - Advanced, Azeotrope problems: azeotrope composition distils over intact. Raoult: \(p_i = \chi_ip_i^0\); total \(P = \sum p_i\). Ideal solutions obey at all compositions (\(\Delta H_{mix} = 0\)); positive deviation (weak A-B, e.g. ethanol+acetone, minimum-boiling azeotrope) and negative deviation (strong A-B, e.g. \(HNO_3\)+water, maximum-boiling azeotrope).
Key formula(s). \[ \Delta T_f=K_fm,\;\pi=iCRT \]
Key points.
  • Colligative properties depend on particle count: always multiply by van It Hoff \(i\).
  • For volatile-nonvolatile: relative lowering \(\Delta p/p^0 = \chi_{solute}\).
  • Vapour is richer in the more volatile component; distillate composition follows the \(y\)-\(x\) curve.
  • Azeotropes distil unchanged (cannot be separated by simple distillation).
Example 1.

\(CS_2\) + acetone shows which deviation, and why?

  1. Mixing breaks the stronger pure-liquid attractions (positive \(\Delta H_{mix}\)).
  2. Positive deviation (higher VP than Raoult).

Answer: Positive deviation.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(HNO_3\) + water is a maximum-boiling azeotrope. What does that imply about A-B forces?

  1. Boiling point rises: VP is lower than ideal.
  2. Strong A-B attraction (negative deviation).

Answer: Strong unlike attraction.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using liquid mole fractions as vapour composition.
  • Missing \(i\) in colligative numericals with electrolytes.

Chapter 14 · Topic 10

Henry's law numericals

Solutions & Colligative Properties - AdvancedStates of MatterTopic 10 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions and Colligative Properties - Advanced, Henry's law numericals: Henry numericals divide pressure by KH for mole fraction. Henry law: solubility of a gas \(\propto\) its partial pressure, \(p = K_H\chi\) (or \(C = K_H'p\)). \(K_H\) rises with temperature (solubility falls); deep-sea divers exhale \(N_2\) slowly to avoid bends from this law.
Key formula(s). \[ p=K_H\chi,\;(\text{higher }K_H \Rightarrow \text{lower solubility}) \]
Key points.
  • Units of \(K_H\) fix the form used; check whether mole fraction or concentration version is given.
  • Scuba/aerated-drink problems are Henry-law flags.
  • Solubility of solids usually rises with \(T\); gases always fall.
  • Convert pressure to the same units as \(K_H\) before multiplying.
Example 1.

\(K_H(N_2) = 76\,kbar\) at 298 K. Find mole fraction dissolved at \(p_{N_2} = 0.8\,bar\).

  1. Convert: \(p = 0.8\,bar = 8\times10^{-4}\,kbar\).
  2. \(\chi = p/K_H = 8\times10^{-4}/76 \approx 1.05\times10^{-5}\).

Answer: About \(1.05\times10^{-5}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why do divers use He-diluted air?

  1. \(He\) has much higher \(K_H\) (lower blood solubility) than \(N_2\).
  2. Less dissolved gas \(\to\) lower bends risk on ascent.

Answer: Lower solubility of He reduces nitrogen-bubble risk.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Inverting \(K_H\) meaning (large \(K_H\) = LESS soluble).
  • Forgetting to match pressure units with \(K_H\).

Chapter 14 · Topic 11

Colligative property derivations

Solutions & Colligative Properties - AdvancedStates of MatterTopic 11 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions and Colligative Properties - Advanced, Colligative property derivations: colligative formulas all descend from chemical-potential lowering. Colligative: \(\Delta T_b = iK_bm\), \(\Delta T_f = iK_fm\), \(\pi = iCRT\), \(\Delta p/p^0 = i\chi_{solute}\). van It Hoff \(i =\) observed/calculated; association gives \(i<1\), dissociation \(i>1\). Abnormal molar mass \(= M_{true}/i\).
Key formula(s). \[ i=1+(n-1)\alpha\;(dissociation),\;i=1-\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)\beta\;(association) \]
Key points.
  • Isotonic solutions have equal \(\pi\) (same \(iC\) at same \(T\)).
  • Reverse osmosis needs applied \(P>\pi\) (desalination).
  • Degree of dissociation from \(i\) first, then \(K\) if asked.
  • Molality (not molarity) in \(\Delta T\) formulas; \(R = 0.0821\,L\,atm\) in \(\pi = CRT\).
Example 1.

Find \(\Delta T_b\) for \(0.2\,m\) glucose (\(K_b = 0.52\)).

  1. Glucose is a non-electrolyte: \(i = 1\).
  2. \(\Delta T_b = 1\times0.52\times0.2 = 0.104\,K\).

Answer: \(0.104\,K\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Find the osmotic pressure of \(0.01\,M\) sucrose at \(300\,K\).

  1. \(\pi = iCRT = 1\times0.01\times0.0821\times300\).
  2. \(\pi \approx 0.246\,atm\).

Answer: \(0.246\,atm\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using molarity in \(\Delta T_f\) (use molality).
  • Taking \(i = n\) without checking \(\alpha\) (weak electrolytes partly dissociate).

Chapter 14 · Topic 12

Molar mass determination

Solutions & Colligative Properties - AdvancedStates of MatterTopic 12 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Solutions and Colligative Properties - Advanced, Molar mass determination: colligative shifts weigh molar mass from measured Delta. Colligative: \(\Delta T_b = iK_bm\), \(\Delta T_f = iK_fm\), \(\pi = iCRT\), \(\Delta p/p^0 = i\chi_{solute}\). van It Hoff \(i =\) observed/calculated; association gives \(i<1\), dissociation \(i>1\). Abnormal molar mass \(= M_{true}/i\).
Key formula(s). \[ \Delta T_f=iK_fm \]
Key points.
  • Reverse osmosis needs applied \(P>\pi\) (desalination).
  • Degree of dissociation from \(i\) first, then \(K\) if asked.
  • Molality (not molarity) in \(\Delta T\) formulas; \(R = 0.0821\,L\,atm\) in \(\pi = CRT\).
  • Isotonic solutions have equal \(\pi\) (same \(iC\) at same \(T\)).
Example 1.

\(0.1\,M\,CaCl_2\) has \(\alpha = 0.9\). Find its van't Hoff factor.

  1. \(n = 3\) ions; \(i = 1 + (n-1)\alpha = 1 + 2(0.9)\).
  2. \(i = 2.8\).

Answer: \(2.8\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Acetic acid (\(M = 60\)) dimerises in benzene; observed molar mass \(= 120\). Find \(i\).

  1. \(i = M_{true}/M_{obs} = 60/120\).
  2. \(i = 0.5\) (association).

Answer: \(0.5\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using molarity in \(\Delta T_f\) (use molality).
  • Taking \(i = n\) without checking \(\alpha\) (weak electrolytes partly dissociate).

  • Molality (not molarity) in \(\Delta T\) formulas; \(R = 0.0821\,L\,atm\) in \(\pi = CRT\).

Find \(\Delta T_f\) for \(0.1\,m\,NaCl\) (\(K_f = 1.86\), \(i = 1.9\)).

  1. \(n = 5\) ions, so \(i \approx 5\).
  2. \(\pi\) is about \(5\times\) larger.

Answer: Five times larger.

Index / Energy & Equilibrium
Chapter 15 · Topic 1

Work in different processes

Thermodynamics - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 1 of 20

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics - Advanced, Work in different processes: each path (isothermal, adiabatic, isobaric) has its own work formula. First law: \(\Delta U = q + w\) (chemistry sign: work done BY the system is negative). \(U, H, G, S\) are state functions; \(q, w\) are path functions. Zeroth law founds temperature; equilibrium needs thermal, mechanical and chemical balance.
Key formula(s). \[ \Delta U = q + w,\;w_{rev} = -nRT\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1} \]
Key points.
  • Reversible work magnitude exceeds irreversible work between the same states.
  • Intensive (\(T, P, \rho\)) vs extensive (\(V, n, U\)): only extensive scales with amount.
  • Cyclic process: \(\Delta U = 0\), so \(q = -w\).
  • Signs: heat absorbed by system \(+\); work done BY system \(-\). Free expansion against vacuum: \(w = 0\).
Example 1.

An ideal gas expands adiabatically into vacuum (free expansion). Give \(w, q, \Delta U\).

  1. Against zero external pressure \(w = 0\); insulated so \(q = 0\).
  2. \(\Delta U = 0\); temperature unchanged for an ideal gas.

Answer: All zero; \(\Delta T = 0\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(1\,mol\) gas is compressed with \(P_{ext} = 5\,atm\) from \(10\,L\) to \(2\,L\). Find \(w\).

  1. \(w = -P_{ext}\Delta V = -5\times(2-10) = +40\,L\,atm\).
  2. \(+40\times101.3 = +4052\,J\) (work done ON the system).

Answer: \(+40\,L\,atm\) (\(+4.05\,kJ\)).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using physics sign convention (work by system positive) in chemistry problems.
  • Forgetting free expansion \(w = 0\) because \(P_{ext} = 0\).

Index / Energy & Equilibrium
Chapter 15 · Topic 2

PV diagrams

Thermodynamics - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 2 of 20

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics - Advanced, PV diagrams: PV diagram area between curve and V-axis is the work. Enthalpy \(H = U + PV\); at constant pressure \(q_p = \Delta H\). Key links: \(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_gRT\), \(C_p - C_v = R\), Hess law (enthalpy is a state function), \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) with spontaneity at \(\Delta G<0\).
Key formula(s). \[ 2nd\,law:\,\Delta S_{univ}>0 \],\;\Delta H=\Delta U+\Delta n_gRT \]
Key points.
  • Bond enthalpy route: \(\Delta H = \sum BE(reactants) - \sum BE(products)\).
  • Kirchhoff: \(\Delta H_2-\Delta H_1 = \Delta C_p(T_2-T_1)\); entropy of heating: \(\Delta S = C\ln(T_2/T_1)\).
  • Standard formation enthalpy of elements in reference state \(= 0\).
  • Strong acid + strong base neutralisation \(\approx -57.1\,kJ/eq\); weaker if weak electrolyte involved (ionisation absorbs heat).
Example 1.

For \(N_2 + 3H_2 \to 2NH_3\), \(\Delta H = -92\,kJ\) at \(298\,K\). Find \(\Delta U\).

  1. \(\Delta n_g = 2-4 = -2\).
  2. \(\Delta U = \Delta H - \Delta n_gRT = -92 - (-2)(2.478) = -87.0\,kJ\).

Answer: About \(-87.0\,kJ\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Ice melts with \(\Delta H = +6.0\,kJ/mol\), \(\Delta S = +22\,J/mol/K\). Above what \(T\) is melting spontaneous?

  1. \(T = 6000/22 \approx 273\,K\).
  2. Melting spontaneous above \(273\,K\) at \(1\,atm\).

Answer: \(273\,K\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Including solids/liquids in \(\Delta n_g\) (gases only).

Chapter 15 · Topic 3

Cyclic processes

Thermodynamics - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 3 of 20

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics - Advanced, Cyclic processes: cycles return delta-U to zero, so net heat equals minus net work. Enthalpy \(H = U + PV\); at constant pressure \(q_p = \Delta H\). Key links: \(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_gRT\), \(C_p - C_v = R\), Hess law (enthalpy is a state function), \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) with spontaneity at \(\Delta G<0\).
Key formula(s). \[ \Delta H=\Delta U+\Delta n_gRT,\;\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S \]
Key points.
  • Standard formation enthalpy of elements in reference state \(= 0\).
  • Strong acid + strong base neutralisation \(\approx -57.1\,kJ/eq\); weaker if weak electrolyte involved (ionisation absorbs heat).
  • Bond enthalpy route: \(\Delta H = \sum BE(reactants) - \sum BE(products)\).
  • Kirchhoff: \(\Delta H_2-\Delta H_1 = \Delta C_p(T_2-T_1)\); entropy of heating: \(\Delta S = C\ln(T_2/T_1)\).
Example 1.

For \(2H_2+O_2\to2H_2O(l)\), \(\Delta U = -750\,kJ\) at \(300\,K\). Find \(\Delta H\).

  1. \(\Delta n_g = 0-3 = -3\).
  2. \(\Delta H = -750 + (-3)(8.314\times10^{-3})(300) = -750-7.48 = -757.5\,kJ\).

Answer: About \(-757.5\,kJ\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(\Delta H = -100\,kJ\), \(\Delta S = -200\,J/K\). Above what \(T\) does the reaction become non-spontaneous?

  1. Set \(\Delta G = 0\): \(T = \Delta H/\Delta S = (-100000)/(-200) = 500\,K\).
  2. Below \(500\,K\) spontaneous; above, \(\Delta G>0\).

Answer: \(500\,K\) (spontaneous below it).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Including solids/liquids in \(\Delta n_g\) (gases only).
  • Using \(kJ\) and \(J\) together without converting in \(\Delta G = \Delta H-T\Delta S\).

Chapter 15 · Topic 4

Reversible vs irreversible work

Thermodynamics - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 4 of 20

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics - Advanced, Reversible vs irreversible work: reversible magnitude always beats irreversible between the same states. First law: \(\Delta U = q + w\) (chemistry sign: work done BY the system is negative). \(U, H, G, S\) are state functions; \(q, w\) are path functions. Zeroth law founds temperature; equilibrium needs thermal, mechanical and chemical balance.
Key formula(s). \[ w_{rev} = -nRT\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1},\;w_{irr} = -P_{ext}\Delta V \]
Key points.
  • Reversible work magnitude exceeds irreversible work between the same states.
  • Intensive (\(T, P, \rho\)) vs extensive (\(V, n, U\)): only extensive scales with amount.
  • Cyclic process: \(\Delta U = 0\), so \(q = -w\).
  • Signs: heat absorbed by system \(+\); work done BY system \(-\). Free expansion against vacuum: \(w = 0\).
Example 1.

An ideal gas expands adiabatically into vacuum (free expansion). Give \(w, q, \Delta U\).

  1. Against zero external pressure \(w = 0\); insulated so \(q = 0\).
  2. \(\Delta U = 0\); temperature unchanged for an ideal gas.

Answer: All zero; \(\Delta T = 0\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(1\,mol\) gas is compressed with \(P_{ext} = 5\,atm\) from \(10\,L\) to \(2\,L\). Find \(w\).

  1. \(w = -P_{ext}\Delta V = -5\times(2-10) = +40\,L\,atm\).
  2. \(+40\times101.3 = +4052\,J\) (work done ON the system).

Answer: \(+40\,L\,atm\) (\(+4.05\,kJ\)).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using physics sign convention (work by system positive) in chemistry problems.
  • Forgetting free expansion \(w = 0\) because \(P_{ext} = 0\).

Chapter 15 · Topic 5

Isothermal work

Thermodynamics - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 5 of 20

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics - Advanced, Isothermal work: isothermal reversible work is -nRT ln(V2/V1). First law: \(\Delta U = q + w\) (chemistry sign: work done BY the system is negative). \(U, H, G, S\) are state functions; \(q, w\) are path functions. Zeroth law founds temperature; equilibrium needs thermal, mechanical and chemical balance.
Key formula(s). \[ w_{rev} = -nRT\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1},\;Zeroth:\,T_1=T_2=T_3 \]
Key points.
  • Intensive (\(T, P, \rho\)) vs extensive (\(V, n, U\)): only extensive scales with amount.
  • Cyclic process: \(\Delta U = 0\), so \(q = -w\).
  • Signs: heat absorbed by system \(+\); work done BY system \(-\). Free expansion against vacuum: \(w = 0\).
  • Reversible work magnitude exceeds irreversible work between the same states.
Example 1.

In an isothermal change \(q = +2\,kJ\) for an ideal gas. Find \(w\) and \(\Delta U\).

  1. Isothermal ideal gas: \(\Delta U = 0\).
  2. \(w = -q = -2\,kJ\).

Answer: \(\Delta U = 0\), \(w = -2\,kJ\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(1\,mol\) expands at \(300\,K\) from \(1\,L\) to \(10\,L\): compare reversible vs \(1\,atm\) irreversible work.

  1. Reversible: \(-8.314\times300\times\ln10 \approx -5744\,J\).
  2. Irreversible: \(-1\times9\,L\,atm = -912\,J\) (much smaller magnitude).

Answer: \(-5.74\,kJ\) vs \(-0.91\,kJ\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using physics sign convention (work by system positive) in chemistry problems.
  • Forgetting free expansion \(w = 0\) because \(P_{ext} = 0\).

Adiabatic work

Thermodynamics - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 6 of 20

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics - Advanced, Adiabatic work: adiabatic work is the Cv times temperature fall. First law: \(\Delta U = q + w\) (chemistry sign: work done BY the system is negative). \(U, H, G, S\) are state functions; \(q, w\) are path functions. Zeroth law founds temperature; equilibrium needs thermal, mechanical and chemical balance.

  • Signs: heat absorbed by system \(+\); work done BY system \(-\). Free expansion against vacuum: \(w = 0\).
  • Reversible work magnitude exceeds irreversible work between the same states.
  • Intensive (\(T, P, \rho\)) vs extensive (\(V, n, U\)): only extensive scales with amount.
  • Cyclic process: \(\Delta U = 0\), so \(q = -w\).
Example 1.

\(2\,mol\) ideal gas expands reversibly and isothermally at \(300\,K\) from \(5\,L\) to \(15\,L\). Find \(w\).

  1. \(w = -nRT\ln(V_2/V_1) = -2\times8.314\times300\times\ln3\).
  2. \(w \approx -5483\,J \approx -5.48\,kJ\). For isothermal ideal gas \(\Delta U = 0\), so \(q = +5.48\,kJ\).

Answer: \(w \approx -5.48\,kJ\), \(q \approx +5.48\,kJ\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) One mole of gas expands against \(1\,atm\) external pressure from \(2\,L\) to \(7\,L\). Find irreversible work in \(L\,atm\) and joules.

  1. \(w = -P_{ext}\Delta V = -1\times5 = -5\,L\,atm\).
  2. In joules: \(-5\times101.3 = -506.5\,J\).

Answer: \(-5\,L\,atm\) (\(-506.5\,J\)).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using physics sign convention (work by system positive) in chemistry problems.
  • Forgetting free expansion \(w = 0\) because \(P_{ext} = 0\).

Relation between Cp and Cv

Thermodynamics - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 7 of 20

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics - Advanced, Relation between Cp and Cv: Cp minus Cv equals R per mole of ideal gas. Enthalpy \(H = U + PV\); at constant pressure \(q_p = \Delta H\). Key links: \(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_gRT\), \(C_p - C_v = R\), Hess law (enthalpy is a state function), \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) with spontaneity at \(\Delta G<0\).

\(2CO + O_2 \to 2CO_2\): \(\Delta U = -564\,kJ\) at \(298\,K\). Find \(\Delta H\).

  1. Gases: products \(2\), reactants \(3\), so \(\Delta n_g = -1\).
  2. \(\Delta H = -564 + (-1)(8.314\times10^{-3})(298) = -566.5\,kJ\).

  1. \(T = \Delta H/\Delta S = 92000/199 \approx 462\,K\).
  2. Spontaneous below \(462\,K\) (Haber-type sign pair).

Answer: \(462\,K\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Including solids/liquids in \(\Delta n_g\) (gases only).

  • Kirchhoff: \(\Delta H_2-\Delta H_1 = \Delta C_p(T_2-T_1)\); entropy of heating: \(\Delta S = C\ln(T_2/T_1)\).
Example 1.

For \(2H_2+O_2\to2H_2O(l)\), \(\Delta U = -750\,kJ\) at \(300\,K\). Find \(\Delta H\).

  1. \(\Delta n_g = 0-3 = -3\).
  2. \(\Delta H = -750 + (-3)(8.314\times10^{-3})(300) = -750-7.48 = -757.5\,kJ\).

Answer: About \(-757.5\,kJ\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(\Delta H = -100\,kJ\), \(\Delta S = -200\,J/K\). Above what \(T\) does the reaction become non-spontaneous?

  1. Set \(\Delta G = 0\): \(T = \Delta H/\Delta S = (-100000)/(-200) = 500\,K\).
  2. Below \(500\,K\) spontaneous; above, \(\Delta G>0\).

Answer: \(500\,K\) (spontaneous below it).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Including solids/liquids in \(\Delta n_g\) (gases only).
  • Using \(kJ\) and \(J\) together without converting in \(\Delta G = \Delta H-T\Delta S\).

Chapter 15 · Topic 16

Entropy change in phase transition

Thermodynamics - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 16 of 20

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics - Advanced, Entropy change in phase transition: transition entropy is Delta-H over the equilibrium temperature. Enthalpy \(H = U + PV\); at constant pressure \(q_p = \Delta H\). Key links: \(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_gRT\), \(C_p - C_v = R\), Hess law (enthalpy is a state function), \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) with spontaneity at \(\Delta G<0\).
Key formula(s). \[ \Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S,\;\Delta S=q_{rev}/T \]
Key points.
  • Strong acid + strong base neutralisation \(\approx -57.1\,kJ/eq\); weaker if weak electrolyte involved (ionisation absorbs heat).
  • Bond enthalpy route: \(\Delta H = \sum BE(reactants) - \sum BE(products)\).
  • Kirchhoff: \(\Delta H_2-\Delta H_1 = \Delta C_p(T_2-T_1)\); entropy of heating: \(\Delta S = C\ln(T_2/T_1)\).
  • Standard formation enthalpy of elements in reference state \(= 0\).
Example 1.

\(2CO + O_2 \to 2CO_2\): \(\Delta U = -564\,kJ\) at \(298\,K\). Find \(\Delta H\).

  1. Gases: products \(2\), reactants \(3\), so \(\Delta n_g = -1\).
  2. \(\Delta H = -564 + (-1)(8.314\times10^{-3})(298) = -566.5\,kJ\).

Answer: About \(-566.5\,kJ\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) A reaction has \(\Delta H = -92\,kJ\), \(\Delta S = -199\,J/K\). Below what \(T\) is it spontaneous?

  1. \(T = \Delta H/\Delta S = 92000/199 \approx 462\,K\).
  2. Spontaneous below \(462\,K\) (Haber-type sign pair).

Answer: \(462\,K\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Including solids/liquids in \(\Delta n_g\) (gases only).
  • Using \(kJ\) and \(J\) together without converting in \(\Delta G = \Delta H-T\Delta S\).

Chapter 15 · Topic 17

Gibbs energy calculations

Thermodynamics - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 17 of 20

Explanation

Concept. In Thermodynamics - Advanced, Gibbs energy calculations: Gibbs arithmetic Delta-G = Delta-H - T Delta-S calls every direction. Enthalpy \(H = U + PV\); at constant pressure \(q_p = \Delta H\). Key links: \(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_gRT\), \(C_p - C_v = R\), Hess law (enthalpy is a state function), \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\) with spontaneity at \(\Delta G<0\).
Key formula(s). \[ \Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S,\;\Delta G^\circ=-RT\ln K,\;\Delta S=q_{rev}/T \]
Key points.
  • Bond enthalpy route: \(\Delta H = \sum BE(reactants) - \sum BE(products)\).
  • Kirchhoff: \(\Delta H_2-\Delta H_1 = \Delta C_p(T_2-T_1)\); entropy of heating: \(\Delta S = C\ln(T_2/T_1)\).
  • Standard formation enthalpy of elements in reference state \(= 0\).
  • Strong acid + strong base neutralisation \(\approx -57.1\,kJ/eq\); weaker if weak electrolyte involved (ionisation absorbs heat).
Example 1.

For \(N_2 + 3H_2 \to 2NH_3\), \(\Delta H = -92\,kJ\) at \(298\,K\). Find \(\Delta U\).

  1. \(\Delta n_g = 2-4 = -2\).
  2. \(\Delta U = \Delta H - \Delta n_gRT = -92 - (-2)(2.478) = -87.0\,kJ\).

Answer: About \(-87.0\,kJ\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Ice melts with \(\Delta H = +6.0\,kJ/mol\), \(\Delta S = +22\,J/mol/K\). Above what \(T\) is melting spontaneous?

  1. \(T = 6000/22 \approx 273\,K\).
  2. Melting spontaneous above \(273\,K\) at \(1\,atm\).

Answer: \(273\,K\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Including solids/liquids in \(\Delta n_g\) (gases only).
  • Using \(kJ\) and \(J\) together without converting in \(\Delta G = \Delta H-T\Delta S\).
