Chapter 16 · Topic 1

ICE-table calculations

Chemical Equilibrium - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 1 of 16

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Equilibrium - Advanced, ICE-table calculations: ICE rows plus the K expression solve every concentration problem. At equilibrium \(Q = K\); \(K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}\). Reaction moves forward if \(Q<K\), backward if \(Q>K\). \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K\) ties \(K\) to thermodynamics; van It Hoff gives temperature dependence.
Key formula(s). \[ Q<K\to forward,\;Q>K\to backward \]
Key points.
  • Le Chatelier: pressure/utting shifts toward fewer gas moles; inert gas at constant \(P\) dilutes like expansion.
  • For \(N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2\) with degree \(\alpha\): \(K_p = 4\alpha^2P/(1-\alpha^2)\).
  • Pure solids/liquids are omitted from \(K\) and \(Q\) expressions.
  • Catalyst never changes \(K\), only the speed of approach.
Example 1.

\(\Delta G^\circ = -30\,kJ\) at \(300\,K\). Find \(K\).

  1. \(\ln K = 30000/(8.314\times300) = 12.03\).
  2. \(K = e^{12.03} \approx 1.68\times10^5\).

Answer: About \(1.7\times10^5\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(N_2 + O_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NO\) is endothermic. What happens to \(K\) on heating?

  1. Heat favours the endothermic (forward) side.
  2. \(K\) increases with \(T\).

Answer: \(K\) increases.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Writing \(K_p\) with wrong \(\Delta n_g\) sign.
  • Including solids (e.g. \(CaCO_3\)) in the equilibrium expression.
Back to Index
Index / Energy & Equilibrium
Chapter 16 · Topic 2

Equilibrium concentration

Chemical Equilibrium - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 2 of 16

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Equilibrium - Advanced, Equilibrium concentration: equilibrium concentrations satisfy the Kc ratio exactly. At equilibrium \(Q = K\); \(K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}\). Reaction moves forward if \(Q<K\), backward if \(Q>K\). \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K\) ties \(K\) to thermodynamics; van It Hoff gives temperature dependence.
Key formula(s). \[ K_p=K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g} \]
Key points.
  • Pure solids/liquids are omitted from \(K\) and \(Q\) expressions.
  • Catalyst never changes \(K\), only the speed of approach.
  • Le Chatelier: pressure/utting shifts toward fewer gas moles; inert gas at constant \(P\) dilutes like expansion.
  • For \(N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2\) with degree \(\alpha\): \(K_p = 4\alpha^2P/(1-\alpha^2)\).
Example 1.

For \(N_2+3H_2\rightleftharpoons2NH_3\), \(K_c = 0.5\) at some \(T\). Find \(K_p\) at \(700\,K\).

  1. \(\Delta n_g = 2-4 = -2\).
  2. \(K_p = 0.5\times(0.0821\times700)^{-2} = 0.5/(57.47)^2 \approx 1.51\times10^{-4}\).

Answer: About \(1.5\times10^{-4}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(1\,mol\,N_2O_4\) dissociates \(20\%\) at total pressure \(1\,atm\). Find \(K_p\).

  1. \(\alpha = 0.2\); \(K_p = 4(0.04)(1)/(1-0.04) = 0.16/0.96\).
  2. \(K_p \approx 0.167\,atm\).

Answer: About \(0.167\,atm\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Writing \(K_p\) with wrong \(\Delta n_g\) sign.
  • Including solids (e.g. \(CaCO_3\)) in the equilibrium expression.

Index / Energy & Equilibrium
Chapter 16 · Topic 3

Equilibrium pressure

Chemical Equilibrium - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 3 of 16

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Equilibrium - Advanced, Equilibrium pressure: equilibrium partial pressures satisfy the Kp ratio exactly. At equilibrium \(Q = K\); \(K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}\). Reaction moves forward if \(Q<K\), backward if \(Q>K\). \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K\) ties \(K\) to thermodynamics; van It Hoff gives temperature dependence.
Key formula(s). \[ K_p=K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g},\;K_p=\frac{4\alpha^2P}{1-\alpha^2}\,(dissociation) \]
Key points.
  • Catalyst never changes \(K\), only the speed of approach.
  • Le Chatelier: pressure/utting shifts toward fewer gas moles; inert gas at constant \(P\) dilutes like expansion.
  • For \(N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2\) with degree \(\alpha\): \(K_p = 4\alpha^2P/(1-\alpha^2)\).
  • Pure solids/liquids are omitted from \(K\) and \(Q\) expressions.
Example 1.

For \(H_2 + I_2 \rightleftharpoons 2HI\), \(K_c = 50\). Start with \(1\,M\) each of \(H_2, I_2\). Find \([HI]\) at equilibrium.

  1. Let \(x\) reacted: \(K_c = (2x)^2/(1-x)^2 = 50\), so \(2x/(1-x) = 7.07\).
  2. \(x = 7.07/9.07 \approx 0.78\); \([HI] = 1.56\,M\).

Answer: About \(1.56\,M\,HI\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(PCl_5\) dissociates \(40\%\) at total pressure \(2\,atm\). Find \(K_p\).

  1. \(K_p = 4\alpha^2P/(1-\alpha^2) = 4(0.16)(2)/(0.84)\).
  2. \(K_p \approx 1.52\,atm\).

Answer: \(1.52\,atm\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Writing \(K_p\) with wrong \(\Delta n_g\) sign.
  • Including solids (e.g. \(CaCO_3\)) in the equilibrium expression.

Chapter 16 · Topic 8

Temperature dependence of K

Chemical Equilibrium - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 8 of 16

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Equilibrium - Advanced, Temperature dependence of K: van't Hoff raises K with T for endothermic reactions. At equilibrium \(Q = K\); \(K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}\). Reaction moves forward if \(Q<K\), backward if \(Q>K\). \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K\) ties \(K\) to thermodynamics; van It Hoff gives temperature dependence.
Key formula(s). \[ \ln\frac{K_2}{K_1}=-\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2}-\frac{1}{T_1}\right) \]
Key points.
  • Pure solids/liquids are omitted from \(K\) and \(Q\) expressions.
  • Catalyst never changes \(K\), only the speed of approach.
  • Le Chatelier: pressure/utting shifts toward fewer gas moles; inert gas at constant \(P\) dilutes like expansion.
  • For \(N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2\) with degree \(\alpha\): \(K_p = 4\alpha^2P/(1-\alpha^2)\).
Example 1.

For \(N_2+3H_2\rightleftharpoons2NH_3\), \(K_c = 0.5\) at some \(T\). Find \(K_p\) at \(700\,K\).

  1. \(\Delta n_g = 2-4 = -2\).
  2. \(K_p = 0.5\times(0.0821\times700)^{-2} = 0.5/(57.47)^2 \approx 1.51\times10^{-4}\).

Answer: About \(1.5\times10^{-4}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(1\,mol\,N_2O_4\) dissociates \(20\%\) at total pressure \(1\,atm\). Find \(K_p\).

  1. \(\alpha = 0.2\); \(K_p = 4(0.04)(1)/(1-0.04) = 0.16/0.96\).
  2. \(K_p \approx 0.167\,atm\).

Answer: About \(0.167\,atm\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Writing \(K_p\) with wrong \(\Delta n_g\) sign.
  • Including solids (e.g. \(CaCO_3\)) in the equilibrium expression.

van't Hoff equation

Chemical Equilibrium - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 9 of 16

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Equilibrium - Advanced, van't Hoff equation: van't Hoff equation quantifies K's temperature slide from Delta-H. At equilibrium \(Q = K\); \(K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}\). Reaction moves forward if \(Q<K\), backward if \(Q>K\). \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K\) ties \(K\) to thermodynamics; van It Hoff gives temperature dependence.
Key formula(s). \[ \Delta G^\circ=-RT\ln K,\;\ln\frac{K_2}{K_1}=-\frac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2}-\frac{1}{T_1}\right) \]
Key points.
  • Catalyst never changes \(K\), only the speed of approach.
  • Le Chatelier: pressure/utting shifts toward fewer gas moles; inert gas at constant \(P\) dilutes like expansion.
  • For \(N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2\) with degree \(\alpha\): \(K_p = 4\alpha^2P/(1-\alpha^2)\).
  • Pure solids/liquids are omitted from \(K\) and \(Q\) expressions.
Example 1.

For \(H_2 + I_2 \rightleftharpoons 2HI\), \(K_c = 50\). Start with \(1\,M\) each of \(H_2, I_2\). Find \([HI]\) at equilibrium.

  1. Let \(x\) reacted: \(K_c = (2x)^2/(1-x)^2 = 50\), so \(2x/(1-x) = 7.07\).
  2. \(x = 7.07/9.07 \approx 0.78\); \([HI] = 1.56\,M\).

Answer: About \(1.56\,M\,HI\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(PCl_5\) dissociates \(40\%\) at total pressure \(2\,atm\). Find \(K_p\).

  1. \(K_p = 4\alpha^2P/(1-\alpha^2) = 4(0.16)(2)/(0.84)\).
  2. \(K_p \approx 1.52\,atm\).

Answer: \(1.52\,atm\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Writing \(K_p\) with wrong \(\Delta n_g\) sign.
  • Including solids (e.g. \(CaCO_3\)) in the equilibrium expression.

Reaction quotient

Chemical Equilibrium - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 10 of 16

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Equilibrium - Advanced, Reaction quotient: Q below K runs forward, above K runs back. At equilibrium \(Q = K\); \(K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}\). Reaction moves forward if \(Q<K\), backward if \(Q>K\). \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K\) ties \(K\) to thermodynamics; van It Hoff gives temperature dependence.
Key formula(s). \[ Q<K\to forward,\;Q>K\to backward,\;K_p=\frac{4\alpha^2P}{1-\alpha^2}\,(dissociation) \]
Key points.
  • Le Chatelier: pressure/utting shifts toward fewer gas moles; inert gas at constant \(P\) dilutes like expansion.
  • For \(N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2\) with degree \(\alpha\): \(K_p = 4\alpha^2P/(1-\alpha^2)\).

  • Catalyst never changes \(K\), only the speed of approach.
Example 1.

\(\Delta G^\circ = -30\,kJ\) at \(300\,K\). Find \(K\).

  1. \(\ln K = 30000/(8.314\times300) = 12.03\).
  2. \(K = e^{12.03} \approx 1.68\times10^5\).

Answer: About \(1.7\times10^5\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(N_2 + O_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NO\) is endothermic. What happens to \(K\) on heating?

  1. Heat favours the endothermic (forward) side.
  2. \(K\) increases with \(T\).

Answer: \(K\) increases.

  • Writing \(K_p\) with wrong \(\Delta n_g\) sign.
  • Including solids (e.g. \(CaCO_3\)) in the equilibrium expression.

Chapter 17 · Topic 1

Approximation in pH calculations

Ionic Equilibrium - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 1 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Ionic Equilibrium - Advanced, Approximation in pH calculations: approximations drop tiny terms but must pass the five-percent check. \(K_w = 10^{-14}\) (25\(^\circ C\)); \(pH+pOH = 14\). Weak acid: \([H^+] = \sqrt{K_aC}\) (\(pH = \frac12(pK_a-\log C)\)); weak base mirrors with \(K_b\). Degree of ionisation \(\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}\).
Key formula(s). \[ pH+pOH=14,\;pH=\frac{1}{2}(pK_a-\log C) \]
Key points.
  • Ostwald dilution: more dilution \(\to\) larger \(\alpha\), but \([H^+]\) still falls.
  • Conjugate pair: \(K_a\times K_b = K_w\); stronger acid \(\to\) weaker conjugate base.
  • Lewis acids accept electron pairs (\(BF_3, AlCl_3\)); \(H^+\) itself is the simplest Lewis acid.
  • Polyprotic: first dissociation dominates \([H^+]\); amphiprotic \(pH = \frac12(pK_{a1}+pK_{a2})\).
Example 1.

Find the pH of \(0.01\,M\,CH_3COOH\) (\(K_a = 1.8\times10^{-5}\)).

  1. \([H^+] = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-5}\times0.01} = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-7}} \approx 4.24\times10^{-4}\).
  2. \(pH = -\log(4.24\times10^{-4}) \approx 3.37\).

Answer: About \(3.37\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) pH of a mixture of \(50\,mL\,0.1\,M\,HCl + 50\,mL\,0.1\,M\,NaOH\)?

  1. Equal moles neutralise exactly to neutral salt solution.
  2. \(pH = 7\) (strong-strong equivalence).

Answer: \(7\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(\sqrt{K_aC}\) when \(\alpha\) is large or for strong acids.
  • Forgetting \(pK_w\) changes with temperature (\(pH<7\) neutral at higher \(T\)).
Back to Index
Index / Energy & Equilibrium
Chapter 17 · Topic 2

Strong acid and strong base mixtures

Ionic Equilibrium - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 2 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Ionic Equilibrium - Advanced, Strong acid and strong base mixtures: strong-strong mixtures neutralise mole-for-mole to pH 7 at equivalence. Buffers resist pH change: acidic \(pH = pK_a+\log(salt/acid)\), basic \(pOH = pK_b+\log(salt/base)\). Salts hydrolyse (\(pH\) from \(K_h = K_w/K_a\) etc.). Precipitate forms when ionic product \(> K_{sp}\); selective precipitation separates ions by \(K_{sp}\) gap.
Key formula(s). \[ pH=pK_a+\log\frac{[salt]}{[acid]},\;weak\,salt:\,pH=\frac12(pK_w+pK_a+\log C) \]
Key points.
  • Salt pH: strong-strong \(\to 7\); weak-acid+strong-base \(\to >7\); strong-acid+weak-base \(\to <7\).
  • Solubility: \(AgCl\): \(s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}\); \(CaF_2\): \(s=(K_{sp}/4)^{1/3}\).
  • Common ion suppresses solubility and weak-electrolyte ionisation.
  • Maximum buffer capacity at \([salt]=[acid]\) (\(pH = pK_a\)).
Example 1.

Acetic buffer has \([salt] = 0.2\,M\), \([acid] = 0.1\,M\), \(pK_a = 4.74\). Find pH.

  1. Ratio \(= 2\).
  2. \(pH = 4.74 + \log2 = 4.74 + 0.30 = 5.04\).

Answer: \(5.04\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(K_{sp}(AgBr) = 5.0\times10^{-13}\). Find its solubility.

  1. \(AgBr \to Ag^+ + Br^-\): \(s = \sqrt{K_{sp}}\).
  2. \(s = \sqrt{5.0\times10^{-13}} \approx 7.07\times10^{-7}\,M\).

Answer: \(7.07\times10^{-7}\,M\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using concentrations instead of the salt/acid ratio after reaction (recompute moles first).
  • Wrong \(s\)-\(K_{sp}\) exponent for \(A_xB_y\) salts.

Index / Energy & Equilibrium
Chapter 17 · Topic 3

Weak acid calculations

Ionic Equilibrium - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 3 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Ionic Equilibrium - Advanced, Weak acid calculations: weak-acid math starts from Ka with Ostwald alpha. Buffers resist pH change: acidic \(pH = pK_a+\log(salt/acid)\), basic \(pOH = pK_b+\log(salt/base)\). Salts hydrolyse (\(pH\) from \(K_h = K_w/K_a\) etc.). Precipitate forms when ionic product \(> K_{sp}\); selective precipitation separates ions by \(K_{sp}\) gap.
Key formula(s). \[ pH=pK_a+\log\frac{[salt]}{[acid]},\;K_h=K_w/K_a\,(hydrolysis),\;weak\,salt:\,pH=\frac12(pK_w+pK_a+\log C) \]
Key points.
  • Solubility: \(AgCl\): \(s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}\); \(CaF_2\): \(s=(K_{sp}/4)^{1/3}\).
  • Common ion suppresses solubility and weak-electrolyte ionisation.
  • Maximum buffer capacity at \([salt]=[acid]\) (\(pH = pK_a\)).
  • Salt pH: strong-strong \(\to 7\); weak-acid+strong-base \(\to >7\); strong-acid+weak-base \(\to <7\).
Example 1.

Ammonia buffer: \([base] = [salt] = 0.1\,M\), \(pK_b = 4.74\). Find pH.

  1. \(pOH = pK_b + \log1 = 4.74\).
  2. \(pH = 14 - 4.74 = 9.26\).

Answer: \(9.26\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Will \(PbCl_2\) (\(K_{sp} = 1.7\times10^{-5}\)) precipitate if \([Pb^{2+}] = 0.01\,M\), \([Cl^-] = 0.1\,M\)?

  1. \(Q = 0.01\times(0.1)^2 = 1.0\times10^{-4} > K_{sp}\).
  2. Yes, it precipitates.

Answer: Yes (\(Q > K_{sp}\)).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using concentrations instead of the salt/acid ratio after reaction (recompute moles first).
  • Wrong \(s\)-\(K_{sp}\) exponent for \(A_xB_y\) salts.

Example 1.

Buffer has \([salt]=[acid]=0.1\,M\), \(pK_a = 4.74\). Find pH; what if \(0.01\,mol\,HCl\) is added per litre?

  2. Adding acid: salt \(0.09\), acid \(0.11\); \(pH = 4.74+\log(0.09/0.11) \approx 4.65\). Tiny shift proves buffering.

Answer: \(4.74 \to\) about \(4.65\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(K_{sp}(AgCl) = 1.8\times10^{-10}\). Find solubility in \(mol/L\) and in pure water vs \(0.1\,M\,NaCl\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.

Chapter 17 · Topic 5

Polyprotic acid calculations

Ionic Equilibrium - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 5 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Ionic Equilibrium - Advanced, Polyprotic acid calculations: first dissociation dominates polyprotic pH. \(K_w = 10^{-14}\) (25\(^\circ C\)); \(pH+pOH = 14\). Weak acid: \([H^+] = \sqrt{K_aC}\) (\(pH = \frac12(pK_a-\log C)\)); weak base mirrors with \(K_b\). Degree of ionisation \(\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}\).
Key formula(s). \[ pH+pOH=14,\;polyprotic:\,K_{a1}>K_{a2}>K_{a3} \]
Key points.
  • Conjugate pair: \(K_a\times K_b = K_w\); stronger acid \(\to\) weaker conjugate base.
  • Lewis acids accept electron pairs (\(BF_3, AlCl_3\)); \(H^+\) itself is the simplest Lewis acid.
  • Polyprotic: first dissociation dominates \([H^+]\); amphiprotic \(pH = \frac12(pK_{a1}+pK_{a2})\).
  • Ostwald dilution: more dilution \(\to\) larger \(\alpha\), but \([H^+]\) still falls.
Example 1.

Find the pH of \(0.01\,M\,NH_4OH\) (\(K_b = 1.8\times10^{-5}\)).

  1. \([OH^-] = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-5}\times0.01} \approx 4.24\times10^{-4}\).
  2. \(pOH \approx 3.37\), so \(pH \approx 10.63\).

Answer: About \(10.63\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Estimate the pH of \(10^{-8}\,M\,HCl\).

  1. Below \(10^{-6}\,M\), water's own \(H^+\) matters: total \([H^+] \approx 1.05\times10^{-7}\).
  2. \(pH \approx 6.98\) (still acidic, never above 7).

Answer: \(6.98\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(\sqrt{K_aC}\) when \(\alpha\) is large or for strong acids.
  • Forgetting \(pK_w\) changes with temperature (\(pH<7\) neutral at higher \(T\)).

Chapter 17 · Topic 6

Amphoteric species

Ionic Equilibrium - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 6 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Ionic Equilibrium - Advanced, Amphoteric species: amphoteric oxides and hydroxides dissolve in both acid and base. \(K_w = 10^{-14}\) (25\(^\circ C\)); \(pH+pOH = 14\). Weak acid: \([H^+] = \sqrt{K_aC}\) (\(pH = \frac12(pK_a-\log C)\)); weak base mirrors with \(K_b\). Degree of ionisation \(\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}\).
Key formula(s). \[ Lewis:\,e^-\,pair\,donor/acceptor,\;conjugate:\,K_aK_b=K_w \]
Key points.
  • Lewis acids accept electron pairs (\(BF_3, AlCl_3\)); \(H^+\) itself is the simplest Lewis acid.
  • Polyprotic: first dissociation dominates \([H^+]\); amphiprotic \(pH = \frac12(pK_{a1}+pK_{a2})\).
  • Ostwald dilution: more dilution \(\to\) larger \(\alpha\), but \([H^+]\) still falls.
  • Conjugate pair: \(K_a\times K_b = K_w\); stronger acid \(\to\) weaker conjugate base.
Example 1.

A weak acid has \(K_a = 10^{-5}\), \(C = 0.1\,M\). Find its degree of ionisation.

  1. \(\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C} = \sqrt{10^{-4}}\).
  2. \(\alpha = 0.01\) (1\% ionised).

Answer: \(0.01\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(K_a(HCOOH) = 1.8\times10^{-4}\). Find \(K_b\) of \(HCOO^-\).

  1. \(K_a\times K_b = K_w\).
  2. \(K_b = 10^{-14}/1.8\times10^{-4} \approx 5.6\times10^{-11}\).

Answer: \(5.6\times10^{-11}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(\sqrt{K_aC}\) when \(\alpha\) is large or for strong acids.
  • Forgetting \(pK_w\) changes with temperature (\(pH<7\) neutral at higher \(T\)).

Chapter 17 · Topic 7

Buffer calculations

Ionic Equilibrium - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 7 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Ionic Equilibrium - Advanced, Buffer calculations: buffer math recomputes the salt-acid ratio after every addition. Buffers resist pH change: acidic \(pH = pK_a+\log(salt/acid)\), basic \(pOH = pK_b+\log(salt/base)\). Salts hydrolyse (\(pH\) from \(K_h = K_w/K_a\) etc.). Precipitate forms when ionic product \(> K_{sp}\); selective precipitation separates ions by \(K_{sp}\) gap.

  • Solubility: \(AgCl\): \(s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}\); \(CaF_2\): \(s=(K_{sp}/4)^{1/3}\).
  • Common ion suppresses solubility and weak-electrolyte ionisation.

Buffer has \([salt]=[acid]=0.1\,M\), \(pK_a = 4.74\). Find pH; what if \(0.01\,mol\,HCl\) is added per litre?

  1. Initial \(pH = 4.74+\log1 = 4.74\).
  2. Adding acid: salt \(0.09\), acid \(0.11\); \(pH = 4.74+\log(0.09/0.11) \approx 4.65\). Tiny shift proves buffering.

Answer: \(4.74 \to\) about \(4.65\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(K_{sp}(AgCl) = 1.8\times10^{-10}\). Find solubility in \(mol/L\) and in pure water vs \(0.1\,M\,NaCl\).

  1. Pure: \(s = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-10}} \approx 1.34\times10^{-5}\,M\).
  2. In \(0.1\,M\,Cl^-\): \(s = K_{sp}/0.1 = 1.8\times10^{-9}\,M\) (suppressed).

Answer: \(1.34\times10^{-5}\,M\) pure; \(1.8\times10^{-9}\,M\) in common ion.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using concentrations instead of the salt/acid ratio after reaction (recompute moles first).
  • Wrong \(s\)-\(K_{sp}\) exponent for \(A_xB_y\) salts.

Precipitate forms when ionic product \(> K_{sp}\); selective precipitation separates ions by \(K_{sp}\) gap.

  1. \(AgBr \to Ag^+ + Br^-\): \(s = \sqrt{K_{sp}}\).
  2. \(s = \sqrt{5.0\times10^{-13}} \approx 7.07\times10^{-7}\,M\).

Answer: \(7.07\times10^{-7}\,M\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.

Ionic Equilibrium - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 9 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Ionic Equilibrium - Advanced, Salt hydrolysis: salts of weak partners hydrolyse and tilt pH off seven. Precipitate forms when ionic product \(> K_{sp}\); selective precipitation separates ions by \(K_{sp}\) gap.
Key formula(s). \[ pH=pK_a+\log\frac{[salt]}{[acid]},\;s=\left(\frac{K_{sp}}{x^xy^y}\right)^{\frac{1}{x+y}},\;Q>K_{sp}\,\Rightarrow\,ppt,\;K_h=K_w/K_a\,(hydrolysis),\;weak\,salt:\,pH=\frac12(pK_w+pK_a+\log C) \]
Key points.
  • Solubility: \(AgCl\): \(s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}\); \(CaF_2\): \(s=(K_{sp}/4)^{1/3}\).

Example 1.

Ammonia buffer: \([base] = [salt] = 0.1\,M\), \(pK_b = 4.74\). Find pH.

  1. \(pOH = pK_b + \log1 = 4.74\).
  2. \(pH = 14 - 4.74 = 9.26\).

Answer: \(9.26\).

(JEE pattern) Will \(PbCl_2\) (\(K_{sp} = 1.7\times10^{-5}\)) precipitate if \([Pb^{2+}] = 0.01\,M\), \([Cl^-] = 0.1\,M\)?

  1. \(Q = 0.01\times(0.1)^2 = 1.0\times10^{-4} > K_{sp}\).
  2. Yes, it precipitates.

Answer: Yes (\(Q > K_{sp}\)).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using concentrations instead of the salt/acid ratio after reaction (recompute moles first).
  • Wrong \(s\)-\(K_{sp}\) exponent for \(A_xB_y\) salts.

Buffer has \([salt]=[acid]=0.1\,M\), \(pK_a = 4.74\). Find pH; what if \(0.01\,mol\,HCl\) is added per litre?

  1. Initial \(pH = 4.74+\log1 = 4.74\).
  2. Adding acid: salt \(0.09\), acid \(0.11\); \(pH = 4.74+\log(0.09/0.11) \approx 4.65\). Tiny shift proves buffering.

Answer: \(4.74 \to\) about \(4.65\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(K_{sp}(AgCl) = 1.8\times10^{-10}\). Find solubility in \(mol/L\) and in pure water vs \(0.1\,M\,NaCl\).

  1. Pure: \(s = \sqrt{1.8\times10^{-10}} \approx 1.34\times10^{-5}\,M\).
  2. In \(0.1\,M\,Cl^-\): \(s = K_{sp}/0.1 = 1.8\times10^{-9}\,M\) (suppressed).

Answer: \(1.34\times10^{-5}\,M\) pure; \(1.8\times10^{-9}\,M\) in common ion.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using concentrations instead of the salt/acid ratio after reaction (recompute moles first).
  • Wrong \(s\)-\(K_{sp}\) exponent for \(A_xB_y\) salts.

Chapter 17 · Topic 17

Mixed acid-base systems

Ionic Equilibrium - AdvancedEnergy & EquilibriumTopic 17 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Ionic Equilibrium - Advanced, Mixed acid-base systems: the focus here is Mixed acid-base systems, worked through the Ionic Equilibrium - Advanced toolkit below. Buffers resist pH change: acidic \(pH = pK_a+\log(salt/acid)\), basic \(pOH = pK_b+\log(salt/base)\). Salts hydrolyse (\(pH\) from \(K_h = K_w/K_a\) etc.). Precipitate forms when ionic product \(> K_{sp}\); selective precipitation separates ions by \(K_{sp}\) gap.
Key formula(s). \[ pH=pK_a+\log\frac{[salt]}{[acid]} \]
Key points.
  • Salt pH: strong-strong \(\to 7\); weak-acid+strong-base \(\to >7\); strong-acid+weak-base \(\to <7\).
  • Solubility: \(AgCl\): \(s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}\); \(CaF_2\): \(s=(K_{sp}/4)^{1/3}\).
  • Common ion suppresses solubility and weak-electrolyte ionisation.
  • Maximum buffer capacity at \([salt]=[acid]\) (\(pH = pK_a\)).
Example 1.

Acetic buffer has \([salt] = 0.2\,M\), \([acid] = 0.1\,M\), \(pK_a = 4.74\). Find pH.

  1. Ratio \(= 2\).
  2. \(pH = 4.74 + \log2 = 4.74 + 0.30 = 5.04\).

Answer: \(5.04\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(K_{sp}(AgBr) = 5.0\times10^{-13}\). Find its solubility.

  1. \(AgBr \to Ag^+ + Br^-\): \(s = \sqrt{K_{sp}}\).
  2. \(s = \sqrt{5.0\times10^{-13}} \approx 7.07\times10^{-7}\,M\).

Answer: \(7.07\times10^{-7}\,M\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using concentrations instead of the salt/acid ratio after reaction (recompute moles first).
  • Wrong \(s\)-\(K_{sp}\) exponent for \(A_xB_y\) salts.

Precipitate forms when ionic product \(> K_{sp}\); selective precipitation separates ions by \(K_{sp}\) gap.

Key points.
  • Solubility: \(AgCl\): \(s=\sqrt{K_{sp}}\); \(CaF_2\): \(s=(K_{sp}/4)^{1/3}\).

Example 1.

Ammonia buffer: \([base] = [salt] = 0.1\,M\), \(pK_b = 4.74\). Find pH.

  1. \(pOH = pK_b + \log1 = 4.74\).
  2. \(pH = 14 - 4.74 = 9.26\).

Answer: \(9.26\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Will \(PbCl_2\) (\(K_{sp} = 1.7\times10^{-5}\)) precipitate if \([Pb^{2+}] = 0.01\,M\), \([Cl^-] = 0.1\,M\)?

  1. \(Q = 0.01\times(0.1)^2 = 1.0\times10^{-4} > K_{sp}\).
  2. Yes, it precipitates.

Answer: Yes (\(Q > K_{sp}\)).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using concentrations instead of the salt/acid ratio after reaction (recompute moles first).
  • Wrong \(s\)-\(K_{sp}\) exponent for \(A_xB_y\) salts.

Index / Electro & Kinetics
Chapter 18 · Topic 1

Cell EMF calculations

Electrochemistry - AdvancedElectro & KineticsTopic 1 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry - Advanced, Cell EMF calculations: EMF math subtracts anode potential from cathode potential. Cell: \(E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode}-E^\circ_{anode}\); Nernst \(E = E^\circ-(0.0591/n)\log Q\) at 298 K. Links: \(\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ\), \(\log K = nE^\circ/0.0591\). Anode \(=\) oxidation (negative in galvanic).
Key formula(s). \[ E=E^\circ-\frac{0.0591}{n}\log Q,\;E_{conc}=\frac{0.0591}{n}\log\frac{C_{cath}}{C_{an}} \]
Key points.
  • Salt bridge completes the circuit and preserves neutrality; no salt bridge \(\to\) no sustained current.
  • Concentration cell: \(E^\circ = 0\), \(E = (0.0591/n)\log(C_{cath}/C_{an})\); current flows to equalise.
  • Multiply half-reactions freely, but NEVER multiply \(E^\circ\) (intensive).
  • \(E^\circ_{cell}>0 \Rightarrow\) spontaneous galvanic; \(E^\circ_{cell}<0 \Rightarrow\) needs electrolysis.
Example 1.

For \(Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \to Cu\), \(E^\circ = +0.34\,V\). Find \(E\) when \([Cu^{2+}] = 0.01\,M\).

  1. \(E = 0.34 - (0.0591/2)\log(1/0.01) = 0.34 - 0.0591\).
  2. \(E \approx 0.281\,V\).

Answer: \(0.281\,V\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) The Daniell cell has \(E^\circ = 1.10\,V\), \(n = 2\). Estimate its equilibrium constant.

  1. \(\log K = 2\times1.10/0.0591 \approx 37.2\).
  2. \(K \approx 1.6\times10^{37}\).

Answer: About \(10^{37}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Multiplying \(E^\circ\) when multiplying half-equations.
  • Wrong \(Q\) (products/reactants of the CELL reaction, solids omitted).

Chapter 18 · Topic 2

Standard electrode potential

Electrochemistry - AdvancedElectro & KineticsTopic 2 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry - Advanced, Standard electrode potential: standard potentials rank all half-cells against hydrogen zero. Cell: \(E^\circ_{cell} = E^\circ_{cathode}-E^\circ_{anode}\); Nernst \(E = E^\circ-(0.0591/n)\log Q\) at 298 K. Links: \(\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ\), \(\log K = nE^\circ/0.0591\). Anode \(=\) oxidation (negative in galvanic).
Key formula(s). \[ E=E^\circ-\frac{0.0591}{n}\log Q,\;\Delta G^\circ=-nFE^\circ \]
Key points.
  • Concentration cell: \(E^\circ = 0\), \(E = (0.0591/n)\log(C_{cath}/C_{an})\); current flows to equalise.
  • Multiply half-reactions freely, but NEVER multiply \(E^\circ\) (intensive).
  • \(E^\circ_{cell}>0 \Rightarrow\) spontaneous galvanic; \(E^\circ_{cell}<0 \Rightarrow\) needs electrolysis.
  • Salt bridge completes the circuit and preserves neutrality; no salt bridge \(\to\) no sustained current.
Example 1.

A silver concentration cell has \(0.1\,M\) vs \(1\,M\,Ag^+\). Find its EMF.

  1. \(E^\circ = 0\); \(E = (0.0591/1)\log(1/0.1)\).
  2. \(E = 0.0591\,V\).

Answer: \(0.0591\,V\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) What are the standard conditions defining the SHE (\(E^\circ = 0\))?

  1. \(Pt|H_2(1\,atm)|H^+(1\,M)\) at \(298\,K\).
  2. All ion activities unity by definition.

Answer: \(1\,M\,H^+\), \(1\,atm\,H_2\), \(Pt\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Multiplying \(E^\circ\) when multiplying half-equations.
  • Wrong \(Q\) (products/reactants of the CELL reaction, solids omitted).

Explanation

Anode \(=\) oxidation (negative in galvanic).
Key formula(s). \[ SHE:\,Pt|H_2(1atm)|H^+(1M)=0.00V \]
Key points.
  • \(E^\circ_{cell}>0 \Rightarrow\) spontaneous galvanic; \(E^\circ_{cell}<0 \Rightarrow\) needs electrolysis.
  • Salt bridge completes the circuit and preserves neutrality; no salt bridge \(\to\) no sustained current.

Example 1.

\(Zn|Zn^{2+}(0.1M)||Cu^{2+}(1M)|Cu\), \(E^\circ = 1.10\,V\), \(n = 2\). Find \(E\).

  1. \(Q = 0.1/1 = 0.1\); \(E = 1.10-(0.0591/2)\log(0.1)\).
  2. \(E = 1.10+0.0296 = 1.1296\,V\).

Answer: About \(1.13\,V\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(E^\circ = 0.46\,V\), \(n = 2\). Find \(K\).

  1. \(\log K = 2\times0.46/0.0591 \approx 15.57\).
  2. \(K \approx 3.7\times10^{15}\).

Answer: About \(10^{15.6}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Multiplying \(E^\circ\) when multiplying half-equations.

Chapter 18 · Topic 9

Electrolysis calculations

Electrochemistry - AdvancedElectro & KineticsTopic 9 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry - Advanced, Electrolysis calculations: electrolysis math is w equals M I t over nF. Faraday: \(w = ZQ = (M/nF)It\). Products follow discharge order (lower \(E^\circ\) cation discharges first at cathode; concentrated \(Cl^-\) can beat \(O_2\) at anode). Corrosion is Fe oxidation; protection via galvanisation, alloying, cathodic protection.
Key formula(s). \[ w=\frac{MIt}{nF} \]
Key points.
  • Series cells: same \(Q\) passes; moles deposited \(\propto M/n\).
  • \(NaCl\)(aq): cathode \(H_2\), anode \(Cl_2\) (conc.) vs \(O_2\) (dilute); molten \(NaCl\): \(Na\) + \(Cl_2\).
  • Batteries: dry cell \(1.5\,V\), lead storage \(2\,V\)/cell, \(H_2\)-\(O_2\) fuel cell clean (water product).
  • Rusting needs both air AND moisture; \(E^\circ(Fe^{2+}/Fe) = -0.44\,V\).
Example 1.

How long must \(2\,A\) pass to deposit \(5.4\,g\,Ag\) (\(M = 108\), \(n = 1\))?

  1. Moles \(e^- = 5.4/108 = 0.05\); \(Q = 0.05\times96485 = 4824\,C\).
  2. \(t = 4824/2 = 2412\,s \approx 40.2\,min\).

Answer: About \(40\,min\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Same \(Q\) through \(AgNO_3\) and \(CuSO_4\) deposits \(10.8\,g\,Ag\). Find \(Cu\) mass.

  1. Moles \(e^- = 0.1\); \(Cu^{2+}\) needs \(2e^-\), so \(0.05\,mol\,Cu\).
  2. Mass \(= 0.05\times63.5 = 3.175\,g\).

Answer: \(3.175\,g\,Cu\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Forgetting \(n\) (valency) in \(w = MIt/nF\).
  • Wrong discharge order in aqueous electrolysis.

Chapter 18 · Topic 10

Faraday laws

Electrochemistry - AdvancedElectro & KineticsTopic 10 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry - Advanced, Faraday laws: both Faraday laws combine into w = ZQ with equivalent reasoning. Faraday: \(w = ZQ = (M/nF)It\). Products follow discharge order (lower \(E^\circ\) cation discharges first at cathode; concentrated \(Cl^-\) can beat \(O_2\) at anode). Corrosion is Fe oxidation; protection via galvanisation, alloying, cathodic protection.
Key formula(s). \[ w=\frac{MIt}{nF},\;Q=It \]
Key points.
  • \(NaCl\)(aq): cathode \(H_2\), anode \(Cl_2\) (conc.) vs \(O_2\) (dilute); molten \(NaCl\): \(Na\) + \(Cl_2\).
  • Batteries: dry cell \(1.5\,V\), lead storage \(2\,V\)/cell, \(H_2\)-\(O_2\) fuel cell clean (water product).
  • Rusting needs both air AND moisture; \(E^\circ(Fe^{2+}/Fe) = -0.44\,V\).
  • Series cells: same \(Q\) passes; moles deposited \(\propto M/n\).
Example 1.

How much copper (\(Cu^{2+}\), \(M = 63.5\)) deposits with \(19300\,C\)?

  1. Moles \(e^- = 19300/96485 = 0.2\); \(Cu = 0.1\,mol\).
  2. Mass \(= 0.1\times63.5 = 6.35\,g\).

Answer: \(6.35\,g\,Cu\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Molten \(MgCl_2\) is electrolysed with \(2\,A\) for \(1\,h\). Find moles of \(Mg\).

  1. \(Q = 2\times3600 = 7200\,C\); \(e^- = 0.0746\,mol\).
  2. \(Mg = 0.0373\,mol\) (2 electrons each).

Answer: \(0.0373\,mol\,Mg\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Forgetting \(n\) (valency) in \(w = MIt/nF\).
  • Wrong discharge order in aqueous electrolysis.

Chapter 18 · Topic 11

Multiple electrolysis cells

Electrochemistry - AdvancedElectro & KineticsTopic 11 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry - Advanced, Multiple electrolysis cells: series cells share charge, so moles scale as M over n. Faraday: \(w = ZQ = (M/nF)It\). Products follow discharge order (lower \(E^\circ\) cation discharges first at cathode; concentrated \(Cl^-\) can beat \(O_2\) at anode). Corrosion is Fe oxidation; protection via galvanisation, alloying, cathodic protection.
Key formula(s). \[ w=\frac{MIt}{nF},\;series:\,same\,Q,\,moles\propto M/n \]
Key points.
  • Batteries: dry cell \(1.5\,V\), lead storage \(2\,V\)/cell, \(H_2\)-\(O_2\) fuel cell clean (water product).
  • Rusting needs both air AND moisture; \(E^\circ(Fe^{2+}/Fe) = -0.44\,V\).
  • Series cells: same \(Q\) passes; moles deposited \(\propto M/n\).
  • \(NaCl\)(aq): cathode \(H_2\), anode \(Cl_2\) (conc.) vs \(O_2\) (dilute); molten \(NaCl\): \(Na\) + \(Cl_2\).
Example 1.

Why does aqueous \(NaCl\) give \(H_2\) at the cathode instead of \(Na\)?

  1. \(H_2O/H_2\) reduces far more easily than \(Na^+/Na\) (\(-0.83\) vs \(-2.71\,V\)).
  2. Water discharges preferentially.

Answer: Water reduces more easily.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) EMF of the lead-storage cell on discharge?

  1. \(Pb + PbO_2 + 2H_2SO_4 \to 2PbSO_4 + 2H_2O\).
  2. About \(2.0\,V\) per cell.

Answer: \(2.0\,V\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Forgetting \(n\) (valency) in \(w = MIt/nF\).
  • Wrong discharge order in aqueous electrolysis.

Products of electrolysis

Explanation

Products follow discharge order (lower \(E^\circ\) cation discharges first at cathode; concentrated \(Cl^-\) can beat \(O_2\) at anode). Corrosion is Fe oxidation; protection via galvanisation, alloying, cathodic protection.
Key formula(s). \[ w=\frac{MIt}{nF},\;Q=It,\;F=96485\,C\,mol^{-1} \]
Key points.
  • Series cells: same \(Q\) passes; moles deposited \(\propto M/n\).
  • \(NaCl\)(aq): cathode \(H_2\), anode \(Cl_2\) (conc.) vs \(O_2\) (dilute); molten \(NaCl\): \(Na\) + \(Cl_2\).
  • Batteries: dry cell \(1.5\,V\), lead storage \(2\,V\)/cell, \(H_2\)-\(O_2\) fuel cell clean (water product).

Example 1.

How long must \(2\,A\) pass to deposit \(5.4\,g\,Ag\) (\(M = 108\), \(n = 1\))?

  1. Moles \(e^- = 5.4/108 = 0.05\); \(Q = 0.05\times96485 = 4824\,C\).
  2. \(t = 4824/2 = 2412\,s \approx 40.2\,min\).

Answer: About \(40\,min\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Same \(Q\) through \(AgNO_3\) and \(CuSO_4\) deposits \(10.8\,g\,Ag\). Find \(Cu\) mass.

  1. Moles \(e^- = 0.1\); \(Cu^{2+}\) needs \(2e^-\), so \(0.05\,mol\,Cu\).
  2. Mass \(= 0.05\times63.5 = 3.175\,g\).

Answer: \(3.175\,g\,Cu\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Forgetting \(n\) (valency) in \(w = MIt/nF\).

Chapter 18 · Topic 13

Conductivity calculations

Electrochemistry - AdvancedElectro & KineticsTopic 13 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry - Advanced, Conductivity calculations: conductivity math multiplies measured G by l over A. Conductance \(G = 1/R\); conductivity \(\kappa = G\cdot(l/A)\); molar \(\Lambda_m = \kappa\times1000/M\). \(\Lambda_m\) rises with dilution (weak: steeply near infinite dilution). Kohlrausch: \(\Lambda^\circ = \sum\nu_i\lambda_i^\circ\); \(\alpha = \Lambda_m/\Lambda^\circ\).
Key formula(s). \[ \Lambda_m=\frac{\kappa\times1000}{M},\;\alpha=\frac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda^\circ} \]
Key points.
  • Cell constant \(= l/A\); calibrate with standard \(KCl\).
  • Weak-electrolyte \(K_a\) from conductivity via \(\alpha\) then Ostwald formula.
  • \(\Lambda^\circ\) of weak electrolytes cannot be measured directly (extrapolation via Kohlrausch).
  • Units: \(\kappa\) \(S\,cm^{-1}\); \(\Lambda_m\) \(S\,cm^2mol^{-1}\).
Example 1.

\(\Lambda^\circ(K^+) = 73.5\), \(\Lambda^\circ(Br^-) = 78.1\). Find \(\Lambda^\circ(KBr)\).

  1. Kohlrausch: \(\Lambda^\circ = \lambda_+^\circ + \lambda_-^\circ\).
  2. \(\Lambda^\circ = 151.6\,S\,cm^2mol^{-1}\).

Answer: \(151.6\,S\,cm^2mol^{-1}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Cell constant \(= 0.5\,cm^{-1}\), \(R = 200\,\Omega\). Find \(\kappa\).

  1. \(\kappa = G\times(l/A) = (1/200)\times0.5\).
  2. \(\kappa = 2.5\times10^{-3}\,S/cm\).

Answer: \(2.5\times10^{-3}\,S/cm\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Missing the 1000 factor in \(\Lambda_m\).
  • Extrapolating weak-electrolyte curves directly to get \(\Lambda^\circ\).

Chapter 18 · Topic 14

Molar conductivity

Electrochemistry - AdvancedElectro & KineticsTopic 14 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry - Advanced, Molar conductivity: molar conductivity is kappa times 1000 over molarity. Conductance \(G = 1/R\); conductivity \(\kappa = G\cdot(l/A)\); molar \(\Lambda_m = \kappa\times1000/M\). \(\Lambda_m\) rises with dilution (weak: steeply near infinite dilution). Kohlrausch: \(\Lambda^\circ = \sum\nu_i\lambda_i^\circ\); \(\alpha = \Lambda_m/\Lambda^\circ\).
Key formula(s). \[ \Lambda_m=\frac{\kappa\times1000}{M},\;\kappa=G\cdot const \]
Key points.
  • Weak-electrolyte \(K_a\) from conductivity via \(\alpha\) then Ostwald formula.
  • \(\Lambda^\circ\) of weak electrolytes cannot be measured directly (extrapolation via Kohlrausch).
  • Units: \(\kappa\) \(S\,cm^{-1}\); \(\Lambda_m\) \(S\,cm^2mol^{-1}\).
  • Cell constant \(= l/A\); calibrate with standard \(KCl\).
Example 1.

Why is \(\Lambda_m\) of \(CH_3COOH\) at \(0.001\,M\) much larger than at \(0.1\,M\)?

  1. Dilution drives ionisation up (Ostwald: \(\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}\)).
  2. More ions per mole \(\to\) larger \(\Lambda_m\).

Answer: Ionisation rises with dilution.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(\Lambda_m = 20\), \(\Lambda^\circ = 400\) (\(S\,cm^2mol^{-1}\)). Find \(\alpha\).

  1. \(\alpha = 20/400\).
  2. \(\alpha = 0.05\).

Answer: \(0.05\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Missing the 1000 factor in \(\Lambda_m\).
  • Extrapolating weak-electrolyte curves directly to get \(\Lambda^\circ\).

Chapter 18 · Topic 15

Kohlrausch law

Electrochemistry - AdvancedElectro & KineticsTopic 15 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry - Advanced, Kohlrausch law: Kohlrausch extrapolation recovers weak-electrolyte limits. Conductance \(G = 1/R\); conductivity \(\kappa = G\cdot(l/A)\); molar \(\Lambda_m = \kappa\times1000/M\). \(\Lambda_m\) rises with dilution (weak: steeply near infinite dilution). Kohlrausch: \(\Lambda^\circ = \sum\nu_i\lambda_i^\circ\); \(\alpha = \Lambda_m/\Lambda^\circ\).
Key formula(s). \[ \Lambda_m=\frac{\kappa\times1000}{M},\;\alpha=\frac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda^\circ},\;cell\,const=l/A \]
Key points.
  • Units: \(\kappa\) \(S\,cm^{-1}\); \(\Lambda_m\) \(S\,cm^2mol^{-1}\).
  • Cell constant \(= l/A\); calibrate with standard \(KCl\).
  • Weak-electrolyte \(K_a\) from conductivity via \(\alpha\) then Ostwald formula.
  • \(\Lambda^\circ\) of weak electrolytes cannot be measured directly (extrapolation via Kohlrausch).
Example 1.

\(\kappa = 0.001\,S/cm\) for \(0.01\,M\,CH_3COOH\). \(\Lambda^\circ = 390\). Find \(\alpha\) and \(K_a\).

  1. \(\Lambda_m = 0.001\times1000/0.01 = 100\); \(\alpha = 100/390 \approx 0.256\).
  2. \(K_a = 0.01(0.256)^2/(0.744) \approx 8.8\times10^{-4}\) (order check vs \(1.8\times10^{-5}\): here data illustrative).

Answer: \(\alpha \approx 0.26\) (method as shown).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why does \(\Lambda_m(NaCl)\) rise only slowly with dilution but \(CH_3COOH\) steeply?

  1. Strong electrolyte already fully ionised; only interionic drag falls.
  2. Weak electrolyte ionisation itself jumps with dilution (Ostwald).

Answer: Dilution ionises weak electrolytes further.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Missing the 1000 factor in \(\Lambda_m\).
  • Extrapolating weak-electrolyte curves directly to get \(\Lambda^\circ\).

Chapter 18 · Topic 16

Degree of dissociation

Electrochemistry - AdvancedElectro & KineticsTopic 16 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Electrochemistry - Advanced, Degree of dissociation: alpha is the dissociated fraction of the starting amount. Conductance \(G = 1/R\); conductivity \(\kappa = G\cdot(l/A)\); molar \(\Lambda_m = \kappa\times1000/M\). \(\Lambda_m\) rises with dilution (weak: steeply near infinite dilution). Key points.
  • Cell constant \(= l/A\); calibrate with standard \(KCl\).
  • Weak-electrolyte \(K_a\) from conductivity via \(\alpha\) then Ostwald formula.
  • \(\Lambda^\circ\) of weak electrolytes cannot be measured directly (extrapolation via Kohlrausch).
  • Units: \(\kappa\) \(S\,cm^{-1}\); \(\Lambda_m\) \(S\,cm^2mol^{-1}\).
Example 1.

\(\Lambda^\circ(K^+) = 73.5\), \(\Lambda^\circ(Br^-) = 78.1\). Find \(\Lambda^\circ(KBr)\).

  1. Kohlrausch: \(\Lambda^\circ = \lambda_+^\circ + \lambda_-^\circ\).
  2. \(\Lambda^\circ = 151.6\,S\,cm^2mol^{-1}\).

Answer: \(151.6\,S\,cm^2mol^{-1}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Cell constant \(= 0.5\,cm^{-1}\), \(R = 200\,\Omega\). Find \(\kappa\).

  1. \(\kappa = G\times(l/A) = (1/200)\times0.5\).
  2. \(\kappa = 2.5\times10^{-3}\,S/cm\).

Answer: \(2.5\times10^{-3}\,S/cm\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Missing the 1000 factor in \(\Lambda_m\).
  • Extrapolating weak-electrolyte curves directly to get \(\Lambda^\circ\).

Chapter 19 · Topic 1

Rate law determination

Chemical Kinetics - AdvancedElectro & KineticsTopic 1 of 17

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Kinetics - Advanced, Rate law determination: initial-rate ratios unlock each reactant order. Rate law \(rate = k[A]^m[B]^n\) comes from experiment only; order \(= m+n\), molecularity \(=\) molecules in an elementary step. First order: \(k = (2.303/t)\log(a/(a-x))\), \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/k\); zero: \(t_{1/2} = a/2k\). Units of \(k\): \((mol/L)^{1-n}s^{-1}\).
Key formula(s). \[ k=\frac{2.303}{t}\log\frac{a}{a-x},\;order=m+n\,(expt) \]
Key points.
  • Pseudo-first-order: excess reactant hides true order (e.g. ester hydrolysis in water).
  • Graphs: 1st order \(\ln[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; 2nd order \(1/[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; zero \([A]\) vs \(t\) linear.
  • Order can be zero, fractional or negative; molecularity is a positive integer \(1,2,3\).
  • Slowest elementary step \(=\) rate-determining; its stoichiometry (with pre-equilibria) sets the law.
Example 1.

A zero-order reaction has \([A]_0 = 0.5\,M\), \(k = 0.01\,M/min\). Find \(t_{1/2}\).

  1. Zero order: \(t_{1/2} = [A]_0/2k\).
  2. \(t_{1/2} = 0.5/0.02 = 25\,min\).

Answer: \(25\,min\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Which plot is linear for a second-order reaction?

  1. Integrated form: \(1/[A] = 1/[A]_0 + kt\).
  2. \(1/[A]\) vs \(t\).

Answer: \(1/[A]\) vs time.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reading order from balanced-equation coefficients.
  • Using \(\log\) vs \(\ln\) inconsistently (factor 2.303).
Back to Index
Index / Electro & Kinetics
Chapter 19 · Topic 2

Order determination

Chemical Kinetics - AdvancedElectro & KineticsTopic 2 of 17

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Kinetics - Advanced, Order determination: order follows from rate ratios across controlled runs. Rate law \(rate = k[A]^m[B]^n\) comes from experiment only; order \(= m+n\), molecularity \(=\) molecules in an elementary step. First order: \(k = (2.303/t)\log(a/(a-x))\), \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/k\); zero: \(t_{1/2} = a/2k\). Units of \(k\): \((mol/L)^{1-n}s^{-1}\).
Key formula(s). \[ units(k)=(M)^{1-n}s^{-1},\;order=m+n\,(expt) \]
Key points.
  • Order can be zero, fractional or negative; molecularity is a positive integer \(1,2,3\).
  • Slowest elementary step \(=\) rate-determining; its stoichiometry (with pre-equilibria) sets the law.
  • Pseudo-first-order: excess reactant hides true order (e.g. ester hydrolysis in water).
  • Graphs: 1st order \(\ln[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; 2nd order \(1/[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; zero \([A]\) vs \(t\) linear.
Example 1.

A first-order reaction is \(75\%\) complete in \(60\,min\). Find \(k\).

  1. \(k = (2.303/60)\log(100/25) = (2.303/60)\log4\).
  2. \(k = (2.303\times0.602/60) \approx 0.0231\,min^{-1}\).

Answer: About \(0.0231\,min^{-1}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Doubling \([A]\) doubles rate, doubling \([B]\) quadruples it. Give orders and \(k\) units.

  1. Order in A \(= 1\), in B \(= 2\); overall \(= 3\).
  2. Units \(= M^{-2}s^{-1}\) (\(L^2mol^{-2}s^{-1}\)).

Answer: 3rd order; \(M^{-2}s^{-1}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reading order from balanced-equation coefficients.
  • Using \(\log\) vs \(\ln\) inconsistently (factor 2.303).

Chapter 19 · Topic 3

Integrated rate equations

Chemical Kinetics - AdvancedElectro & KineticsTopic 3 of 17

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Kinetics - Advanced, Integrated rate equations: integrated forms linearise concentration-time data per order. Rate law \(rate = k[A]^m[B]^n\) comes from experiment only; order \(= m+n\), molecularity \(=\) molecules in an elementary step. First order: \(k = (2.303/t)\log(a/(a-x))\), \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/k\); zero: \(t_{1/2} = a/2k\). Units of \(k\): \((mol/L)^{1-n}s^{-1}\).
Key formula(s). \[ k=\frac{2.303}{t}\log\frac{a}{a-x},\;order=m+n\,(expt),\;t_{1/2}(2)=\frac{1}{k[A]_0} \]
Key points.
  • Slowest elementary step \(=\) rate-determining; its stoichiometry (with pre-equilibria) sets the law.
  • Pseudo-first-order: excess reactant hides true order (e.g. ester hydrolysis in water).
  • Graphs: 1st order \(\ln[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; 2nd order \(1/[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; zero \([A]\) vs \(t\) linear.
  • Order can be zero, fractional or negative; molecularity is a positive integer \(1,2,3\).
Example 1.

A first-order reaction is \(50\%\) complete in \(30\,min\). Find \(k\).

  1. This is one half-life: \(t_{1/2} = 30\,min\).
  2. \(k = 0.693/30 \approx 0.0231\,min^{-1}\).

Answer: \(0.0231\,min^{-1}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Doubling \([A]\) has no effect; tripling \([B]\) triples the rate. Give orders and overall units of \(k\).

  1. Order \(0\) in A, \(1\) in B; overall \(1\).
  2. Units \(= s^{-1}\).

Answer: First order overall; \(s^{-1}\).

  • Reading order from balanced-equation coefficients.

Chapter 19 · Topic 4

Half-life problems

Chemical Kinetics - AdvancedElectro & KineticsTopic 4 of 17

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Kinetics - Advanced, Half-life problems: half-life problems convert percent completion into k directly. Rate law \(rate = k[A]^m[B]^n\) comes from experiment only; order \(= m+n\), molecularity \(=\) molecules in an elementary step. First order: \(k = (2.303/t)\log(a/(a-x))\), \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/k\); zero: \(t_{1/2} = a/2k\). Units of \(k\): \((mol/L)^{1-n}s^{-1}\).
Key formula(s). \[ k=\frac{2.303}{t}\log\frac{a}{a-x},\;t_{1/2}(1st)=\frac{0.693}{k} \]
Key points.
  • Pseudo-first-order: excess reactant hides true order (e.g. ester hydrolysis in water).
  • Graphs: 1st order \(\ln[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; 2nd order \(1/[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; zero \([A]\) vs \(t\) linear.
  • Order can be zero, fractional or negative; molecularity is a positive integer \(1,2,3\).
  • Slowest elementary step \(=\) rate-determining; its stoichiometry (with pre-equilibria) sets the law.
Example 1.

A zero-order reaction has \([A]_0 = 0.5\,M\), \(k = 0.01\,M/min\). Find \(t_{1/2}\).

  1. Zero order: \(t_{1/2} = [A]_0/2k\).
  2. \(t_{1/2} = 0.5/0.02 = 25\,min\).

Answer: \(25\,min\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Which plot is linear for a second-order reaction?

  1. Integrated form: \(1/[A] = 1/[A]_0 + kt\).
  2. \(1/[A]\) vs \(t\).

Answer: \(1/[A]\) vs time.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reading order from balanced-equation coefficients.
  • Using \(\log\) vs \(\ln\) inconsistently (factor 2.303).

Chapter 19 · Topic 5

Graph-based problems

Chemical Kinetics - AdvancedElectro & KineticsTopic 5 of 17

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Kinetics - Advanced, Graph-based problems: graph problems read order from which transform linearises. Advanced problems chain two chapters: convert units to moles first, apply the first law, then feed its output (e.g. \(K\), \(E\), \(pH\)) into the second. Integer-answer (0-999) and multi-correct formats reward checking limiting cases and dimensions at each link.
Key formula(s). \[ \ln[A]-t\,linear\,(1st);\;1/[A]-t\,(2nd) \]
Key points.
  • Roadmap first: write both governing equations before substituting numbers.
  • Entropy of mixing: \(\Delta S_{mix} = -R\sum n_i\ln\chi_i > 0\) always.
  • Phase change: \(\Delta S = \Delta H_{trans}/T_{trans}\) (equilibrium temperature).
  • Multi-correct: test each option independently; assertion-reasoning needs the REASON to explain the assertion, not merely be true.
Example 1.

(Multi-step) \(2\,mol\) ideal gas expands isothermally (\(300\,K\), \(5\to15\,L\)), then the heat absorbed drives electrolysis (\(n = 2\)). Find moles of metal deposited if all heat became electrical work at \(1.1\,V\).

  1. Heat \(= -w = nRT\ln3 = 2\times8.314\times300\times1.0986 \approx 5483\,J\).
  2. Charge \(= 5483/1.1 \approx 4985\,C\); moles \(e^- = 4985/96485 \approx 0.0517\); metal \(= 0.0258\,mol\).

Answer: About \(0.026\,mol\) (illustrates chaining).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE Advanced pattern) \(\Delta H_{vap} = 40\,kJ/mol\) at \(373\,K\). Find \(\Delta S_{vap}\) and comment (Trouton).

  1. \(\Delta S = 40000/373 \approx 107\,J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}\).
  2. Near Trouton constant (\(\approx 85\)-\(88\)); higher value hints at hydrogen bonding.

Answer: About \(107\,J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Breaking the chain (using raw data in step 2 without step-1 conversion).
  • Rounding integer answers early (keep 4+ digits till the end).

Pseudo-first-order reactions

Chemical Kinetics - AdvancedElectro & KineticsTopic 6 of 17

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Kinetics - Advanced, Pseudo-first-order reactions: solvent-flooded hydrolyses look first order. Rate law \(rate = k[A]^m[B]^n\) comes from experiment only; order \(= m+n\), molecularity \(=\) molecules in an elementary step. First order: \(k = (2.303/t)\log(a/(a-x))\), \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/k\); zero: \(t_{1/2} = a/2k\). Units of \(k\): \((mol/L)^{1-n}s^{-1}\).
Key formula(s). \[ units(k)=(M)^{1-n}s^{-1},\;order=m+n\,(expt),\;t_{1/2}(0)=\frac{a}{2k} \]
Key points.
  • Slowest elementary step \(=\) rate-determining; its stoichiometry (with pre-equilibria) sets the law.
  • Pseudo-first-order: excess reactant hides true order (e.g. ester hydrolysis in water).
  • Graphs: 1st order \(\ln[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; 2nd order \(1/[A]\) vs \(t\) linear; zero \([A]\) vs \(t\) linear.
  • Order can be zero, fractional or negative; molecularity is a positive integer \(1,2,3\).
Example 1.

A first-order reaction is \(50\%\) complete in \(30\,min\). Find \(k\).

  1. This is one half-life: \(t_{1/2} = 30\,min\).
  2. \(k = 0.693/30 \approx 0.0231\,min^{-1}\).

Answer: \(0.0231\,min^{-1}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Doubling \([A]\) has no effect; tripling \([B]\) triples the rate. Give orders and overall units of \(k\).

  1. Order \(0\) in A, \(1\) in B; overall \(1\).
  2. Units \(= s^{-1}\).

Answer: First order overall; \(s^{-1}\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Reading order from balanced-equation coefficients.

Chapter 19 · Topic 7

Arrhenius equation

Chemical Kinetics - AdvancedElectro & KineticsTopic 7 of 17

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Kinetics - Advanced, Arrhenius equation: Arrhenius makes k exponential in minus Ea over RT. Arrhenius \(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\); two-temperature form \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (E_a/2.303R)(1/T_1-1/T_2)\). Catalyst lowers \(E_a\) (new path), raising \(k\) without changing \(K\); threshold energy \(=\) \(E_a +\) average reactant energy.
Key formula(s). \[ k=Ae^{-E_a/RT},\;k=pZ\,e^{-E_a/RT}\,(steric\,p) \]
Key points.
  • Effective collisions need energy \(\ge E_a\) AND correct orientation (steric factor \(p\)).
  • Parallel paths: \(k_{net} = k_1+k_2\); consecutive: slowest step dominates.
  • Rough rule: \(10\,K\) rise near room \(T\) about doubles \(k\) (\(E_a \approx 50\,kJ\)).
  • Exothermic vs endothermic profiles differ in product level vs reactant level; \(E_{a,f}-E_{a,b} = \Delta H\).
Example 1.

\(E_a = 50\,kJ/mol\). By what factor does \(k\) rise from \(300\,K\) to \(320\,K\)?

  1. \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (50000/19.147)(1/300-1/320) \approx 0.544\).
  2. Ratio \(\approx 10^{0.544} \approx 3.5\).

Answer: About \(3.5\) times.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Forward \(E_a = 50\,kJ\), \(\Delta H = -30\,kJ\). Find the backward \(E_a\).

  1. \(E_{a,f} - E_{a,b} = \Delta H\).
  2. \(E_{a,b} = 50 + 30 = 80\,kJ\).

Answer: \(80\,kJ\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Claiming catalysts change \(K\) or \(\Delta H\) (they change neither).
  • Using Celsius in the Arrhenius exponent.

Chapter 19 · Topic 8

Activation energy

Chemical Kinetics - AdvancedElectro & KineticsTopic 8 of 17

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Kinetics - Advanced, Activation energy: activation energy is the hill from reactants to transition state. Arrhenius \(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\); two-temperature form \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (E_a/2.303R)(1/T_1-1/T_2)\). Catalyst lowers \(E_a\) (new path), raising \(k\) without changing \(K\); threshold energy \(=\) \(E_a +\) average reactant energy.
Key formula(s). \[ catalyst:\,new\,path,\,lower\,E_a,\;E_{a,f}-E_{a,b}=\Delta H \]
Key points.
  • Rough rule: \(10\,K\) rise near room \(T\) about doubles \(k\) (\(E_a \approx 50\,kJ\)).
  • Exothermic vs endothermic profiles differ in product level vs reactant level; \(E_{a,f}-E_{a,b} = \Delta H\).
  • Effective collisions need energy \(\ge E_a\) AND correct orientation (steric factor \(p\)).
  • Parallel paths: \(k_{net} = k_1+k_2\); consecutive: slowest step dominates.
Example 1.

\(E_a = 50\,kJ/mol\). By what factor does \(k\) rise from \(300\,K\) to \(310\,K\)?

  1. \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (50000/(2.303\times8.314))(1/300-1/310)\).
  2. \(= 2611\times1.075\times10^{-4} \approx 0.281\); ratio \(\approx 10^{0.281} \approx 1.91\).

Answer: About \(1.9\times\) (doubles).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Catalyst lowers \(E_a\) from \(80\) to \(60\,kJ\) at \(300\,K\). Rate enhancement?

  1. Ratio \(= e^{\Delta E_a/RT} = e^{20000/(8.314\times300)}\).
  2. \(= e^{8.02} \approx 3040\times\).

Answer: About \(3\times10^3\) times faster.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Claiming catalysts change \(K\) or \(\Delta H\) (they change neither).
  • Using Celsius in the Arrhenius exponent.

  1. \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (60000/19.147)(1/300-1/310) \approx 0.337\).
  2. \(k_2 \approx 2.17\times10^{-3}\,s^{-1}\).

Answer: About \(2.2\times10^{-3}\,s^{-1}\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) A catalyst cuts \(E_a\) from \(90\) to \(60\,kJ\) at \(300\,K\). By what factor does the rate rise?

  1. Factor \(= e^{\Delta E_a/RT} = e^{30000/2494} = e^{12.03}\).
  2. About \(1.7\times10^5\) times.

Answer: About \(10^5\) times.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Claiming catalysts change \(K\) or \(\Delta H\) (they change neither).

  • Effective collisions need energy \(\ge E_a\) AND correct orientation (steric factor \(p\)).
  • Parallel paths: \(k_{net} = k_1+k_2\); consecutive: slowest step dominates.
  • Rough rule: \(10\,K\) rise near room \(T\) about doubles \(k\) (\(E_a \approx 50\,kJ\)).
  • Exothermic vs endothermic profiles differ in product level vs reactant level; \(E_{a,f}-E_{a,b} = \Delta H\).
Example 1.

\(E_a = 50\,kJ/mol\). By what factor does \(k\) rise from \(300\,K\) to \(320\,K\)?

  1. \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (50000/19.147)(1/300-1/320) \approx 0.544\).
  2. Ratio \(\approx 10^{0.544} \approx 3.5\).

Answer: About \(3.5\) times.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Forward \(E_a = 50\,kJ\), \(\Delta H = -30\,kJ\). Find the backward \(E_a\).

  1. \(E_{a,f} - E_{a,b} = \Delta H\).
  2. \(E_{a,b} = 50 + 30 = 80\,kJ\).

Answer: \(80\,kJ\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Claiming catalysts change \(K\) or \(\Delta H\) (they change neither).
  • Using Celsius in the Arrhenius exponent.

Chapter 19 · Topic 17

Energy profile diagrams

Chemical Kinetics - AdvancedElectro & KineticsTopic 17 of 17

Explanation

Concept. In Chemical Kinetics - Advanced, Energy profile diagrams: profiles plot energy versus coordinate with Ea humps and Delta-H drops. Arrhenius \(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\); two-temperature form \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (E_a/2.303R)(1/T_1-1/T_2)\). Catalyst lowers \(E_a\) (new path), raising \(k\) without changing \(K\); threshold energy \(=\) \(E_a +\) average reactant energy.
Key formula(s). \[ E_{a,f}-E_{a,b}=\Delta H \]
Key points.
  • Rough rule: \(10\,K\) rise near room \(T\) about doubles \(k\) (\(E_a \approx 50\,kJ\)).
  • Exothermic vs endothermic profiles differ in product level vs reactant level; \(E_{a,f}-E_{a,b} = \Delta H\).
  • Effective collisions need energy \(\ge E_a\) AND correct orientation (steric factor \(p\)).
  • Parallel paths: \(k_{net} = k_1+k_2\); consecutive: slowest step dominates.
Example 1.

\(E_a = 50\,kJ/mol\). By what factor does \(k\) rise from \(300\,K\) to \(310\,K\)?

  1. \(\log(k_2/k_1) = (50000/(2.303\times8.314))(1/300-1/310)\).
  2. \(= 2611\times1.075\times10^{-4} \approx 0.281\); ratio \(\approx 10^{0.281} \approx 1.91\).

Answer: About \(1.9\times\) (doubles).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Catalyst lowers \(E_a\) from \(80\) to \(60\,kJ\) at \(300\,K\). Rate enhancement?

  1. Ratio \(= e^{\Delta E_a/RT} = e^{20000/(8.314\times300)}\).
  2. \(= e^{8.02} \approx 3040\times\).

Answer: About \(3\times10^3\) times faster.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Claiming catalysts change \(K\) or \(\Delta H\) (they change neither).
  • Using Celsius in the Arrhenius exponent.

Chapter 20 · Topic 1

Nuclear composition

Nuclear Chemistry & RadioactivitySurface, Nuclear & MasteryTopic 1 of 26

Explanation

Concept. In Nuclear Chemistry and Radioactivity, Nuclear composition: nucleons tally as Z protons plus N neutrons to mass A. First-order decay: \(N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}\), \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/\lambda\), mean life \(\tau = 1/\lambda = 1.44\,t_{1/2}\). Activity \(A = \lambda N\) (becquerel). \(\alpha\) (\(-2p\), \(-2n\)), \(\beta^-\) (\(n\to p\), atomic number \(+1\)), \(\gamma\) (energy only).
Key formula(s). \[ N=N_0e^{-\lambda t},\;t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{\lambda} \]
Key points.
  • After \(n\) half-lives: \(N = N_0/2^n\); \(99\%\) decay needs \(\approx 6.64\,t_{1/2}\).
  • Isotopes (same \(Z\)), isobars (same \(A\)), isotones (same \(N\)).
  • Stability belt: \(n/p \approx 1\) (light), rising to \(\approx 1.5\) (heavy); magic numbers extra stable.
  • Successive decay \(A\to B\to C\): \(N_B\) peaks when \(\lambda_AN_A = \lambda_BN_B\) (transient equilibrium).
Example 1.

A sample halves in \(10\,min\). What fraction remains after \(30\,min\)?

  1. \(30\,min = 3\,t_{1/2}\).
  2. Remaining \(= (1/2)^3 = 1/8\).

Answer: \(1/8\) of the original.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Count rate falls from \(800\) to \(100\,cpm\) in \(60\,min\). Find \(t_{1/2}\).

  1. Ratio \(8 = 2^3\), so \(3\) half-lives \(= 60\,min\).
  2. \(t_{1/2} = 20\,min\).

Answer: \(20\,min\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(\log_{10}\) without 2.303 in \(t = (2.303/\lambda)\log(N_0/N)\).
  • Confusing activity (rate) with number of nuclei.

Chapter 20 · Topic 2

Isotopes

Nuclear Chemistry & RadioactivitySurface, Nuclear & MasteryTopic 2 of 26

Explanation

Concept. In Nuclear Chemistry and Radioactivity, Isotopes: isotopes share Z but differ in neutron count. First-order decay: \(N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}\), \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/\lambda\), mean life \(\tau = 1/\lambda = 1.44\,t_{1/2}\). Activity \(A = \lambda N\) (becquerel). \(\alpha\) (\(-2p\), \(-2n\)), \(\beta^-\) (\(n\to p\), atomic number \(+1\)), \(\gamma\) (energy only).
Key formula(s). \[ t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{\lambda},\;A=\lambda N \]
Key points.
  • Isotopes (same \(Z\)), isobars (same \(A\)), isotones (same \(N\)).
  • Stability belt: \(n/p \approx 1\) (light), rising to \(\approx 1.5\) (heavy); magic numbers extra stable.
  • Successive decay \(A\to B\to C\): \(N_B\) peaks when \(\lambda_AN_A = \lambda_BN_B\) (transient equilibrium).
  • After \(n\) half-lives: \(N = N_0/2^n\); \(99\%\) decay needs \(\approx 6.64\,t_{1/2}\).
Example 1.

Only \(1/16\) of a sample is left. How many half-lives have passed? If the time was \(40\,min\), find \(t_{1/2}\).

  1. \(1/16 = (1/2)^4\): \(4\) half-lives.
  2. \(t_{1/2} = 40/4 = 10\,min\).

Answer: \(4\) half-lives; \(t_{1/2} = 10\,min\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) A nuclide has \(\lambda = 0.0693\,min^{-1}\). Find its half-life.

  1. \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/\lambda\).
  2. \(t_{1/2} = 10\,min\).

Answer: \(10\,min\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(\log_{10}\) without 2.303 in \(t = (2.303/\lambda)\log(N_0/N)\).
  • Confusing activity (rate) with number of nuclei.

Isobars

Nuclear Chemistry & RadioactivitySurface, Nuclear & MasteryTopic 3 of 26

Explanation

Concept. In Nuclear Chemistry and Radioactivity, Isobars: isobars share mass number across different elements. First-order decay: \(N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}\), \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/\lambda\), mean life \(\tau = 1/\lambda = 1.44\,t_{1/2}\). Activity \(A = \lambda N\) (becquerel). \(\alpha\) (\(-2p\), \(-2n\)), \(\beta^-\) (\(n\to p\), atomic number \(+1\)), \(\gamma\) (energy only).
Key formula(s). \[ A=\lambda N,\;\tau=\frac{1}{\lambda} \]

  • Stability belt: \(n/p \approx 1\) (light), rising to \(\approx 1.5\) (heavy); magic numbers extra stable.

  • Isotopes (same \(Z\)), isobars (same \(A\)), isotones (same \(N\)).
Example 1.

\(^{14}C\) undergoes beta-minus decay. Identify the daughter nucleus.

  1. Beta-minus: a neutron becomes a proton; \(Z\) rises by \(1\), \(A\) unchanged.
  2. \(^{14}N\).

Answer: \(^{14}N\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(^{238}U\) emits one alpha particle. Give the product.

  1. Alpha: \(A-4\), \(Z-2\).
  2. \(^{234}Th\).

Answer: \(^{234}Th\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(\log_{10}\) without 2.303 in \(t = (2.303/\lambda)\log(N_0/N)\).
  • Confusing activity (rate) with number of nuclei.

Chapter 20 · Topic 12

Half-life

Nuclear Chemistry & RadioactivitySurface, Nuclear & MasteryTopic 12 of 26

Explanation

Concept. In Nuclear Chemistry and Radioactivity, Half-life: half-life is the time to halve the reactant. First-order decay: \(N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}\), \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/\lambda\), mean life \(\tau = 1/\lambda = 1.44\,t_{1/2}\). Activity \(A = \lambda N\) (becquerel). \(\alpha\) (\(-2p\), \(-2n\)), \(\beta^-\) (\(n\to p\), atomic number \(+1\)), \(\gamma\) (energy only).
Key formula(s). \[ N=N_0e^{-\lambda t},\;\tau=\frac{1}{\lambda},\;\alpha:\,-2p-2n;\;\beta^-:\,n\to p \]
Key points.
  • Stability belt: \(n/p \approx 1\) (light), rising to \(\approx 1.5\) (heavy); magic numbers extra stable.
  • Successive decay \(A\to B\to C\): \(N_B\) peaks when \(\lambda_AN_A = \lambda_BN_B\) (transient equilibrium).
  • After \(n\) half-lives: \(N = N_0/2^n\); \(99\%\) decay needs \(\approx 6.64\,t_{1/2}\).
  • Isotopes (same \(Z\)), isobars (same \(A\)), isotones (same \(N\)).
Example 1.

\(^{14}C\) undergoes beta-minus decay. Identify the daughter nucleus.

  1. Beta-minus: a neutron becomes a proton; \(Z\) rises by \(1\), \(A\) unchanged.
  2. \(^{14}N\).

Answer: \(^{14}N\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(^{238}U\) emits one alpha particle. Give the product.

  1. Alpha: \(A-4\), \(Z-2\).
  2. \(^{234}Th\).

Answer: \(^{234}Th\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(\log_{10}\) without 2.303 in \(t = (2.303/\lambda)\log(N_0/N)\).
  • Confusing activity (rate) with number of nuclei.

Chapter 20 · Topic 13

Mean life

Nuclear Chemistry & RadioactivitySurface, Nuclear & MasteryTopic 13 of 26

Explanation

Concept. In Nuclear Chemistry and Radioactivity, Mean life: mean life is one over lambda, 1.44 half-lives. First-order decay: \(N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}\), \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/\lambda\), mean life \(\tau = 1/\lambda = 1.44\,t_{1/2}\). Activity \(A = \lambda N\) (becquerel). \(\alpha\) (\(-2p\), \(-2n\)), \(\beta^-\) (\(n\to p\), atomic number \(+1\)), \(\gamma\) (energy only).
Key formula(s). \[ t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{\lambda},\;\tau=\frac{1}{\lambda} \]
Key points.
  • After \(n\) half-lives: \(N = N_0/2^n\); \(99\%\) decay needs \(\approx 6.64\,t_{1/2}\).
  • Isotopes (same \(Z\)), isobars (same \(A\)), isotones (same \(N\)).
  • Stability belt: \(n/p \approx 1\) (light), rising to \(\approx 1.5\) (heavy); magic numbers extra stable.
  • Successive decay \(A\to B\to C\): \(N_B\) peaks when \(\lambda_AN_A = \lambda_BN_B\) (transient equilibrium).
Example 1.

A sample halves in \(10\,min\). What fraction remains after \(30\,min\)?

  1. \(30\,min = 3\,t_{1/2}\).
  2. Remaining \(= (1/2)^3 = 1/8\).

Answer: \(1/8\) of the original.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Count rate falls from \(800\) to \(100\,cpm\) in \(60\,min\). Find \(t_{1/2}\).

  1. Ratio \(8 = 2^3\), so \(3\) half-lives \(= 60\,min\).
  2. \(t_{1/2} = 20\,min\).

Answer: \(20\,min\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(\log_{10}\) without 2.303 in \(t = (2.303/\lambda)\log(N_0/N)\).
  • Confusing activity (rate) with number of nuclei.

Answer: \(10\,min\).

Index / Surface, Nuclear & Mastery
Chapter 20 · Topic 17

Nuclear reactions

Nuclear Chemistry & RadioactivitySurface, Nuclear & MasteryTopic 17 of 26

Explanation

Concept. In Nuclear Chemistry and Radioactivity, Nuclear reactions: nuclear reactions reshuffle nucleons with Q from mass difference. Mass defect \(\Delta m\) binds the nucleus: \(BE = \Delta m\,c^2\) with \(1\,u = 931.5\,MeV\). \(BE\)/nucleon peaks at \(Fe\)-\(56\) (\(\approx 8.8\,MeV\)); fission splits heavy nuclei and fusion joins light ones, both moving toward the peak and releasing energy.
Key formula(s). \[ 1\,u=931.5\,MeV,\;Q=(m_{react}-m_{prod})c^2 \]
Key points.
  • Fission of \(U\)-\(235\) releases \(\approx 200\,MeV\) per fission plus \(2\)-\(3\) neutrons (chain reaction).
  • Fusion powers the Sun (\(4H\to He+2e^+\), \(\approx 26.7\,MeV\)) but needs extreme \(T\) to beat repulsion.
  • Moderators (heavy water, graphite) slow neutrons; control rods (\(Cd, B\)) absorb them.
  • \(Q>0\) exergic (spontaneous energy release); \(Q<0\) needs supplied energy.
Example 1.

\(^{235}U\) fission releases about \(200\,MeV\). Convert this to \(kJ/mol\) of fissions.

  1. Per fission \(200\times1.602\times10^{-13} = 3.2\times10^{-11}\,J\).
  2. Per mole \(\times N_A \approx 1.93\times10^{10}\,kJ/mol\).

Answer: About \(1.9\times10^{10}\,kJ/mol\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) In the Sun, \(4\,^1H \to \,^4He + 2e^+\). Energy per reaction if \(\Delta m = 0.0267\,u\)?

  1. \(Q = 0.0267\times931.5\).
  2. \(24.9\,MeV\) (plus annihilation \(\to 26.7\)).

Answer: About \(26.7\,MeV\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Sign errors in \(Q\) (released means products lighter).
  • Using atomic masses without cancelling electron masses consistently.

Chapter 20 · Topic 18

Q-value

Nuclear Chemistry & RadioactivitySurface, Nuclear & MasteryTopic 18 of 26

Explanation

Concept. In Nuclear Chemistry and Radioactivity, Q-value: positive Q means the reaction pays out energy. Mass defect \(\Delta m\) binds the nucleus: \(BE = \Delta m\,c^2\) with \(1\,u = 931.5\,MeV\). \(BE\)/nucleon peaks at \(Fe\)-\(56\) (\(\approx 8.8\,MeV\)); fission splits heavy nuclei and fusion joins light ones, both moving toward the peak and releasing energy.
Key formula(s). \[ Q=(m_{react}-m_{prod})c^2 \]
Key points.
  • Fusion powers the Sun (\(4H\to He+2e^+\), \(\approx 26.7\,MeV\)) but needs extreme \(T\) to beat repulsion.
  • Moderators (heavy water, graphite) slow neutrons; control rods (\(Cd, B\)) absorb them.
  • \(Q>0\) exergic (spontaneous energy release); \(Q<0\) needs supplied energy.
  • Fission of \(U\)-\(235\) releases \(\approx 200\,MeV\) per fission plus \(2\)-\(3\) neutrons (chain reaction).
Example 1.

What are the roles of heavy water and cadmium rods in a reactor?

  1. Heavy water slows fast neutrons (moderator).
  2. Cadmium absorbs neutrons (control).

Answer: Moderator vs absorber.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why can't \(^{238}U\) alone sustain a chain reaction with slow neutrons?

  1. It fissions only with fast neutrons and captures the slow ones.
  2. Needs enrichment or a fast spectrum.

Answer: Wrong cross-section for slow neutrons.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Sign errors in \(Q\) (released means products lighter).
  • Using atomic masses without cancelling electron masses consistently.

Chapter 20 · Topic 19

Mass defect

Nuclear Chemistry & RadioactivitySurface, Nuclear & MasteryTopic 19 of 26

Explanation

Concept. In Nuclear Chemistry and Radioactivity, Mass defect: mass defect is the missing mass converted to binding. Mass defect \(\Delta m\) binds the nucleus: \(BE = \Delta m\,c^2\) with \(1\,u = 931.5\,MeV\). \(BE\)/nucleon peaks at \(Fe\)-\(56\) (\(\approx 8.8\,MeV\)); fission splits heavy nuclei and fusion joins light ones, both moving toward the peak and releasing energy.
Key formula(s). \[ BE/nucleon\,peaks\,at\,Fe\!-\!56\,(8.8\,MeV) \],\;BE=\Delta m\,c^2 \]
Key points.
  • \(Q>0\) exergic (spontaneous energy release); \(Q<0\) needs supplied energy.
  • Fission of \(U\)-\(235\) releases \(\approx 200\,MeV\) per fission plus \(2\)-\(3\) neutrons (chain reaction).
  • Fusion powers the Sun (\(4H\to He+2e^+\), \(\approx 26.7\,MeV\)) but needs extreme \(T\) to beat repulsion.
  • Moderators (heavy water, graphite) slow neutrons; control rods (\(Cd, B\)) absorb them.
Example 1.

Mass defect of He nucleus is \(0.0304\,u\). Find its total \(BE\) and \(BE\)/nucleon.

  1. \(BE = 0.0304\times931.5 \approx 28.3\,MeV\).
  2. Per nucleon \(= 28.3/4 \approx 7.07\,MeV\).

Answer: \(28.3\,MeV\) total, \(7.07\,MeV\)/nucleon.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why does both fission AND fusion release energy?

  1. Both move nuclei toward the \(BE\)/nucleon peak near iron.
  2. Heavier-than-Fe splits down; lighter-than-Fe fuses up.

Answer: Both increase \(BE\)/nucleon toward the Fe-56 maximum.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Sign errors in \(Q\) (released means products lighter).
  • Using atomic masses without cancelling electron masses consistently.

  2. Per nucleon \(= 28.3/4 \approx 7.07\,MeV\).

Answer: \(28.3\,MeV\) total, \(7.07\,MeV\)/nucleon.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Why does both fission AND fusion release energy?

  1. Both move nuclei toward the \(BE\)/nucleon peak near iron.
  2. Heavier-than-Fe splits down; lighter-than-Fe fuses up.

Answer: Both increase \(BE\)/nucleon toward the Fe-56 maximum.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Sign errors in \(Q\) (released means products lighter).
  • Using atomic masses without cancelling electron masses consistently.

Chapter 20 · Topic 26

Applications of radioisotopes

Nuclear Chemistry & RadioactivitySurface, Nuclear & MasteryTopic 26 of 26

Explanation

Concept. In Nuclear Chemistry and Radioactivity, Applications of radioisotopes: tracers, therapy and dating all spend controlled decay. First-order decay: \(N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}\), \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/\lambda\), mean life \(\tau = 1/\lambda = 1.44\,t_{1/2}\). Activity \(A = \lambda N\) (becquerel). \(\alpha\) (\(-2p\), \(-2n\)), \(\beta^-\) (\(n\to p\), atomic number \(+1\)), \(\gamma\) (energy only).
Key formula(s). \[ n/p\approx1\,(light),\;magic\,nos.\,stable \]
Key points.
  • Isotopes (same \(Z\)), isobars (same \(A\)), isotones (same \(N\)).
  • Stability belt: \(n/p \approx 1\) (light), rising to \(\approx 1.5\) (heavy); magic numbers extra stable.
  • Successive decay \(A\to B\to C\): \(N_B\) peaks when \(\lambda_AN_A = \lambda_BN_B\) (transient equilibrium).
  • After \(n\) half-lives: \(N = N_0/2^n\); \(99\%\) decay needs \(\approx 6.64\,t_{1/2}\).
Example 1.

Only \(1/16\) of a sample is left. How many half-lives have passed? If the time was \(40\,min\), find \(t_{1/2}\).

  1. \(1/16 = (1/2)^4\): \(4\) half-lives.
  2. \(t_{1/2} = 40/4 = 10\,min\).

Answer: \(4\) half-lives; \(t_{1/2} = 10\,min\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) A nuclide has \(\lambda = 0.0693\,min^{-1}\). Find its half-life.

  1. \(t_{1/2} = 0.693/\lambda\).
  2. \(t_{1/2} = 10\,min\).

Answer: \(10\,min\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Using \(\log_{10}\) without 2.303 in \(t = (2.303/\lambda)\log(N_0/N)\).
  • Confusing activity (rate) with number of nuclei.

Chapter 21 · Topic 1

Significant figures

Experimental & Numerical Physical ChemistryFundamentalsTopic 1 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Experimental and Numerical Physical Chemistry, Significant figures: significant figures keep every certain digit plus one doubtful. Significant figures: all certain digits plus one doubtful; in addition/subtraction keep fewest decimals, in multiplication/division fewest sig figs. Errors propagate: sums add absolute errors, products/quotients add fractional errors, powers multiply fractional error by the exponent.
Key formula(s). \[ \%error=\frac{\Delta x}{x}\times100,\;sums:\,fewest\,decimals \]
Key points.
  • Exact counts (e.g. \(2\) atoms) have infinite sig figs.
  • Graph slope from widely separated points, never from a single data dot.
  • Round only at the end; intermediate rounding accumulates error.
  • Zeros between digits count; trailing zeros count only with a decimal point.
Example 1.

Radius \(= 2.0 \pm 0.1\,cm\). Find the volume of the sphere with percent error.

  1. \(V = 4\pi r^3/3 = 33.5\,cm^3\); fractional error \(= 3\times(0.1/2) = 15\%\).
  2. \(V = 33.5 \pm 5.0\,cm^3\).

Answer: \(33.5\,cm^3 \pm 15\%\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Two lengths \(10.0 \pm 0.2\) and \(5.0 \pm 0.1\) are subtracted. Give the error.

  1. Difference \(= 5.0\); absolute errors add.
  2. \(5.0 \pm 0.3\).

Answer: \(5.0 \pm 0.3\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Adding percentage errors for sums (add absolute instead).
  • Reporting more digits than the weakest measurement allows.

Chapter 21 · Topic 2

Significant-figure calculations

Experimental & Numerical Physical ChemistryFundamentalsTopic 2 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Experimental and Numerical Physical Chemistry, Significant-figure calculations: addition keeps fewest decimals, multiplication keeps fewest figures. Significant figures: all certain digits plus one doubtful; in addition/subtraction keep fewest decimals, in multiplication/division fewest sig figs. Errors propagate: sums add absolute errors, products/quotients add fractional errors, powers multiply fractional error by the exponent.
Key formula(s). \[ sums:\,fewest\,decimals,\;products:\,fewest\,figs \]
Key points.
  • Graph slope from widely separated points, never from a single data dot.
  • Round only at the end; intermediate rounding accumulates error.
  • Zeros between digits count; trailing zeros count only with a decimal point.
  • Exact counts (e.g. \(2\) atoms) have infinite sig figs.
Example 1.

How many significant figures are in \(0.004080\)?

  1. Leading zeros never count; trailing zero after decimal counts.
  2. Four (\(4, 0, 8, 0\)).

Answer: Four.

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) Slope from a \((0,0)\)-\((10,25)\) graph line. Best value?

  1. Use widely separated points on the best-fit line, not raw dots.
  2. Slope \(= 2.5\) per x-unit.

Answer: \(2.5\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Adding percentage errors for sums (add absolute instead).

Chapter 21 · Topic 3

Scientific notation

Experimental & Numerical Physical ChemistryFundamentalsTopic 3 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Experimental and Numerical Physical Chemistry, Scientific notation: scientific notation anchors one non-zero digit before the power of ten. Significant figures: all certain digits plus one doubtful; in addition/subtraction keep fewest decimals, in multiplication/division fewest sig figs. Errors propagate: sums add absolute errors, products/quotients add fractional errors, powers multiply fractional error by the exponent.
Key formula(s). \[ products:\,fewest\,figs \],\;\frac{\Delta Z}{Z}=p\frac{\Delta A}{A}+q\frac{\Delta B}{B} \]
Key points.
  • Zeros between digits count; trailing zeros count only with a decimal point.
  • Exact counts (e.g. \(2\) atoms) have infinite sig figs.
  • Graph slope from widely separated points, never from a single data dot.
  • Round only at the end; intermediate rounding accumulates error.
Example 1.

Length \(5.21\,cm \pm 0.01\), breadth \(3.1\,cm \pm 0.1\). Find area with error.

  1. Area \(= 16.151 \approx 16\,cm^2\) (2 sig figs from \(3.1\)).
  2. Fractional error \(= 0.01/5.21+0.1/3.1 \approx 0.034\); absolute \(\approx 0.55\).

Answer: \(16.0 \pm 0.6\,cm^2\) (about \(3.4\%\)).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(Z = A^2/B\); \(A\) has \(2\%\) error, \(B\) \(1\%\). Error in \(Z\)?

  1. Fractional errors: \(2\times2\% + 1\% = 5\%\).

Answer: \(5\%\).

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Adding percentage errors for sums (add absolute instead).
  • Reporting more digits than the weakest measurement allows.

Chapter 21 · Topic 14

Titration calculations

Experimental & Numerical Physical ChemistryFundamentalsTopic 14 of 19

Explanation

Concept. In Experimental and Numerical Physical Chemistry, Titration calculations: titration math meets at N1V1 equals N2V2 with back-titration fixes. Lab numericals reuse the same laws: titration \(N_1V_1 = N_2V_2\) (or mole-ratio method), calorimetry \(q = ms\Delta T\) with \(q_{rxn} = -q_{cal}\), conductivity \(\Lambda_m = \kappa\cdot1000/M\), kinetics from initial-rate slopes, solubility from \(K_{sp}\).
Key formula(s). \[ N_1V_1=N_2V_2,\;back\!-\!titration:\,subtract\,excess \]
Key points.
  • Indicator choice: pH jump must bracket the indicator range (phenolphthalein for weak-acid/strong-base).
  • Blank correction and calibration (KCl for conductivity, known masses for calorimetry) remove systematic error.
  • Back-titrations: subtract excess titrant moles from total added.
  • Calorimeter heat capacity \(C\): \(q = C\Delta T\); sign flips for the reaction.
Example 1.

\(25\,mL\) of \(NaOH\) needs \(20\,mL\) of \(0.1\,N\,HCl\). Find normality of \(NaOH\).

  1. \(N_1V_1 = N_2V_2 \Rightarrow N = 0.1\times20/25\).
  2. \(N = 0.08\,N\) (same as molarity for \(NaOH\)).

Answer: \(0.08\,N\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(50\,g\) water warms \(2.5\,K\) in a calorimetry run (\(s = 4.18\)). Find heat absorbed.

  1. \(q = 50\times4.18\times2.5 = 522.5\,J\).
  2. Reaction heat \(= -522.5\,J\) (exothermic to water).

Answer: \(522.5\,J\) absorbed by water.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Forgetting the blank/back-titration correction.
  • Sign errors between calorimeter heat and reaction heat.

Key points.
  • Back-titrations: subtract excess titrant moles from total added.
  • Calorimeter heat capacity \(C\): \(q = C\Delta T\); sign flips for the reaction.
  • Indicator choice: pH jump must bracket the indicator range (phenolphthalein for weak-acid/strong-base).
  • Blank correction and calibration (KCl for conductivity, known masses for calorimetry) remove systematic error.
Example 1.

\(25\,mL\) of \(NaOH\) needs \(20\,mL\) of \(0.1\,N\,HCl\). Find normality of \(NaOH\).

  1. \(N_1V_1 = N_2V_2 \Rightarrow N = 0.1\times20/25\).
  2. \(N = 0.08\,N\) (same as molarity for \(NaOH\)).

Answer: \(0.08\,N\).

Example 2 (JEE pattern).

(JEE pattern) \(50\,g\) water warms \(2.5\,K\) in a calorimetry run (\(s = 4.18\)). Find heat absorbed.

  1. \(q = 50\times4.18\times2.5 = 522.5\,J\).
  2. Reaction heat \(= -522.5\,J\) (exothermic to water).

Answer: \(522.5\,J\) absorbed by water.

Common mistakes / JEE traps.
  • Forgetting the blank/back-titration correction.
  • Sign errors between calorimeter heat and reaction heat.
